adapt-1.title: Mindset for Change
adapt-1.summary: Use a growth mindset, understand the change curve and build tolerance for uncertainty.
objectives: Tell a fixed mindset thought from a growth mindset thought and rewrite it.
Place your reaction to a change on the change curve.
Practise one habit for tolerating uncertainty.

explanation.heading: Why adaptability matters
explanation.body: Technology, jobs and teams change faster than any course can keep up with. A tool you learn this year may be replaced in three. In SAP work, for example, ABAP itself keeps evolving with newer syntax and cloud-based development models. People who succeed over the long run are rarely those who know the most today; they are those who adapt quickest. Adaptability is a skill, and it begins with how you think about change.

explanation.heading: Growth mindset
explanation.body: A **fixed mindset** treats ability as a fixed trait: "I am not a maths person", "I cannot speak in public". Failure then feels like a verdict. A **growth mindset** treats ability as something built through effort, strategies and feedback: "I have not learned this yet". Research on learning supports the idea that skills improve with practice, though talent and circumstances differ. The word **yet** is a powerful tool. Compare "I failed the aptitude test, so I am bad at logic" with "I scored low on this test; I will study the question types and retry". The second leads to action. Practise by catching fixed thoughts, adding "yet", and writing one next step. Growth mindset does not mean unlimited effort in any direction; it means treating setbacks as information.

explanation.heading: The change curve
explanation.body: Most people go through predictable emotions when change arrives, whether a new manager, new software or a new city. The **change curve** has stages: **shock or denial** ("this will not really happen"), **resistance or frustration** ("why are they doing this?"), **dip or confusion**, then **acceptance and experiment**, and finally **commitment**. Performance usually falls before it rises. Knowing the curve helps you in two ways. You can name where you are, which reduces panic, and you can shorten the dip by doing small experiments rather than waiting. Different people move at different speeds and nobody needs to feel guilty about stage two.

explanation.heading: Tolerating uncertainty
explanation.body: Change brings not knowing: Will I get the job? Will this tool last? Many people try to remove uncertainty by over-planning or avoiding action. A better skill is **tolerance of uncertainty**: acting sensibly without full information. Practices include separating what you know, what you can find out and what nobody can know; making reversible decisions quickly; setting a review date instead of seeking certainty now; and doing small experiments. Calm the body first, since anxious bodies read uncertainty as danger. Over time you learn that you can cope without all the answers.

examples.title: Adding the word yet
examples.body: Pooja thinks "I cannot understand pointers." She rewrites: "I do not understand pointers yet. I will draw memory diagrams for three examples and ask for one explanation." Within a week she explains pointers to a friend.
examples.takeaway: Yet plus a next step turns a verdict into a plan.

examples.title: Naming the stage
examples.body: After a project switch to a new tool, Rahul feels irritated and slow. He recognises the dip on the change curve, writes "week two: expected" and schedules two small practice tasks. His frustration eases.
examples.takeaway: Naming your stage shortens the dip.

adapt-2.title: Learning Agility
adapt-2.summary: Learn new tools quickly using a fast-learning method, the Feynman technique, deliberate practice and a short learning plan.
objectives: Break a new tool down into a map of core ideas.
Use the Feynman technique to find gaps.
Write a two-week learning plan with practice.

explanation.heading: Learning how to learn
explanation.body: In a first job you will repeatedly meet new tools: a version control system, a testing framework, a new module. Your speed at getting competent matters as much as what you already know. **Learning agility** is the ability to pick up new skills quickly and apply them. It comes from a few methods you can practise: map the territory, test your understanding by explaining it, practise on real tasks and plan your time.

explanation.heading: Map the territory first
explanation.body: Before details, draw a **learning map** on one page: what is this tool for, what are its five to ten core concepts and how do they connect? For an unfamiliar SAP transaction or a new framework, find the official overview, a beginner tutorial and one real example. List the concepts, then rank them by how often you will use them. The 20% of features that cover 80% of daily work come first. Keep a glossary of new terms. Skip advanced features until you can complete a basic task from start to end. Beginners often feel pressure to master everything at once; resist it. A narrow but working skill gives you something to build on and shows your team you can already contribute, while the rest can be learned on the job as real needs appear.

explanation.heading: The Feynman technique
explanation.body: The **Feynman technique** tests whether you really understand something. Step one: choose a concept. Step two: explain it in simple words as if to a beginner, in writing or aloud, without jargon. Step three: note where you stumble or fall back on technical words; these are the gaps. Step four: go back to the source, fill the gap and explain again. If you cannot explain a concept simply, you do not yet understand it. A rubber duck, a friend or a voice memo all work as audiences.

explanation.heading: Practice loop and learning plan
explanation.body: Learning sticks through use. Use a **practice loop**: try a small task, check the result, fix errors and repeat with a slightly harder task. Mix in **retrieval**, such as writing a command from memory before looking it up. Then build a **learning plan** for two weeks: a target ("create and test a simple report program"), daily 45-minute sessions with a single focus, one small project to apply it and a checkpoint at day seven where you demonstrate what you can do. Share progress with someone, because explaining what you did makes you notice what you skipped. Write a two-line note at the end of each session: what I learned and what is still unclear. These notes become your own reference guide. If you are stuck for more than 25 minutes, ask for help; hiding confusion slows you down.

examples.title: A one-page map
examples.body: To learn Git, Ashish lists: repository, commit, branch, merge, remote. He ranks commit and branch first, completes a small project using only those and learns merge later when he needs it.
examples.takeaway: Start with the few concepts used most.

examples.title: A Feynman gap
examples.body: Asked to explain an index in a database, Leena says "it makes lookups faster using a structure". When asked how, she cannot answer. She reads about B-trees, then explains it as the index at the back of a book.
examples.takeaway: Stumbling reveals what to study next.

adapt-3.title: Resilience After Setbacks
adapt-3.summary: Reframe failure, run a blameless post-mortem, prepare a plan B and bounce back with small steps.
objectives: Reframe a failure into information and a next step.
Run a simple post-mortem on a setback.
Build a plan B and a bounce-back routine.

explanation.heading: Setbacks are inevitable
explanation.body: Everyone who tries ambitious things fails sometimes: a rejected application, a failed exam, a bug that breaks production. **Resilience** is not avoiding setbacks or hiding feelings; it is recovering and continuing with learning. It can be trained like a muscle. This lesson gives you four tools: reframing, a post-mortem, a plan B and a bounce-back routine. If setbacks leave you hopeless for weeks, talk to a trusted person or a counsellor.

explanation.heading: Reframing failure
explanation.body: Failure feels personal, but it is usually specific and temporary. Use three checks. **Specific**: "I failed this interview" is not "I am a failure". **Temporary**: this result is not permanent. **Informative**: what does it tell me? Replace "Why me?" with "What can I learn, and what will I try next?" Do not suppress feelings: allow a day or two to feel disappointed, talk to a friend and then move to action. Compare "I failed the viva, so I am not cut out for this" with "I forgot the key definition under pressure; I will practise answers aloud."

explanation.heading: The post-mortem
explanation.body: A **post-mortem** studies what happened to learn, not to blame. Sit down within a few days and write four headings. **What happened?** (facts only). **What went well?** (so you keep it). **What went wrong and why?** (look at causes, not character; ask why five times). **What will I change?** (two or three specific actions with dates). Keep it blameless: focus on processes, preparation and decisions. For a failed placement test: facts: scored 40 per cent, ran out of time on section two; cause: no timed practice; change: three timed mock tests by Sunday.

explanation.heading: Plan B and bouncing back
explanation.body: A **plan B** is a prepared alternative that reduces the fear of failing. For each important goal, write what you will do if it does not work: other companies to apply to, another exam date, a related role. Having a plan B does not mean lack of commitment; it frees you to commit fully. To **bounce back**, restore the basics first: sleep, food, movement and talking to someone. Then take one small step within 48 hours, such as booking a mock test. Small actions rebuild momentum. Track progress over weeks, not hours. Also remember that most successful people have a long list of rejections and failures behind them; what separates them is that they kept trying with better preparation each time. Treat each setback as one data point on a longer line, and let your plan B give you the security to keep going.

examples.title: A blameless post-mortem
examples.body: After a failed demo, Zoya writes: Facts: the database was not seeded. Cause: no pre-demo checklist. Change: build a five-point checklist and run it one hour before every demo.
examples.takeaway: A post-mortem turns embarrassment into a system fix.

examples.title: Plan B in action
examples.body: Aditya applies to ten SAP trainee roles. His plan B includes two junior web-development roles and an ABAP certification course. When early replies are slow, he feels less pressure and keeps learning.
examples.takeaway: Alternatives reduce fear and keep you moving.

adapt-4.title: Navigating New Environments
adapt-4.summary: Handle the first 90 days, shifting requirements, new cultures and flexibility that keeps your principles.
objectives: Plan your first 90 days in a new role.
Respond well when requirements change.
Fit a new culture while holding your principles.

explanation.heading: The first 90 days
explanation.body: A new job, internship or project is a high-stakes adaptation. The first 90 days shape how people see you. Think in three phases. **Days 1 to 30, learn**: meet people, understand the team's goals, tools and rules, and ask many questions. Write a glossary of terms and acronyms. **Days 31 to 60, contribute**: take on small tasks, deliver reliably and ask for feedback. **Days 61 to 90, own**: take responsibility for a defined piece of work and propose one improvement. Agree expectations with your manager in week one: what does success look like at 30, 60 and 90 days?

explanation.heading: Shifting requirements
explanation.body: In client projects, requirements change: a feature is added, a deadline moves, a priority flips. Reacting with irritation hurts trust. Use a calm routine. **Clarify**: what exactly has changed and why? **Assess impact**: what does it affect in time, effort and quality? **Communicate**: state the impact and options, for example "We can add this if we move the report to next sprint". **Confirm in writing**: record the new decision. **Adjust**: update plans. Keep modular work and short feedback cycles so changes cost less. Distinguish normal change from endless scope growth; polite, documented trade-offs are the tool for that.

explanation.heading: Culture and fit
explanation.body: Every workplace has unwritten rules: how formal people are, when meetings start, whether disagreement is voiced openly, how decisions are made. Observe in the first weeks. Notice who speaks in meetings, how people write emails, what is praised and how seniors are addressed. Ask a friendly colleague, "Is there anything about how things work here that I should know?" Adopt local habits that are harmless, such as meeting times, message style and dress norms. Find a **buddy or mentor** early. Being a good fit means respecting norms and contributing, not becoming someone else.

explanation.heading: Flexibility without losing principles
explanation.body: Adapting does not mean agreeing to everything. Separate **preferences**, such as tools, schedules and style, where you should be flexible, from **principles**, such as honesty, safety and respect, where you should not bend. If a client asks you to hide a defect or misreport work, you stay firm, politely and early, and escalate to your manager if needed. A useful test: "Would I be comfortable explaining this decision to my manager, a client and my family?" Being flexible on the first group while steady on the second makes you both adaptable and trustworthy.

examples.title: Changing requirement
examples.body: A client adds a new report in the final week. Ritu replies: "I can add it. It needs two days, so testing would move to next Wednesday. Shall we proceed?" She confirms by email. The client agrees to a smaller version.
examples.takeaway: Impact plus options turns a surprise into a decision.

examples.title: A principle held
examples.body: Asked to mark a task as tested when it was not, Karan says: "I cannot mark it as tested until I run it. I can finish by tomorrow morning." His lead accepts the delay.
examples.takeaway: Hold the principle, offer a practical alternative.

ai-1.title: How Modern AI Works (and Fails)
ai-1.summary: Understand how machine learning differs from rules, why language models predict words rather than look up facts, and where hallucination and bias come from.
objectives: Explain the difference between a rule-based program and a machine-learning system.
Describe a language model as a next-word predictor trained on text, and explain why it can sound confident and be wrong.
Name the typical strengths and weaknesses of AI and decide which tasks need human checking.

concepts.label: Language models predict the next word

explanation.heading: Rules versus learning
explanation.body:
Traditional software follows **rules a programmer wrote**. An ABAP report that adds 18 percent tax to an invoice does exactly that, every time, and you can read the line of code that does it. If the output is wrong, you find the wrong rule.

**Machine learning** works the other way round. Instead of writing the rules, you show the system thousands or millions of examples and let it adjust internal numbers (called parameters) until its outputs match the examples. A spam filter is a good case: nobody can write a complete rule for 'what spam looks like', but a model trained on many labelled emails learns patterns that no person spelled out.

The trade-off matters. Rules are predictable and explainable but cannot handle messy, open-ended problems. Learned systems handle messy problems but are **probabilistic**: they give the most likely answer, not a guaranteed one, and it is often hard to say exactly why.

explanation.heading: A language model is a next-word predictor
explanation.body:
A large language model is trained on a huge amount of text to do one thing very well: given the words so far, **predict a likely next word** (strictly, a small piece of a word). It then appends that word and predicts again, and again, until a full answer appears.

This explains both its power and its weakness. To predict well across all of human writing, it has had to absorb grammar, style, common facts, code patterns and reasoning patterns. But it is not looking anything up in a database of verified facts, and it has no built-in sense of 'I do not know'. It produces text that is **plausible**, which is not always the same as **true**.

Worked example: ask for 'the capital of India' and the most likely continuation is correct, because that pairing appears constantly in training text. Ask for 'the third author of an obscure 2011 paper' and the most plausible-looking continuation is a confident invented name.

explanation.heading: Hallucination: fluent and wrong
explanation.body:
When a model produces false content in a confident tone, we call it a **hallucination**. Typical forms: invented references and quotations, made-up function names or library options, wrong dates and numbers, and summaries that quietly add claims the source never made.

Hallucination is more likely when the question is obscure, very recent, highly specific (exact figures, names, section numbers), or when you ask for sources and none exist in what the model learned. It is less likely, though never zero, when you paste the source text into the question and ask it to work only from that text.

The practical rule: **the smoother the answer sounds, the less that tells you about whether it is right.** Confidence of tone is a style, not evidence.

explanation.heading: Training data, bias and what to delegate
explanation.body:
A model reflects its training data. If the data over-represents certain regions, languages, genders or viewpoints, the outputs will lean the same way. A tool trained mostly on English text may handle a Hindi or Tamil business letter less well, and a model that learned from past hiring decisions can repeat past unfairness. Its knowledge also stops at a cut-off date, so it may not know about recent changes.

A useful sorting habit for tasks:

- **Good fits:** drafting, rephrasing, summarising text you provide, brainstorming options, explaining a concept at different levels, generating test data, first-pass code for a well-known pattern.
- **Poor fits without checking:** exact facts and figures, legal or medical decisions, anything needing current information, maths done in its head, and citing sources.

Practise by choosing three tasks from your week and labelling each 'safe to draft', 'must verify' or 'do not delegate'. Your own judgement is the final checker.

examples.title: Rule-based or learned?
examples.body: A bank app blocks any UPI transfer above a fixed daily limit: that is a rule, written by a person, fully explainable. The same app flags a transfer as 'unusual for this customer' by comparing it with thousands of past patterns: that is a learned model, and the flag is a probability, so a human may need to review it.
examples.takeaway: Fixed thresholds are rules; pattern-based judgement under uncertainty is usually learning. Both can sit inside one product.

examples.title: A confident wrong answer
examples.body: A student asks a chatbot: 'Give me the exact section number of the Indian Contract Act that defines consideration, with a quote.' The reply gives a section number, a neat quotation and a case name, all in a crisp tone. The student checks the Act's text and finds the quote is reworded and the case does not exist.
examples.takeaway: Exact numbers, quotes and case names are classic hallucination zones. Verify against the original text before using them.

examples.title: Grounding the model in your own text
examples.body: Instead of asking 'What are the key points of our project policy?', you paste the 400-word policy and ask: 'Using only the text below, list the key points. If something is not in the text, say so.' The answer now stays close to the source and you can check each point against it line by line.
examples.takeaway: Supplying the source and restricting the answer to it reduces, but does not remove, the risk of invented content.

exercises.prompt: What is the most accurate description of what a language model does when it answers you?
options: It searches a database of verified facts and copies the matching entry.
It repeatedly predicts a likely next word based on patterns learned from text.
It understands the question the way a human expert does and reasons from experience.
It runs a fixed list of if-then rules written by engineers for each topic.
exercises.hint: Think about what the model was trained to do.
exercises.why: A language model is trained to predict likely next words, so its output is plausible text. It is not a fact database (option 1), not a human-style understanding (option 3), and not a hand-written rule list (option 4).

exercises.prompt: What is the term for a model confidently producing false or invented content such as a made-up reference? (one word)
exercises.hint: It begins with H.
exercises.why: Hallucination is the standard term for fluent but false output. The tone of the answer gives no clue to its accuracy.

exercises.prompt: A friend says: 'AI is just a big program where engineers typed in the answers.' In 3 to 5 sentences, correct this. Explain how a machine-learning system differs from a rule-based program, using one concrete example such as spam filtering or a tax calculation.

rubric.label: Clear contrast between rules and learning

descriptors.0: No real contrast; repeats the friend's claim.
descriptors.1: Mentions both ideas but does not say who or what supplies the logic.
descriptors.2: States that rules are written by people while learned systems adjust from examples.
descriptors.3: Clearly states that rules are hand-written and predictable, while learning finds patterns from data and gives probable answers.

auto.label: Mentions learning from data or examples

descriptors.1: Example named but not connected to the point.
descriptors.2: Example used correctly for one side of the contrast.
descriptors.3: Example used to show both sides, such as a fixed tax rule versus a learned spam filter.

descriptors.0: Contains false claims about how AI works.
descriptors.1: Mostly right but overstates, for example says AI is always correct.
descriptors.3: Accurate, and notes that learned systems are probabilistic and can be wrong.

exercises.modelAnswer: Not quite. In a rule-based program, a person writes the logic, like a tax calculation that always adds a fixed percentage, so the result is predictable and explainable. In machine learning, nobody writes the rules for something like spam filtering. The system is shown many labelled examples and adjusts itself until it finds patterns that match. Because it works from patterns, its answers are probabilities and it can sometimes be wrong.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers say plainly who creates the logic in each approach and use one example consistently. A common mistake is to say AI 'thinks' or is 'always right', or to treat all software as AI. Score yourself on whether a classmate with no background could follow your explanation and then repeat it.

exercises.prompt: You are preparing a college presentation. A chatbot gives you a statistic with a named report as its source: 'According to the 2019 National Study on Student Stress, 63.4 percent of engineering students report burnout.' It sounds perfect for your slide. What do you do?

options.text: Put it on the slide; the exact decimal and report name make it credible.
options.feedback: Precision is not proof. Exact-looking numbers and named reports are typical hallucination patterns.

options.text: Ask the chatbot 'Are you sure?' and use it if it says yes.
options.feedback: The model may repeat or defend the same invention. Asking it to confirm itself is not independent checking.

options.text: Look for the report in an independent, original source. If you cannot find it, drop the figure or describe the topic without a number.
options.feedback: Correct. Verify high-risk specifics against the original, and never present an unverified statistic as fact.

options.text: Keep the number but add 'approximately' so it is safer.
options.feedback: Hedging the wording does not fix a figure that may not exist.

exercises.why: Statistics and named sources are where models invent details most smoothly. The reliable fix is independent verification against the original; self-confirmation and softer wording do not help.

task.title: Catch a model being plausible
task.brief: Test an AI tool on one question you can verify and one you cannot, and record the difference in reliability.
steps: Choose an AI chat tool you can access. Ask a factual question where you already know the answer, such as a concept from your own syllabus.
Ask a second question demanding precise details, such as an exact quote, page number or statistic on a niche topic.
Check the second answer against a textbook, official document or your notes, and mark each detail as confirmed, wrong or unverifiable.
Write down the one sign in the wording that you would have missed if you had not checked.
checklist: I asked one question I could verify myself
I checked each detail against an original source
I recorded what was confirmed, wrong or unverifiable
task.evidencePrompt: State both questions briefly, how many details were wrong or unverifiable, and what you will now always verify.

quiz.prompt: Which system is built mainly with machine learning rather than hand-written rules?
options: A calculator that applies GST at a fixed percentage
A program that sorts a list of names alphabetically
A model that recognises handwritten digits after seeing thousands of labelled images
A form that rejects an empty mobile-number field
quiz.why: Handwriting varies too much for anyone to write complete rules, so the model learns patterns from labelled examples. The other three are clear rules a programmer can state directly.

quiz.prompt: Why can a language model write fluent text about a topic and still be wrong?
options: It is trained to produce plausible continuations of text, not to verify truth.
It deliberately lies when it is unsure.
It only copies sentences it has stored word for word.
Fluent text always means the model has checked the facts.
quiz.why: Plausibility and truth are different targets. Models do not deliberately lie (option 2), do not simply copy stored sentences (option 3), and fluency is not a fact-check (option 4).

quiz.prompt: Which request is MOST likely to produce a hallucination?
options: Explain what a primary key is in simple words.
Rewrite this paragraph in a more polite tone.
Summarise the text I pasted below in three bullets.
Give me the exact page number and quote from a specific little-known book.
quiz.why: Exact page numbers and quotes from obscure sources are specific details the model may not have learned reliably, so it fills the gap with something plausible. The others work from common knowledge or supplied text.

quiz.prompt: A model trained mostly on data from one group performs worse for people outside that group. This unfair pattern inherited from the data is called what? (one word)
quiz.why: Bias in the training data carries into the outputs. It is a reason to check results, especially in decisions about people.

bank.prompt: A company trains a model on ten years of its past hiring decisions to shortlist candidates. Which risk is most direct?
options: The model will refuse to read CVs.
The model may repeat unfair patterns present in past decisions.
The model will become a rule-based program.
The model will always shortlist the best candidate.
bank.why: A model learns patterns in its data, including unfair ones. It does not become rule-based, and it has no guarantee of finding the best candidate.

bank.prompt: You ask a model about a government scheme announced last month and it answers confidently with details. What is the best response?
options: Trust it, because it answered quickly and in detail.
Assume it has live access to the news.
Check an official source, because the model's knowledge has a cut-off and may not include recent events.
Ask the same question five times and take the most common answer.
bank.why: Training data stops at a cut-off date, so recent events may be missing or invented. Repeating the question does not add new evidence.

bank.prompt: A learned model gives its answer as the most likely result rather than a guaranteed one. What one-word adjective describes this kind of system? (starts with p)
bank.why: Learned systems are probabilistic: they estimate what is likely. Rule-based programs are deterministic for the same inputs.

cards.front: How does machine learning differ from a rule-based program?
cards.back: Rules are written by people and are predictable. Machine learning adjusts itself from many examples and gives probable answers, which are harder to explain and can be wrong.

cards.front: What does a language model fundamentally do?
cards.back: It predicts a likely next word, repeatedly, from patterns learned in text. It produces plausible output, not verified facts.

cards.front: Where is hallucination most likely, and what is the defence?
cards.back: Likeliest with exact figures, quotes, citations, obscure or recent topics. Defence: verify against an original source, or supply the source text and restrict the answer to it.

cards.front: Name two limits that come from training data.
cards.back: Bias inherited from uneven or unfair data, and a knowledge cut-off date that leaves out recent events.

ai-1.reflection: Which tasks in your own study or job preparation would you happily let AI draft, and which would you never delegate or never use without checking? Why?

keyPoints: Rules are written by people; machine learning learns patterns from examples and is probabilistic.
A language model predicts likely next words: plausible, not guaranteed true.
Hallucination hides in exact figures, quotes and citations.
Training data brings bias and a knowledge cut-off.
Sort tasks into safe to draft, must verify, do not delegate.
revision.redo: Pick one AI answer you received recently, find its single most checkable claim, and verify it against an original source.

ai-2.title: Using AI Tools Responsibly
ai-2.summary: Write clear task specifications with context, iterate on results, verify outputs, protect private data and use AI with academic and professional integrity.
objectives: Write a prompt that states role, task, context, constraints and output format.
Iterate on a first answer and verify the final output before using it.
Decide what must never be pasted into an AI tool and when disclosure or avoidance is the right call.

concepts.label: Integrity and when not to use AI

explanation.heading: Treat a prompt as a task specification
explanation.body:
In the previous lesson you saw that a language model predicts plausible text. That means the quality of what comes out depends heavily on what you put in. A vague request such as 'write about databases' gets a generic answer. A good request works like a short brief to a capable but new colleague who knows nothing about your situation.

A reliable structure has five parts:

1. **Role or audience:** who the answer is for.
2. **Task:** the one thing you want done.
3. **Context:** the facts and source text the model needs.
4. **Constraints:** length, tone, things to avoid, what to do if unsure.
5. **Output format:** bullets, table, email, code with comments.

Worked example. Weak: 'Explain joins.' Strong: 'I am a final-year MCA student preparing for an ABAP interview. Explain INNER JOIN versus LEFT OUTER JOIN using customers and sales orders. Maximum 150 words, one small example table for each, and finish with one common mistake. If any part is uncertain, say so.' The second version leaves the model far less to guess.

explanation.heading: Iterate, then verify
explanation.body:
Treat the first answer as a draft. Improve it with targeted follow-ups: 'Shorten to three sentences', 'Make the tone more formal for a client', 'Give two alternatives', 'Which assumptions did you make?'. Changing one thing at a time makes it easier to see what helped.

Then **verify before you use it**. Match the effort to the risk:

- **Low risk** (rephrasing your own paragraph): read it carefully and check it still says what you meant.
- **Medium risk** (explaining a concept): compare with your notes or textbook.
- **High risk** (figures, legal or policy statements, code that touches data): check the original source, run and test the code, and never trust it blindly.

For code, ask the model to explain each line, then run it with a small test case and an edge case such as an empty input. If you cannot explain why it works, you are not ready to submit it as yours.

explanation.heading: Privacy: only paste what you could safely publish
explanation.body:
Text you type into an online AI tool is sent to a service run by another company. Depending on the tool's settings it may be stored, reviewed, or used to improve the service. You usually cannot take it back, so decide **before** pasting.

Never paste: passwords, OTPs, API keys, Aadhaar, PAN or bank details; a client's confidential documents, source code or data covered by an NDA; other people's personal information; unpublished exam material. If your employer or client has an approved tool and a policy, follow it exactly.

A practical technique is **anonymising**. Replace 'Ramesh Kumar, Account 0123456789 at Nova Retail Pvt Ltd' with 'Customer A, Account XXXX at Company B' and keep only the structure the model needs. If you cannot remove the sensitive part and still ask a useful question, do not use the tool for that task.

explanation.heading: Integrity, ownership and when not to use AI
explanation.body:
You remain responsible for anything you submit or send, whoever drafted it. If AI produced a false claim in your report, the error is yours.

In college, check your institution's rule for each assignment. Many allow AI for brainstorming or language polish but not for the core answer; some forbid it entirely. If the rule is unclear, ask the teacher, and when AI helped, say how. At work, follow the same logic with your manager: disclose significant AI help when the client or policy expects it.

Sometimes the right choice is **not to use AI**: when the task is meant to build your own skill (practising ABAP syntax before an interview), when the data is confidential and there is no approved tool, when the stakes demand certainty, or when a sensitive human message such as an apology needs your own voice. A useful test: if you could not explain or defend the result in front of your teacher or manager, do not submit it.

examples.title: From vague to specified
examples.body:
Before: 'Write an email about the delay.'

After: 'Draft a 90-word email from me, a junior consultant, to our client's project manager. Context: the data migration is two days late because the test environment was unavailable; the new date is 18th. Tone: calm, accountable, no blame. Include one next step and ask for confirmation of the new date. Output only the email with a subject line.'
examples.takeaway: The second prompt names the audience, facts, tone, length and format, so the model has almost nothing left to invent.

examples.title: Anonymising before asking
examples.body:
Original: 'Our client Sunrise Pharma Ltd has a customer, Mrs Anita Rao, whose invoice INV-88231 for Rs 4,52,000 was posted twice. Why might this happen in SAP?'

Safe version: 'A company posted one customer invoice twice. List five common causes in an order-to-cash process and how I would check each.'
examples.takeaway: The question you need answered rarely needs names, amounts or invoice numbers. Keep the pattern, drop the identifiers.

examples.title: Verifying AI code
examples.body: A model gives a function that returns the average of a list. You test it with [4, 6, 8] and get 6, which is right. Then you test an empty list and it crashes with a divide-by-zero error. You ask the model to handle empty input, re-run both tests, and add a comment explaining the choice.
examples.takeaway: Passing the happy case proves little. Testing an edge case is what turns a plausible draft into code you can defend.

exercises.prompt: Which prompt is best specified for getting a useful result?
options: Explain SQL joins for me, thanks, make it good.
Write a long detailed essay about SQL and everything related to it.
I am a fresher preparing for interviews. Explain GROUP BY in under 120 words with one example on an orders table, and state one common mistake.
exercises.hint: Look for audience, limit, example and output shape.
exercises.why: The last prompt has an audience, task, length limit, example requirement and a focus. The others leave scope, depth and format to guesswork; 'long and detailed' increases length, not usefulness.

exercises.prompt: Replacing real names and account numbers with placeholders such as 'Customer A' before asking an AI tool is called what? (one word, starts with 'anon')
exercises.hint: It makes the data anonymous.
exercises.why: Anonymising keeps the structure of the problem while removing identifiers, so you can ask for help without exposing private or confidential information.

exercises.prompt: You want an AI tool to help you prepare a 100-word self-introduction for a campus placement interview. Write the prompt you would send. Invent realistic context (course, strengths, target role) and make sure it includes audience or role, task, context, at least two constraints and an output format.

descriptors.0: Only a bare request such as 'write my introduction'.
descriptors.1: Task stated but little about who you are or who the audience is.
descriptors.2: Task plus relevant personal context or audience.
descriptors.3: Clear task, audience (interviewer) and specific facts about you and the target role.

auto.label: Mentions the interview setting and who you are

descriptors.1: One vague constraint such as 'make it good'.
descriptors.2: One or two concrete constraints (length, tone).
descriptors.3: At least two concrete constraints, such as 100 words, confident but humble tone, and no clichés or invented facts.
Format stated and the prompt tells the model not to invent facts or to ask if details are missing.

exercises.modelAnswer: I am a final-year MCA student applying for an entry-level SAP ABAP consultant role at an IT services firm. Write a 100-word spoken self-introduction for a campus placement interview. Context: I have built two web projects using Node.js and Supabase, I am learning ABAP and SQL, and I enjoy debugging. Tone: confident, warm, not boastful. Do not invent any achievements or numbers that I have not given. Output a single paragraph that I can read aloud in under a minute, then list two points I should be ready to expand on.
exercises.guidance: A strong prompt reads like a brief you would hand a new colleague: who you are, who it is for, what to produce, limits, and format. Common mistakes are leaving out your real facts, which invites invented ones, and asking for polish without saying the tone. Check that every instruction in your prompt is something you could verify in the reply.

exercises.prompt: On your internship, your mentor asks you to understand why a client's nightly job failed. You have the log, which contains customer names, mobile numbers and account balances, plus an error code. The company has not told you whether any AI tool is approved. What is the best step?

options.text: Paste the whole log into a public AI chat; it is the fastest way to a diagnosis.
options.feedback: The log holds personal and client data. Pasting it exposes information you have no right to share.

options.text: Paste only the lines with names removed; the balances are probably fine.
options.feedback: Balances and mobile numbers are still sensitive, and partial redaction is easy to get wrong without a policy.

options.text: Ask your mentor what the policy is. Until you know, work from the error code and documentation, or write a fully anonymised description of the failure pattern.
options.feedback: Correct. Check the rule first and, if needed, share only a sanitised problem description that contains no client data.

options.text: Use a personal phone so that the company does not see you using the tool.
options.feedback: Hiding the use is worse: the data still leaves the client's control, and it breaks trust if discovered.

exercises.why: Client data is not yours to share. The professional move is to ask about policy, and meanwhile use only anonymised, non-confidential descriptions or ordinary documentation.

task.title: Write and test a five-part prompt
task.brief: Turn one real study or work request into a well-specified prompt, run it, improve it once, and verify the output.
steps: Pick a real task, for example summarising a topic from your syllabus or drafting a polite email.
Write a prompt with role or audience, task, context, constraints and output format. Remove any private details first.
Run it, then send one follow-up that changes only one thing (for example tone or length).
Verify one claim or one line of the final output against your notes or an original source, and note whether it passed.
checklist: My prompt had all five parts
I removed or anonymised private details
I made exactly one targeted follow-up
I verified at least one claim independently
task.evidencePrompt: Paste or describe your prompt in a sentence, say what the follow-up changed, and state what you verified and the result.

quiz.prompt: Which element tells the model how the answer should look?
quiz.why: Output format (bullets, table, email, code with comments) controls the shape of the answer. Context supplies facts, audience sets the reader, and verification is something you do afterwards.

quiz.prompt: AI gives you a function that works on your first test. What is the best next step before submitting it?
options: Submit it, because one passing test proves it works.
Test an edge case such as empty input and make sure you can explain each line.
Ask the AI whether it is correct and accept its reply.
Rename the variables so it looks like your own work.
quiz.why: Edge-case testing and your own understanding are what make code defensible. One passing case proves little, self-confirmation is not independent, and renaming does not add understanding.

quiz.prompt: Which item is safest to paste into a public AI tool?
options: A generic question about how pagination works, with no real data
A classmate's marks and phone number
quiz.why: A generic technical question contains nothing confidential. The others are confidential code, a security credential and another person's personal data.

quiz.prompt: Your college has not said whether AI may be used for an assignment. What is the responsible action?
options: Use it and say nothing; no rule means it is allowed.
Ask the teacher, and if you do use AI, state how it helped.
Use it only for the hardest question.
Use a second AI tool to rewrite the first tool's text.
quiz.why: When a rule is unclear, ask and be transparent. Silence is not permission, and rewriting with another tool hides rather than resolves the question of honest authorship.

bank.prompt: An AI-written summary of a 10-page report says the project 'saved 40 percent of costs'. You cannot recall that figure from the report. What do you do?
options: Search the report text for the figure and check its context before repeating it.
Keep it, because summaries are usually accurate.
Round it to 'about half' to be safe.
Delete the whole summary and never use AI again.
bank.why: Summaries can add or distort numbers. Check against the source. Rounding changes a possibly wrong figure into another wrong one, and abandoning the tool is an overreaction.

bank.prompt: A reply from an AI tool is too long and formal for a quick Teams message. Which follow-up is most effective?
options: Rewrite in two friendly sentences for a colleague on Teams, keeping the deadline of Friday.
bank.why: A follow-up should state the specific change: length, tone, audience and the fact to keep. Vague feedback gives the model nothing to adjust.

bank.prompt: If you submit AI-drafted work with a mistake in it, who is responsible for the mistake? (one word)
bank.why: The person who submits or sends the work owns it, however it was drafted. This is why verification matters.

cards.front: What five parts make a strong prompt?
cards.back: Role or audience, task, context, constraints, output format. Treat it as a brief to a capable new colleague who knows nothing about your situation.

cards.front: How much should you verify an AI output?
cards.back: Match effort to risk. Low: read it. Medium: compare with notes. High (figures, policy, code touching data): check the original and test, including edge cases.

cards.front: What must never be pasted into an AI tool?
cards.back: Passwords, OTPs, keys, ID and bank details, client or NDA material, other people's personal data. Anonymise or do not use the tool.

cards.front: When is not using AI the right call?
cards.back: When the task is meant to build your own skill, the data is confidential without an approved tool, the stakes demand certainty, or the message needs your own voice.

ai-2.reflection: Think of a recent task where you could have used AI. Which of the five prompt parts would you most often skip, and what would it cost you in accuracy or ownership?

keyPoints: Prompt = role or audience, task, context, constraints, format.
Iterate with one specific change at a time.
Verify in proportion to risk; test code with an edge case.
Paste only what you could safely publish; anonymise the rest.
You own what you submit; follow rules and disclose when expected.
revision.redo: Take any one-line request you made to an AI tool and rewrite it with all five parts in under two minutes.

ai-3.title: Digital Safety and Privacy
ai-3.summary: Protect your accounts and money with unique passwords, two-factor authentication, scam recognition, sensible privacy settings and backups.
objectives: Build strong, unique credentials using a password manager and two-factor authentication.
Recognise phishing and UPI or OTP scams by their pressure tactics and stop before acting.
Reduce your exposure with privacy settings, a tested backup routine and a managed digital footprint.

concepts.label: Phishing and UPI or OTP scams

explanation.heading: Passwords: long, unique and never memorised twice
explanation.body:
Earlier in this skill you saw that AI tools only know what you give them, so you learned to be careful about what you paste. The same care applies to every account you own. Most account break-ins do not come from clever hacking. They come from **reused passwords**: a small website you joined years ago is breached, and attackers try that same email and password on your email, your bank and your cloud storage.

The fix has two parts. First, make every password **unique**. Second, make it **long**, because length matters more than clever symbols. *Tr0ub4dor!* is short and predictable; *four unrelated words such as 'monsoon-lantern-cricket-slate'* is long, easy to remember and very hard to guess. Nobody can remember fifty unique passwords, so use a **password manager** (the one built into your phone or browser is acceptable; a dedicated manager is better). You remember one strong master passphrase; the manager generates and stores the rest.

Turn on **two-factor authentication (2FA)** for email first, because email resets every other account, then for banking, cloud storage and your college or work login. Prefer an authenticator app or a hardware key over SMS codes where you have the choice. Save the backup codes offline, so losing your phone does not lock you out for good.

explanation.heading: Phishing and OTP scams: pressure is the signal
explanation.body:
**Phishing** is a message designed to make you act before you think. It may arrive by email, SMS, WhatsApp or a phone call. Scam content changes constantly, but the tricks are stable: **urgency** ('your account will be blocked in two hours'), **authority** (a bank, a courier, the police, a recruiter), a **reward** (a refund, a lottery, a high-paying job) and a **request** (click, install, share a code or move money).

Some rules never change. **No genuine bank, UPI app or company will ask for your OTP, UPI PIN, card CVV or password**, by phone or message. An OTP is a key that authorises something; if someone asks for it, they are the ones trying to authorise something. You enter a UPI PIN only to *send* money, never to *receive* it, so any request screen that asks for your PIN to 'receive a refund' is a trap. Be wary of screen-sharing apps and unknown APK files sent on chat, since both give a stranger control of your phone.

Worked example: you get an SMS, 'Your electricity will be cut tonight, call this number immediately.' The pressure (tonight), the authority (the utility) and the demand (call now) are the pattern. Your response is a three-step pause: **stop, verify through a channel you already trust** (the official app or the number printed on your bill), then act. If you already shared something, call your bank at once to block the card or account and report the fraud through the national cybercrime helpline or portal. Speed limits the damage.

explanation.heading: Privacy settings and backups
explanation.body:
Privacy settings decide what apps, strangers and companies can see. Spend twenty minutes once and review them every few months. Check which apps can use your **location, contacts, microphone and camera** and switch off what an app does not need: a torch app has no reason to read your contacts. Set social accounts to the narrowest audience you are comfortable with, and check who can see your phone number and profile photo on messaging apps.

On public Wi-Fi, avoid logging into banking or sensitive accounts; use mobile data instead. Keep your phone and apps updated, because updates close known holes. Lock your phone with a PIN or biometric and set it to lock quickly.

Backups protect you from a different threat: loss, theft, a failed drive or ransomware. A useful rule is **3-2-1**: keep **three** copies of important files, on **two** different kinds of storage, with **one** copy away from your main device (cloud or a drive kept elsewhere). An untested backup is only a hope, so once in a while open a file from the backup to confirm that it restores. For a student, the important items are project code, certificates, ID scans and assignments. Put code in a private repository; keep scans in an encrypted or access-controlled folder.

explanation.heading: Your digital footprint is permanent enough to matter
explanation.body:
Your **digital footprint** is everything about you that can be found online: what you post, what others post about you, tags, comments, old accounts and data collected by apps. Recruiters and IT-services firms often search a candidate's name before an interview, and clients may do the same with consultants.

Manage it deliberately. **Search for yourself** using your name with your city and college, and look at the first two pages of results and the images. **Delete or lock** old accounts and posts you would not want a hiring manager to read. **Separate** identities where useful: one professional email for applications and professional profiles, another for shopping and sign-ups. Before you post, ask: would I be comfortable if my manager, a client and my family all saw this in five years?

Also limit what you reveal that helps scammers: your full birth date, home address, ID numbers, boarding passes and photos of cards or documents. Scammers assemble small facts into a convincing story. A good habit is a **quarterly security check**: update passwords on your top three accounts if needed, review app permissions, confirm that backups work and search your own name.

examples.title: A 'refund' scam, stage by stage
examples.body:
A caller says: 'Sir, your online order was double-charged. I will send you a collect request. Please approve it with your UPI PIN to get the refund.' You receive a request that asks for your PIN. If you enter it, money leaves your account.

The safe path: say nothing about your PIN, end the call, open your payment app yourself and look at the request. It says 'pay', not 'receive'. Contact the merchant through the official app or website.
examples.takeaway: A PIN is only for sending money. A 'refund' that needs your PIN, an OTP or a caller who rushes you is a scam by definition.

examples.title: Fixing a weak password setup
examples.body:
Before: one password, 'Deepak@123', used on email, a shopping site, a gaming forum and a college portal. No 2FA.

After: a password manager generates a unique 16-character password for each account; the email account gets an authenticator app as 2FA; the master passphrase is four unrelated words; backup codes are printed and kept in a folder at home.
examples.takeaway: One breach no longer unlocks everything, and the account that resets all others, your email, is the best protected.

examples.title: A footprint audit before placement season
examples.body: A student searches 'Rohan Mehta Faridabad MCA' and finds a public forum post from Class 11 with insulting language, an old gaming handle that links to a profile with a public phone number, and no professional profile at all. In an hour he deletes the post, locks the old account, removes the phone number, and creates a clean profile showing his projects.
examples.takeaway: Employers search first. Cleaning up and adding something positive takes an hour and changes the first impression.

exercises.prompt: Which single habit reduces the damage when one website you use is breached?
options: Using a different password on every account
Adding a symbol such as ! to the end of your usual password
Changing your one shared password every year
Choosing a password that is easy to type on mobile
exercises.hint: Think about what attackers try on other sites after a breach.
exercises.why: Unique passwords stop one breach from unlocking your other accounts. A symbol at the end is predictable and the password is still shared; yearly changes leave a reused password exposed for months; and ease of typing says nothing about safety.

exercises.prompt: Complete the rule with one word: a UPI PIN is needed only to ____ money, never to receive it.
exercises.hint: Which direction does money move when you authorise with a PIN?
exercises.why: You authorise outgoing payments with your PIN. A screen asking for your PIN in order to 'receive' money is a scam to take money out of your account.

exercises.prompt: You receive this WhatsApp message: 'Dear candidate, you are shortlisted for a work-from-home job paying a high monthly salary. Pay a refundable registration fee on the link below within one hour or your slot will be given to someone else.' Explain in 3-5 sentences whether to trust it, naming at least two warning signs and the exact steps you will take.

descriptors.0: Does not name any warning sign.
descriptors.1: Names one sign vaguely, such as 'looks fake'.
descriptors.2: Names two signs, for example the upfront fee and the one-hour deadline.
descriptors.3: Names three or more signs: upfront fee, urgency, unsolicited offer, unrealistic pay, unverified link.

auto.label: Mentions at least two warning signs

descriptors.0: No action given, or advice to pay to check.
descriptors.1: Says to ignore it but gives no verification or reporting step.
descriptors.2: Gives one safe step such as not clicking, or verifying the company independently.
descriptors.3: Gives several steps: do not pay or click, verify through the company's official channel, block and report the number.

descriptors.1: Reasons are listed but not connected to the decision.
descriptors.2: Reasons support the conclusion with minor gaps.
descriptors.3: A clear conclusion supported by the pattern of pressure, reward and request.

exercises.modelAnswer: I would not trust this message. A genuine employer does not ask for a registration fee, so the upfront payment is the first warning. The one-hour deadline is pressure meant to stop me thinking, and the very high pay for work from home with no interview is another. I will not click the link or pay. I will search for the company myself through its official website or a trusted careers page to see whether the role exists, then block and report the number.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers recognise the pattern: reward plus urgency plus a request for money. A common mistake is to say 'it may be real, I'll pay a small amount to check', which is exactly what the scam relies on. Another is only to ignore the message without verifying or reporting. Score yourself honestly on whether you named specific signs and gave at least one verification step that does not use the link provided.

exercises.prompt: At 11 pm you get a call: 'This is your bank's fraud team. We have blocked a suspicious payment. To keep your account safe we will send an OTP; please read it out so we can cancel the transaction.' Your phone then shows an OTP SMS that says it is for approving a payment. The caller is calm and knows your name. What do you do?

options.text: Read out the OTP quickly, because the caller knows your name and the bank is protecting you.
options.feedback: Knowing your name proves nothing, since names are easy to find. The OTP is for approving a payment, and reading it out completes the fraud.

options.text: Ask the caller to verify by telling you your last transaction, then share the OTP if he is right.
options.feedback: Scammers often have partial data from earlier leaks, so a correct detail is not proof. The rule is never to share an OTP at all.

options.text: End the call without sharing anything, then call the bank using the number on your card or the official app, and report the attempt.
options.feedback: Correct. You break the pressure, verify through a channel you trust and report. If any real fraud exists, the bank can see it on its own side.

options.text: Stay on the line and keep arguing until the caller admits it is a scam.
options.feedback: Engaging keeps you under their pressure and risks a slip. Ending the call is safer than winning the argument.

exercises.why: The OTP message itself tells you its purpose: to authorise a payment. A bank protecting you never needs it from you. Hanging up and calling the number you already trust removes the caller's control.

task.title: Your 20-minute security upgrade
task.brief: Make three real improvements to your digital safety today and record what changed.
steps: Open the account settings of your main email and turn on two-factor authentication using an authenticator app; save the backup codes somewhere offline.
Check your password manager (or set one up) and replace the password on your email and one other important account with a unique long one.
Review the permissions of five apps on your phone and switch off one location, contacts, camera or microphone permission that is not needed.
Search your own name with your city or college and note one thing you will delete, lock or improve.
checklist: Two-factor authentication is on for my email
Two important accounts now have unique passwords
I reviewed at least five app permissions
I noted one footprint item to fix
task.evidencePrompt: List the three changes you made and the one footprint item you will fix next.

quiz.prompt: Which password is the strongest choice if each is used on only one account?
quiz.why: Four unrelated words are long and hard to guess. The others are short, follow common patterns or rely on obvious substitutions, which cracking tools try first.

quiz.prompt: Which feature most reliably marks a message as a likely scam?
options: It comes from an unknown number
It combines urgency with a request for money, an OTP or a PIN
quiz.why: Genuine messages can have links and some come from unfamiliar numbers, but pressure combined with a request for secrets or money is the core pattern of fraud.

quiz.prompt: In the 3-2-1 backup rule, how many copy should be kept off-site or away from your main device? (a number)
quiz.why: 3-2-1 means three copies, two types of storage, one copy away from your main device, so a theft, fire or ransomware attack does not take everything.

quiz.prompt: What is the most useful first step in managing your digital footprint before applying for jobs?
options: Delete every social media account you own
Search for your own name and review what appears
Make all your posts public so recruiters can see them
Use a nickname on your CV
quiz.why: You cannot fix what you have not seen. Deleting everything removes positive evidence, public posts raise exposure and a nickname does not stop a search.

bank.prompt: A friend says: 'I use the same strong password everywhere, so I am safe.' What is the main flaw?
options: A strong password should never be written down
Once any one site leaks it, attackers can use it on all your other accounts
Strong passwords expire after thirty days
Two-factor authentication cannot be used with strong passwords
bank.why: Strength does not protect against reuse. A single breach exposes the password everywhere. Strong passwords do not automatically expire, and 2FA works well with them.

bank.prompt: A courier message says your parcel is held and you must pay a small customs fee through a link within two hours. What is the best response?
options: Pay quickly, since the amount is small
Ignore the link and check the parcel through the courier's official app or the seller's order page
Forward the message to friends to ask what to do
bank.why: Verify through a source you already trust. A small amount is the lure; replying confirms your number is active; forwarding spreads the risk.

bank.prompt: Name the practice of occasionally opening a file from your backup to confirm it works. Answer with one word that completes: 'an untested backup is only a ____'.
bank.why: A backup only has value if you can restore from it. Test restores occasionally so you discover problems before you need the files.

cards.front: What are the three habits that protect most accounts?
cards.back: Long unique passwords stored in a password manager, two-factor authentication starting with email, and offline backup codes.

cards.front: Which details does a genuine bank never ask you for?
cards.back: Your OTP, UPI PIN, card CVV or password. Hang up, then verify through the official app or the number on your card.

cards.front: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule mean?
cards.back: Three copies of important files, on two kinds of storage, with one copy kept away from your main device. Test restores occasionally.

cards.front: How do you audit your digital footprint?
cards.back: Search your name with city and college, review results and images, delete or lock what you would not want an employer to see, and add something professional.

ai-3.reflection: Which of your accounts would do you the most harm if someone took it over, and is it protected as well as it deserves to be today?

keyPoints: Unique, long passwords in a manager; 2FA on email first.
Urgency plus a request for money, OTP or PIN is the scam pattern.
Stop, verify through a trusted channel, then act.
Back up with 3-2-1 and test the restore.
Search your own name before employers do.
revision.redo: Pick one account, check whether it has a unique password and 2FA, and fix whichever is missing.

ai-4.title: Digital Productivity and Data Literacy
ai-4.summary: Organise files so you can find anything, think in tables, spot work worth automating, evaluate tools sensibly and handle synthetic media and data ethically.
objectives: Set up a file and folder system with naming rules that makes any document findable in seconds.
Structure data as a clean table and use simple spreadsheet logic, then identify repeated tasks worth automating.
Judge a new tool or a piece of media critically and handle other people's data ethically.

explanation.heading: A file system you can search in ten seconds
explanation.body:
In the last lesson you protected your accounts and backups. Now we make your digital work easy to find and easy to trust. Most lost time on a computer is not slow typing; it is hunting for a file called *final_v2_REAL.docx* in a Downloads folder with four hundred other items.

A good system has three parts. First, **few top-level folders** organised by purpose, not by file type: *01-Study, 02-Projects, 03-Career, 04-Admin, 99-Archive*. Second, **consistent names** that sort correctly: put the date first in year-month-day form, then the subject, then a version: *2026-10-12_ABAP-internal-tables_notes_v2.pdf*. A year-first date means files sort in time order automatically. Third, **one inbox**: new downloads land in a single Inbox folder that you empty once a week, by filing or deleting.

Avoid the two classic mistakes. Over-nesting (eight levels deep) makes you click for ages, so aim for no more than three levels. And never put the word *final* in a name; use version numbers and move old versions into the archive. For code, version control does this job better than file names. If you use cloud storage, make sure that the same structure exists there, so a lost laptop does not mean a lost system.

explanation.heading: Think in tables: one row, one thing
explanation.body:
A spreadsheet is a small database. The idea that makes it powerful is **tidy data**: every column is one attribute, every row is one record, and every cell holds one value. If you ever learn SQL or ABAP internal tables, the same thinking applies, because a table is a table.

Suppose you track freelance work. A messy sheet has one row per month with columns 'Client A paid', 'Client B paid' and merged cells. A tidy sheet has columns *Date, Client, Hours, Rate, Amount, Paid?* and one row per job. The tidy sheet can be sorted, filtered and summed by client or month with a few formulas, and the messy one cannot.

Learn a handful of building blocks. **SUM** adds a range. **SUMIF** adds only the rows that meet a condition: summing the Amount where Client equals 'Meera' gives her total. **COUNTIF** counts matching rows. **IF** returns different results by condition, such as marking late payments. **Lookup functions** fetch a value from another table by a key. A **pivot table** summarises a tidy table by category in a few clicks.

Worked example: ten jobs, three for Meera at ₹4,000, ₹6,500 and ₹2,500. SUMIF for Meera returns ₹13,000, and COUNTIF returns 3. Always sanity-check results: if the total looks off, check for numbers stored as text, hidden rows and blank cells inside the range.

explanation.heading: Automation thinking and choosing tools
explanation.body:
Automation thinking means noticing repeated work and asking whether a machine can do it. Use a simple test: is the task **repeated** often, **rule-based** (the same steps each time), and **boring** enough that errors creep in? Renaming fifty files, copying data from one sheet into a monthly report, or sending the same reminder each Friday are all good candidates. Judgement-heavy work, such as deciding how to answer a client's complaint, is a poor candidate.

Work in this order: **map** the steps in plain words, **simplify** them (remove unneeded steps first), then **automate** with the simplest tool that works: a spreadsheet formula, a template, a calendar repeat, a keyboard shortcut, a saved filter, a small script, or a no-code workflow tool. Time check: a task that takes 10 minutes a week costs about 8.7 hours a year, so spending two hours to automate it is worthwhile, but a once-a-year task is not.

When you evaluate any new tool, ask five questions. What **problem** does it solve for me? What does it **cost**, including time to learn and the price when the free plan ends? Can I **export** my data if I leave? What happens to my **data and privacy**? Does it have a **track record**, such as support, updates and a clear business model? New and fashionable is not a reason. If you cannot say which task it replaces, you do not need it yet.

explanation.heading: Deepfakes, synthetic media and data ethics
explanation.body:
Today, images, audio and video can be produced or altered by software so convincingly that they cannot be trusted by eye or ear. A **deepfake** is synthetic media that shows a real person doing or saying something they never did. Voice cloning can copy a relative's voice from a few seconds of audio, which is why scammers now phone with an 'urgent family emergency'.

The defence is **verification, not detection by feel**. Check the source: who first published it, and does a reliable outlet carry the same item? Look for context mismatches. Pause when the content makes you angry or urgent, since that is the intention. For a voice call asking for money, hang up and call the person on their known number, or use a family code word. Never share synthetic media of real people without their consent, especially intimate or humiliating content, which can cause serious harm and can be a legal offence.

**Data ethics** is about treating data about people with care. Collect only what you need (**minimisation**), say why you collect it (**purpose**), get **consent**, keep it secure and delete it when it is no longer needed. In a college project, that means not scraping and publishing classmates' phone numbers, anonymising names in a survey, and storing responses in a protected folder. In an IT-services job, client and customer data is never yours to copy to a personal device or a public tool. Ask: would the people in this dataset be comfortable with how I am using it?

examples.title: Cleaning up a chaotic Downloads folder
examples.body:
Before: Downloads holds 'Resume final.docx', 'Resume final (2).docx', 'IMG_4432.jpg', 'notes.pdf' and 300 more files.

After: the CV lives in 03-Career as '2026-10_Deepak-Raj_CV_v3.docx'; the older versions are in 99-Archive; 'notes.pdf' is renamed '2026-09-28_SAP-ABAP-data-types_notes.pdf' and filed in 01-Study. Downloads is emptied on Sunday evening.
examples.takeaway: Purpose-based folders and date-first names turn searching into a ten-second job.

examples.title: A tidy table answers questions in seconds
examples.body: Table columns: Date, Subject, Minutes, Type. Rows: one per study session. Formula: =SUMIF(B:B, "ABAP", C:C) returns total ABAP minutes; =COUNTIF(D:D, "Practice") counts practice sessions. If ABAP shows 540 minutes and there are 9 sessions, the average session is 540 / 9 = 60 minutes.
examples.takeaway: One row per record and one value per cell allow simple formulas to do all the summarising.

examples.title: Checking a suspicious clip
examples.body: A video shows a well-known business leader endorsing an investment scheme that doubles money in a month. The accounts sharing it are new, the clip has no original source, and the promise is extreme. Instead of trusting the face and voice, you search for the same statement on the person's official channels and reliable news outlets and find nothing.
examples.takeaway: Verify the source and the claim. A realistic face and voice are not evidence.

exercises.prompt: Which file name will sort correctly by date and still make sense in a year?
exercises.hint: Think about which part of the name the computer sorts first.
exercises.why: A year-month-day date at the start sorts chronologically and the subject and version make it understandable later. Day-first dates sort by day across months, and words like final or NEW tell you nothing and become false later.

exercises.prompt: A tidy sheet has Amounts of ₹4,000, ₹6,500 and ₹2,500 for client Meera and ₹3,000 for client Arun. What does a SUMIF for Meera return? Give the number only.
exercises.hint: Add only Meera's rows.
exercises.why: SUMIF adds only the rows where the client is Meera: 4,000 + 6,500 + 2,500 = 13,000. Arun's 3,000 is excluded.

exercises.prompt: Choose one repeated task from your own study or work (for example, copying exam dates into a calendar, renaming downloaded notes, or building a weekly progress summary). In 4-6 sentences, map its steps, decide whether it is worth automating using the repeated, rule-based, boring test and the time arithmetic, and name the simplest tool you would use.

descriptors.1: A vague description of the task without a sequence.
descriptors.2: Steps are listed but some are unclear or missing.
descriptors.3: A clear ordered sequence of concrete steps that someone else could follow.

rubric.label: Applies the three-part test and time maths

descriptors.1: Says it would be useful without applying repeated, rule-based and boring.
descriptors.2: Applies the test or the time arithmetic, but not both.
descriptors.3: Applies repeated, rule-based and boring and estimates time saved against time to build.

auto.label: Uses decision words such as repeat, rule, minutes or hours

descriptors.1: Names an over-complicated tool without a reason.
descriptors.2: Names a suitable tool with a thin reason.
descriptors.3: Names the simplest tool that works and says why a heavier one is unnecessary.

exercises.modelAnswer: Every Sunday I copy my assignment deadlines from the college portal into my calendar, which takes about 15 minutes. The steps are: open the portal, read each deadline, create a calendar event, and add a reminder two days earlier. The task is repeated weekly, follows the same rules each time and is boring enough that I sometimes miss a date. At 15 minutes a week it costs around 13 hours a year, so it is worth improving. The simplest tool is a calendar template with a default two-day reminder, and a small checklist, rather than a script.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers pick a real task, list steps in order and show the arithmetic (minutes per week multiplied by 52, then divided by 60 for hours). A common mistake is jumping to a complicated tool before simplifying the steps. Another is choosing a task that needs judgement each time. Score yourself on whether the decision is justified, not whether the task is impressive.

exercises.prompt: You are doing a survey for a college project and have an Excel sheet with 120 classmates' names, phone numbers, CGPA and opinions. A friend suggests posting the complete sheet in the class group so others can use it, and uploading it to a public AI tool to quickly summarise opinions. What is the best course of action?

options.text: Post the full sheet in the group; everyone is a classmate, so there is no harm.
options.feedback: People gave answers for a project, not for wide sharing. Phone numbers and CGPA are personal, and a group chat copy can travel anywhere.

options.text: Remove names, phone numbers and CGPA into a separate protected file, keep only anonymised opinions for analysis and summarising, and share only the aggregated results.
options.feedback: Correct. This applies minimisation and anonymisation: use only what the analysis needs, protect what remains and share summaries rather than raw personal data.

options.text: Upload the full sheet to the AI tool but not to the group.
options.feedback: This avoids one exposure but still sends identifiable personal data to an outside service without the respondents' consent.

options.text: Delete the data immediately, so nobody can complain.
options.feedback: Deleting is safe but throws away legitimate work. Anonymising and sharing aggregated results meets your goal without the risk.

exercises.why: Ethical data handling means collecting and using only what is needed for the stated purpose, protecting identifiers and sharing results at the level of summaries. The anonymised file is both useful and safe.

task.title: Tidy one corner of your digital life
task.brief: Create a small, working file structure and one tidy table, then notice one task to automate.
steps: Create three top-level folders on your computer or cloud drive (for example 01-Study, 02-Projects, 99-Archive) and move ten loose files into them.
Rename at least five of those files using the date-first pattern with subject and version.
Create a tidy table in a spreadsheet with at least five rows from your own life (study sessions, expenses or applications) and add one SUMIF or COUNTIF.
Write down one repeated task you do each week and estimate how much time it takes.
checklist: I created at least three purpose-based folders
I renamed five files with date, subject and version
My table has one row per record and one value per cell
I estimated the weekly time cost of one repeated task
task.evidencePrompt: Write your folder names, one renamed file, the formula you used and the task you may automate.

quiz.prompt: What is the best use of an Inbox folder in a file system?
options: A permanent store for every download
A single landing place for new files that you file or delete once a week
A folder for files you are never going to open again
A folder holding only your most important documents
quiz.why: An inbox keeps new files from spreading everywhere and is emptied on a schedule. It is not permanent storage, and it is not for old or important files.

quiz.prompt: Which layout follows tidy data principles?
options: One row per month with a separate column for each client's payment
Merged cells showing client names above groups of rows
One row per job with columns for date, client, hours and amount
quiz.why: Tidy data has one record per row and one value per cell. The others hide multiple values, merge cells or spread one attribute across columns, which breaks filters and formulas.

quiz.prompt: A task takes 10 minutes every week. About how many hours does it take in a year (52 weeks)? Round to the nearest whole number.
quiz.why: 10 minutes multiplied by 52 weeks is 520 minutes, which is about 8.7 hours, so roughly 9 hours a year.

quiz.prompt: You get a voice message that sounds exactly like your cousin asking you to send money urgently. What is the best action?
options: Send a small amount now and ask questions later
Trust it, because the voice is clearly his
Hang up or ignore it and call your cousin on his usual number to verify
Reply on the same chat asking him to prove it
quiz.why: Voices can be cloned, so a familiar sound is no proof. Verify through a separate channel you already trust. Asking on the same compromised channel lets the scammer answer.

bank.prompt: A project folder has twelve levels of nested subfolders. What is the main problem and the fix?
options: Too much nesting slows finding files; flatten to about three levels and use clear names
Nothing is wrong, because deeper folders are safer
It must be converted to a single folder with all files in it
The folders should be sorted by file type instead of purpose
bank.why: Deep nesting makes files hard to locate. A flatter structure with clear names is faster. A single huge folder is also hard to search, and sorting by file type scatters related work.

bank.prompt: Which spreadsheet function adds up only the rows that meet a condition, such as total expenses where Category is Food? Answer with the function name.
bank.why: SUMIF (or SUMIFS for several conditions) totals values only where the condition holds. SUM adds everything, and COUNTIF counts rows rather than adding values.

bank.prompt: A friend recommends a new productivity app because everyone is talking about it. Which question should you ask first?
options: How many people have downloaded it?
Which task of mine does it replace, and can I export my data if I leave?
Does it have a dark mode?
Is it the newest app in its category?
