People tend to use five styles, defined by how much they care about their own goals and about the relationship:

- **Competing**: my goal wins. Fast and firm, but it can leave resentment.
- **Collaborating**: we work together to meet both sets of needs. Takes time, produces the best outcomes.
- **Compromising**: each gives up something to meet in the middle. Quick and fair-ish.
- **Avoiding**: step away from the issue. Useful for trivial matters or to cool down; harmful when it is a habit.
- **Accommodating**: I give way to keep peace or because the issue matters more to the other person.

No style is good or bad in itself. The common mistake is to use *your favourite* style for every situation. A person who always avoids lets small problems grow; a person who always competes wins arguments and loses colleagues.

explanation.heading: Choose your style on purpose
explanation.body:
Before reacting, ask two questions: **How important is this issue?** and **How important is this relationship?** If the stakes are high and the relationship matters, collaborate. If the issue is trivial, avoid or accommodate. If time is short and a decision is needed, compromise or, in an emergency such as a production outage, compete by taking clear command. If you are wrong, accommodate gracefully.

Practise by noticing your default. For one week, each time you disagree with someone, note the style you used. Most people discover they have one or two habitual styles. Knowing yours is the first step to using the others.

examples.title: Separating task from relationship
examples.body:
Situation: Ritu and Sameer share a project repository. Sameer pushed code that broke Ritu's module. Ritu messages: 'You are so careless, you break everything.'

Task part: the build is failing and needs a fix before the demo.
Relationship part: Ritu feels her work is not respected.

Rewrite: 'The build failed after your push, and my module stopped working. Can we look at it together and fix it before the demo? I would also like us to agree on running tests before pushing.'
examples.takeaway: The rewrite keeps the legitimate task issue and the real need (a shared rule), and drops the character attack that would have pushed the conflict up a rung.

examples.title: Coming down the ladder
examples.body:
Conflict at rung 3: Karan says to Divya in a team chat, 'Typical of you to miss the deadline again.'

A de-escalating reply: 'I did miss Tuesday's deadline and I want to fix the impact. Can we talk for five minutes about what the testing team needs by tomorrow?'

The reply accepts the fact, ignores the insult, and moves to the task. That drops the conversation back to rung 1.
examples.takeaway: To come down a rung, respond to the issue and not to the insult, and propose a concrete next step.

examples.title: Style fits the situation
examples.body:
1. A production server is down at midnight and two engineers disagree on the fix. The senior engineer says, 'We roll back now. Discuss it after.' (Competing is right: speed matters.)
2. Two friends disagree on which cafe to meet at. One says, 'Either is fine, you choose.' (Accommodating is right: the issue is small.)
3. Two teammates disagree on the architecture of a six-month project. They book an hour, list what each needs and design something that serves both. (Collaborating is right: high stakes, long relationship.)
examples.takeaway: The same person can use different styles in different situations, and that flexibility is the skill.

exercises.prompt: Which of these statements is a task conflict statement rather than a relationship one?
options: You never listen to anyone's ideas in meetings.
People like you always want credit for the team's work.
I think the report should lead with the cost figures, not the timeline.
I cannot trust you to finish things on time.
exercises.hint: Task conflict is about the work itself, not about the person's character.
exercises.why: The third option disagrees about the content of the report. The others make claims about the person's character or reliability ('never', 'always', 'cannot trust you'), which is how a task disagreement turns into a relationship conflict.

exercises.prompt: Anita always says 'Fine, whatever you prefer' even when she disagrees, and gives up her own needs to keep the peace. Which of the five conflict styles is this? (one word)
exercises.hint: She yields to the other person's wishes.
exercises.why: Accommodating means giving way to the other side. It is not avoiding, because Anita engages and then yields; it is helpful when the issue matters little to you, but harmful as a habit because her real needs never get heard.

exercises.prompt: A teammate has made a personal comment in a group chat. Use the escalation ladder to bring the conversation back to the task.
exercises.setup: You are a final-year student leading a four-person project. In the group chat, your teammate Ananya wrote: 'You always take over the code and nobody else gets a say.' You did write most of the backend last week because the others were busy with exams. Your goal is to bring the conflict back from personalising to the task, and to find out what she actually needs.

turns.they: I am just saying, you always take over. Last week I did not even know what you had pushed.

options.text: That is not true. I did the backend because nobody else had time.
options.feedback: You defend yourself and contradict her, which keeps the conversation at the personalising rung.
options.reply: See, this is exactly what I mean. You never accept that you do this.

options.text: I did write a lot of the backend last week, and I can see that you did not know what had changed. Is that the part that bothered you?
options.feedback: You accept the fact, separate the task issue (visibility of changes) and ask about her real concern.
options.reply: Yes. I felt left out. I want to review the changes before they go in, and I would like to take the login module myself.

options.text: Let us not argue in the group chat. Forget it.
options.feedback: Avoiding the chat is sensible, but 'forget it' leaves the real issue unresolved and she may feel dismissed.
options.reply: Fine. But I am still not happy about it.

turns.they: I want to be involved in decisions, not just told afterwards.

options.text: So you want to change how we split the work? Let us do a call tonight and decide the modules together.
options.feedback: A concrete next step is good, but you moved to the solution before showing you understood her need.
options.reply: A call is fine, I suppose. I just hope this time it is not already decided.

options.text: Fair point. Let me suggest two things: I will post a short note before each major push, and we pick modules together on a call tonight. Does that work for you?
options.feedback: You acknowledge the need, offer a specific change and invite her agreement.
options.reply: Yes, that works. Thank you. I can take login and the report layout, if that is fine.

options.text: I am happy to share, but you must also reply faster when I ask for updates.
options.feedback: Adding a counter-accusation turns a repair into a trade and pushes the conflict back up the ladder.
options.reply: So now it is my fault? I thought we were fixing this.

turns.they: Okay. And please do not call me out in the chat next time either, ask me directly.

options.text: You started it in the chat, though.
options.feedback: Scoring points keeps the conflict alive just as it was settling.

options.text: Agreed, I will raise concerns with you directly first, and I would appreciate the same from you. Thanks for telling me what you needed.
options.feedback: You agree on a working rule in both directions and close with appreciation.
options.reply: Deal. Thanks for listening. I will take the login module tonight.

options.text: Sure, okay.
options.feedback: Accepting is fine, but you miss the chance to make the agreement mutual and thank her.

exercises.why: The ladder tells you the target: move from personalising (rung 3) to the task (rung 1). That means accepting the true fact, asking what lies behind the insult, offering a concrete change, and agreeing a rule that goes both ways. Defending, counter-attacking or scoring points sends you back up.

exercises.prompt: Read this case. In an IT services team, Sneha rewrote a module that Rohit had written, without telling him, because she thought it was too slow. Rohit then wrote in the team chat: 'Some people cannot trust others to do their work.' Two other teammates have started to side with Rohit. Write 4 to 6 sentences covering: (1) whether this is task or relationship conflict, (2) which rung of the ladder it is on, (3) the conflict style you would use first and why, and (4) one opening sentence you would say to Sneha or Rohit.

descriptors.1: Says task or relationship without any reasoning.
descriptors.2: Identifies a mix but does not explain which part is which.
descriptors.3: Explains that the slow module is the task issue and that the lack of notice and the public remark are relationship issues.

descriptors.1: Names a rung that does not fit the facts, with no reason.
descriptors.2: Names a plausible rung but gives a thin reason.
descriptors.3: Names rung 3 or 4 (personalising moving into sides) and gives evidence such as the public remark and teammates siding.

descriptors.1: Names a style with no link to the situation.
descriptors.2: Names a style with a partial justification.
descriptors.3: Chooses collaborating (or a brief cooling-off first, then collaborating) and links it to a long-term team and an issue that matters.

descriptors.0: The opening sentence is accusing or missing.
descriptors.1: Neutral but vague, such as 'We need to talk'.
descriptors.2: Constructive but does not mention the specific issue.
descriptors.3: Specific, non-blaming and inviting, for example mentioning the module change and asking to talk privately.

exercises.modelAnswer: This is a mix. The task issue is that the module was slow; the relationship issue is that Sneha changed Rohit's work without telling him and Rohit then made a public remark. It is on rung 3 moving to rung 4, because the comment is personal and teammates are taking sides. I would use collaborating, after a short cooling-off, because the project is long and both the module quality and the trust matter. I would start by messaging Rohit privately: 'I would like to talk about the module change and how we handle changes in future. Can we speak for ten minutes today?'
exercises.guidance: A strong answer separates the two kinds of conflict instead of choosing only one, ties the rung to evidence in the case (the public remark, the siding), and picks a style for a reason. A common mistake is to say 'compete' or 'avoid' with no reasoning, or to write an opening line that blames Sneha or Rohit. Another is to forget that the fix should also include a future rule about informing the owner before changing their code. Compare with the model answer and score honestly.

task.title: Map one real disagreement
task.brief: Analyse a real disagreement from your recent life using the task and relationship test, the ladder and the five styles.
steps: Pick a real disagreement from the last month with a friend, family member, teammate or classmate. Choose a small one.
Write two lines: what the disagreement was about (task part) and how it affected the relationship (relationship part).
Mark the highest rung of the ladder it reached and what happened at that point.
Name the style you used and the style you would use now, with one sentence on why.
Write one sentence you could say to bring it down one rung.
checklist: I separated the task part from the relationship part
I named a rung on the ladder
I named the style I used and the one I would choose now
task.evidencePrompt: Write the disagreement in one line, its highest rung, the style you used, and your de-escalating sentence.

quiz.prompt: Two teammates disagree about which framework to use. One says: 'Your suggestion only shows you do not understand the project.' What has happened?
options: Nothing has changed; it is still purely a task conflict
A task conflict has been converted into a relationship conflict
The conflict has been resolved by compromise
The conflict has moved to avoiding
quiz.why: The comment targets the person's understanding rather than the framework. That is conversion from task to relationship conflict. It is not a compromise, and nobody is avoiding anything.

quiz.prompt: People in a team have started complaining about a colleague to friends and forming camps. Which rung of the ladder is this?
quiz.why: Pulling other people in and forming camps is the 'sides' rung. A third party is often needed here, because a direct two-person talk is harder once camps exist.

quiz.prompt: Which conflict style works with both people to meet both sets of needs, even though it takes more time? (one word, ending in -ing)
quiz.why: Collaborating looks for a solution that serves both sides. Compromising splits the difference, which is quicker but each side gives something up.

quiz.prompt: A friend asks which film to watch tonight; you have no strong view. Which style is the most sensible?
options: Competing, to make sure your opinion is heard
Collaborating, with a full hour of discussion
Accommodating, by letting your friend choose
quiz.why: When the issue is trivial and the relationship matters, giving way is efficient and kind. Competing and long collaboration waste effort on a small matter, and ignoring your friend damages the relationship.

bank.prompt: A manager notes that when two developers argue about code style, the argument ends once the team adopts a written style guide. What kind of conflict was it mainly?
options: Relationship conflict, because two people were arguing
Task conflict, because a shared rule resolved it
bank.why: If a neutral rule dissolves the disagreement, the issue was about the work rather than the people. The fact that two people argued does not make it a relationship conflict.

bank.prompt: In a meeting, a colleague says: 'Of course you would say that, you always side with the client.' What is the best de-escalating response?
options: 'I do not always side with the client. You are being unfair.'
'Let us look at the two options and the client's constraint, and decide which fits the deadline.'
Say nothing and look at the table
'Well, you always side with the manager.'
bank.why: The best response ignores the insult and returns to the task with a concrete structure. Defending or counter-attacking keeps the conversation on the personal rung, and silence leaves the accusation unanswered.

bank.prompt: A senior engineer says 'Roll back the release now, we will discuss it afterwards' during a live outage. Which of the five conflict styles is she using? (one word, ending in -ing)
bank.why: She is taking decisive command because speed matters more than consensus. In an emergency, competing is appropriate; as an everyday style, it damages relationships.

cards.front: How do you tell task conflict from relationship conflict?
cards.back: Task conflict is about the work; relationship conflict is about the people. Test: would the disagreement exist with different people? If yes, it is mostly task. Watch for task issues converting into personal ones.

cards.front: Name the five rungs of the escalation ladder.
cards.back: Difference, debate, personalising, sides, attack or withdrawal. Intervene early, and come down one rung at a time by responding to the issue, not the insult.
Competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating. They vary by concern for your own goals and for the relationship. None is always right.

cards.front: What two questions help you choose a style?
cards.back: How important is the issue, and how important is the relationship? High and high: collaborate. Low issue: avoid or accommodate. Emergency: compete briefly.

conflict-1.reflection: Think of a disagreement where you used your habitual style. Would a different style have produced a better result, and what would it have cost you to try it?

keyPoints: Task conflict is about the work; relationship conflict is about people.
Watch for conversion from task to personal.
The ladder: difference, debate, personalising, sides, attack or withdrawal.
Five styles: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating.
Choose a style by issue importance and relationship importance.
revision.redo: Recall a recent disagreement and say aloud: its type, its highest rung, the style you used and one better move.

conflict-2.title: Difficult Conversations
conflict-2.summary: Prepare and open a hard conversation with a clear script, I-statements, good timing, listening before responding and a focus on facts.
objectives: Prepare a difficult conversation by separating facts, your interpretation and your feelings.
Open with a four-part script and an I-statement that avoids blame.
Choose timing and listen and paraphrase before responding.

explanation.heading: Why difficult conversations go wrong
explanation.body:
In the previous lesson you learned to tell task conflict from relationship conflict and to place a disagreement on the ladder. This lesson is about the moment you actually have to talk. Most people either avoid the conversation until they are angry, or start with an accusation. Both make the other person defensive within the first ten seconds, and a defensive person cannot listen.

A difficult conversation is easier when you have prepared three things, chosen a good moment, opened it well, and listened properly. Each is a skill you can practise.

explanation.heading: Prepare: facts, story, feelings
explanation.body:
Before you speak, separate three layers.

- **Facts**: what a camera would record. 'Your module was not merged on Friday and the demo build failed.'
- **Story**: what you make of the facts. 'He does not care about the team.'
- **Feelings**: what you feel. 'I am worried and frustrated.'

The story is where most trouble starts, because it feels like a fact. Words such as *always*, *never*, *careless* and *lazy* are story words. In the conversation, lead with facts, share feelings briefly, and offer the story only as a question: 'I wondered whether the deadline was unclear. Was it?'

Also ask yourself: what is my purpose? 'To prove I am right' leads to a fight. 'To get the module merged on time and keep a good working relationship' leads to a conversation. Finally, ask what part you may have played. If you did not tell him the deadline moved, that is part of the picture.

explanation.heading: Open with a four-part script and an I-statement
explanation.body:
The first thirty seconds set the tone. A simple opening script has four parts:

1. **Shared purpose**: 'I want our demo to go well.'
2. **Observation** (fact, no blame): 'Your module was not merged by Friday.'
3. **Impact** (an I-statement): 'I had to stay late and I felt anxious about the demo.'
4. **Invitation**: 'Can you tell me what happened from your side?'

An **I-statement** says what you saw, how it affected you and what you need, without judging the person. Compare 'You are so unreliable' (a you-statement that is a verdict) with 'When the module was not merged on Friday, I had to rework the build at night, and I felt stressed. I need us to agree on a merge time.' The second is hard to argue with, because it describes your experience.

Common mistakes: hiding a criticism inside a compliment sandwich so that nothing is clear, using sarcasm, and saying 'I feel that you are careless' (that is still a you-statement wearing an I).

explanation.heading: Timing and setting
explanation.body:
Choose the moment as carefully as the words. Do not have the conversation when you are furious, in front of other people, by chat when the matter is emotional, or when the other person is about to present or sleep. Take a pause of a few hours or until the next day to cool down, but do not let that become permanent avoidance.

Ask permission: 'Is now a good time, or shall we talk at 4 pm? It is about the demo build.' Naming the subject avoids ambushing the person. Choose a private place, a calm voice and equal seating or a walk, not a standing confrontation.

explanation.heading: Listen before you respond
explanation.body:
After you have opened, stop talking. The other person has a story too, and you need to hear it, because you may be missing a fact. Use three moves: ask an open question ('What happened from your side?'), **paraphrase** what you heard ('So the requirements changed on Thursday night and nobody told you?'), and acknowledge the feeling ('That sounds frustrating') before you give your view. Acknowledging does not mean agreeing.

Paraphrasing is the most useful tool, because it shows you listened and it corrects misunderstandings before they harden. If the person becomes angry, do not match it. Lower your voice, slow down and return to facts. If the conversation is going in circles, name it: 'We are both getting heated. Shall we take ten minutes and come back?'

examples.title: Before and after: an opening line
examples.body:
Before: 'You are always late with your tasks and it is ruining the project. Why are you so careless?'

After: 'I want us to finish the demo on time. Your module was not merged on Friday, and I had to fix the build at night, which stressed me. Can you tell me what got in the way?'
examples.takeaway: The after version states a shared purpose, one fact, one impact and an invitation, and contains no 'always' and no label.

examples.title: Paraphrasing in action
examples.body:
Vikram: 'I did not merge it because the API contract changed on Thursday night and I had to redo the endpoints.'

You: 'So the contract changed late on Thursday, and you needed Friday to redo the endpoints. Did you hear about the change from the client, or from Priya?'

Vikram: 'From Priya, at 11 pm. I did not want to disturb you.'
examples.takeaway: Paraphrasing and a curious question revealed a new fact (the late change) that makes the earlier accusation unfair.

examples.title: Facts, story and feelings sheet
examples.body:
Situation: A teammate ignored your messages for two days.

Fact: 'I sent three messages on Monday and Tuesday and had no reply.'
Story: 'He is ignoring me on purpose.' (Possibly wrong; alternatives: he is ill, busy, or missed the notifications.)
Feeling: 'I am frustrated and a bit anxious about the deadline.'
Purpose: 'Get the review done by Thursday.'

Opening: 'I sent three messages about the review and have not heard back, and the deadline is Thursday. Is everything okay on your side?'
examples.takeaway: Writing the three layers separately lets you speak only the fact, a short feeling and a question, and keep the story to yourself until you have checked it.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a proper I-statement that you could use with a teammate who arrived 40 minutes late to a team call?
options: When you joined 40 minutes after the start, we had to repeat the discussion, and I felt rushed. I would like us to start on time.
I feel that you are very disrespectful of everyone's time.
You always do this and it is really unprofessional.
I think everyone is annoyed with you, so please be on time.
exercises.hint: Look for observable fact, your own impact and a request.
exercises.why: The second option describes what happened, the impact on the speaker and a request. The first is a you-statement dressed with 'I feel that'. The third uses 'always' and a label. The fourth speaks for others and adds pressure.

exercises.prompt: Your project manager criticised your report sharply in front of the whole team this morning. You are angry and want to answer immediately in the team chat. What is the best move?

options.text: Reply at once in the team chat to defend your work.
options.feedback: Replying in public while angry usually escalates and makes you look defensive.

options.text: Stay silent, say nothing ever, and hope it passes.
options.feedback: Avoiding feels safe but the feeling will leak out later, and the manager will not know the impact.

options.text: Wait until you have cooled down, then ask your manager for ten minutes in private and open with facts and impact.
options.feedback: A pause, a private setting and a calm opening give the conversation the best chance.

options.text: Complain about the manager to colleagues over lunch.
options.feedback: Complaining to others pulls people into sides and does not reach the person who can change the situation.

exercises.why: Timing is part of the message. Cool down first, choose a private setting, and speak to the person directly with facts and impact. Public replies and gossip escalate, and silence leaves the issue unresolved.

exercises.prompt: Open a difficult conversation with a teammate who has missed deadlines, and listen to find out what is really happening.
exercises.setup: You lead a small group building a college project. Teammate Vikram has missed two merge deadlines this week and you stayed up late to fix the build. You have asked for ten minutes in a quiet corner. You want to fix the pattern and keep a good relationship.

turns.they: Okay, you wanted to talk? Is it about the build again?

options.text: Yes. You always miss deadlines and I am tired of covering for you.
options.feedback: 'Always' and a complaint put him on the defensive straight away.
options.reply: Covering for me? I have been working as hard as anyone. This is unfair.

options.text: I want the demo to go well. Your module was not merged by Friday or Monday, and I fixed the build late at night, which stressed me. Can you tell me what got in the way?
options.feedback: Shared purpose, specific facts, impact as an I-statement, and an open invitation.
options.reply: Honestly, the API contract changed on Thursday night, and I had to redo my endpoints. I did not want to bother you.

options.text: No, it is nothing serious. Let us just carry on.
options.feedback: Backing out wastes the chance to talk and the pattern will probably repeat.
options.reply: Okay, good. I thought there was a problem.

turns.they: I redid the endpoints Friday, then my laptop crashed on Monday, and I lost some work.

options.text: Ah, so the contract changed late, and then your laptop crashed and you lost work. That is a rough week. Did you tell anyone?
options.feedback: You paraphrase, acknowledge the difficulty and ask a gentle question about the gap.
options.reply: No, I did not. I thought I could catch up quietly. I should have told you.

options.text: Everybody has problems. You should have planned better.
options.feedback: Dismissing the explanation closes him down and ignores the new facts.
options.reply: Right. Sure. I will try harder then.

options.text: That is unlucky. Next time just message me.
options.feedback: Reasonable advice, but you skipped acknowledging his situation and asking what he needs.

turns.they: I will tell you earlier next time. I also feel I get tasks with no notice, so I cannot plan.

options.text: Thanks for saying that. Let us agree: I will post tasks by Monday morning, and you will message me the same day if something blocks you. Does that work?
options.feedback: You accept his point, offer your part, and make a clear mutual agreement.
options.reply: Yes, that works. And I will push my code to a branch daily so nothing is lost.

options.text: That is not true. I always post the tasks on time.
options.feedback: Contradicting him after a good conversation spoils the progress and uses 'always' again.
options.reply: Fine. I will not argue about it.

options.text: Okay, let us see how it goes.
options.feedback: Open-ended; without a specific agreement the same problem is likely to return.

exercises.why: A strong conversation opens with shared purpose, facts and an I-statement, then listens: the real cause (a late contract change and a crash) only appeared because the learner asked and paraphrased. The close turns both sides' points into one clear agreement.

exercises.prompt: Situation: a teammate, Pooja, has twice presented your analysis in team meetings without mentioning your name. You feel upset and want to talk to her. Write (1) the fact, story and feeling layers in one line each, and (2) a four-part opening script (shared purpose, observation, impact as an I-statement, invitation) of 4 to 6 sentences in total.

descriptors.0: The layers are missing or mixed together.
descriptors.1: Only one or two layers are given, or the fact contains judgement.
descriptors.2: All three layers are given but the fact still contains words like 'always' or 'stole'.
descriptors.3: A neutral observable fact, a clearly labelled story with an alternative explanation, and a named feeling.

descriptors.1: One or two of the four parts are present.
descriptors.2: Three parts are present, or all four with one unclear.
descriptors.3: All four parts are clearly present and in a natural order.

descriptors.0: Accuses, uses labels such as 'thief' or 'selfish'.
descriptors.1: Mostly neutral but contains 'always', 'never' or a verdict.
descriptors.2: Neutral but the impact is not stated as an I-statement.
descriptors.3: Neutral throughout, with a true I-statement and an open question.

exercises.modelAnswer:
Fact: in the last two team meetings, Pooja presented my analysis without naming me. Story: she wanted the credit (but she may simply have forgotten, or been nervous). Feeling: I feel hurt and a bit invisible.

Opening: 'I want us to keep working well together. In the last two meetings, the analysis I prepared was presented without my name, and I felt overlooked because I had spent a weekend on it. Could you tell me how you saw it, and could we agree to credit each other's work in meetings?'
exercises.guidance: Strong answers keep the fact camera-like ('presented without my name'), label the story as a guess and offer another explanation, and speak the impact from the first person. A common mistake is to write 'she stole my work' as the fact; that is a story. Another is to finish with a demand rather than an invitation. Compare with the model answer, and score each criterion honestly.

task.title: Prepare and script one real conversation
task.brief: Choose something you have been avoiding saying to someone, and prepare it using facts, story, feeling and the opening script.
steps: Pick one small, real issue you have been avoiding with a friend, classmate, family member or colleague. Do not pick a very painful one for a first attempt.
Write the fact, the story, the feeling and your purpose in one line each.
Write a four-part opening: shared purpose, observation, impact as an I-statement, invitation.
Choose a time and place and write the sentence you will use to ask permission to talk.
Say the script aloud twice. If it is safe and sensible, have the conversation within the week.
checklist: I wrote fact, story, feeling and purpose separately
My observation contains no 'always', 'never' or labels
My impact line is a true I-statement
I chose a private time and place
task.evidencePrompt: Write your four-part opening script exactly as you plan to say it.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a fact rather than a story?
options: He does not care about the team.
He was careless with the report.
The report was submitted two days after the deadline.
He is trying to make me look bad.
quiz.why: A camera could record the submission date. Not caring, carelessness and bad intentions are interpretations of the facts, which may be wrong.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of the 'shared purpose' part of an opening script?
options: To soften the person before the real criticism
To show that you are both working towards the same goal, which lowers defensiveness
To avoid mentioning the actual problem
To prove that you are right
quiz.why: A shared purpose signals that you are on the same side of the problem. It is not a sandwich to hide the criticism, and it does not replace stating the issue.

quiz.prompt: Repeating back in your own words what you heard, such as 'So the contract changed late on Thursday?', is called what? (one word)
quiz.why: Paraphrasing shows you listened and corrects misunderstandings early. It is different from agreeing: you are checking, not conceding.

quiz.prompt: Which is the best way to start a difficult talk with a colleague?
options: Raise it in front of the team so everyone hears
Message at midnight when you are most upset
Ask 'Is now a good time? I would like ten minutes about the demo build', and meet privately
Wait three months until it stops mattering
quiz.why: Asking permission, naming the subject and choosing a private setting avoids ambush and defensiveness. Public or late-night timing escalates, and waiting for months lets resentment grow.

bank.prompt: Which sentence best turns the complaint 'You never listen to my ideas in meetings' into an I-statement?
options: I think you are ignoring me on purpose.
In Monday's meeting my suggestion was not discussed, and I felt overlooked. I would like us to hear each person's idea before deciding.
It seems nobody here respects my ideas.
bank.why: It names one specific moment, states the personal impact and makes a request. The others assign motives, give an order or generalise to everyone.

bank.prompt: While you describe a problem, the other person says, 'You are wrong, I told you the date.' What is the best next step?
options: Raise your voice to be heard
Say 'Okay, let me check what I missed. You are saying you told me the date. When was that?' and listen
Prove them wrong with a list of past mistakes
bank.why: Paraphrasing and asking when keeps you in fact-finding mode and may reveal a miscommunication. Matching anger, leaving or bringing up past mistakes escalates the conflict.

bank.prompt: In the facts, story, feelings model, 'He is deliberately ignoring me' is which layer? (one word)
bank.why: It is an interpretation of why something happened. The fact would be: 'I sent three messages and received no reply.'

cards.front: What three layers do you separate before a difficult conversation?
cards.back: Facts (what a camera records), story (your interpretation) and feelings. Lead with facts, state feelings briefly, and offer the story only as a question.

cards.front: What is the four-part opening script?
cards.back: Shared purpose, observation (fact), impact as an I-statement, invitation to hear their side. Avoid 'always', 'never' and labels.

cards.front: How should you choose the timing of a difficult talk?
cards.back: After you have cooled down, in private, and with permission: 'Is now a good time? It is about the demo build.' Pause, but do not avoid forever.

cards.front: What are the three listening moves before you respond?
cards.back: Ask an open question, paraphrase what you heard, and acknowledge the feeling. Acknowledging is not agreeing. Then give your view.

conflict-2.reflection: Which conversation are you currently avoiding, and what is the first sentence, containing only a fact and an I-statement, that you could say to begin it?

keyPoints: Separate facts, story and feelings before you speak.
Open with shared purpose, observation, impact and invitation.
An I-statement describes your experience and makes a request.
Choose a private, calm moment and ask permission.
Paraphrase and acknowledge before you respond.
revision.redo: Take one complaint you have about someone and rewrite it as a fact, an I-statement and a request in three sentences.

conflict-3.title: Resolving and Repairing
conflict-3.summary: Move from positions to interests, generate options, agree clearly, apologise and repair, and know when to involve a neutral third party.
objectives: Separate positions from interests and generate options.
Close a conflict with a specific, checkable agreement.
Offer an effective apology and know when to bring in a neutral third party.

explanation.heading: Positions and interests
explanation.body:
A **position** is what someone says they want: "I want the window seat", "We must release on Friday". An **interest** is the reason behind it: comfort, a deadline, fear of blame, respect. Two positions can clash while the interests are compatible. Two students quarrel over one room for group study: one wants it at 5 pm, the other at 6 pm. Asking why reveals that one has a bus at 6:30 and the other has a lab until 5:30. Both interests are met by starting at 5:30.

To find interests ask: "What matters most to you about this?" and "What are you worried might happen?" Then share your own interests, not only your demand.

explanation.heading: Options and agreements
explanation.body: Once interests are on the table, generate **options** before choosing. Brainstorm without judging, then evaluate against both sides' interests and fair criteria such as cost, time and precedent. Aim for options that create value, such as trading what is cheap for you and valuable for them. When you choose, make the **agreement** specific: who does what, by when, how you will check, and what happens if it slips. "We will communicate better" is not an agreement; "I will send the status update every Monday by 10 am and you will reply by Tuesday" is. Write it down and share it. Review after one or two weeks.

explanation.heading: Apology and repair
explanation.body: When your actions harmed someone, repair matters as much as the solution. A good apology has five parts: **acknowledge** what you did specifically, **recognise** the impact on them, take **responsibility** without excuses, **express regret** sincerely and offer **repair** with a change of behaviour. Example: "I missed the review deadline and you had to stay late. That was my fault. I am sorry. I will send updates two days early and check with you on Wednesday." Avoid "I am sorry if you were hurt" and "but" sentences, which turn apologies into defences. Then follow through; repaired trust is built by behaviour afterwards.

explanation.heading: When to involve a third party
explanation.body: Some conflicts stall: emotions are too high, power is unequal or the issue involves rules, safety or harassment. A **neutral third party**, such as a mentor, teacher, HR representative or trusted senior, can help. Before going to them, try a direct conversation first unless safety is at risk. Ask the other person: "Would it help to bring in someone neutral?" Present facts, not accusations, and state what you want from the helper: listening, mediating or deciding. For harassment, discrimination or safety concerns, go straight to the proper channel. Using a third party is a sign of maturity, not failure.

examples.title: Interests revealed
examples.body: Two teammates both want to demo first. Asking why shows that Dev has an exam the next day and Mira wants to show her feature to the manager who leaves early. They schedule Dev first, but Mira presents to the manager separately beforehand.
examples.takeaway: Interests allowed both needs to be met.

examples.title: A specific agreement
examples.body: After disputes about shared files, a team agrees: "Every Friday at 4 pm, each member uploads work to the shared folder with the date in the file name. Aman checks and posts a summary." They review in two weeks.
examples.takeaway: Specific tasks and timing make an agreement checkable.

exercises.prompt: Which is an interest rather than a position?
options: I need time to prepare before the manager review.
I want the meeting on Monday.
exercises.why: It describes the underlying need.

exercises.prompt: A good apology offers ____ by changing future behaviour. (one word)
exercises.why: Repair shows that the apology is real.

exercises.prompt: Two roommates argue about noise at night: one studies late and the other sleeps early. Write each person's likely interests, three options and one specific agreement.

descriptors.3: Clear interests for both.
Three varied options.
Who, what, when and a review.

exercises.modelAnswer: Interests: one needs quiet focus for late study; the other needs seven hours of sleep before an early class. Options: study in the library until 11 pm; use headphones and a desk lamp after 11; swap study times on alternate days. Agreement: from Monday, the late student studies in the library until 11 pm on weekdays, uses headphones after that and we review on Sunday after two weeks.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers show different interests, several options and a concrete agreement with a review date.

exercises.prompt: A senior repeatedly makes personal comments that make you uncomfortable, and direct talk has not helped. What is best?

options.text: Keep quiet and hope it stops.
options.feedback: Silence may allow harm to continue.

options.text: Use the proper channel such as a mentor or HR and record the incidents with dates.
options.feedback: Using proper channels protects you.

options.text: Reply with insults.
options.feedback: Insults escalate and weaken your case.

options.text: Resign from the job immediately.
options.feedback: Leaving may be a choice later, but report first.

exercises.why: Serious misconduct needs the proper channel.

task.title: Resolve one conflict
task.brief: Apply interests, options and a specific agreement to a real or realistic conflict.
steps: Write the conflict in two sentences.
List the position and interests of each side.
Brainstorm three options and pick one.
Write a specific agreement with names, dates and a review.
task.evidencePrompt: Write the interests of both sides and your agreement.

quiz.prompt: Asking "What matters most to you about this?" helps to find:
quiz.why: It reveals the need behind the demand.

quiz.prompt: A good agreement includes:
options: Who does what by when and how it is checked
quiz.why: Specific and checkable agreements hold.

quiz.prompt: Which apology is best?
options: I missed the deadline; I am sorry and will send updates early.
Sorry but you did not remind me.
quiz.why: It names the act, takes responsibility and offers repair.

quiz.prompt: A neutral person who helps resolve a conflict is called a ____ party. (one word)
quiz.why: Third parties include mentors, teachers or HR.

bank.prompt: Two positions that clash may have:
bank.why: Underlying interests may be compatible.

bank.prompt: Before choosing a solution you should:
bank.why: Options widen the possibilities.

bank.prompt: For harassment or safety concerns you should:
bank.why: Serious matters need formal reporting.

cards.back: A position is what someone demands; an interest is the need or worry behind it.
Who does what by when, how it will be checked and a review date.
Acknowledge, recognise impact, take responsibility, express regret, offer repair.

cards.front: When to involve a third party?
cards.back: When emotions or power gaps block progress or when safety or harassment is involved.

conflict-3.reflection: Think of a recent disagreement. What were the interests behind each position, and what option did you miss?

keyPoints: Interests lie behind positions.
Generate options before choosing.
Write specific agreements.
Apologise with repair and use third parties wisely.
revision.redo: Rewrite a past conflict resolution using interests and a specific agreement.

conflict-4.title: Conflict in Teams and Remote Work
conflict-4.summary: Handle written conflict, feedback disputes and prevention with working agreements and escalation paths for teams and remote work.
objectives: Defuse a tense written exchange and know when to switch to a call.
Handle a feedback dispute constructively.
Create team working agreements and an escalation path.

explanation.heading: Why remote conflict is harder
explanation.body: In person, tone of voice, facial expressions and body language soften words. In chat and email these signals disappear, so neutral messages feel cold and short ones feel rude. Time zones, delays and unclear ownership add friction. Remote and hybrid teams therefore need deliberate habits for communication and conflict, because small misunderstandings can grow into resentment before anyone notices.

explanation.heading: Handling written conflict
explanation.body: When a message upsets you, follow four steps. **Pause**: do not reply for at least ten minutes. **Assume good intent** as a hypothesis, and consider other readings, such as hurry or stress. **Clarify** with a question: "I read this as a criticism of my delivery; is that what you meant?" **Switch medium** when the thread has gone back and forth three times, or emotions are high: propose a five-minute call and then confirm decisions in writing. Write replies that are short, factual and polite: facts, impact, request. Avoid capital letters, sarcasm and copying senior people to pressure someone. Never send an angry message and hope to retract it. If you must vent, write the angry draft in a notes file, wait, then delete it and write the calm version. Remember that screenshots travel: assume anything you type could be read by your manager, the client and the whole team.

explanation.heading: Feedback disputes
explanation.body: Disagreements about feedback are common: "This work is not good enough" versus "I followed the brief". Handle them by separating three things: **facts** (what was asked, what was delivered), **standards** (what good looks like) and **feelings** (how it landed). Ask for specific examples and the criteria used. State your view with evidence: "The brief said X; I delivered X. If the expectation was Y, can we agree on that for the next version?" Agree on the next step and write the acceptance criteria. If feedback feels unfair repeatedly, discuss with your manager as a pattern, using examples, not as a complaint about a person.

explanation.heading: Prevention and escalation
explanation.body: The best conflict management is prevention. A **working agreement** is a short document the team writes together: response times, core hours, meeting rules, how decisions are made, how to give feedback and how disagreements are raised. Review it monthly. Add an **escalation path** that everyone knows: first talk directly, then involve the team lead, then the manager or HR, with time limits such as two working days at each step. Clear paths prevent both silence and public blow-ups. Escalating is not tattling; it is using the process the team agreed.

examples.title: Defusing a thread
examples.body: A colleague writes, "Why was this not tested?" Instead of replying defensively, Tara waits, then writes: "I tested the main flow. Which case were you concerned about? Happy to jump on a five-minute call." The tension drops.
examples.takeaway: Pause, clarify and move to a call.

examples.title: A working agreement
examples.body: A four-person remote team writes: reply to direct messages within four working hours, core hours 11 to 4, decisions recorded in the project doc, disagreements raised first with the person, then the lead. Conflicts fall sharply in the next sprint.
examples.takeaway: Agreed rules reduce guesswork and friction.

exercises.prompt: What should you do first when an upsetting message arrives?
exercises.why: A pause prevents regret.

exercises.prompt: A team ____ agreement sets response times and meeting rules. (one word)
exercises.why: Working agreements prevent friction by making rules explicit.

exercises.prompt: A teammate writes in the group chat: "Did you even read the requirements?" Write your reply to them (short, calm, with a clarifying question and an offer to talk) and say why you chose that approach.

descriptors.3: Calm and professional.
Specific question.

rubric.label: Offer to switch medium and reason

descriptors.3: Offer plus reason.

exercises.modelAnswer: Reply: "I read the requirements and built section 1 to 3. Which part do you feel I missed? I can show my notes in a quick five-minute call if easier." Reason: asking a question avoids defending, a call prevents tone problems and I will confirm decisions in writing afterward.
exercises.guidance: Strong replies stay calm, ask what was meant and propose a call, then confirm in writing. Avoid sarcasm and long justifications.

exercises.prompt: You and a colleague disagree about task ownership and have not resolved it after two direct talks. What is next?

options.text: Complain about them publicly.
options.feedback: Public blame damages the team.

options.text: Follow the agreed path: bring the lead in with facts and propose options.
options.feedback: Using the agreed path keeps it fair.

options.text: Do their part silently.
options.feedback: This quietly builds resentment later.

options.text: Ignore the issue.
options.feedback: Unresolved ownership grows worse.

exercises.why: Escalate through the agreed path with facts.

task.title: Draft a working agreement
task.brief: Write a one-page working agreement and escalation path for a real or imagined team.
steps: List five rules covering response time, core hours, meetings, decisions and feedback.
Write a three-step escalation path with time limits.
Write a calm reply to a tense message using the four steps.
Share the draft with one teammate and ask for a change.
task.evidencePrompt: Write your five rules and your escalation path.

quiz.prompt: When should you switch from chat to a call?
options: When the thread goes back and forth or emotions are high
quiz.why: Calls prevent tone-based misunderstanding.

quiz.prompt: In a feedback dispute, separate:
quiz.why: Separating these makes the discussion clear.

quiz.prompt: Why review a working agreement monthly?
options: To keep rules fit for the team
quiz.why: Teams change, so rules need updates.

quiz.prompt: Escalating through an agreed path is not ____. (one word)
quiz.why: It is using a process the team agreed.

bank.prompt: A better message style in conflict is:
bank.why: Facts, impact and a request keep it constructive.

bank.prompt: To resolve a feedback dispute, ask for:
bank.why: Examples and criteria make feedback usable.

bank.prompt: A good escalation path has:
bank.why: Clear steps and limits prevent delay.

cards.back: Pause, assume good intent, clarify, switch to a call when needed.
Separate facts, standards and feelings; ask for examples; agree acceptance criteria.

cards.front: What goes in a working agreement?
cards.back: Response times, core hours, meeting rules, decision method, feedback and disagreement rules.
Talk directly, then team lead, then manager or HR, with time limits at each step.

conflict-4.reflection: Recall a chat message that you misread. What would have happened if you had paused and asked a clarifying question?

keyPoints: Text removes tone, so pause and clarify.
Move heated threads to a call.
Separate facts, standards and feelings.
Prevent conflict with agreements and escalation paths.

creativity-1.title: Generating Ideas
creativity-1.summary: Separate idea generation from judging, aim for quantity, use SCAMPER and constraints, and set idea quotas.
objectives: Explain divergent and convergent thinking and keep them apart.
Generate many ideas using SCAMPER and constraints.
Use an idea quota to push past obvious answers.

explanation.heading: Two kinds of thinking
explanation.body:
Creative work uses two modes. **Divergent thinking** opens up possibilities: many ideas, wild ones included, no judging. **Convergent thinking** narrows: compare, test and choose. Problems begin when both run together. If you criticise each idea as it appears, you stop after two or three safe ones. The rule is simple: generate first, judge later, and never in the same breath.

Schedule them separately. Spend ten minutes only producing ideas, then take a break, then spend ten minutes selecting. Even a small gap protects the first stage from your inner critic.

explanation.heading: Quantity first
explanation.body: The first ideas that come to mind are usually the obvious ones that everybody else has too. Better ideas often appear after the obvious ones are exhausted, so aim for **quantity**. Set a target, for example 20 ideas in 10 minutes, and keep writing when it feels empty. Write short phrases, not essays. Include silly or impossible ideas; they often contain a usable part. Do not edit while writing. If you are working in a group, let everyone write alone first, then share, so that loud voices do not steer the list.

explanation.heading: The SCAMPER method
explanation.body:
**SCAMPER** is a set of prompts for changing something that already exists. **S**ubstitute: what could replace a part? **C**ombine: what could be merged? **A**dapt: what can be borrowed from elsewhere? **M**odify: change size, shape or frequency. **P**ut to another use: who else could use this? **E**liminate: what can be removed? **R**earrange or reverse: change order or roles.

Apply it to a student attendance app: Combine attendance with timetable reminders; Eliminate manual roll calls by using a QR code; Put to another use: track lab equipment returns; Reverse: let students mark teachers' lateness. One familiar object, seven fresh directions.

explanation.heading: Constraints and quotas
explanation.body:
It seems odd, but limits improve creativity. A blank page offers too many options, while a constraint such as "design a study tool using only paper and no more than three steps" forces new thinking. Try limits on cost, time, materials or words.

An **idea quota** works the same way: "five ideas every morning before checking my phone". Over a month that is 150 ideas, and even a few useful ones change your work. Keep an idea list so that none are lost. Treat the quota as practice for the habit, not a test of quality. The more you practise producing, the less frightening an empty page becomes.

examples.title: SCAMPER on a notebook
examples.body: Substitute paper with a tablet; combine with a planner; adapt a ledger layout; modify to pocket size; put to another use as a bug log; eliminate lines; reverse so the back page is the index. Five minutes gave seven concepts, two of them new.
examples.takeaway: A framework gives you somewhere to start when your mind is blank.

examples.title: Constraint at work
examples.body: Asked to improve onboarding, Neha limits herself to "one page, no meeting". Ideas: a checklist, a welcome video, a buddy list. Without limits she had only suggested more meetings.
examples.takeaway: Constraints push you off the obvious path.

exercises.prompt: Which is divergent thinking?
exercises.why: Divergent thinking opens possibilities without judging.

exercises.prompt: In SCAMPER, the letter E stands for ____. (one word)
exercises.why: E means eliminate: what can you remove?

exercises.prompt: Pick an everyday object (for example a water bottle or a to-do list app). Write at least six ideas using SCAMPER prompts, labelling each with its letter.

descriptors.3: Six or more.
Five or more prompts.
Several unusual but plausible.

exercises.modelAnswer: Water bottle. S: substitute the cap with a filter. C: combine with a reminder light that glows each hour. A: adapt a cycling bottle clip for backpacks. M: make it collapsible. P: reuse as a desk pen holder. E: eliminate the label to save ink. R: reverse the flow so the bottle fills from the bottom.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers label each idea with its SCAMPER letter and include some unusual but plausible options. Avoid stopping after the first three.

exercises.prompt: In a group brainstorm someone says "That will never work" to your first idea. What helps most?

options.text: Stop sharing ideas.
options.feedback: This ends idea generation completely.

options.text: Suggest the group separate generating from judging and continue listing.
options.feedback: It protects the divergent stage.

options.text: Argue until they agree.
options.feedback: Arguing mixes the two stages.

options.text: Switch to the safest idea.
options.feedback: Safe ideas are usually obvious.

exercises.why: Keep generation and evaluation separate.

task.title: Ten-minute idea sprint
task.brief: Generate 20 ideas on a real problem and then choose three.
steps: Write the problem as a question.
Set a timer for ten minutes and list 20 ideas without judging.
Use two SCAMPER prompts if you get stuck.
After a break, mark your three best ideas and say why.
checklist: I did not judge while writing
I picked three and gave reasons
task.evidencePrompt: Write your problem and your three best ideas.

quiz.prompt: Judging every idea as it appears will:
quiz.why: Early judging blocks divergent thinking.

quiz.prompt: Why aim for quantity first?
options: Obvious ideas come first and better ones later
quiz.why: Better ideas appear after the obvious ones.

quiz.prompt: Which is a SCAMPER prompt?
quiz.why: Combine is the C in SCAMPER.

quiz.why: Constraints focus thinking and push beyond the obvious.

bank.prompt: Convergent thinking is for:

bank.prompt: An idea quota of five a day builds:
bank.why: Regular practice builds the idea habit.

bank.prompt: The R in SCAMPER means:
bank.why: Rearrange or reverse changes order or roles.

cards.back: Divergent opens many options without judging; convergent narrows, compares and chooses.
Obvious ideas come first; better ones come after you push past them.
Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate, Rearrange/Reverse.

creativity-2.title: Reframing and Connecting
creativity-2.summary: Reframe problems with How Might We questions, analogies, random input and inversion, and combine unrelated ideas.
objectives: Turn a problem into several How Might We questions.
Use analogies and random input to find new angles.
Use inversion to expose hidden assumptions.

explanation.heading: The question shapes the answers
explanation.body:
A problem stated one way allows only a few solutions. "How do we stop students coming late?" leads to penalties. Reframed as "How might we make the first ten minutes worth arriving for?", it opens up quizzes, announcements and short activities. Creativity often begins with a better question rather than a better answer.

Reframing is a skill you can practise. Always ask yourself whether the problem is stated too narrowly, whether it describes a symptom rather than a cause and whether it assumes one particular solution.

explanation.heading: How Might We questions
explanation.body:
A **How Might We (HMW)** question has three parts: "How" suggests an answer exists, "Might" allows many options, "We" shares ownership. Good HMW questions are neither too broad ("How might we fix education?") nor too narrow ("How might we add a button on page 3?"). Take one problem and write five or more HMWs by changing the focus: the user, the cause, the moment, the opposite and the emotion. Choose one and generate ideas for it.

Example: "Students forget revision." HMWs: How might we make revision part of their daily routine? How might we make forgetting visible before the exam? How might we make revising a social activity?

explanation.heading: Analogies and random input
explanation.body: An **analogy** borrows a solution from another field. How does a hospital triage emergencies? Could a help desk use the same colour system? How does a gym keep people returning? Could a study app do the same? Ask "Who has already solved a similar problem?" The **random input** technique adds a surprise: pick a random word, such as "umbrella", and force connections. An umbrella protects, folds, is shared in rain. For a software release this could suggest a rollback "cover", a compact deployment kit and shared rollback ownership. Most connections will be weak, but one or two can be useful.

explanation.heading: Inversion and combining
explanation.body:
**Inversion** flips the problem: instead of "How can we make users love our app?" ask "How could we make users hate it?" The list (slow loading, confusing menus, constant pop-ups) is easy to produce, and reversing it yields a quality checklist. Inversion also exposes assumptions: "Customers must visit a shop." What if the shop visits them?

**Combining** unrelated ideas creates new ones: a map and a diary became a travel journal app; a camera and a phone became the smartphone. List two columns of unrelated things, such as tools and places, and pair items at random. Ask what each pair could become and keep the interesting ones.

examples.title: HMW in practice
examples.body: Problem: "Team meetings run too long". HMWs: How might we make decisions before meetings? How might we make every minute visible? How might we make standing the default? The team chose the second and added a visible timer.
examples.takeaway: Reframing creates choices that the original problem hid.

examples.title: Inversion for quality
examples.body: To improve a college website, students listed how to make it worst: hide the timetable, ask for login three times, use tiny fonts. Reversing gave a five-point improvement list.
examples.takeaway: Listing failures is easy and reveals what to protect.

exercises.prompt: Which is a good How Might We question?
options: How might we make the first ten minutes of class worth attending?
exercises.why: It is open, specific and focuses on one angle.

exercises.prompt: Asking "How could we make this fail?" is called ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Inversion flips the problem to reveal assumptions.

exercises.prompt: Take the problem "People in my hostel waste a lot of food." Write five different How Might We questions that each change the focus (user, cause, moment, emotion, opposite).

descriptors.3: Five.
Clearly different angles.
All open and well sized.

exercises.modelAnswer: How might we help students order only what they will eat? How might we make leftovers valuable to someone else? How might we show the cost of waste at the moment of serving? How might we make taking small portions feel normal? How might we make wasting food harder than saving it?
exercises.guidance: Good HMWs differ in angle (user, cause, moment, emotion, opposite), stay open and avoid naming the solution.

exercises.prompt: Your college library queue is long. Which approach uses analogy well?

options.text: Add more chairs.
options.feedback: It treats a symptom only.

options.text: Look at how bakeries or railway counters manage queues and borrow one idea.
options.feedback: Borrowing from similar problems is analogy.

options.text: Remove the library.
options.feedback: This ignores the goal.

options.text: Ask everyone to arrive early.
options.feedback: It shifts rather than solves the problem.

exercises.why: Look to other fields that solved a similar problem.

task.title: Reframe a real problem
task.brief: Take one real problem and run HMW, inversion and a random word on it.
steps: Write the problem in one sentence.
Write five HMW questions and pick one.
List ten ways to make the problem worse, then reverse them.
Add a random word and write two connections.
task.evidencePrompt: Write your chosen HMW and the best idea from inversion.

quiz.prompt: In HMW, the word "might" signals:
quiz.why: Might allows many possibilities.

quiz.prompt: An analogy borrows:
quiz.why: Analogy transfers solutions across fields.

quiz.prompt: Why is inversion useful?
options: It is quick and exposes assumptions
quiz.why: Listing failures is easy and reveals what to fix.

quiz.prompt: Pairing two unrelated items to see what they become is called ____ ideas. (one word)
quiz.why: Combining unrelated ideas can create something new.

bank.prompt: An HMW that is too narrow is:
options: How might we add a button on page 3?
How might we help students revise?
bank.why: It names a solution already.

bank.prompt: Random input works by:
options: Forcing connections to a random word
bank.why: The random word triggers new links.

bank.prompt: Reversing a list of ways to fail gives:
bank.why: The opposites become standards.

cards.back: How (answer exists), Might (many options), We (shared ownership); not too broad or narrow.
Who has already solved a similar problem in another field?
Ask how to make it fail, list answers, reverse them into guidelines.
List two unrelated columns, pair items randomly, keep interesting combinations.

creativity-2.reflection: Which problem in your life is stated in a way that already assumes a solution?

keyPoints: A better question opens better answers.
HMW questions reframe from many angles.
Analogy and random input import new ideas.
Inversion exposes assumptions.

creativity-3.title: Developing and Testing Ideas
creativity-3.summary: Select ideas with criteria, build quick prototypes, gather feedback, kill weak ideas and finish creative work.
objectives: Select ideas using clear criteria.
Build a quick prototype and run a feedback loop.
Decide when to kill an idea and how to finish what you start.

explanation.heading: Choosing what to develop
explanation.body: After generating many ideas you must choose. Avoid choosing by gut alone, or by the loudest voice. Use two or three **criteria**, such as impact, effort and risk, and give each idea a score from one to five. A simple grid helps: high impact and low effort first. Also look for the idea you can test cheaply, not the one that sounds best. Choose one or two to develop; trying to develop ten means finishing none. Be honest about your own constraints too: a brilliant idea that needs six months and a team is the wrong idea for a student with a free weekend. Write down why each rejected idea lost, so you can revisit it later when your skills or time have changed.

explanation.heading: Quick prototypes
explanation.body: A **prototype** is the cheapest version that lets you learn something. It does not need to work perfectly. For an app idea it could be paper screens, a clickable mock-up or a one-page demo; for a service idea, a role-play; for a business idea, a simple sign-up page to see if anyone cares. Ask before building: "What is the main thing I need to find out?" and build only enough to answer that. Aim to build the first version in hours or days, not weeks. Early prototypes are meant to be thrown away.

explanation.heading: Feedback loops
explanation.body: Show the prototype to three to five real users. Do not explain too much; watch what they do. Ask open questions: "What did you expect to happen?" "What was confusing?" "What would you change?" Avoid asking "Do you like it?", which produces polite answers. Record patterns, not single opinions: if three of five people get stuck at the same point, fix that. Then improve and test again. Each loop of **build, show, learn** should be short. Welcome negative feedback; it is the cheapest information you will ever get.

explanation.heading: Killing ideas and finishing
explanation.body: Not every idea deserves completion. Set **kill criteria** before you start: "If fewer than three of ten people want this after two weeks, I will stop." Dropping a weak idea early frees time for better ones; it is not failure. For ideas that survive, finish. Many creative projects die at 80 per cent. Counter this by defining "done" in advance, setting a deadline, shrinking the scope and shipping a rough version. A finished imperfect project teaches more than a perfect unfinished one. Share it publicly, then improve. Sharing creates gentle accountability and gives you feedback from people you did not expect, which often points to the next version.

examples.title: Scoring ideas
examples.body: Three app ideas for campus: a notes exchange, a canteen queue tracker and a bus alert. Scores for impact, effort and risk give the bus alert 13/15. The team builds it first.
examples.takeaway: Criteria make choices visible and fair.

examples.title: A fast prototype
examples.body: Instead of building a full app, Imran makes a WhatsApp group where he posts bus times by hand for a week. Fifty students join, proving demand before any code.
examples.takeaway: The cheapest test can use no technology.

exercises.prompt: A sensible way to select ideas is to:
exercises.why: Criteria make selection fair and visible.

exercises.prompt: A prototype is the ____ version that lets you learn something. (one word)
exercises.why: Prototypes are cheap on purpose.

exercises.prompt: Choose a creative idea. Describe the prototype you would build in one day, whom you would show it to, three open questions you would ask, and one kill criterion.

descriptors.3: Cheap and tests the key question.
Three open questions.
Specific number and time.

exercises.modelAnswer: Idea: a daily SQL practice bot for the class group. Prototype: a shared document with one question posted each day for a week. Show to ten classmates. Questions: What did you expect to see? What stopped you from trying? What would make you return? Kill criterion: if fewer than four people answer on at least three days, I stop.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers use a cheap prototype, open questions and a numeric kill criterion with a deadline.

exercises.prompt: Your side project is 80% done, you now have a new exciting idea. What is best?

options.text: Switch immediately to the new idea.
options.feedback: This repeats the pattern of unfinished work.

options.text: Write the new idea down, finish a rough version of the current project, then decide.
options.feedback: Capture and finish; then choose.

options.text: Abandon both projects.
options.feedback: This wastes the progress.

options.text: Do both at once.
options.feedback: Splitting attention slows both.

exercises.why: Capture new ideas but finish what you started.

task.title: Prototype and test
task.brief: Build a one-day prototype of one idea and test with three people.
steps: Score three ideas on impact, effort and risk and pick one.
Write the key question your prototype must answer.
Build the cheapest version in one day.
Show it to three people, record patterns and decide: continue, change or kill.
task.evidencePrompt: Write your key question, what three people said and your decision.

quiz.prompt: Which pair of criteria is useful?
quiz.why: Impact and effort help prioritise.

quiz.prompt: Before prototyping, ask:
options: What is the main thing I need to find out?
quiz.why: Build only enough to answer the key question.

quiz.prompt: A better feedback question is:
options: What did you expect to happen?
quiz.why: Open questions reveal real reactions.

quiz.prompt: Rules that tell you when to stop an idea are called ____ criteria. (one word)
quiz.why: Kill criteria are set in advance.

bank.prompt: Developing ten ideas at once usually results in:
bank.why: Focus is needed to finish.

bank.prompt: Three of five users stumble at one step. You should:
bank.why: Patterns matter more than single opinions.

bank.prompt: Defining "done" in advance helps:
bank.why: A clear finish line prevents drifting.

cards.back: Score against two or three criteria such as impact, effort and risk; choose one or two.
The cheapest version that answers your key question; built in hours or days and thrown away.
Build, show three to five people, watch and ask open questions, learn patterns, repeat.
Set kill criteria and a definition of done; shrink scope; ship a rough version.

creativity-3.reflection: Which of your unfinished projects deserves a kill decision, and which deserves to be finished this week?

Prototype ideas cheaply.
Learn from patterns in feedback.
Kill weak ideas and finish the rest.

creativity-4.title: A Creative Practice
creativity-4.summary: Build a capture system, use incubation and routines, beat blocks and complete a small portfolio project.
objectives: Set up a capture system for ideas.
Use incubation, routines and blocks-breakers.
Plan a small portfolio project with a finish date.

explanation.heading: Creativity as a habit
explanation.body: Creative people are not waiting for lightning; they have habits that make ideas likely and catch them when they come. A creative practice has four parts: capture ideas, give them time to develop, keep going when stuck and produce visible work. This lesson turns the techniques you have learned into a routine you can keep for years.

explanation.heading: Capture system
explanation.body: Ideas are fragile. You have a thought in the shower and it is gone by breakfast. A **capture system** is one place, always within reach, where every idea goes: a notes app, a pocket notebook or voice memos. Rules: one place only, write it immediately, no editing while capturing. Once a week spend ten minutes reviewing, tagging the promising ones and deleting the rest. Review is what turns a pile of scraps into a resource. Add small context to each note, such as where it came from and why it excited you. A bare note reading "app idea" is useless in a month, while "app idea: queue tracker for the canteen, from waiting 25 minutes today" can be developed immediately.

explanation.heading: Incubation and routines
explanation.body: **Incubation** means stepping away from a problem so that your mind keeps working in the background. Work hard on a problem, then walk, shower, sleep or do something unrelated. Insight often arrives during the break. For this to work you must first immerse yourself in the problem. Pair it with a **routine**: the same time and place each day, a short warm-up and a clear start signal such as making tea. Even 30 minutes daily beats a rare eight-hour session. Protect the slot like an appointment. On low-energy days, do a smaller version, such as five minutes, rather than skipping, because keeping the chain unbroken matters more than the length of the session.

explanation.heading: Beating blocks and building a portfolio
explanation.body:
When stuck, try these: lower the bar ("write the worst version"), change the medium or location, set a five-minute timer, impose a constraint, work on a different part, or show someone a rough draft. Blocks often come from perfectionism and fear of judgement, not lack of ideas.

A **portfolio project** is a small, finished, shareable piece that shows your ability: a mini web app, a case study or a short guide. Keep it small enough to finish in two weeks. Define the audience, the scope and the finish date, build in public view if you can, and write a short note about what you learned. For a student targeting a first job, two or three small finished projects count for more than many half-built ones.

examples.title: A capture habit
examples.body: Kavita keeps a pocket notebook. On Sunday she reviews it, stars three notes and moves two into a project list. One starred note became a college blog series.
examples.takeaway: Capture plus weekly review turns scraps into projects.

examples.title: A small portfolio piece
examples.body: Sameer builds a tiny expense tracker in ten days, deploys it and writes a one-page note about design choices. He adds it to his resume as evidence of finishing.
examples.takeaway: A small finished project is evidence of ability.

exercises.prompt: A good capture system is:
exercises.why: One reliable place prevents losing ideas.

exercises.prompt: Stepping away from a problem so that your mind keeps working on it is called ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Incubation lets background thinking work.

exercises.prompt: Plan a small portfolio project you could finish in two weeks. State what it is, the audience, the scope (what is in and out), the finish date and how you will share it.

descriptors.3: Small with clear in and out.
Specific date and share plan.
Named and linked to the project value.

exercises.modelAnswer: Project: a small SAP ABAP learning log site with ten short posts. Audience: other beginners and recruiters. In scope: ten posts, one summary page. Out of scope: comments and login. Finish date: 28 October. Share: post on LinkedIn and add it to my resume.
exercises.guidance: Strong plans are small, give a date and name where it will be shown. Avoid projects that need months.

exercises.prompt: You have stared at a blank page for twenty minutes. What helps most?

options.text: Wait for inspiration.
options.feedback: Waiting rarely breaks a block.

options.text: Set a five-minute timer and write the worst possible version.
options.feedback: Lowering the bar starts the flow.

options.text: Delete the project.
options.feedback: This avoids the problem.

options.text: Scroll social media.
options.feedback: This only adds distraction.

exercises.why: Lower the bar and start small.

task.title: Set up your practice
task.brief: Create a capture system and plan a small portfolio project.
steps: Choose one capture tool and add ten ideas today.
Schedule a 30-minute daily creative slot at a fixed time.
Plan one small project with scope and a finish date.
Block a weekly ten-minute review.
task.evidencePrompt: Write your tool, slot time and project finish date.

quiz.prompt: Weekly review of captured ideas helps to:
quiz.why: Review selects and develops promising ideas.

quiz.prompt: Incubation works best after:
quiz.why: You must work on the problem first.

quiz.prompt: A common cause of creative blocks is:
quiz.why: Fear of judgement often blocks starting.

quiz.prompt: A portfolio project should be small enough to ____ in about two weeks. (one word)
quiz.why: Finished small projects are better evidence than large unfinished ones.

bank.prompt: Why keep one capture place?
bank.why: One place means ideas are not lost.

bank.prompt: A routine helps creativity by:
bank.why: A routine reduces the effort of starting.

bank.prompt: For a first job, which is stronger?
options: Two or three small finished projects
bank.why: Finished work shows ability.

cards.back: One place, always within reach, write immediately, review weekly.
Immerse in the problem, step away, let background thinking work, return.
Write the worst version, timer for five minutes, change place, add a constraint, show a rough draft.
Small scope, named audience, finish date, share publicly, write what you learned.

creativity-4.reflection: What is the smallest daily creative habit you could keep for a month, and at what time will you do it?

keyPoints: Creativity is a habit.
Capture every idea in one place.
Use incubation and routines.
Finish a small project to show your work.

critical-1.title: Claims, Arguments and Evidence
critical-1.summary: Learn to separate premises from conclusions, weigh different kinds of evidence, and expose the hidden assumptions that hold an argument up.
objectives: Identify the conclusion and premises in a short argument.
Rank common types of evidence by how much weight they deserve.
Find the hidden assumption that an argument depends on.

explanation.heading: An argument is a conclusion plus its reasons
explanation.body:
In everyday talk, an 'argument' is a quarrel. In critical thinking it means something calmer: a **conclusion** (the claim you are asked to accept) supported by one or more **premises** (the reasons or facts offered in its favour). Your first job when you meet any pitch, article or forwarded message is to separate the two.

Look for signal words. Conclusions often follow *therefore, so, hence, which shows that*. Premises often follow *because, since, given that, as*. Take this: 'Our app crashed twice this week, so we should delay the launch.' The conclusion is 'delay the launch'; the premise is 'it crashed twice this week'. Writing the argument out in two lines, premise then conclusion, instantly shows you what must be true for the claim to stand.

Not every sentence is part of an argument. Opinions without reasons ('This framework is terrible') are bare claims, and a claim with no premises gives you nothing to evaluate.

explanation.heading: Not all evidence weighs the same
explanation.body:
Evidence comes in kinds, and a rough ladder helps you judge it. At the bottom are **anecdotes** ('my cousin got placed after that course'). Next come **expert opinion** and **testimonials**, useful when the expert is qualified in that exact area and has no stake in the outcome. Higher are **systematic data**: surveys with decent samples, logged measurements, placement statistics with the method disclosed.
