At the top are **controlled comparisons** where one factor was changed and the rest held constant.

Four quick questions test any piece of evidence. Is it **relevant** to this exact claim? Is it **sufficient**, meaning enough of it? Is it **representative**, or only the best cases? Is the **source reliable**, with the means to know and no reason to bend the truth? A coaching institute that advertises 'our students got 12-lakh packages' fails representativeness if it quietly leaves out the other 95 students.

explanation.heading: Strong versus weak: two tests
explanation.body:
An argument can fail in two separate ways, so test both. First, **do the premises actually support the conclusion?** If every premise were true, how likely would the conclusion be? Second, **are the premises themselves true?** A beautifully shaped argument built on a false premise is still unsound, and a true premise that barely connects to the conclusion is still weak.

Worked example. 'Rohan scored 90% in college; therefore he will be an excellent ABAP consultant.' The premise may be true, but the link is thin: marks measure exam skills, while consulting also needs communication, debugging patience and client handling. The argument is weak, not because Rohan is poor, but because the evidence does not reach the conclusion. Compare: 'Rohan debugged three live tickets in his internship and his lead rated them accurate and on time; therefore he can handle junior support tasks.' Here the premise is directly relevant to the conclusion, so the argument is stronger.

explanation.heading: Hidden assumptions: the missing bridge
explanation.body:
Most arguments skip a step. That skipped step is the **assumption**, a belief that must be true for the premise to lead to the conclusion. 'Every top developer I know uses this laptop, so I should buy it.' The bridge is: 'what works for those developers will work for my needs and budget.' Once written out, you can question it.

To find an assumption, ask: 'What would have to be true for this reasoning to work?' Then ask whether that is actually true here. The most dangerous assumptions are the ones that sound like common sense. Common mistake: treating a claim as proven because the speaker sounds confident. Practise by writing the one-line bridge between premise and conclusion for every argument you read this week.

examples.title: Mapping a placement pitch
examples.body:
Pitch: 'Join Skyline Institute. Last year our ABAP batch had 40 students and 34 were placed, so you will get a job too.'

Premise: 34 of 40 were placed last year (that is 85%).
Conclusion: you will get a job.
Hidden assumption: your batch and the job market will resemble last year's, and 'placed' means a relevant role at a decent firm.
Questions to ask: how was 'placed' defined, and how many of the 34 got ABAP roles?
examples.takeaway: Writing the pitch as premise, conclusion and assumption turns a persuasive sales line into specific questions you can ask.

examples.title: Ranking three pieces of evidence
examples.body:
Claim: 'Pair programming reduces bugs.'
A) A friend says his team had fewer bugs after trying it.
B) A senior engineer says it works well.
C) A company tracked bug counts for 20 teams over 6 months, with half of the teams pairing and half not, assigned at random.

C is strongest because it compares groups and randomises the assignment. B is useful but based on one person's impression. A is an anecdote and could reflect many other changes in his team.
examples.takeaway: Prefer evidence that compares groups and rules out other explanations over evidence that merely tells a story.

examples.title: Hunting the hidden bridge
examples.body:
'The new hostel mess app has a 4.8 rating, so it will fix our food complaints.'

Premise: the app has a high rating.
Conclusion: it will fix complaints.
Bridge: high ratings come from people like us, and the app addresses the actual complaint (taste and hygiene), not just ordering convenience.
If the ratings praise fast delivery, the bridge breaks.
examples.takeaway: A true premise can still fail to support the conclusion when the bridge between them is untested.

exercises.prompt: Identify the conclusion: 'Our test coverage is only 30%, and two production bugs slipped through last month, so we should add tests before the next release.'
options: We should add tests before the next release.
Two production bugs slipped through last month.
The next release is arriving shortly.
exercises.hint: Look for the word 'so'. What comes after it?
exercises.why: The claim the speaker wants you to accept is 'we should add tests', signalled by 'so'. The other two statements are premises offered as reasons. The last option is not even stated in the text.

exercises.prompt: A coaching ad shows only the three students who got top packages out of a batch of 60. Which of the four evidence questions (relevant, sufficient, representative, reliable) does it fail most clearly? Answer with one word.
exercises.hint: The ad shows only the best cases.
exercises.why: Showing only the top three of sixty is a handpicked sample, so it is not representative of what a typical student experiences. It may be perfectly true and relevant, but it is not a fair picture.

exercises.prompt: Read this: 'Our college canteen raised prices by 10% last month and sales of snacks fell. Therefore the price rise caused the drop, and we should reverse it.' Write the conclusion, the premise, and one hidden assumption, then give one question you would ask before agreeing.

descriptors.0: Conclusion and premise are mixed up or missing.
descriptors.1: One of the two is identified correctly.
descriptors.2: Both identified, with slight imprecision in wording.
descriptors.3: Conclusion (reverse the price rise) and premise (prices rose and sales fell) are clearly stated.

auto.label: Uses the words conclusion and premise

descriptors.0: No assumption named, or it restates the premise.
descriptors.1: An assumption is hinted at but vague.
descriptors.2: A reasonable assumption is named but not tied to the argument.
descriptors.3: Names a real bridge, such as 'nothing else changed, like exams or holidays', and explains why the argument needs it.

descriptors.0: No question, or a rhetorical one.
descriptors.1: A question that cannot be answered with evidence.
descriptors.3: A specific, answerable question such as 'did sales fall in other canteens that did not raise prices?'

exercises.modelAnswer: Conclusion: the price rise caused the drop in snack sales and should be reversed. Premise: prices rose by 10% last month and snack sales fell afterwards. Hidden assumption: nothing else changed in that month, such as holidays, exams or a new competing stall, so the price is the only explanation. Question: did snack sales also fall at other outlets on campus that did not change their prices?
exercises.guidance: A strong answer names the conclusion as the claim about cause and action, not simply a restatement of the facts. The assumption should be the missing bridge, the idea that price was the only thing that changed. A common mistake is to list opinions about prices instead of the reasoning gap. Score yourself on whether each part is specific enough that a colleague could go and check it.

exercises.prompt: Your team lead says: 'Everyone in the forum recommends switching to framework X, so we should rewrite our module in it.' The deadline is six weeks away. How do you respond?

options.text: Agree; a popular forum recommendation is reliable enough.
options.feedback: Popularity is not evidence of fit. You have no information about those users' projects, constraints or the cost of rewriting.

options.text: Dismiss it completely because forum posts are not trustworthy.
options.feedback: Rejecting the source outright skips the real work. Forum opinion is weak evidence, but it can point you to claims worth testing.

options.text: Ask what the forum users actually measured, whether their projects resemble ours, and what a rewrite would cost against the deadline; propose a small trial on one component.
options.feedback: This checks relevance and sufficiency, surfaces the hidden assumption (their results transfer to us), and offers a cheap way to gather stronger evidence.

options.text: Ask for the names of the forum users so you can verify who they are.
options.feedback: Knowing who posted helps a little, but it does not test whether their experience applies to your module or timeline.

exercises.why: The best response treats the claim as a conclusion, identifies the weak premise (many people recommend it) and the hidden assumption (it will suit our project), and replaces opinion with a small, low-risk test.

task.title: Map one real argument
task.brief: Take one persuasive message you received recently and lay out its structure on paper.
steps: Pick a real message: a forwarded post, an advert, a course pitch or an opinion in a group chat.
Write the conclusion in one line, then each premise on its own line.
Write the hidden assumption that links premises to conclusion.
Rate each piece of evidence using the four questions: relevant, sufficient, representative, reliable.
Write one question you would ask the sender.
checklist: I wrote the conclusion in a single sentence
I rated the evidence on the four questions
I wrote a specific question for the sender
task.evidencePrompt: Write the conclusion, the key premise, and the hidden assumption you found.

quiz.prompt: Which word most often signals a premise rather than a conclusion?
quiz.why: 'Because' introduces a reason, so it points to a premise. 'Therefore', 'hence' and 'so' introduce what follows from the reasons, which is the conclusion.

quiz.prompt: Which piece of evidence is generally strongest for the claim 'A new onboarding checklist reduces early errors'?
options: A manager's belief that it helps
A comparison of error rates between new joiners who used it and similar joiners who did not
A single new joiner saying it was useful
A popular blog post praising checklists
quiz.why: A comparison between similar groups isolates the effect of the checklist. A manager's belief, one testimonial and a blog post are opinion or anecdote, and each could reflect many other factors.

quiz.prompt: 'The sun was hot today, therefore the exam results will be good.' What is the main problem?
options: The premise is true but irrelevant to the conclusion
quiz.why: Hot weather is probably true, but it has no link to exam results, so the premises do not support the conclusion. An argument can fail through weak support even when every premise is true.

quiz.prompt: What is the name for the unstated belief that must be true for a premise to lead to a conclusion? Answer with one word.
quiz.why: The unstated bridge between premise and conclusion is the assumption. Finding it shows you what the speaker is relying on without saying so.

bank.prompt: In 'Because the client changed the scope twice, we will need two more weeks', what is the conclusion?
options: The client changed the scope twice
We will need two more weeks
bank.why: The claim being supported is the need for two more weeks. The scope changes are the reason offered. The last two options are not stated in the sentence.

bank.prompt: A survey of 15 students at one hostel is used to claim 'Indian students prefer night-time study.' Which check does it fail most obviously?
options: Representativeness and sufficiency of the sample
bank.why: Fifteen students from one hostel cannot stand for all Indian students, so the sample is both too small and unrepresentative. Surveys are only as good as who they ask and how many.

bank.prompt: 'Our competitor raised prices and lost customers, so if we raise prices we will lose customers too.' What must be assumed about our company? Answer with one word that completes: our situation is ____ to theirs.
bank.why: The argument only works if our customers, product and market behave like the competitor's. That similarity is the hidden assumption connecting the premise to the conclusion.

cards.front: What are the two parts of an argument, and which signal words point to each?
cards.back: Conclusion (the claim; signalled by therefore, so, hence) and premises (the reasons; signalled by because, since, given that). Separate them first.

cards.front: What four questions test a piece of evidence?
cards.back: Is it relevant, sufficient, representative and reliable? Anecdotes sit low; comparisons with controlled or random groups sit high.

cards.front: What two tests decide whether an argument is strong?
cards.back: Do the premises, if true, really support the conclusion? And are the premises themselves true? Failing either one weakens the argument.

cards.front: How do you find a hidden assumption?
cards.back: Ask: what would have to be true for this premise to lead to this conclusion? Write that bridge down in one line and question it.

critical-1.reflection: Think of a belief you hold because many people around you share it. What is the premise really supporting it, and what hidden assumption would you need to test?

keyPoints: Split every argument into conclusion and premises.
Judge evidence by relevance, sufficiency, representativeness and reliability.
Test both the truth of premises and their support for the conclusion.
Write the hidden bridge assumption and question it.
revision.redo: Take one headline or advert you see today and write its conclusion, premise and hidden assumption in three short lines.

critical-2.title: Fallacies and Cognitive Biases
critical-2.summary: Recognise common reasoning errors in arguments and the mental biases that make you accept them, then respond calmly.
objectives: Name and spot five common logical fallacies in everyday arguments.
Recognise confirmation bias, anchoring, sunk cost and availability in your own decisions.
Respond to a flawed argument without attacking the person.

explanation.heading: Errors in arguments and in minds
explanation.body:
Last time you learned to split an argument into premises and a conclusion and to check the evidence. This lesson covers two sources of bad reasoning. **Fallacies** are errors in the argument itself: the premises do not support the conclusion even though it sounds convincing. **Cognitive biases** are errors in our own thinking: shortcuts the brain takes that push us off course. Knowing both makes you harder to fool, including by yourself.

A warning: naming fallacies is a tool for improving thinking, not for winning fights. Calling someone's argument "a fallacy" without explaining why just starts a quarrel.

explanation.heading: Five common fallacies
explanation.body:
- **Ad hominem**: attacking the person instead of the claim. "You failed last semester, so your suggestion on the database design is worthless." The suggestion must be judged on its merits.
- **Straw man**: misrepresenting a view to make it easy to defeat. Someone says "We should review the code before release" and the reply is "So you want to slow the whole project down for weeks?"
- **False dilemma**: presenting only two options when more exist. "Either we use this framework or the project fails."
- **Slippery slope**: claiming one step will inevitably lead to extreme results without evidence. "If we allow one late submission, nobody will submit on time."
- **Appeal to authority or popularity**: "A famous coder said it, so it is true" or "Everyone is learning this tool, so it must be best." Expertise matters only within the expert's field and when evidence backs it; popularity shows what is trendy, not what is correct.

Response technique: restate the real claim, then ask for evidence. "I am not asking for a delay. I suggest a one-day review. What risk do you see in that?"

explanation.heading: Biases that live in your head
explanation.body:
**Confirmation bias**: we notice and remember evidence that supports what we already believe, and discount the rest. If you believe a certain training institute is best, you will read only its success stories. Counter it by actively searching for the strongest case against your view.

**Anchoring**: the first number you hear shapes later judgements. If a recruiter says "freshers in this company get about 3 lakh", every figure afterwards feels measured against it, even if the number was arbitrary. Counter it by researching your own range before the conversation.

**Sunk cost**: continuing something because of what you have already spent, not what you will gain. You paid Rs 30,000 for a course that is clearly not helping and keep going "so the fees do not go to waste". The money is gone either way; ask only "from today, is this the best use of my next hundred hours?"

**Availability**: judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind. After reading news about a layoffs round you may overestimate your own risk, even though the news reports exceptions loudly and ordinary days quietly. Counter it with base rates and data.

examples.title: Spotting a straw man in a group project
examples.body: Riya says: "Maybe we should write tests before demo day." Karan answers: "You want us to spend a month on tests and miss the deadline?" Riya had suggested a couple of hours on the main features. A good reply: "I meant two hours on the three main functions, not a month. Does that risk the deadline?"
examples.takeaway: Restating your actual claim calmly removes the exaggeration without attacking the person.

examples.title: Sunk cost in a decision
examples.body: Arjun has spent three months and Rs 20,000 on a coaching programme with outdated material and poor trainers. A friend offers a better, cheaper batch. Arjun wants to stay "because I have already paid". A clearer frame: the Rs 20,000 is gone in both cases; compare only future cost, time and learning of staying versus switching.
examples.takeaway: Judge options by their future costs and benefits, not by what is already lost.

exercises.prompt: A teammate says, "Your idea for the login page is bad because you only joined this team last week." This is:
options: An ad hominem attack on you rather than your idea
A fair challenge to your idea
exercises.why: It attacks the person rather than judging the idea. Newness to a team says nothing about whether the idea works.

exercises.prompt: Seeking out only information that agrees with what you already believe is called ____ bias. (one word)
exercises.why: Confirmation bias is the habit of favouring evidence that supports your existing view.

exercises.prompt: You have spent six months on a side project that no longer fits your goals. A friend says, "You have come this far, you cannot quit now." What is the best reasoning?

options.text: Continue, because six months must not be wasted.
options.feedback: This is the sunk cost trap; the past time is gone either way.

options.text: Compare what the next 100 hours would achieve on the project versus on your current goal, then decide.
options.feedback: Looking forward at future benefit is the sound way to decide.

options.text: Quit immediately without thinking.
options.feedback: Impulsive quitting is not reasoning; compare options first.

options.text: Ask more friends until someone agrees with you.
options.feedback: This is confirmation bias in action.

exercises.why: Decide from future costs and benefits, not past investment or the opinions you collected to agree with yourself.

exercises.prompt: Read this claim: "Everyone in my class is joining this paid certification, and a famous YouTuber recommends it, so it must be the best way to get a job." Identify two fallacies or biases in it, explain each in one sentence, and write the question you would ask to test the claim.

descriptors.3: Appeal to popularity and appeal to authority correctly named.

auto.label: Names appeal to popularity and authority

descriptors.3: Both explained with reference to the claim.
Asks for specific evidence such as placement outcomes.
Curious and respectful.

exercises.modelAnswer: Appeal to popularity: many classmates joining shows it is trendy, not that it works. Appeal to authority: a YouTuber may not have evidence about hiring outcomes. Question: what share of past participants got entry-level roles, and in how long?
exercises.guidance: A strong answer names the fallacies, links each to the exact words of the claim and ends with an evidence question. Mistakes include only labelling or insulting the person. Score yourself against the model.

task.title: Fallacy and bias hunt
task.brief: Find real examples of reasoning errors around you and one in your own thinking.
steps: Collect three claims from social media, a WhatsApp group, advertising or a class discussion.
Label the fallacy in each and write a calm reply that restates the real claim and asks for evidence.
Identify one decision where you may have anchoring, confirmation or sunk cost bias.
Write what you would do differently, for example searching for disconfirming evidence.
checklist: I wrote a calm reply to at least one
I identified a bias in my own decision
task.evidencePrompt: Write one claim, its fallacy, your calm reply and one personal bias.

quiz.prompt: A straw man misrepresents someone's argument so that it is:
quiz.why: It replaces the real view with a weaker one.

quiz.prompt: Why is popularity weak evidence of quality?
options: Many people can be wrong, so popularity shows trend not truth
quiz.why: Popularity may reflect marketing or habit instead of merit.

quiz.prompt: The first number mentioned in a salary talk strongly shaping your judgement is:
quiz.why: The first figure becomes an anchor for later comparisons.

quiz.prompt: Which statement avoids the sunk cost fallacy?
options: I will continue because I already paid
Whatever I spent is gone, so I will choose what gives most value from here
I must finish what I start
quiz.why: Only future costs and benefits should decide.

bank.prompt: A manager says, "Either we approve this change today or the client leaves." No other options are discussed. This is:
bank.why: It forces two options when others, like a phased plan, may exist.

bank.prompt: After seeing three news stories about plane crashes, you feel flying is very risky. This mental shortcut is the ____ heuristic. (one word)
bank.why: Vivid, easily recalled examples distort your sense of how often something happens.

bank.prompt: Which habit best fights confirmation bias?
options: Reading only sources you agree with
Looking for the best argument against your view
bank.why: Deliberately seeking disconfirming evidence tests your belief.

cards.back: Ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, slippery slope and appeal to authority or popularity.

cards.front: Why are authority and popularity weak?
cards.back: Experts can be wrong outside their field and crowds follow trends; ask for evidence instead.
Confirmation: favouring evidence you already agree with. Anchoring: the first number shapes later judgement.
Sunk cost: continuing because of past spending. Availability: judging likelihood by memorable examples. Use future value and data instead.

critical-2.reflection: Which bias from this lesson most affects your own choices, and what question could you ask before your next decision to catch it?

keyPoints: Fallacies break the link between premises and conclusion.
Restate the real claim and ask for evidence, calmly.
Biases such as confirmation, anchoring, sunk cost and availability distort your own thinking.
Decide using future value and data.
revision.redo: Pick a decision you made this month and check it for sunk cost and confirmation bias.

critical-3.title: Numbers, Statistics and Causation
critical-3.summary: Question statistics: separate correlation from causation, respect base rates and sample size, choose the right average and read percentages and charts carefully.
objectives: Explain why correlation does not prove causation and name alternative explanations.
Use base rates, sample size and the right average to judge a statistic.
Distinguish percentage from percentage points and spot misleading charts.

explanation.heading: Why numbers deserve questions
explanation.body: In the last lesson you looked at reasoning errors. Numbers add a new risk: they look objective, so we stop questioning them. A statistic can be perfectly accurate and still mislead. This lesson gives you five questions to ask whenever a number is used to persuade you, whether in a placement brochure, a news headline, or a client report.

explanation.heading: Correlation, causation, base rates and samples
explanation.body:
**Correlation** means two things move together. **Causation** means one makes the other happen. Students who attend extra coaching score higher marks. Does coaching cause higher marks? Perhaps. Or students who are already motivated choose coaching and also study more; motivation is a **confounder**. Or marks and coaching both rise with family income. When you see a link, ask: could it be coincidence, reverse causation or a third factor? Only controlled comparisons, such as randomly assigning coaching, can show cause strongly.

**Base rates** are how common something is in general. Suppose a screening test is 90 percent accurate for a condition that affects 1 in 100 people. Test 1,000 people: 10 have it and about 9 are caught; of the 990 who do not, 10 percent, about 99, get a false alarm. So most positive results, 99 out of 108, are false alarms. Ignoring the base rate hides this. Always ask "how common is this in the first place?"

**Sample size** matters too. "9 out of 10 students loved the course" means little if only ten were asked, or if they were picked by the trainer. Small or hand-picked samples swing wildly.

explanation.heading: Averages that hide the truth
explanation.body: The **mean** adds everything and divides by the count; the **median** is the middle value when sorted. One extreme value drags the mean. A team of five freshers earns 4, 4, 5, 5 and 6 lakh a year, and the mean is 4.8. Add one executive at 50 lakh and the mean jumps to 12.3, yet five of six people still earn around 4 to 6. The median of 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 50 is 5, which describes the typical person better. When a distribution is skewed, as with salaries or house prices, prefer the median and ask for the spread.

explanation.heading: Percentages and charts
explanation.body:
A **percentage change** and a **percentage point** change differ. If a pass rate goes from 40 percent to 50 percent, that is a 10 percentage point rise, but a 25 percent increase (10 divided by 40). Headlines may choose the larger sounding one. Also watch what the percentage is of: "200 percent more risk" from a tiny starting risk, say 1 in 10,000 to 3 in 10,000, is still very small in absolute terms.

Charts can mislead through a **truncated axis** (a bar chart starting at 90 rather than 0 makes a 2-point difference look huge), cherry-picked time windows, or two axes scaled to suggest a link. Always read the axis labels and starting values, and ask what was left out.

examples.title: Placement brochure average
examples.body: A college says the "average package is 9 lakh". The placed students earned: 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 8, 12, 36 lakh (ten students). The mean is 9 lakh, but the median is 5.5 lakh, and 7 of 10 earned 6 lakh or less. A better question: "What is the median package and how many students sat for placement?"
examples.takeaway: A high outlier can lift the mean far above what most people experience; ask for the median and the number placed.

examples.title: Percent vs percentage points
examples.body: A training firm says: "Our pass rate rose by 50 percent." Last year 20 percent passed, this year 30 percent. The change is 10 percentage points, which is a 50 percent relative increase (10 divided by 20). Both are true; the second sounds larger. Check both figures and the batch size before judging.
examples.takeaway: Always find the actual starting and ending numbers behind a relative claim.

exercises.prompt: Ice-cream sales and drowning incidents both rise in summer. What best explains this?
options: A third factor, hot weather, drives both
exercises.why: Hot weather is a confounder that raises both. The other options assume a direct link without evidence.

exercises.prompt: Five freshers earn 3, 4, 4, 5 and 14 lakh a year. The median salary in lakh is ____. (number)
exercises.why: Sorted values are 3, 4, 4, 5, 14, and the middle one is 4.

exercises.prompt: A coaching centre says, "9 out of 10 students who took our course got placed." You find the 10 were chosen by the centre from 400 enrolled students. What do you conclude?

options.text: The result is reliable because 9 out of 10 is high.
options.feedback: A hand-picked, tiny sample says little about all 400.

options.text: It is a biased, small sample; ask how many of all 400 got placed and into which roles.
options.feedback: The denominator and selection method decide whether the claim means anything.

options.text: The centre is lying and should be reported.
options.feedback: Assuming dishonesty is premature; the claim is just uninformative.

options.text: Join immediately because most succeeded.
options.feedback: Acting on a cherry-picked statistic ignores selection bias.

exercises.why: Check who was counted and how many in total; selected small samples cannot represent a population.

exercises.prompt: A company says: "Employee satisfaction rose from 60 percent to 75 percent." Write (a) the change in percentage points, (b) the relative percentage increase with the working, and (c) three questions you would ask before trusting the claim, including at least one about the sample or chart.

descriptors.3: 15 percentage points stated clearly.
15 divided by 60 equals 25 percent, shown.
Three, covering sample size, who was surveyed and the chart or time window.
Clear and concise.

exercises.modelAnswer: (a) 75 minus 60 is 15 percentage points. (b) 15 divided by 60 is 0.25, so a 25 percent relative increase. (c) How many employees responded and were they chosen randomly? Was the survey anonymous? Does the chart start its axis at zero and which months does it cover?
exercises.guidance: A strong answer states both measures correctly and shows the division. Questions should target sample size, selection, anonymity and the time window or axis. A frequent mistake is to say the satisfaction rose by 15 percent. Mark yourself honestly.

task.title: Audit one statistic
task.brief: Find a real statistic from the news, a brochure or an advertisement and test it with the five questions.
steps: Choose one claim with a number, and write it down exactly.
Ask: what is the comparison, the sample size, who was counted and how?
Check whether the average used is a mean or median and whether outliers matter.
Rewrite any percentage as both relative change and percentage points.
Note whether the chart or wording could mislead and write a fairer version of the claim.
checklist: I identified the type of average or percentage
I wrote a fairer version of the claim
task.evidencePrompt: Paste the claim, your main doubt and your fairer wording.

quiz.prompt: A confounder is:
options: A third factor affecting both variables
quiz.why: It creates a link without direct cause.

quiz.prompt: Which sample is most trustworthy for judging a course?
options: A random sample of 200 of all students
Ten students picked by the trainer
quiz.why: Random and larger samples reflect the whole group better.

quiz.prompt: When a few very high salaries exist, which average better describes a typical person?
quiz.why: The median resists extreme values.

quiz.prompt: A rate rises from 20 percent to 25 percent. This is:
quiz.why: 25 minus 20 is 5 percentage points; the relative rise is 25 percent.

bank.prompt: Students who sleep more score better. Which is the most careful statement?
options: Sleep makes every student score higher
Sleep and marks are linked; other factors like health or routine may play a part
There is no link at all
bank.why: A link needs further evidence before claiming cause.

bank.prompt: Four values are 10, 12, 14 and 40. What is the mean? (number)
bank.why: 10 plus 12 plus 14 plus 40 is 76, divided by 4 is 19.

bank.prompt: A bar chart compares two apps with bars starting at 95 instead of 0 on the axis. What is the risk?
options: The bars will be too long
bank.why: A truncated axis exaggerates small differences.

cards.back: Correlation: things move together. Causation: one makes the other happen. Check coincidence, reverse cause and confounders.

cards.front: Why base rates and sample size?
cards.back: Base rates show how common something is; samples must be large and unbiased to represent a group.
Mean is sensitive to outliers; median is the middle value and describes skewed data better.
From 40 to 50 percent is 10 points but 25 percent relative. Check chart axes starting at zero and time windows.

critical-3.reflection: Which statistic have you recently believed without checking the sample, the average type or the base rate?

keyPoints: Link does not prove cause; look for confounders.
Use base rates and ask how many and how chosen.
Prefer the median when outliers exist.
Differentiate percent from percentage points and read chart axes.
revision.redo: Take one headline number from today and ask for its sample size, average type and starting value.

critical-4.title: Reasoning Under Uncertainty
critical-4.summary: Steelman opposing views, state calibrated confidence, run a pre-mortem, think through second-order effects and update your mind with evidence.
objectives: Steelman a view you disagree with before responding.
Give confidence levels and run a pre-mortem on a plan.
Trace second-order effects and update beliefs when evidence changes.

concepts.label: Second-order thinking and changing your mind

explanation.heading: Deciding without certainty
explanation.body: You learned to judge arguments, avoid fallacies and question numbers. Real decisions rarely come with certainty: which job offer, which specialisation, whether to relocate to Bengaluru or Pune. Critical thinkers do not wait for certainty; they reason well about uncertain things. Four habits help: steelman, calibrate, pre-mortem and think second-order.

explanation.heading: Steelmanning and calibration
explanation.body:
A straw man weakens the opposing view; a **steelman** does the opposite, restating it in its strongest, fairest form before you reply. Use it when you disagree. Example: a friend argues that you should accept a government job with lower pay rather than an IT-services offer. A steelman: "Job security, fixed hours and a pension-like stability let you plan family finances, study further and avoid layoff stress." Only after you can state that so your friend says "yes, exactly" should you explain your disagreement. The effect is that you test your view against the best version of the other, and people listen to you more.

**Calibration** means that your confidence matches reality. If you say "90 percent sure" about ten things and only five turn out true, you are overconfident. Express beliefs as probabilities or ranges: "I am about 70 percent sure that I can finish the report by Friday." Keep a short log of predictions and outcomes; over a few months you will see whether your 70 percent means 70 percent. Avoid 0 and 100 percent unless you truly mean it.

explanation.heading: Pre-mortem and second-order thinking
explanation.body:
A **pre-mortem** is run before a project starts. Imagine it is six months later and the plan has failed badly. Write down why, in specific stories: "We did not test on slow networks", "I dropped the plan when exams began", "The client changed scope". Then change the plan to prevent the top three reasons. It works because imagining a failure that has already happened frees people to voice doubts they would otherwise suppress as negativity.

**Second-order thinking** asks "and then what?" First-order effects are immediate; second-order effects follow. Skipping sleep for a night to finish a project (first order: more done) leads to poorer concentration the next day and a slower week (second order). Taking a loan for a laptop beyond your needs may feel like a benefit now, yet its monthly burden limits your choices next year. Ask "and then what?" at least twice for any significant decision.

explanation.heading: Changing your mind with evidence
explanation.body: Changing your mind is not weakness; it is the purpose of reasoning. Before an important decision, decide what evidence would make you change: "If three recent graduates tell me this institute did not help their placement, I will drop it." Afterwards, update in proportion: strong evidence moves you a lot, weak evidence a little. Beware of two errors: stubbornness (ignoring good evidence to protect your ego) and flip-flopping (changing with every opinion). Say aloud, "I used to think X; now, given Y, I think Z." This habit makes colleagues and clients trust your judgement because they see that evidence moves you.

examples.title: Pre-mortem for a hackathon
examples.body: Before a 24-hour hackathon, a team imagines it failed. Reasons: no one owned deployment, the API key expired, two members fell asleep in the afternoon, the demo was not rehearsed. Changes: assign a deployment owner, test keys on day one, schedule sleep shifts and run a five-minute demo rehearsal at hour 20.
examples.takeaway: Naming failure stories in advance turns vague worry into specific prevention.

examples.title: Steelmanning before disagreeing
examples.body: Sana thinks learning a niche tool like ABAP is risky. Her cousin supports it. Sana says: "Your best case is that SAP is used by many large companies, ABAP skills are specialised so competition for entry roles may be narrower, and the pay can grow with experience. Did I get that right?" Cousin: "Yes." Then Sana raises her concern about being tied to one ecosystem.
examples.takeaway: Stating the strongest version first makes the conversation honest and productive.

exercises.prompt: What does steelmanning mean?
options: Stating the opposing view in its strongest fair form before replying
Repeating the other person's weakest point
exercises.why: Steelmanning tests your view against the best opposing case. Repeating the weakest point is a straw man.

exercises.prompt: If you say "90 percent sure" about many predictions but only half come true, you are ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Your stated confidence is higher than your actual success rate, so you are overconfident.

exercises.prompt: Your team is about to start a three-month college project and everyone feels confident. What is the best step?

options.text: Start immediately; doubt slows us down.
options.feedback: Unchecked confidence leaves weak points unseen.

options.text: Hold a 15-minute pre-mortem: imagine the project failed and list specific reasons, then fix the top three.
options.feedback: It surfaces risks early while plans are still cheap to change.

options.text: Ask the weakest member to name every possible problem.
options.feedback: This blames one person instead of using the whole team.

options.text: Plan only for the best case.
options.feedback: This ignores the very risks that cause failure.

exercises.why: A pre-mortem imagines failure in advance to expose and fix risks while changes are cheap.

exercises.prompt: You are considering taking a Rs 40,000 loan at a high interest rate to buy a premium laptop in your final year. Write the first-order benefit, two second-order effects ("and then what?"), a confidence level for your recommendation as a percentage with a reason, and what evidence would change your mind.

descriptors.3: Clear and realistic.
Two specific effects with a chain of consequences.
Percentage with a reason for the uncertainty.
Specific observable evidence that would change the decision.

exercises.modelAnswer: First order: a faster laptop helps my project work. Second order: EMIs reduce my monthly budget for two years and may force me to take any job quickly, and interest cost exceeds the performance gain for my needs. I am about 75 percent sure I should not take the loan because my current laptop runs my tools. I would change my mind if a core course required hardware my laptop cannot run, or if I found an interest-free option.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers chain consequences beyond the first benefit, attach a defensible percentage and name the evidence that would flip the decision. Weak answers repeat the benefit and claim certainty. Score yourself honestly.

task.title: Decide under uncertainty
task.brief: Apply all four habits to one real decision you face in the next few months.
steps: Write the decision and the two main options.
Steelman the option you currently dislike in three sentences.
Write your confidence in your preferred option as a percentage and why.
Run a five-minute pre-mortem: list three reasons it could fail and one prevention each.
Write two second-order effects and the evidence that would make you change your mind.
checklist: I stated a confidence percentage with a reason
I listed three failure reasons and preventions
I named evidence that would change my mind
task.evidencePrompt: Write your decision, confidence, top failure reason and change-my-mind evidence.

quiz.prompt: When should you steelman?
options: Before you reply to a view you disagree with
quiz.why: It makes your disagreement fair and better informed.

quiz.prompt: Being well calibrated means:
options: Your 70 percent predictions come true about 70 percent of the time
quiz.why: Confidence should match outcomes over many predictions.

quiz.prompt: A pre-mortem is done:
options: Before starting, by imagining a future failure
quiz.why: Imagined failure in advance exposes risks while they are cheap to fix.

quiz.prompt: Second-order thinking asks:
options: What did I do last time?
quiz.why: It follows effects beyond the immediate result.

bank.prompt: A friend argues against learning ABAP. Which reply shows steelmanning?
options: Your strongest point is that it is specialised and tied to one ecosystem; is that right?
Everyone learns it, so it is good
I do not listen to you
bank.why: It restates the best form of their argument first.

bank.prompt: In a pre-mortem you imagine the plan has already ____. (one word)
bank.why: You assume failure, then ask what caused it.

bank.prompt: New evidence strongly contradicts your belief. The best response is to:
options: Update your belief in proportion to the strength of the evidence
bank.why: Proportional updating avoids both stubbornness and flip-flopping.

cards.back: Restating an opposing view in its strongest fair form before you respond, until its holder says yes, exactly.
Matching your confidence to reality; state probabilities and keep a log of predictions and results.
Imagine the plan failed, list specific causes, and change the plan to prevent the top few.
Ask and then what; decide in advance what evidence would change your mind and update in proportion.

critical-4.reflection: Which upcoming decision would benefit most from a pre-mortem and a written confidence level?

keyPoints: Steelman before disagreeing.
State confidence as a percentage and track results.
Run a pre-mortem to find failure causes early.
Ask and then what, and update in proportion to evidence.
revision.redo: Write one prediction for this week with a percentage and check it on Sunday.

discipline-1.title: Habits and Identity
discipline-1.summary: Understand the cue-routine-reward loop, shrink habits until they are easy, anchor them with if-then plans, and tie them to the person you are becoming.
objectives: Break any habit into its cue, routine and reward, and redesign one part of the loop.
Write a habit-stacking script and an implementation intention that name a trigger, an action and a place.
Phrase a habit as an identity vote rather than a vague wish.

explanation.heading: Every habit is a loop: cue, routine, reward
explanation.body:
A habit is not a personality trait. It is a loop with three parts. The **cue** is the trigger (a time, a place, a feeling, a person, the action just before). The **routine** is what you do. The **reward** is what your brain gets out of it, which is why it repeats.

Take a common evening loop: you finish dinner (cue), open Instagram reels (routine), and feel relaxed and entertained (reward). To change it, do not fight the whole loop. Keep the cue and the reward, and swap the routine. After dinner, you make a cup of tea and do ten minutes of ABAP syntax revision. The reward is the tea plus a tick on your tracker.

When a habit will not stick, ask which part is broken. No clear cue means you forget. A heavy routine means you avoid it. No reward means there is no reason for the brain to repeat it.

explanation.heading: Make it tiny first, then let it grow
explanation.body:
Most people fail because they start too big: 'two hours of study every day'. On a bad day, two hours looks impossible, so you do nothing, and doing nothing teaches you that the plan does not work.

A **tiny habit** is a version so small that you can do it even when tired, stressed or busy. Examples: open the ABAP notes and read one statement; put on running shoes; write one line of code. The aim is not the five minutes. The aim is to make *showing up* automatic. Once you have started, you will often keep going, but you are allowed to stop. Growth comes later.

The arithmetic is encouraging. Five minutes a day for 30 days is 150 minutes, 2.5 hours of real practice, and a loop that now runs without a fight. Compare that with a two-hour plan that you follow for three days and abandon: 6 hours, and a feeling of failure.

explanation.heading: Say exactly when, where and after what
explanation.body:
A wish like 'I will study more' has no cue. An **implementation intention** fixes the cue in advance using the pattern: **When X happens, I will do Y, at place Z.** Research on this technique is consistent: specific if-then plans are followed far more often than general goals, because the decision is already made.

The easiest cue is something you already do daily. This is **habit stacking**: *After I [current habit], I will [tiny new habit].*

- After I pour my morning chai, I will open my ABAP notes and read one statement.
- After I sit down at my desk at 7 pm, I will write one line of code in the editor.
- After I plug in my phone to charge at night, I will write tomorrow's one task on a sticky note.

A good anchor is specific (not 'in the morning'), reliable (happens every day), and sits right before the new habit. A common mistake is anchoring to something that happens irregularly, such as 'after I get free time'.

explanation.heading: Habits are votes for who you are
explanation.body:
Goals say what you want. **Identity** says who you are. 'I want to learn ABAP' is a wish. 'I am a person who writes code every day' is a statement that each action either supports or weakens. Every small repetition is a **vote** for that identity, and a few votes will not decide an election, but a steady pile of them does.

Use this in two ways. First, phrase habits as identity: not 'I am trying to avoid my phone' but 'I am someone who protects my study time'. Second, collect evidence: a tick on a calendar after each tiny habit is proof, to yourself, that the identity is true. When you slip, do not say 'I am lazy'. Say 'I am a person who writes code daily, and I missed yesterday, so today I show up with the tiny version.' The identity survives the slip.

examples.title: A habit-stacking script card
examples.body:
Goal: practise ABAP daily.

Anchor: After I finish my evening chai at 6:30 pm.
Tiny habit: I open the practice file and write one SELECT statement.
Place: my study table, laptop already open from the morning.
Reward: tick the day on the wall calendar, then my 10-minute cricket highlights.
Identity line: I am someone who writes code every day.

If-then backup: If I get home after 8 pm, then I do the tiny habit on my phone's notes app, reading one flashcard.
examples.takeaway: The script names a trigger, an action so small it cannot be refused, a place, a reward, an identity line, and a backup plan for the days that go wrong.

examples.title: Swapping the routine, keeping the loop
examples.body:
Old loop: Cue = I feel bored at 10:30 pm. Routine = scroll YouTube Shorts. Reward = novelty and relief from boredom.

New loop: Cue = same boredom at 10:30 pm, with my phone charging across the room. Routine = read one page of a novel on the bed. Reward = novelty, a calmer mind, and sleeping earlier.

The new routine meets the same need (novelty, relief) which is why it can replace the old one. Pure willpower against an unchanged reward rarely works.
examples.takeaway: Find the real reward the old habit gives you and offer the brain a healthier route to the same reward.

examples.title: From wish to identity vote
examples.body:
Wish: 'I should exercise more.'
Goal: 'I will run 5 km three times a week.'
Identity vote: 'I am a person who moves every day.' Today's vote: put on shoes and walk for five minutes after lunch.

On a rainy day the 5 km goal is cancelled and the day is wasted. The identity vote is still available: five minutes of stretching indoors.
examples.takeaway: Identity-based habits flex on bad days; rigid goals break and take your motivation with them.

exercises.prompt: Rahul checks WhatsApp the moment he sits down to study, gets a small hit of social connection, and then loses an hour. Which part of the loop is the CUE?
options: The small hit of social connection
exercises.hint: The cue is what happens right before the routine and sets it off.
exercises.why: Sitting down is the trigger. Checking WhatsApp is the routine, and the social connection is the reward that makes the brain repeat it. Losing an hour is a consequence, not a part of the loop. To change the habit, Rahul should keep the cue but change the routine, for example by putting the phone in another room before sitting down.

exercises.prompt: You commit to a tiny habit of 5 minutes of coding practice every day for 30 days. How many minutes of practice is that in total? (number only)
exercises.hint: Multiply the minutes per day by the number of days.
exercises.why: 5 x 30 = 150 minutes, or 2.5 hours. The point of a tiny habit is not the size of one session but the 30 repetitions that make starting automatic.

exercises.prompt: You want to revise SAP ABAP flashcards every day, but you keep saying you will do it 'when you have time'. Write a habit-stacking script: name an existing daily anchor, the tiny version of the habit, the place, and one reward. Use the format 'After I ..., I will ...'.

descriptors.0: No anchor, or a vague one such as 'when I have time'.
descriptors.1: An anchor is named but it is irregular or vague (for example 'in the evening').
descriptors.2: A daily anchor is named but it is not clearly right before the habit.
descriptors.3: A specific daily action that reliably happens just before the habit, such as 'After I pour my morning chai'.

descriptors.0: A big action such as 'study for two hours'.
descriptors.1: A moderate action that still needs willpower on a bad day.
descriptors.2: A small action but the size or count is not clear.
descriptors.3: A clearly tiny action with a size, such as 'review three flashcards' or 'two minutes'.

descriptors.0: Neither a place nor a reward is mentioned.
descriptors.1: Only one of place or reward is mentioned, vaguely.
descriptors.2: Both are mentioned but one is vague.
descriptors.3: A specific place and a satisfying, immediate reward are both stated.

auto.label: Mentions a place and a reward

descriptors.0: No plan for a difficult day.
descriptors.1: A vague promise to try harder.
descriptors.2: A backup is mentioned but it is not smaller than the main habit.
descriptors.3: An explicit if-then backup that is smaller or easier than the main habit.

exercises.modelAnswer: After I finish my evening chai at my study table, I will review three ABAP flashcards. Then I will tick the day on my wall calendar and enjoy ten minutes of music. If I reach home late, then I will review one flashcard on my phone while brushing my teeth, so the day still counts.
exercises.guidance: A strong script has a daily anchor that really exists, a habit you cannot refuse (three flashcards, not thirty), a named place, an immediate reward, and a smaller backup version. The common mistake is writing an ambitious goal and calling it a script. If your habit would feel hard on your worst day, shrink it until it would not. Score yourself against the model answer.

exercises.prompt: You planned to study ABAP for 90 minutes daily. You managed it for four days, then missed three in a row because of a college deadline. You feel like a person who 'never sticks to anything'. What is the best next step?

options.text: Restart on Monday with a stricter 120-minute plan to make up for the lost days.
options.feedback: A bigger plan after a failure repeats the same mistake. It will collapse on the next busy day and strengthen the 'I never stick' story.

options.text: Wait until you feel motivated again, then restart properly.
options.feedback: Motivation is unreliable. Waiting leaves the gap open and the identity damage unrepaired.

options.text: Tonight, after dinner, do a five-minute version of the habit and tick the calendar, telling yourself 'I am someone who studies daily, and I am back'.
options.feedback: This restores a vote for your identity today, uses a tiny version that survives a busy week, and rebuilds the loop. You can grow the time later.

options.text: Change your goal to something easier, such as learning ABAP 'sometime this year'.
options.feedback: Shrinking the goal into vagueness removes the cue and the accountability. Shrink the action, not the commitment.

exercises.why: A missed streak is a data point about the plan, not a verdict on you. The best response is an immediate, tiny, specific action that casts a vote for the identity you want. Bigger plans and waiting both depend on motivation, which is exactly what failed.

task.title: Build your habit script card
task.brief: Create one complete habit-stacking script for a habit that matters to your SAP ABAP goal and set it up to start tomorrow.
steps: List three things you do every single day without fail, such as chai, brushing teeth or opening your laptop. Choose the one that happens closest to when you could practise.
Write the script in your notes: After I [anchor], I will [tiny habit of 2 to 5 minutes] at [place].
Add a reward that you actually enjoy and a backup line: If [bad-day situation], then I will [even smaller version].
Add one identity line, starting with 'I am someone who...', and place the note or a sticky where you will see it at the anchor.
Do the tiny habit once today to test the script and tick the day.
checklist: My anchor is something I do every day
My tiny habit takes five minutes or less
I wrote a reward and a bad-day backup
I did the habit once today
task.evidencePrompt: Write your complete script: anchor, tiny habit, reward and identity line.

quiz.prompt: A friend says: 'I scroll my phone every night because I am just weak.' Using the habit loop, what is the most useful question to ask?
options: How can I punish myself when I scroll?
What cue starts it and what reward does it give me?
Why do I have less willpower than others?
How can I delete all my apps forever?
quiz.why: A habit is a loop, so the useful move is to find the cue and the reward, then change one part. Punishment and blaming willpower do not change the loop, and deleting everything is extreme and often reversed.

quiz.prompt: What is the main purpose of a tiny habit such as 'write one line of code'?
options: To make starting automatic, so the habit can grow later
To test how much willpower you have
quiz.why: Tiny habits make showing up automatic and easy on bad days. They do not replace the goal; they build the loop that carries you toward it. Testing willpower defeats the purpose, which is to need none.

quiz.prompt: Complete the habit-stacking formula with one word: 'After I [current habit], I will [new ____ habit].'
quiz.why: The new habit should be tiny, so that the stack works even on a day when you have little energy.

quiz.prompt: Which statement is an identity-based habit rather than a goal?
options: I want to lose 5 kg by December.
I will run three times a week.
I will read for one hour daily.
I am a person who moves every day, so I took a short walk after lunch.
quiz.why: The last statement ties the action to who you are and counts the small action as a vote. The others state outcomes or schedules that can fail on a bad day.

bank.prompt: Which of these is the strongest implementation intention?
options: I will try to wake up early.
When my 6:15 am alarm rings, I will put my feet on the floor and drink a glass of water at my desk.
I will exercise whenever I feel energetic.
bank.why: It names a specific cue (alarm), an action, and a place. The others are wishes or conditions based on feelings, which do not reliably appear.

bank.prompt: Meera replaces her 4 pm tea-and-biscuit break with a plain walk, but she keeps relapsing. She realises the break gave her a social chat with colleagues. What should she do?
options: Remove the walk and return to biscuits
Walk with a colleague and chat on the way
Force herself to walk alone to build discipline
bank.why: The real reward was the social contact. A new routine must satisfy the same reward, so walking with a colleague keeps the loop intact. The other options ignore the reward or rely on willpower.

bank.prompt: A student plans two minutes of Python practice daily for 60 days. How many total minutes is that? (number only)
bank.why: 2 x 60 = 120 minutes. The value of the plan lies mostly in 60 consecutive cues answered, not in the 120 minutes.

cards.front: What are the three parts of a habit loop?
cards.back: Cue (trigger), routine (the action), reward (the payoff that makes it repeat). To change a habit, keep the cue and reward and swap the routine.

cards.front: Why start with a tiny habit?
cards.back: A tiny version survives tired, busy days, so it makes starting automatic. Five minutes daily for 30 days is 150 minutes and a working loop.
After I [specific, reliable current habit], I will [tiny new habit] at [place]. Add a reward and an if-then backup for bad days.
Each small action is evidence for the person you are becoming, such as 'I am someone who writes code daily'. A slip does not cancel the identity; a tiny return restores it.

discipline-1.reflection: Which daily habit of yours could serve as the most reliable anchor for a new tiny habit, and what identity would that tiny habit be a vote for?

keyPoints: Every habit is cue, routine, reward; change the routine, keep the reward.
Make the habit tiny so you can do it on your worst day.
After I [anchor], I will [tiny habit] at [place].
Each repetition is a vote for who you are becoming.
revision.redo: Say your habit-stacking script aloud from memory, then do the tiny habit once and tick the day.

discipline-2.title: Designing Your Environment
discipline-2.summary: Shape your surroundings so good habits are easy and distractions are hard, using friction, commitment devices, temptation bundling and urge surfing.
objectives: Add friction to a distraction and remove friction from a helpful habit.
Design a commitment device and a temptation bundle for one of your own habits.
Ride out an urge with a short urge-surfing routine and set clear phone boundaries.

explanation.heading: Environment beats willpower: friction up, friction down
explanation.body:
In the last lesson you built a tiny habit with a cue. Now look at where you do it. We do what is easy and visible. Willpower is a limited and unreliable resource, but your surroundings work for you 24 hours a day.

**Friction** is the number of steps and the effort between you and an action. To build a habit, **remove friction**: leave your laptop open on the study table with the practice file ready, so starting is one step. To break a habit, **add friction**: log out of Instagram, move the app into a folder on the last screen, and charge your phone in another room, so a scroll takes seven steps instead of one.

A useful rule: make the good action take under 20 seconds to start and make the bad action take over 60 seconds. You are not trying to be strong; you are trying to be the person whose room makes the right choice easy.

explanation.heading: Phone boundaries in three layers
explanation.body:
The phone is the biggest source of friction problems for most students, so set boundaries in layers.

1. **Remove**: delete apps you never planned to use, and turn off notifications for everything except calls and people. A buzz is a cue you did not choose.
2. **Hide and delay**: move social apps off the home screen, use a screen-time limit that needs a password someone else knows, and keep the phone in another room during focus blocks.
3. **Replace**: put a book, notebook or practice file where the phone used to sit.

Illustrative arithmetic: if you unlock your phone 60 times a day and each unlock costs about 3 minutes once you count getting back on track, that is 180 minutes, three hours, a day. Cutting unlocks in half returns an hour and a half. Your numbers will differ; the logic is the same.

explanation.heading: Commitment devices and temptation bundling
explanation.body:
A **commitment device** is a choice made now that binds your future self. You use it when you know that at 9 pm you will want to give up. Examples: pay for a mock test series in advance, book a study slot with a friend who will wait for you, or agree that you pay your friend ₹200 for every missed session. If you plan five sessions a week and miss two, you pay ₹400, which is real enough to matter but small enough to be safe. A good device is specific, easy to check, and cannot be quietly cancelled by you.

**Temptation bundling** joins something you *need* to do with something you *want* to do, allowed only together. Examples: your favourite podcast only while doing flashcards; a cricket highlights video only after the day's code practice; a special coffee only while updating your resume. The want becomes the reward in the habit loop from Lesson 1.

explanation.heading: Urge surfing: when the craving arrives anyway
explanation.body:
Even with a good environment, urges come: the urge to check a message, open a video, or skip the session. An urge behaves like a wave. It rises, peaks and falls, usually within a few minutes, whether you obey it or not. **Urge surfing** means watching the wave instead of acting on it.

A simple routine:

1. Name it: 'This is an urge to check Instagram.'
2. Rate it from 1 to 10 and notice where you feel it (restless hands, tight chest).
3. Breathe slowly and set a 10-minute timer. Do not argue with the urge. Just watch the number change.
4. When the timer ends, re-rate it. If it is still high, take a two-minute walk, then restart the timer.

Notice that this is not about suppressing anything. You are showing your brain that an urge can exist without being obeyed, and each time you do this the next wave is a little weaker.

examples.title: A room redesign for a study evening
examples.body:
Before: phone on the bed, laptop in the bag, charger in the study corner, YouTube tab always open.

After:
- Phone charges in the hall at 6 pm (friction up: 12 steps to reach it).
- Laptop sits open on the desk with the ABAP practice file loaded (friction down: 1 step to start).
- A sticky note on the screen: 'One SELECT statement first.'
- YouTube logged out on the laptop.

Result: the first action in the room is the practice file, not the phone.
examples.takeaway: Two moves, adding friction to the distraction and removing it from the habit, change behaviour without any extra willpower.

examples.title: A commitment device with arithmetic
examples.body:
Priya plans to practise on 5 days a week for 4 weeks, which is 20 sessions. She tells her friend Ananya: 'For every missed session, I pay you ₹150.' In week 1 she misses one session, so she pays ₹150. In week 2 she misses none. By week 4 her total is ₹150, and because the stake was real she studied on days she would normally have skipped.

If she had missed 4 sessions, she would have paid 4 x ₹150 = ₹600.
examples.takeaway: A stake is useful when it is fixed in advance, small enough to be safe, and enforced by another person.

examples.title: Surfing a 9 pm urge
examples.body: 9:05 pm: 'I want to check reels.' Rating: 8/10. Timer for 10 minutes. 9:08: 7/10, feel restless in the hands, so I stretch. 9:12: 5/10. 9:15: 3/10, the timer ends and I go back to flashcards. I did not delete anything or shout at myself. I just waited.
examples.takeaway: The urge fell from 8 to 3 without being obeyed. Watching numbers change turns an emergency into an event.

exercises.prompt: You want to practise coding every evening and also scroll less. Which setup uses friction correctly?
options: Keep the phone on the desk with notifications off and open the laptop only when you feel motivated.
Charge the phone in another room and leave the laptop open on your practice file.
Delete the phone's browser and keep the laptop in your bag.
Keep both on the desk and rely on willpower.
exercises.hint: Add friction to the distraction and remove it from the habit.
exercises.why: Charging the phone away adds friction to the distraction, and an open practice file removes friction from the habit. The first option leaves the phone in reach and waits for motivation, the third makes the good habit harder, and the fourth uses no design at all.

exercises.prompt: Illustration: you unlock your phone 60 times a day and each unlock costs 3 minutes of lost focus. How many hours is that per day? (number only)
exercises.hint: 60 x 3 gives minutes. Divide by 60 for hours.
exercises.why: 60 x 3 = 180 minutes, which is 3 hours. Even if your own numbers are smaller, the cost of frequent unlocks is much larger than any single glance suggests.

exercises.prompt: Design one temptation bundle and one commitment device for the habit of doing 30 minutes of ABAP practice on 5 evenings a week. State the want you will bundle, the rule that links it to the habit, and the stake with its rupee amount and the person who enforces it.

rubric.label: Temptation bundle: a want tied only to the habit

descriptors.0: No bundle, or the want is available anytime anyway.
descriptors.1: A want is named but it is not restricted to the habit.
descriptors.2: A want is tied to the habit, but the rule is loose.
descriptors.3: A specific enjoyable thing allowed only during or right after the practice, with a clear rule.

rubric.label: Commitment device with a clear stake

descriptors.1: A vague stake such as 'I will feel guilty'.
descriptors.2: A stake is stated but the amount or trigger is unclear.
descriptors.3: A specific rupee amount, a clear trigger (per missed session) and a total that checks out.

rubric.label: Enforcement by another person or fixed system

descriptors.1: Someone is named but has no real role.
descriptors.2: Someone is named and checks, but the process is unclear.
descriptors.3: A named person or system enforces the stake without your permission.

descriptors.1: Too large or too small to be sensible.
descriptors.2: Reasonable but not tested against a bad week.
descriptors.3: A modest stake that you could afford to lose and that fits a bad week.

exercises.modelAnswer: Bundle: I watch my favourite cricket analysis video only while I am doing the 30-minute practice, or right after it, never before. Device: I will pay my friend Ananya ₹150 for each of the 5 weekly evening sessions I miss. If I miss 2 in a week, I pay ₹300. Ananya checks my session log on Sunday and I send the money by UPI the same night.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer joins a genuine pleasure to the habit with a firm rule, and sets a stake that is real but safe, fixed in advance, and enforced by someone else. Common mistakes are bundling something you can have anytime (so it is no incentive), and punishing yourself with a stake you could cancel. Check that your arithmetic is correct: amount per miss times missed sessions.

exercises.prompt: It is 9:30 pm and you are 20 minutes into a practice session. A strong urge hits to open a video platform 'just for 5 minutes'. Your phone is on the desk. What is the best response?

options.text: Give in for five minutes; it is only five minutes.
options.feedback: Giving in rewards the urge and strengthens the loop; five minutes rarely stays five.

options.text: Name the urge, rate it, move the phone to the hall, set a 10-minute timer and keep working.
options.feedback: Right: you surf the urge as it fades and add friction so the next one is easier to resist.

options.text: Scold yourself for being weak and force yourself to sit still.
options.feedback: Self-criticism relies on willpower and adds stress, without changing the environment or the urge.

options.text: Quit for the evening and promise to do double tomorrow.
options.feedback: One wave becomes a lost day, and the double-tomorrow promise usually fails too.

exercises.why: Surf the urge and add friction at the same time. Naming and rating makes the urge an event, and moving the phone adds friction for next time. Giving in rewards the urge and feeds the loop, scolding relies on willpower, and quitting turns one wave into a lost day.

task.title: Redesign one study spot
task.brief: Change your environment tonight so that your ABAP practice is easier to start and your biggest distraction is harder to reach.
steps: Identify your biggest distraction (an app, a game or a site) and note how many steps it takes to open it now.
Add at least two friction steps: for example log out, move the app into a hidden folder, set a password-protected time limit, or charge the phone in another room.
Remove friction from your habit: open the practice file or notes and leave the laptop ready on the desk.
Write one temptation bundle rule and one stake with an amount and a friend who checks.
Tomorrow, count how many times you reached for the distraction compared with today.
checklist: I wrote the number of steps before and after
I added at least two friction steps to the distraction
My habit takes one step to begin
I wrote a bundle rule and a stake with an amount
task.evidencePrompt: Describe your two friction changes, your bundle rule and your stake.

quiz.prompt: Which action ADDS friction to a distracting habit?
options: Logging out and moving the app into a folder on the last screen
Placing the app on your home screen
Keeping the phone on the desk for convenience
Turning on notifications so you do not miss anything
quiz.why: Logging out and burying the app adds steps. The other options make the app easier or louder, which strengthens the cue.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is the best commitment device?
options: Telling yourself you will try harder next week
Making a private promise in your diary
Writing a long list of goals
Pre-paying for a 10-session mock test series and booking each slot with a friend
quiz.why: Pre-paying and booking with a friend commits your future self and involves another person. Private promises and lists can be quietly ignored.

quiz.prompt: Which is a true temptation bundle?
options: Watching your favourite series whenever you like, and studying whenever you can
Studying for an hour and then deciding what to do next
Listening to your favourite podcast only while doing flashcards
Buying a new notebook because you studied once
quiz.why: Bundling links something you want to something you need to do, and allows the want only with the need. The other options do not tie the two together.

quiz.prompt: Urge surfing treats an urge like a ____ that rises, peaks and falls. Fill in the one-word image.
quiz.why: An urge rises, peaks and falls like a wave, usually within minutes, whether or not you obey it. You watch it instead of acting.

bank.prompt: Arjun wants to drink more water at work. His bottle is in his bag under the desk. What is the best friction fix?
options: Place a filled bottle on the desk in view
Set a reminder to drink water more often
Buy a bigger bottle and keep it in the bag
bank.why: Putting the bottle in view removes friction and adds a visual cue. Reminders and guilt rely on willpower, and a bigger bottle in the bag does not change visibility.

bank.prompt: You agree to pay a friend ₹100 for every skipped workout. Over a month you skip 3 workouts. How much do you pay in rupees? (number only)
bank.why: 3 x ₹100 = ₹300. Predictable arithmetic is part of what makes a commitment device effective.

bank.prompt: During urge surfing, you rate an urge 8 out of 10, wait 10 minutes and rate it 4. What does this show?
options: The method failed because the urge is still there
Urges fade on their own when you watch them instead of obeying
You must suppress urges completely to succeed
bank.why: The drop from 8 to 4 shows that urges pass without being acted on. The goal is not zero urge or special willpower, but seeing that you can let it pass.

cards.front: How do you use friction to change habits?
cards.back: Remove steps between you and the habit you want (laptop open, file ready). Add steps before the distraction (log out, hide the app, charge the phone elsewhere).

cards.front: What makes a commitment device work?
cards.back: It is decided in advance, specific, with a modest real stake, and enforced by another person or system so you cannot quietly cancel it.
Pairing something you want with something you need to do, and allowing the want only together with the need, for example a favourite podcast only during flashcards.

cards.front: What are the steps of urge surfing?
cards.back: Name the urge, rate it 1 to 10, breathe, set a 10-minute timer and watch the number change without acting. Re-rate at the end.

discipline-2.reflection: Which distraction in your space has the lowest friction right now, and what is the single smallest change that would make it harder to reach tonight?

keyPoints: Add friction to distractions; remove it from the habit you want.
Use layers for the phone: remove, hide and delay, replace.
A commitment device is specific, small, and enforced by someone else.
Bundle a want with a need, only together.
Name, rate and wait out an urge for 10 minutes.
revision.redo: Look at your desk or phone and make one change that adds a step to a distraction or removes a step from your habit.

discipline-3.title: Systems Beat Motivation
discipline-3.summary: Plan for low-energy days with minimum versions, a never-miss-twice rule and a streak method that survives lapses.
objectives: Explain why motivation and energy rise and fall, and plan around your own cycle.
Write a three-tier habit with a minimum version you can do on your worst day.
Apply the never-miss-twice rule and a four-step recovery script after a lapse.

explanation.heading: Motivation is weather; a system is the roof
explanation.body:
Last time you shaped your environment so good habits were easier. Today's question is what happens on the days when even a well-designed environment is not enough, because you are tired, anxious or simply flat.

Motivation behaves like weather: it changes by the day and you cannot schedule it. Energy follows body rhythms too. Most people have a high-energy window (often mid-morning or early evening), a dip after lunch, and a slump late at night. A **system** is whatever still works when the weather is bad: a fixed cue, a tiny starting action and a pre-decided fallback.

A useful fact: motivation often *follows* action. Many people feel keen only after five minutes of starting. So the rule is not 'wait until I feel like it' but 'start small and let the feeling catch up'.

*Worked example:* Aman plans two hours of ABAP practice every evening. During a heavy project week he gets home at 8:30 pm, exhausted, and does nothing for five days. His plan had one version only, so any bad day became a failed day. The fix is not more willpower; it is a plan with more than one size.

explanation.heading: Minimum versions: the three-tier habit
explanation.body:
Write every important habit in three sizes:

- **Minimum** (2 to 10 minutes): so easy that you can do it when ill, travelling or stressed.
- **Standard** (your normal plan): done on ordinary days.
- **Stretch** (a bonus): done only when energy is high.

For ABAP study the tiers might be: Minimum, open the editor and write or read one SELECT statement (10 minutes). Standard, 60 minutes on one exercise from your course. Stretch, 120 minutes building a small report with a selection screen.

Two rules make this work. First, **choose the tier by your energy at the cue, not by guilt**. Second, **the minimum counts as a full success**. If a minimum feels like cheating, it is too big or your scoring is too harsh. A good minimum fails the 'worst day test': could I still do this on the worst day of the month? If not, shrink it.

A common mistake is to set the minimum at half of the standard, which is still 30 minutes. Shrink by *effort*, not by fraction: the goal is to keep the identity of 'someone who shows up'.

explanation.heading: Never miss twice
explanation.body:
Everyone misses. What separates people who keep habits for years is what happens next. **One miss is an accident; two misses is the start of a new habit.** The rule is simple: after a missed day, the next day's minimum is non-negotiable.

The danger is the *what-the-hell effect*: after one slip you think 'my streak is ruined, so I may as well skip the week'. The slip was small; the story you tell about it is what does the damage.

Use a four-step **recovery script** within 24 hours of a miss:

1. **Notice**: say 'I missed yesterday' without adding 'because I am lazy'.
2. **Name the cause**: practical, not personal (late bus, no charger, family function).
3. **Shrink**: do the minimum version at the next cue, with no catching up.
4. **Fix one thing**: move the cue, prepare the night before, or lower the standard for that day of the week.

Catching up ('I'll do double tomorrow') is the wrong response; it makes tomorrow harder and teaches your brain that habits are punishments.

explanation.heading: Streaks and lapses: track the ratio, not the chain
explanation.body:
Streak counters are motivating until the day they reset to zero, and then they can be crushing. Use a streak as a tool, never as the judge of your character.

A more forgiving measure is **consistency ratio**: days done divided by days planned. Suppose your week is Mon yes, Tue yes, Wed no, Thu yes, Fri yes, Sat no, Sun yes. That is 5 of 7 days, which is 71%. The next week you do 6 of 7, which is 86%. Over four weeks of 5, 6, 5 and 7 days you have done 23 of 28 days, which is 82%. The chain broke several times, yet the habit is clearly alive.

Set a floor such as 'at least 5 days a week' and a trigger such as 'if I drop below 4, I shrink the plan'. Review weekly, not daily, so one bad day cannot rewrite the story. Remember that you are building the identity of a person who returns, not a person who is perfect.

examples.title: Same person, two plans
examples.body:
Plan A: 'Study ABAP 2 hours daily after college.' Result: 4 good days, then a bad week, then nothing for a month.

Plan B: Minimum 10 minutes (one SELECT), Standard 60 minutes, Stretch 120 minutes, cue: after dinner plates are washed. On a bad Wednesday Aman does the 10-minute minimum, ticks it, and goes to bed. On Saturday he does the stretch.
examples.takeaway: Plan B has the same ambition but survives low-energy days; it also lets high-energy days pay extra.

examples.title: A lapse recovery in practice
