examples.body: Priya misses Monday and Tuesday because of a family function. Wednesday morning she writes: 'Missed 2 days. Cause: travel, no laptop. Fix: keep a notes app list of five ABAP questions to review on my phone when travelling.' That evening she does the 10-minute minimum, not a double session.
examples.takeaway: She names a practical cause, adds one fix, and returns at minimum size instead of punishing herself with catch-up work.

examples.title: Reading a month of data
examples.body: Habit log for 30 days: 24 days done, 6 missed, longest streak 9 days, current streak 3. Consistency: 24 / 30 = 80%. A reader fixated on the current streak of 3 would feel like a failure; the ratio shows an 80% habit.
examples.takeaway: The ratio tells the truth about the habit; the streak counter only tells you about the last few days.

exercises.prompt: You want to practise coding for 90 minutes each evening. Which is the best 'minimum version' for your worst days?
options: Code for 45 minutes, which is half the plan.
Plan the whole week of practice on paper.
Skip the day and make it up on Sunday.
Open your editor and write one working 5-line program, about 10 minutes.
exercises.hint: Think about the worst day of the month, not the average day.
exercises.why: A minimum must pass the worst-day test, so it is an effort-sized action you can always do. Half the plan (45 minutes) is still too heavy on a flat day, planning is not practising, and skipping to make up later is the pattern that breaks habits.

exercises.prompt: You planned a habit on 7 days this week and did it on 5 days. What is your consistency ratio, to the nearest whole percent? Write the number only.
exercises.hint: Divide days done by days planned.
exercises.why: 5 divided by 7 is 0.714, so the ratio is about 71%. Looking at the ratio instead of a broken chain shows that the habit is still mostly working.

exercises.prompt: You want to practise SQL or ABAP for one hour each evening, but on lab days you reach home at 8:30 pm and are exhausted. Write a three-tier version (minimum, standard, stretch) of this habit with a time for each tier, one cue, and one rule for how you choose the tier on a given day.

descriptors.1: Two tiers, or tiers without times.
descriptors.2: Three tiers with times, but the sizes are not clearly different.
descriptors.3: Three distinct tiers with realistic times (for example 10, 60 and 120 minutes).

descriptors.0: The minimum is as hard as the normal plan.
descriptors.1: The minimum is smaller but still needs 30+ minutes or heavy setup.
descriptors.2: The minimum is small, but it needs some preparation or setup.
descriptors.3: The minimum is under 10 minutes, needs almost no setup, and could be done at 8:30 pm exhausted.

descriptors.1: A rule exists but it is based on guilt or mood only.
descriptors.2: A rule based on energy or time, but vague.
descriptors.3: A clear if-then rule based on energy or time available, for example 'if I reach home after 8 pm, I do the minimum'.

descriptors.1: A vague time such as 'in the evening'.
descriptors.3: A specific existing routine used as the cue (for example, after dinner dishes).

exercises.modelAnswer: Cue: after I finish dinner. Minimum (10 minutes): open the editor and write one SELECT query or one small program. Standard (60 minutes): one full course exercise. Stretch (120 minutes): build a small report with a selection screen on a weekend. Rule: if I reach home after 8 pm or feel drained, I do the minimum and count it as done; on ordinary days I do the standard; stretch only on Saturday when I have energy.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer shows three different sizes, with the minimum small enough for 8:30 pm on a lab day. The most common mistake is a minimum like '30 minutes instead of 60', which is still a real study session. Check that your rule says what to do when you are tired, and that finishing the minimum is counted as a success. Score each criterion by comparing with the model answer honestly.

exercises.prompt: You had a 40-day study streak, but a family function made you miss three days in a row. The tracker has reset to zero and you think, 'I will restart properly next Monday.' It is Wednesday evening. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for Monday to restart so the new streak begins cleanly.
options.feedback: Waiting turns a three-day lapse into a five-day one and invites the what-the-hell effect.

options.text: Do double sessions for the next three days to catch up.
options.feedback: Catching up makes tomorrow harder and treats the habit as a debt to repay, which usually leads to another miss.

options.text: Tonight, do the 10-minute minimum, note the cause (travel, no laptop), add one fix, and judge the habit by 37 of 40 days.
options.feedback: This follows the recovery script: notice, name the cause, shrink and fix one thing, and it uses the ratio rather than the broken streak.

options.text: Drop the habit for now; you will pick it up after exams when life is calmer.
options.feedback: One lapse is not evidence that the habit does not fit; shrinking the habit is a better response than quitting.

exercises.why: The best response restarts at once at minimum size and reads the lapse as data. Waiting, catching up and quitting all let one miss become several.

task.title: Build your three-tier habit and test it
task.brief: Create a minimum, standard and stretch version of one real habit, then test the minimum tomorrow on purpose.
steps: Pick one habit that matters to your goals, such as daily coding practice, reading or exercise.
Write its three tiers with exact times. Check the minimum against the worst-day test.
Write one if-then rule for choosing the tier, based on your energy.
Write your four-step recovery script (notice, name cause, shrink, fix one thing) on a card.
Do the minimum version tomorrow at your usual cue and log it.
checklist: I wrote three tiers with times
I wrote the four recovery steps
task.evidencePrompt: Write your three tiers with times and your tier-choosing rule.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about motivation is most accurate?
options: It stays the same if you set big goals.
It often arrives after you start a small action, so starting can come before feeling ready.
It should be present before any habit is attempted.
It is mainly a matter of character that cannot change.
quiz.why: Motivation fluctuates daily and frequently follows action. Waiting for it to appear first is a common trap; the other options treat it as constant, a precondition or a fixed trait.

quiz.prompt: In a three-tier habit, what is the smallest, easiest version called? (one word)
quiz.why: The minimum version is the smallest action that still counts, so that bad days do not break the habit.

quiz.prompt: You missed yesterday's habit. What does 'never miss twice' tell you to do today?
options: Do the minimum version at your next cue, without catching up.
Do double today to make up for yesterday.
Reset your goal to a bigger one.
quiz.why: After one miss, return immediately at minimum size. Doubling up adds pressure, waiting invites a second miss, and a bigger goal makes the return harder.

quiz.prompt: Why is a consistency ratio often a better measure than a streak counter?
options: It shows only your best days.
It does not reset to zero after one miss, so one lapse cannot erase the evidence that the habit works.
It removes the need to track.
quiz.why: A ratio such as 24 of 30 days stays informative after a lapse. A streak resets to zero and can make a mostly successful habit look like a failure.

bank.prompt: A student studies best at 7 am but keeps scheduling hard problems at 11 pm after being tired all day. What is the most useful change?
options: Put the hardest work in the high-energy window and light tasks in the low one.
bank.why: Matching the task to your energy cycle gets more from the same hours. Trying harder at 11 pm relies on willpower, and dropping a schedule removes the system.

bank.prompt: Over four weeks you did a gym habit on 5, 4, 6 and 5 days out of 28 planned days. How many days did you do in total?
bank.why: 5 + 4 + 6 + 5 = 20 days, a ratio of 20/28 which is about 71%.

bank.prompt: After missing a day, someone thinks 'the streak is gone, so I may as well skip this week.' What is this pattern called?
bank.why: The what-the-hell effect is giving up entirely after a small slip. The planning fallacy is about underestimating time, attention residue is about task switching, and temptation bundling pairs a habit with a treat.

cards.front: How should you treat motivation when designing habits?
cards.back: As unreliable weather. Build a system with a fixed cue, a tiny start and a fallback, because motivation often follows action.

cards.front: What are the three tiers of a habit, and what is the test for the minimum?
cards.back: Minimum, standard and stretch. The minimum must pass the worst-day test: you could still do it when ill, tired or travelling.

cards.front: What are the four steps of the lapse recovery script?
cards.back: Notice the miss without self-blame, name a practical cause, shrink to the minimum version at the next cue, and fix one thing in your setup.

cards.front: How do you calculate a consistency ratio?
cards.back: Days done divided by days planned. For example, 5 of 7 days is 71%. Review it weekly instead of watching the streak daily.

discipline-3.reflection: Think of the last time you dropped a habit completely. What was the story you told yourself after the first miss, and what minimum version would have kept you going?

keyPoints: Motivation is weather; build a system that works on bad days.
Write three tiers: minimum, standard, stretch. The minimum counts as success.
One miss is an accident; never miss twice.
Recover in four steps: notice, name the cause, shrink, fix one thing.
Track the consistency ratio (days done / days planned), not just the streak.
revision.redo: Look at one habit you care about and write its minimum version in one line, then say aloud what you will do after your next miss.

discipline-4.title: Focus and Deep Work
discipline-4.summary: Protect long blocks of attention, log distractions, practise deliberately and close each day with a shutdown ritual.
objectives: Explain attention residue and why switching tasks costs more than it seems.
Run a 50-minute focus block with a distraction log.
Use a shutdown ritual so work stops cleanly at the end of the day.

explanation.heading: Why switching is expensive
explanation.body:
When you leave one task for another, part of your attention stays behind on the first one. This is called **attention residue**. Checking a single WhatsApp message in the middle of writing a SQL query does not cost ten seconds; it can cost several minutes before your thinking is as sharp as before. A day full of small switches leaves you busy but shallow, with the feeling of having worked hard and produced little.

Deep work means giving one demanding task your full, uninterrupted attention. For a student preparing for SAP ABAP, this is the difference between reading a chapter while glancing at the phone and actually understanding internal tables well enough to write a program without notes.

explanation.heading: Focus blocks and the distraction log
explanation.body:
A **focus block** is a fixed period, usually 50 minutes, with one task, the phone out of reach, notifications off and a short break afterwards. Start with 25 minutes if 50 feels long, and add five minutes each week. Before the block write one sentence: "At the end I will have ___". A clear finish line stops drifting.

Keep a **distraction log**: a paper slip beside you. Each time the urge to check something appears, write one word (for example "cricket score", "email", "reel") and return to work. The log does two things. It lets the urge pass without acting, and at the end of the week it shows your real triggers. Most people discover two or three repeating ones, and those can be removed at the source: phone in another room, site blockers, or a set time to check messages.

explanation.heading: Deliberate practice
explanation.body:
Time spent is not the same as skill gained. **Deliberate practice** means working at the edge of your ability with a specific target, immediate feedback and repetition of the weak part. Re-reading notes feels productive but is easy. Writing an ABAP loop from memory, checking it against the answer and redoing the line you got wrong is hard and effective.

Use four steps: choose one small skill, attempt it without help, check the result against a correct version, then repeat only the part that failed. Thirty minutes of this beats two hours of passive review.

explanation.heading: The shutdown ritual
explanation.body: Unfinished tasks keep nagging at the mind in the evening. A **shutdown ritual** is a short fixed routine, five minutes at most, that tells your brain the day is closed. Review what is done, write tomorrow's top three tasks, note any loose thread in one line, tidy your desk and say a closing phrase such as "Done for today". Because the plan exists on paper, your mind can rest, and tomorrow starts without a decision about where to begin.

examples.title: A real focus block
examples.body: Aman sets a 50-minute timer, leaves his phone in the next room and writes: "At the end I will have solved six SQL join problems." He logs three urges: "reel", "email", "tea". After the block he sees "reel" appears daily at the same time, so he moves his phone charger outside his study room.
examples.takeaway: The log turns urges into data you can act on.

examples.title: Deliberate versus passive
examples.body: Priya reads a chapter on data types twice and feels confident. Her friend writes ten declarations from memory, compares them with the book, finds three errors and repeats those three. The friend learns more in 30 minutes.
examples.takeaway: Attempt, check, repeat the weak part.

exercises.prompt: What is attention residue?
options: Part of your attention staying on the previous task after you switch
exercises.why: After switching, thoughts of the earlier task linger and slow the new one.

exercises.prompt: A shutdown ritual includes writing tomorrow's top ____ tasks. (one word)
exercises.why: Writing the top three tasks lets the mind rest tonight and start fast tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Design your next focus block: the task, the finish sentence ("At the end I will have..."), the length, where your phone will be and what you will write in the distraction log.

descriptors.3: One clear task with a visible finish line.
Specific place for phone and notifications off.
Method and what you will do with the results.

exercises.modelAnswer: Task: solve six SQL join problems. Finish: "At the end I will have six solved queries and notes on two errors." Length: 50 minutes. Phone in my bag in the other room, notifications off. I will keep a paper slip and write one word per urge, then review the slip on Sunday and remove the most frequent trigger.
exercises.guidance: Strong plans have one task, a finish line that you can check, a phone out of reach and a plan to review the log. Avoid listing three tasks in one block.

exercises.prompt: You have 30 minutes to improve at writing SELECT queries. Which plan is best?

options.text: Re-read your notes twice.
options.feedback: Re-reading feels easy but gives weak feedback.

options.text: Write five queries from memory, check each, and redo the ones you missed.
options.feedback: This has a target, feedback and repetition of weak parts.

options.text: Watch a long video at double speed.
options.feedback: Passive watching builds little recall.

options.text: Copy solved queries into your notebook.
options.feedback: Copying involves no retrieval or checking.

exercises.why: Deliberate practice combines attempt, feedback and repeating the failed part.

task.title: Run one 50-minute focus block
task.brief: Complete one distraction-logged focus block today and a shutdown ritual tonight.
steps: Write your finish sentence and set a 50-minute timer.
Put your phone in another room and keep a paper distraction log.
After the block count urges and name the top trigger.
Tonight write tomorrow's top three tasks and say your closing phrase.
task.evidencePrompt: Write your finish sentence, urge count, top trigger and tomorrow's top three tasks.

quiz.prompt: Checking messages during a coding task mainly costs you:
quiz.why: Residue from the switch slows full focus for minutes.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of the distraction log?
options: To let urges pass and reveal repeating triggers
quiz.why: Logging lets you resist the urge and shows triggers to remove.

quiz.prompt: Which element is essential to deliberate practice?
options: Feedback and repeating the weak part
quiz.why: Feedback on a specific weak point is what drives improvement.

quiz.prompt: The shutdown ritual lasts at most ____ minutes. (one word)
quiz.why: It is short, five minutes at most, so you will actually do it.

bank.prompt: To reduce attention residue you should:
options: Finish or park a task cleanly before switching
bank.why: Parking a task with a note frees attention for the next.

bank.prompt: A good focus block has:
options: One task, one finish line and phone away
bank.why: One clear task and fewer distractions make it work.

bank.prompt: Why write tomorrow's plan tonight?
options: So your mind can rest and tomorrow starts fast
bank.why: A written plan closes open loops in the mind.

cards.back: Part of your attention stays on the old task after you switch, which lowers quality on the new one.
One task, finish sentence, 25-50 minutes, phone away, urges logged on paper.
Pick a small skill, attempt without help, check against a correct version, repeat the failed part.

cards.front: What goes in a shutdown ritual?
cards.back: Review done work, write tomorrow's top three, note loose threads, tidy up, say a closing phrase.

discipline-4.reflection: Which distraction appears most often in your day, and what is one change that would remove it at the source?

keyPoints: Switching leaves attention residue.
Use a single-task focus block with a distraction log.
Practise deliberately with feedback.
End the day with a shutdown ritual.
revision.redo: Run another focus block and compare your urge count with the first.

english-1.title: Sentence Backbone and Articles
english-1.summary: Build correct, natural sentences by mastering word order, articles, prepositions and agreement.
objectives: Build sentences on a clear subject-verb-object backbone.
Choose a, an, the or no article correctly in common situations.
Avoid five frequent workplace errors, including 'discuss about' and 'revert back'.

explanation.heading: Every clear sentence has a backbone
explanation.body:
English depends on word order more than many languages do. The default order is **Subject - Verb - Object**: *Priya fixed the bug.* Who did it, what they did, to what. When a sentence feels confusing, find the backbone first and then add detail around it.

A useful habit is to say the backbone out loud before you add extras. 'The team finished the report' is the backbone. 'The team finished the quarterly report yesterday after a long meeting' adds time and context, but the backbone is still intact. Long sentences go wrong when the backbone gets buried or when the subject and verb drift apart.

explanation.heading: Articles: a, an, the, or nothing
explanation.body:
Use **a/an** for one non-specific thing the listener does not yet know: *I need a laptop.* Use **an** before a vowel *sound*, not just a vowel letter: *an hour*, *an MBA*, but *a university*, *a user*.

Use **the** when the listener knows which one: because you mentioned it before, because it is unique, or because the situation makes it obvious. *I bought a laptop. The laptop is fast.* *The sun rises in the east.* *Please close the door.*

Use **no article** for general plural or uncountable ideas: *Engineers solve problems. Honesty matters.* A quick test: ask 'Which one?' If the listener can answer, use *the*. If it is any one of many, use *a/an*. If you mean the whole category, use no article.

explanation.heading: Verbs that hold a preposition, and verbs that must not
explanation.body:
Some verbs already contain the meaning of a preposition, so adding one is an error. Say *discuss the plan*, not *discuss about the plan*. Say *reach the office*, not *reach to the office*. Say *emphasise the point*, not *emphasise on the point*. Other verbs need a fixed preposition: *depend on*, *agree with a person*, *agree to a proposal*, *apologise for a mistake*, *wait for a reply*.

A second family of errors is redundancy. *Revert back* repeats itself because *revert* already means go back; say *revert* or, more plainly, *reply*. *Return back*, *repeat again* and *cousin brother* are similar. Plain, short phrases sound more professional than padded ones.

explanation.heading: Agreement: make the verb match the real subject
explanation.body:
The verb agrees with the subject, not with the nearest noun. *The list of requirements **is** long.* The subject is *list*, so the verb is singular. *Everyone **has** a role.* Words like everyone, each, nobody and someone are singular.

Watch the third-person -s in the present tense: *She works, they work.* This small -s is the single most common slip in fast speech. Slow down on the verb, and check it against the subject in your mind. Reading your own writing aloud will catch most agreement errors.

examples.title: A status update, before and after
examples.body:
Before: 'We discussed about the issue and revert back to you with solution by tomorrow.'

After: 'We discussed the issue. I will reply with a solution by tomorrow.'
examples.takeaway: Remove 'about' after discuss, replace 'revert back' with a plain verb, and add the missing article and a clear subject.

examples.title: Articles across a short story
examples.body: 'I opened a ticket for a login problem. The problem happens only on mobile. Developers on the team asked for screenshots.'
examples.takeaway: First mention uses a; second mention uses the; general plural (Developers) takes no article, while 'the team' is a specific known group.

examples.title: Finding the true subject
examples.body: 'The quality of these reports has improved.' The subject is quality, so the verb is has, not have, even though 'reports' sits closer to the verb.
examples.takeaway: Ignore the phrase that starts with 'of' when you are choosing the verb form.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct and natural in a workplace email?
options: Let us discuss about the schedule tomorrow.
Let us discuss the schedule tomorrow.
Let us discuss on the schedule tomorrow.
Let us discuss regarding the schedule tomorrow.
exercises.hint: Discuss already means talk about something.
exercises.why: 'Discuss' takes its object directly: discuss the schedule. Adding about, on or regarding is an error because the verb already carries that meaning.

exercises.prompt: Complete with a, an or the: 'I attended ____ interview yesterday. ____ interviewer asked about my project.' Write your two answers separated by a comma.
exercises.hint: Interview begins with a vowel sound. The interviewer was introduced by the first sentence.
exercises.why: 'An interview' is a first mention that begins with a vowel sound. 'The interviewer' is now a specific, known person, so the is correct.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite this sentence so it is clear and correct, in two or three shorter sentences: 'The meeting that we had with the client yesterday about the delay in the delivery of the modules which were promised last month were not so good and I will revert back to you with the next steps after discuss about it with team.'

descriptors.0: Still one long tangled sentence with no clear backbone.
descriptors.1: Split into shorter sentences but some still bury the subject and verb.
descriptors.2: Mostly clear sentences; one is still wordy or unclear.
descriptors.3: Every sentence has a clear subject, verb and object and is easy to follow.

rubric.label: Errors removed (revert back, discuss about, agreement, articles)

descriptors.1: One or two of the errors were fixed; others remain.
descriptors.2: Most errors were fixed; one remains.
descriptors.3: All errors fixed: no 'revert back', no 'discuss about', correct agreement, and 'the team' or 'my team'.

auto.label: None of 'revert back', 'discuss about' or 'were not so good' remain

descriptors.1: Some key information missing (client, delay, next steps).
descriptors.2: Meaning preserved with a small omission.
descriptors.3: All key points kept: the client meeting, the delay, the next steps.

exercises.modelAnswer: The meeting with the client yesterday did not go well. The delivery of the modules promised last month is delayed. I will discuss it with my team and reply with the next steps.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer finds the backbone ('The meeting did not go well'), splits the long sentence into two or three, removes 'revert back' and 'discuss about', and fixes the agreement between 'meeting' and the verb. A common mistake is to shorten the text by dropping the client or the next steps; keep the meaning. Compare your version with the model answer and score each criterion honestly.

exercises.prompt: Your manager asks you to send a short update to a client. You have a draft: 'We are discussing about the issue internally and will revert back by evening.' You have two minutes. What do you do?

options.text: Send it as it is; the client will understand.
options.feedback: The meaning is clear but two errors reduce your credibility with a client.

options.text: Change it to 'We are discussing the issue internally and will reply by evening.'
options.feedback: Correct: both errors removed, and the sentence stays short and professional.

options.text: Make it longer and more formal with extra phrases to sound polished.
options.feedback: Longer is not better; padded sentences hide the backbone and add more places for errors.

options.text: Ask a colleague to rewrite the whole update.
options.feedback: Getting help is fine, but with two minutes you should fix the known error patterns yourself.

exercises.why: The fastest professional fix is to apply the two rules you know: no 'about' after discuss, and a plain verb instead of 'revert back'.

task.title: Error hunt in your own writing
task.brief: Find and fix real errors in something you wrote recently.
steps: Open an email, chat message or assignment you wrote in the last week and copy 150 words into a note.
Underline every article, every verb followed by a preposition, and every subject-verb pair.
Correct each error you find and note which rule it broke.
Write your top two repeating errors at the top of the note.
checklist: I chose real writing of at least 100 words
I listed my top two repeating errors
task.evidencePrompt: Write your two repeating errors and one corrected sentence.

quiz.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.why: University begins with the sound 'yoo', a consonant sound, so the article is a. The is wrong because it is not a specific known student; and the article cannot be dropped for a singular countable noun.

quiz.prompt: Which phrase is redundant and best replaced?
quiz.why: Revert already means go back, so 'revert back' repeats itself. Use 'revert' or, more plainly, 'reply'.

quiz.prompt: Select the correct verb: 'The list of tasks ____ long.'
quiz.why: The subject is the singular noun 'list', not 'tasks'. A singular subject takes 'is'.

quiz.prompt: Name the verb in the backbone of this sentence: 'The new engineer quickly fixed the production bug.' (one word)
quiz.why: The backbone is 'engineer fixed bug'. 'Fixed' is the verb; 'quickly' modifies it and 'new' and 'production' modify nouns.

bank.prompt: Pick the best version: '____ honesty is important in ____ team.'
bank.why: Honesty as a general idea takes no article. 'A team' fits when you mean any team; 'the team' would need a known team. Option 2 is the natural general statement.

bank.prompt: Correct the phrase by writing only the correct verb phrase: 'We emphasise on quality.'
bank.why: Emphasise takes its object directly: emphasise quality.

bank.prompt: Which is correct?
bank.why: Everyone is grammatically singular, so it takes has.

cards.front: What is the default English word order?
cards.back: Subject - Verb - Object. Find the backbone first, then add detail.

cards.front: Article test: how do you decide between a, the and no article?
cards.back: Ask 'Which one?' If the listener knows, use the. If any one of many, use a/an. If the whole category, use no article.
discuss the plan; reply (or revert); emphasise the point. The verbs already carry the meaning.

cards.front: Which word controls the verb in 'The list of tasks ___ long'?
cards.back: The head noun 'list' (singular), not the noun in the 'of' phrase.

english-1.reflection: Which of your repeating errors do you think costs you the most credibility, and what is one cue that will remind you to check it?

keyPoints: Find the subject-verb-object backbone, then add detail.
Which one? test for articles.
No 'about' after discuss; no 'back' after revert.
The head noun controls the verb.
revision.redo: Rewrite one sentence from yesterday's messages, fixing any article, preposition or agreement slip, and say the corrected version aloud.

english-2.title: Tenses in Real Use
english-2.summary: Choose the right tense by meaning: present perfect versus past simple, plans, reported speech and time expressions.
objectives: Choose between present perfect and past simple by asking whether the time is finished or connected to now.
Use present continuous and 'going to' correctly for arrangements and plans.
Report what someone said using the correct backshift and time words.

concepts.label: Time expressions that signal the tense

explanation.heading: Choose the tense by meaning, not by memorised rule
explanation.body:
In the last lesson you built the sentence backbone. Now we choose the verb form that sits inside it. Most tense mistakes come from memorising rules instead of asking one question: **what is the relationship between this action and now?**

If the action belongs to a finished time, use the **past simple**: *I joined the project in March.* If the action is connected to the present, because the result is still visible, the period is still open, or the experience counts today, use the **present perfect**: *I have joined three client calls this week.*

explanation.heading: Present perfect versus past simple
explanation.body:
Use the **present perfect (have/has + past participle)** for three situations:

- A result that matters now: *The build has failed.* (So we cannot deploy.)
- An experience with no finished time named: *I have worked with Oracle databases.*
- An unfinished period: *this week*, *this month*, *so far*, *since Monday*.

Use the **past simple** the moment you name a finished time: *yesterday*, *last week*, *in 2024*, *two days ago*. You cannot say *I have submitted the form yesterday*. Say *I submitted the form yesterday* or *I have submitted the form.*

Worked example: a manager asks, 'Is the report ready?' You answer, 'Yes, I have finished it' because the result matters now. If she asks, 'When did you finish it?' you answer, 'I finished it at 4 pm', because now the time is finished and named.

explanation.heading: Plans and arrangements
explanation.body:
Indian English often uses the simple present for plans, as in *I go to Pune tomorrow*. Standard usage prefers the **present continuous** for fixed arrangements: *I am going to Pune tomorrow; my ticket is booked.* Use **going to** for intentions and predictions based on evidence: *I am going to learn ABAP this year. Look at those clouds, it is going to rain.* Use **will** for decisions made at the moment of speaking and for promises: *I'll send the file now.*

A quick test: has the plan already been arranged with other people or tickets? Use the present continuous. Is it an intention in your head? Use going to. Are you deciding right now? Use will.

explanation.heading: Reporting what people said
explanation.body:
When you report speech, the tense usually moves one step back and the time words change. *'I will send the file tomorrow'* becomes *She said she would send the file the next day.* *'I am working on it'* becomes *He said he was working on it.* *'I have finished'* becomes *She said she had finished.*

Notice that *said* is not followed by *to* unless you name the listener: *She told me she would send it*, but *She said she would send it.* Questions lose their question order: *'Where is the file?'* becomes *He asked where the file was*, not *where was the file*.

If the statement is still true or very recent, you may keep the original tense: *She said the meeting is at 3.* Practise by retelling one real conversation each evening in two sentences.

examples.title: Stand-up update, wrong and right
examples.body:
Wrong: 'Yesterday I have fixed the login bug and today I am testing it. I am working here since January.'

Right: 'Yesterday I fixed the login bug and today I am testing it. I have been working here since January.'
examples.takeaway: 'Yesterday' names a finished time, so past simple. 'Since January' starts in the past and continues now, so present perfect (continuous).

examples.title: Turning a client call into a report
examples.body:
The client said: 'We need the modules by Friday. We are testing the first batch now. Did you send the document?'

Your note: 'The client said they needed the modules by Friday. They said they were testing the first batch. They asked whether we had sent the document.'
examples.takeaway: Each verb moves one step back, 'now' would become 'then' in a later report, and the question uses statement order after 'whether'.

examples.title: Three ways to talk about next week
examples.body:
'I am meeting the HR team on Monday.' (fixed arrangement)
'I am going to prepare for the SAP interview.' (intention)
'Let me check the calendar. I will confirm by evening.' (decision now)
examples.takeaway: The same future time needs different forms depending on how settled the plan is.

exercises.prompt: Write the correct form of the verb 'submit' to complete: 'I ____ the assignment last Friday.' (one word)
exercises.hint: 'Last Friday' is a finished time.
exercises.why: A named finished time (last Friday) needs the past simple, so 'submitted'. 'Have submitted' would be wrong with 'last Friday'.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I am living in Faridabad since 2022.
I have lived in Faridabad since 2022.
exercises.hint: 'Since' starts a period that continues to now.
exercises.why: 'Since 2022' needs the present perfect (have lived). Present simple, present continuous and past simple do not connect a past start to the present, so the other options are incorrect.

exercises.prompt: Report this speech by completing the sentence. The manager said, 'I am reviewing your code.' Write: 'The manager said that she ____ my code.' (use two or three words)
exercises.hint: Move the present continuous one step back.
exercises.why: Present continuous 'am reviewing' moves back to past continuous 'was reviewing' in reported speech.

exercises.prompt: Write a short progress update (four to six sentences) to your mentor about an assignment or project. Use at least one present perfect sentence about progress so far, one past simple sentence with a finished time, and one sentence about a plan for next week using the present continuous or going to.

rubric.label: Present perfect used for result or progress so far

descriptors.0: No present perfect sentence, or it is formed wrongly.
descriptors.1: Present perfect attempted but combined with a finished time word.
descriptors.2: Correct present perfect with a small slip.
descriptors.3: Correct present perfect clearly tied to the present result or an open period.

rubric.label: Past simple with a finished time

descriptors.1: Finished time mentioned but the verb is perfect or wrongly formed.
descriptors.2: Correct past simple with a small slip elsewhere.
descriptors.3: A clear finished time (yesterday, on Monday, last week) with a correct past simple verb.

rubric.label: Plan expressed with present continuous or going to

descriptors.0: No future plan, or the plan uses simple present.
descriptors.1: Plan present but form is incorrect.
descriptors.2: Correct form but the plan is vague.
descriptors.3: Correct form and a specific plan with a day or action.

auto.label: Uses going to or a present continuous plan

descriptors.2: Clear with a few awkward phrases.
descriptors.3: Clear, ordered from past to present to future, and polite.

exercises.modelAnswer: Hi Rahul sir, here is my progress update. I have completed the database design and I have written most of the queries so far. On Monday I presented the first version to my team, and they suggested two changes. Next week I am testing the changes on sample data, and I am going to prepare a short demo for Friday. Please let me know if you want any other detail.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers move from past to present to future. Check each sentence: if you named a finished time, the verb must be past simple; if you talk about progress so far or a result, use present perfect. A common mistake is writing 'I have presented on Monday'. Another is using simple present for plans ('I test it next week'). Score yourself honestly against the model.

task.title: Retell a real conversation in two tenses
task.brief: Practise reporting and tense choice using a real conversation from today.
steps: Recall a real conversation from today with a friend, teacher or colleague and note three things they said.
Write each as direct speech, then rewrite it as reported speech with the correct backshift.
Write three sentences about your own day: one present perfect, one past simple with a finished time, and one plan using the present continuous.
Read everything aloud once and fix any tense that sounds wrong.
checklist: I wrote three direct and three reported sentences
I moved each reported verb one step back
I used a finished time only with past simple
task.evidencePrompt: Write one reported sentence and one present perfect sentence from your practice.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I have seen the client yesterday.
I have saw the client yesterday.
I am seeing the client yesterday.
quiz.why: 'Yesterday' is a finished time, so the past simple 'saw' is correct. Present perfect cannot be used with a finished time word, and 'have saw' uses the wrong participle.

quiz.prompt: You have already booked a train ticket to Jaipur for Saturday. Which sentence is best?
options: I go to Jaipur on Saturday.
I will going to Jaipur on Saturday.
I went to Jaipur on Saturday.
I am going to Jaipur on Saturday.
quiz.why: A fixed arrangement uses the present continuous. Simple present is a timetable form, 'will going' is ungrammatical, and the past simple points to the wrong time.

quiz.prompt: Complete the reported sentence: 'I will send the file.' becomes 'She said she ____ send the file.' (one word)
quiz.why: In reported speech 'will' moves back to 'would'.

quiz.prompt: Which time expression normally goes with the present perfect?
quiz.why: 'So far this month' describes an unfinished period. 'Two days ago', 'in 2023' and 'last night' name finished times, which need the past simple.

bank.prompt: Complete with the correct form of 'work': 'I ____ at an IT firm for two years now.' Write the verb phrase (two words).
bank.why: 'For two years now' describes a period continuing to the present, so present perfect or present perfect continuous.

bank.prompt: A recruiter said, 'Where do you live?' Which report is correct?
options: She asked where did I live.
She asked me where I lived.
She asked me where do I live.
She told me where I lived.
bank.why: Reported questions use statement order and backshift: where I lived. 'Told' reports a statement, not a question.

bank.prompt: Your friend asks about your weekend. You have not decided anything but suddenly feel like seeing a film. Which reply fits?
options: I am going to see a film, I think maybe.
I will go and see a film, I think.
I see a film on Sunday.
I am seeing a film as I decided yesterday.
bank.why: A spontaneous decision made while speaking takes 'will'. Present continuous would suggest a booked plan, and simple present suggests a timetable.

cards.front: How do you choose between present perfect and past simple?
cards.back: Finished, named time: past simple. Result now, experience, or unfinished period: present perfect.

cards.front: Which time words signal present perfect and which signal past simple?
cards.back: Present perfect: since, for (continuing), so far, this week, ever. Past simple: yesterday, last week, ago, in 2024.

cards.front: Present continuous, going to or will for the future?
cards.back: Present continuous for fixed arrangements, going to for intentions or evidence, will for instant decisions and promises.

cards.front: What happens to verbs and questions in reported speech?
cards.back: Verbs usually shift one step back (will becomes would). Questions use statement order: he asked where the file was.

english-2.reflection: Which tense do you reach for automatically when you are nervous, and what is one sentence you can prepare today to practise the better choice?

keyPoints: Ask how the action relates to now.
Finished named time takes past simple.
Since, for, so far and this week take present perfect.
Present continuous for fixed arrangements.
Reported speech moves verbs back and uses statement order.
revision.redo: Say two sentences about today aloud: one present perfect about progress, one past simple with a named time. Then report one thing someone said to you.

english-3.title: Precise Vocabulary and Collocations
english-3.summary: Choose exact words, natural word partners and workplace phrasal verbs, and keep a notebook that makes new vocabulary stick.
objectives: Use natural collocations such as make a decision and raise an issue instead of word-for-word translations.
Replace vague words like good, thing and nice with precise words that carry real information.
Run a vocabulary notebook that records phrases in context and is reviewed on a schedule.

concepts.label: Replacing vague words and using word families

explanation.heading: Words travel in pairs: collocations
explanation.body:
Last time you chose tenses by meaning. Vocabulary works the same way: you choose by what sounds natural to a fluent ear, not by what is logically possible. A **collocation** is a pair or group of words that native speakers habitually use together. We **make** a decision, **take** a break, **do** research, **pay** attention, **raise** a concern and **meet** a deadline. Saying *do a decision* or *take a research* is understandable but sounds off, like wearing a shoe on the wrong foot.

The verbs make, do, take and have cause the most trouble. A rough guide: **make** is for creating or producing something new (a plan, a mistake, an effort, progress); **do** is for tasks and activities (homework, the dishes, a favour, business); **take** is for actions you carry out (a decision is *made*, but a *step*, *notes*, a *risk*, a *look* are taken); **have** is for experiences and events (a meeting, a conversation, a problem).

The fix is to learn words in chunks. Do not write down *deadline*; write *meet a deadline* and *miss a deadline*. When you store the chunk, the right verb comes automatically.

explanation.heading: Replace vague words with precise ones
explanation.body:
Vague words such as *good*, *nice*, *thing*, *stuff*, *very* and *big* take up space but carry little information. 'The demo was good' tells the manager nothing. 'The demo was smooth: no errors and the client asked for a follow-up' tells her everything.

A three-step method:

1. **Spot** the vague word when you reread your draft.
2. **Ask** 'In what way?' (fast, clear, thorough, reliable, polite, profitable).
3. **Replace** it with the specific word, or with a number or fact.

Worked example: 'We had a big problem with the thing in the login.' becomes 'We had a critical bug in the login module: users could not reset passwords.' *Critical* replaces *big*, *bug* replaces *problem*, *module* replaces *thing*, and the final clause adds evidence.

Use **word families** to widen your reach. From one root you get several useful forms: *decide, decision, decisive, decisively*; *analyse, analysis, analyst, analytical*; *succeed, success, successful, successfully*. When you learn *efficient*, also pick up *efficiency, efficiently, inefficient*. Each family lets you fit the same idea into different sentence shapes, which keeps your writing flexible.

explanation.heading: Phrasal verbs you will meet in every IT office
explanation.body:
A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word that changes the meaning: *look into* (investigate), *follow up* (check again later), *sort out* (solve), *roll out* (release gradually), *carry out* (perform), *set up* (arrange or install), *come up with* (invent), *run into* (meet by chance), *back up* (save a copy), *point out* (draw attention to), *hold up* (delay), *get back to* (reply later).

In a status call you might hear: 'We are **looking into** the outage; I will **get back to** you by five.' Or: 'The vendor **held up** the release, so we will **roll** it **out** next week.' Learn the meaning in one sentence, and notice that many have a more formal single-word partner: *look into = investigate*, *carry out = perform*, *set up = establish*, *point out = indicate*. In emails to clients prefer the formal verb; in team chats the phrasal verb is more natural.

Common mistake: guessing the particle. *Fill in a form* (or *fill out* in American English), *depend on*, *cope with*, *get along with* a colleague. If unsure, check how the whole chunk is written, not the verb alone.

explanation.heading: A notebook that actually sticks
explanation.body:
Most learners keep long word lists they never reread. A notebook that sticks has four rules.

- **Record phrases in context.** Write the sentence where you met the word, plus one sentence of your own about your life or work.
- **Keep it small.** Add three to five items per day, not thirty. Quality beats quantity.
- **Add the family and the partners.** Under *efficient*, write *efficiency*, and *highly efficient*, *energy-efficient*.
- **Review on a schedule.** Cover the answer and recall it after one day, one week and one month. Retrieving a word from memory is what locks it in; rereading does not.

Worked example of one entry: *meet a deadline* - 'We must meet the deadline for the sprint demo.' - My sentence: 'I met the deadline for my project report.' - Opposite: *miss a deadline*. Then use each new item in a real message within 48 hours. A word you have used aloud or in writing once is far more likely to stay.

examples.title: Fixing word-for-word translations
examples.body:
Before: 'I did a mistake in the report, so I will do a correction and take the decision after the meeting.'

After: 'I made a mistake in the report, so I will make a correction and take a decision after the meeting.' A fluent speaker would also say 'make a decision'.
examples.takeaway: Mistakes and corrections are made, decisions are made. Learn the verb together with the noun.

examples.title: From vague to precise in a status update
examples.body:
Before: 'The new feature is good and the testing was nice. There are some things left.'

After: 'The new feature is stable: it passed all 40 test cases. Three items remain: the error message, the logout button and the report export.'
examples.takeaway: Replace evaluation words with evidence, and replace 'things' with a named list.

examples.title: Phrasal verbs in a client call
examples.body: 'We ran into a problem during setup, but we have sorted it out. I will follow up tomorrow and point out the changes in a short note.'
examples.takeaway: Four phrasal verbs carry four precise actions: met unexpectedly, solved, checked later, drew attention to.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses a natural collocation?
options: We need to take a decision about the vendor immediately.
We need to do a decision about the vendor immediately.
We need to make a decision about the vendor immediately.
We need to put a decision about the vendor immediately.
exercises.hint: Think of creating or producing a result.
exercises.why: 'Make a decision' is the standard collocation (take a decision is also used in British English, but make is safest). 'Do a decision' is a translation error; 'put a decision' is not used.

exercises.prompt: Complete with one verb: 'We must ____ the deadline for the demo on Friday.'
exercises.hint: The opposite is 'miss'.
exercises.why: 'Meet a deadline' is the collocation. Do not use 'catch' or 'reach' for deadlines in standard workplace English.

exercises.prompt: Complete with a two-word phrasal verb meaning 'investigate': 'The support team is ____ the outage and will update you by five.' (two words, ing form)
exercises.hint: You look at a surface; you look ___ a problem to find the cause.
exercises.why: 'Looking into' means investigating. 'Looking at' only means examining visually, and 'looking after' means taking care of.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite this vague update for your project guide in 3 to 4 sentences, replacing every vague word with something precise (invent realistic facts): 'The project is going well. I did some good work on the thing this week and there are a few problems but nothing big. The next steps are nice and simple.'

rubric.label: Vague words replaced with specific words or facts

descriptors.0: Vague words such as good, thing, nice or some remain.
descriptors.1: One or two vague words are replaced; others remain.
descriptors.2: Most vague words are replaced with specific words but one claim has no evidence.
descriptors.3: Every vague word is replaced with a precise word, number or named item.

auto.label: None of the original vague phrases remain

rubric.label: Natural collocations and at least one phrasal verb

descriptors.0: Word-for-word or unnatural verb choices such as 'do a decision'.
descriptors.1: One natural collocation or phrasal verb used.
descriptors.2: Several natural collocations; phrasal verb missing or slightly misused.
descriptors.3: Natural collocations (make progress, meet a deadline, fix a bug) and a correct phrasal verb (sort out, follow up, look into).

descriptors.0: No clear progress or next steps.
descriptors.1: Progress or next steps are stated, but not both.
descriptors.3: Progress, one named problem and concrete next steps in short clear sentences.

exercises.modelAnswer: This week I completed the login module and fixed 12 of the 15 reported bugs. Three bugs remain: the password reset email is delayed, the logout button fails on mobile and the report export crashes on large files. I will sort these out by Wednesday and then run the full test cycle before I send you the demo link on Friday.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer turns every evaluation word into a fact: a count, a named module, a date. It uses natural collocations such as 'complete a module', 'fix bugs' and a phrasal verb like 'sort out'. Common mistakes are replacing 'good' with another vague word like 'excellent' or 'great' and listing next steps without dates. Score yourself against the model: could your guide act on your message without asking a question?

task.title: Start a ten-item vocabulary notebook
task.brief: Build and use a small notebook from real material you read this week.
steps: Read one work-related email, article or documentation page (about 300 words) and pick five chunks, not single words, that you would like to use.
Write each chunk in a notebook or notes app with the original sentence, one sentence of your own and any word-family forms.
Find five vague words in your own recent writing (good, thing, nice, very, some) and write a precise replacement for each.
Use at least three new chunks in a real message or conversation within 48 hours, and mark when you did.
Set a reminder to cover and recall the five chunks tomorrow, next week and next month.
checklist: I recorded chunks, not single words
Each entry has a sentence of my own
I replaced five vague words in my own writing
I used at least three chunks in a real message
task.evidencePrompt: List three chunks you recorded and one real sentence in which you used one of them.

quiz.prompt: Which verb completes the collocation: '____ attention to the error message'?
quiz.why: 'Pay attention' is the fixed collocation. 'Give attention' is rare and 'do' or 'take a' are not used with attention in this sense.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence replaces the vague word best? Original: 'The app is very good.'
options: The app is really very good.
The app is nice and good.
The app responds in under two seconds on a slow network.
The app is a good thing.
quiz.why: Only the third option adds evidence. The others stack vague words on top of each other and tell the reader nothing new.

quiz.prompt: Complete the phrasal verb meaning 'check again later': 'I will ____ up with the vendor tomorrow.' (one word)
quiz.why: 'Follow up' means to check or act again after an earlier contact.

quiz.prompt: Which notebook habit helps memory most?
options: Adding thirty new words in one sitting
Writing each chunk with a sentence of your own and recalling it after one day, one week and one month
Copying definitions from a dictionary neatly
Highlighting words in different colours and rereading them
quiz.why: Retrieval at spaced intervals plus personal context builds memory. Large batches, copying and rereading feel productive but fade quickly.

bank.prompt: Pick the natural sentence for a team meeting.
options: Let me do a suggestion about the schedule.
Let me make a suggestion about the schedule.
Let me put a suggestion about the schedule.
Let me take a suggestion about the schedule.
bank.why: 'Make a suggestion' is the standard collocation. 'Do' and 'take' do not combine with suggestion in this meaning.

bank.prompt: Give the noun form from the word family of 'efficient' (one word, meaning how well something uses time or resources).
bank.why: The family is efficient, efficiently, efficiency, inefficient. The noun is efficiency.

bank.prompt: A colleague says: 'We ran into a problem during setup.' What does 'ran into' mean here?
options: Crashed a vehicle into a wall
bank.why: In this context 'run into' means to meet something unexpected. It does not mean escaping or solving.

cards.front: Which verbs go with decision, mistake, deadline and research?
cards.back: Make a decision, make a mistake, meet a deadline, do research. Learn the verb and noun together as one chunk.

cards.front: Three-step method to replace a vague word?
cards.back: Spot it, ask 'In what way?', replace it with a precise word, number or fact.

cards.front: Meanings of look into, sort out, follow up, roll out?
cards.back: Investigate; solve; check again later; release gradually. Use the formal single verb in client emails.

cards.front: Four rules of a notebook that sticks?
cards.back: Record phrases in context, keep it small, add family and partners, review by recall after a day, a week and a month.

english-3.reflection: Which vague words or word-for-word translations appear most in your own speech or writing, and what is one precise replacement you will practise this week?

keyPoints: Learn words as chunks: make a decision, meet a deadline.
Replace vague words with a precise word, number or fact.
Phrasal verbs: look into, sort out, follow up, roll out.
Review notebook entries by recall at one day, one week, one month.
revision.redo: Pick three vague words from a message you wrote today, replace each with a precise word, and say the improved sentence aloud.

english-4.title: Speaking With Fluency
english-4.summary: Speak in chunks, pause instead of using fillers, structure answers clearly and build a five-minute daily recording routine.
objectives: Speak in meaningful chunks and replace filler words with short silent pauses.
Structure a spoken answer using point, reason, example, point.
Practise with shadowing and a five-minute daily self-recording routine.

explanation.heading: Fluency means flow, not speed
explanation.body:
In the last lesson you built better vocabulary. Now we use it aloud. Many learners believe fluent speakers talk fast. In fact fluency is about **flow**: ideas arriving in steady, meaningful groups with few stops in the wrong places. Rushing makes errors and hides your ideas; a slightly slower, steady pace is easier to understand, especially on phone calls with clients from other regions.

Fluent speakers do not say words one at a time. They speak in **chunks** of three to seven words that carry one idea, with a tiny pause at the boundary. Compare:

- Word by word: 'I... have... completed... the... testing... of... the... module.'
- In chunks: 'I have completed the testing / of the login module / and found three bugs.'

The second version is not faster, it just breaks at natural places: after a complete idea, before a preposition phrase, before 'and' or 'but'. To practise, take a paragraph and mark chunk boundaries with slashes, then read it aloud, pausing only at the slashes. A comfortable pace for explaining something is roughly 120 to 150 words per minute.

explanation.heading: Pause instead of filling
explanation.body:
Fillers such as *umm*, *aaa*, *like*, *you know* and *basically* appear when the brain needs time and the mouth refuses to be silent. A listener hears the filler as hesitation; a short silent pause sounds like confident thinking. A one-second pause is shorter than it feels to you.

The replacement technique has three steps:

1. **Notice** your habitual filler by recording yourself once (you will find one or two favourites).
2. **Plan the pause**: decide that when you feel the filler coming, you will close your lips and breathe for one beat.
3. **Bridge with a phrase** if you need longer: 'Let me think for a second', 'That is a good question', or restate the question: 'So, why did we choose Node.js?'

Do not aim for zero fillers on day one. Aim to halve them. In an interview, a pause before you answer shows you are thinking; a stream of 'umm' suggests you are searching for words.

explanation.heading: Structure your answer: point, reason, example, point
explanation.body:
Long, wandering answers lose listeners. The **PREP** structure gives every answer a spine:

1. **Point**: state your answer in one sentence.
2. **Reason**: give the main reason.
3. **Example**: give one concrete example.
4. **Point**: repeat the point, briefly, as a conclusion.

Worked example. Question: 'Why do you want to become an SAP ABAP consultant?'

'I want to start my career as an ABAP consultant (point) because it combines programming with real business processes (reason). In my college project I built a small inventory module, and I enjoyed turning a business rule into working logic (example). So ABAP lets me use my coding skills where they directly support business (point).'

That is four sentences and about 45 seconds. The same structure works for 'Tell me about a challenge', for stand-up updates ('Status, blocker, plan'), and for client questions. Common mistake: starting with the example and never stating the point. Lead with the point so the listener knows where you are going.

explanation.heading: Shadowing and the five-minute recording routine
explanation.body:
**Shadowing** means listening to a clear speaker for a few seconds and repeating immediately after, copying rhythm, stress and chunking, not just the words. It trains your mouth and ear together. Choose short audio of 20 to 40 seconds that is clearly spoken, play one sentence, pause it, and repeat in the same rhythm. Then repeat the whole clip along with the speaker, a half-beat behind.

Combine it with a **five-minute daily routine**:

- Minute 1: pick a topic (your day, a project, a concept you studied).
- Minutes 2-3: record yourself answering with the PREP structure.
- Minute 4: listen once and note two things: one filler habit and one word you stumbled on.
- Minute 5: record the answer again fixing just those two things.

The second take is where improvement happens. Keep the recordings in a folder; after two weeks, listen to the first and the latest. Most learners hear the difference immediately, and hearing your own progress is a powerful motivator.

examples.title: Chunking a stand-up update
examples.body: Slashes mark pauses: 'Yesterday I finished / the validation logic / for the order form. / Today I will write / the unit tests. / I have one blocker: / the test database is not accessible.'
examples.takeaway: Each chunk holds one idea of three to six words. The pauses make the update easy to follow and give you time to think.

examples.title: Filler-heavy versus paused answer
examples.body:
Filler: 'So, umm, basically, you know, I think, like, the project was, umm, about a, like, web app.'

Paused: 'My project was a web app (pause) for tracking college library books. (pause) I built the back end in Node.js.'
examples.takeaway: The second version is shorter, clearer and sounds more confident, even though the speaker had to think just as long.

examples.title: PREP in an interview
examples.body:
Question: 'Are you comfortable working in a team?'

Answer: 'Yes, I am. Teamwork helps me learn faster. In my final-year project, three of us divided the modules, and I reviewed a teammate's code every Friday. So I enjoy working in a team and can contribute actively.'
examples.takeaway: A clear point, a reason, a real example and a short closing line, in about 30 seconds.

exercises.prompt: Which version is chunked in the most natural way?
options: I have completed the / testing of the / login module and / found three bugs.
I have completed the testing / of the login module / and found three bugs.
I / have completed / the testing / of the login / module and found / three bugs.
I have completed the testing of the login module and found three bugs without any break.
exercises.hint: Break after complete ideas, not in the middle of a noun phrase.
exercises.why: The second splits at meaning boundaries. The first and third break noun phrases apart ('the / testing'), and the fourth gives the listener no chance to absorb the idea.

exercises.prompt: In the PREP structure, what is the first step? Answer in one word.
exercises.why: You start with your point, a one-sentence answer, so the listener knows the direction before hearing the reasons.

exercises.prompt: In an online interview the panel asks a question you did not expect: 'Where do you see ABAP in five years?' You need a few seconds to think. What do you do?

options.text: Say 'umm, like, basically, you know...' until a thought arrives.
options.feedback: Fillers signal hesitation and use up time without adding content.

options.text: Say 'That is a good question, let me think for a second', pause for two seconds, then answer with a clear point.
options.feedback: A bridge phrase plus a silent pause shows composure, and buys the time you need.

options.text: Answer immediately with the first idea even if it is vague.
options.feedback: Speed is not required; a vague answer is worse than a short pause.

options.text: Ask them to skip the question.
options.feedback: Skipping hurts you; asking for a moment to think is acceptable, avoiding the question is not.

exercises.why: A short silent pause or bridge phrase is professional, and the thinking time lets you structure the answer with PREP.

exercises.prompt: Write the script of a 30 to 40 second spoken answer to: 'Tell me about a challenge you faced in a project and how you handled it.' Use PREP, mark chunk boundaries with slashes in at least one sentence, and include one bridge phrase you might use before answering.

rubric.label: Point, reason, example, point are all present

descriptors.0: No clear point; the answer wanders.
descriptors.1: Two of the four parts are present.
descriptors.2: Three parts present or the parts are present but blurred.
descriptors.3: A clear opening point, a reason, a specific example and a closing point.

auto.label: Uses linking words such as because, for example, so

descriptors.0: No chunk marks or bridge phrase.
descriptors.1: Chunk marks present but break noun phrases, or no bridge phrase.
descriptors.2: Chunk marks at sensible places; bridge phrase present but generic.
descriptors.3: Chunks mark meaning boundaries and a natural bridge phrase opens the answer.

auto.label: Contains at least one slash marking a chunk boundary

descriptors.0: No example is given at all.
descriptors.1: A generic example with no detail.
descriptors.2: A real example with some detail but no result.
descriptors.3: A specific situation, action and result, with a number or named detail.

exercises.modelAnswer: That is a good question, / let me think for a second. My biggest challenge was a deadline clash in my final-year project, / and I handled it by planning in small steps. Two weeks before submission / our database design failed, because we had not tested large data. For example, I listed the five most urgent fixes, / split them with my teammate and we met every evening for a quick check. We finished two days early. So I handle challenges by breaking them into small steps and staying in contact with my team.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer opens with a clear point, gives a reason, then a specific story with action and result, and closes with a short summary. Mark slashes where you would pause, usually after a full idea. Common mistakes: starting with the story, using only generic statements like 'I worked hard', and forgetting to close. Read your script aloud with a timer; 30 to 40 seconds is about 80 to 100 words.

task.title: Your first five-minute recording
task.brief: Record, review and re-record one spoken answer to find your filler habits.
steps: Choose a question, such as 'Tell me about yourself' or 'Explain a project you built', and set a timer for five minutes.
Record a 45-second answer on your phone using point, reason, example, point.
Play it back once and note your top filler word, how many times you used it and one word you stumbled on.
Record the answer again, pausing silently instead of using the filler and chunking at natural places.
Shadow one 20-second clip of a clear speaker, sentence by sentence, from any audio or video you already have.
checklist: I recorded two takes of the same answer
I counted my top filler word in take one
I used silent pauses in take two
I practised shadowing one short clip
task.evidencePrompt: State your question, your top filler word with its count in take one and take two, and one thing you will fix tomorrow.

quiz.prompt: What does fluency mainly depend on?
quiz.why: Fluency is steady flow in meaningful groups. Speed and difficult words make speech harder to follow, and pauses are a natural part of fluent speech.

quiz.prompt: What is the best replacement for the filler 'umm' while you think?
options: A short silent pause or a bridge phrase
Repeating the last word several times
quiz.why: A silent pause or a phrase such as 'let me think' sounds composed. Speaking faster or louder does not give you thinking time.

quiz.prompt: Which answer begins correctly with PREP?
options: In my college project I used Node.js...
Yes, I enjoy teamwork because it helps me learn faster.
Well, there are many things to say about teamwork.
I do not know exactly, but maybe...
quiz.why: It starts with the point (yes, I enjoy teamwork) and the reason. Starting with an example, or with vague openings, hides the point.

quiz.prompt: What is the name of the technique of repeating a speaker's words immediately after hearing them, copying rhythm and stress? (one word)
quiz.why: Shadowing trains rhythm, stress and chunking together.

bank.prompt: A client asks a technical question on a call and you need time to find the answer. Which opening is best?
options: Good question. Let me check that and confirm in a moment.
I have no idea at all.
bank.why: A bridge phrase shows control and buys time. Fillers sound unsure, and refusing or skipping damages trust.

bank.prompt: In a three-line stand-up update 'Status, blocker, plan', which of these three items would you say second? (one word)
bank.why: The order is status first, blocker second and plan third, which follows the point-reason logic of a short update.

bank.prompt: In a five-minute recording routine, what is the most useful step after listening to your first take?
options: Delete it and never listen again
Record again, fixing just one or two points you noticed
bank.why: Focused repetition on one or two points drives improvement. Deleting, spreading attention over ten new topics or sharing early do not.

cards.front: What is a chunk and how long is it?
cards.back: A group of three to seven words carrying one idea, followed by a tiny pause. Break after complete ideas, not inside noun phrases.

cards.front: How do you replace a filler word?
cards.back: Notice your habitual filler, plan a one-beat silent pause, and use a bridge phrase such as 'Let me think for a second' if you need longer.
Point, Reason, Example, Point. Lead with the answer, support it, show one concrete example, then close with the point again.
Pick a topic, record a PREP answer, listen and note one filler plus one stumble, then re-record fixing just those two things.

english-4.reflection: When do you feel least fluent: with strangers, in technical discussions or in interviews, and what is one small thing you can do before the next such moment to reduce the pressure?

keyPoints: Fluency is flow in chunks, not speed.
Pause silently or use a bridge phrase instead of fillers.
Answer with Point, Reason, Example, Point.
Shadow short clips and re-record a second take daily.
revision.redo: Answer one question aloud for 30 seconds using PREP, pausing instead of filling, and notice your filler count.

eq-1.title: Self-Awareness
eq-1.summary: Name your emotions precisely, spot triggers and body signals, link feelings to your values, and keep a simple emotion log.
objectives: Name an emotion with a precise word instead of 'fine', 'bad' or 'stressed'.
Identify the trigger and the body signal that come before a strong reaction.
Use a three-line emotion log to connect a feeling to the value behind it.

concepts.label: Triggers and the values behind them

explanation.heading: Why self-awareness comes first
explanation.body:
Emotional intelligence has four parts: knowing your own emotions, managing them, understanding other people's, and handling relationships. The first part is the foundation. You cannot manage a feeling you have not noticed, and you cannot choose a response if the reaction is already over.

Self-awareness is not about analysing yourself for hours. It is a quick, honest check: *what am I feeling, what set it off, and what does it want me to do?* People who do this check even for ten seconds make fewer rash decisions in group projects, client calls and family discussions.

explanation.heading: Name it precisely
explanation.body:
Most of us use a few broad words: *fine*, *stressed*, *bad*, *angry*. Researchers call the skill of using finer words **emotional granularity**, and the practical benefit is simple: a precise name points to a precise action.

Take 'stressed'. It could mean:

- **Anxious**: worried about something that might happen (tomorrow's viva).
- **Overwhelmed**: too many demands at once (three submissions this week).
- **Resentful**: you feel you are carrying a teammate's share.
- **Embarrassed**: you were corrected in front of others.

Anxiety asks for preparation. Overwhelm asks for a shorter list. Resentment asks for a conversation. Embarrassment asks for perspective. If you only say 'stressed', you will try the same remedy (work harder) for all four.

A simple method: start with the broad family (anger, fear, sadness, joy, shame), then ask 'which shade?' Irritated, furious or let down? Nervous, dreading or panicky? Pick the closest word, and rate it 1 to 10.

explanation.heading: Triggers, body signals and the value underneath
explanation.body:
A **trigger** is the specific event that sets a feeling off: a message left on 'seen', a senior saying 'this is not what I asked for', your mother comparing your results with a cousin's. The trigger is usually smaller than the reaction, because it touches something you care about. Ask: *what value felt threatened?* Fairness, respect, competence, belonging, freedom? If you were furious when a teammate took credit, the value was fairness. Naming the value tells you what you actually need.

Your **body signals** usually arrive before the words do: a tight jaw, hot face, sinking stomach, shallow breathing, restless legs, a heavy chest. Learn your own two or three. They are your early-warning system. If you notice your jaw clenching in a meeting, you have a few seconds of choice that you would otherwise lose.

explanation.heading: The emotion log: three lines, once a day
explanation.body:
Keep a short log, ideally at the end of the day or right after a strong moment. Use three lines:

1. **Trigger**: what happened, in factual words, as a camera would record it.
2. **Feeling and body**: the precise emotion, its strength out of 10, and where you felt it.
3. **Value or need**: what mattered to you.

Worked example: *Trigger: Rohit presented my part of the slides as 'our work' without naming me. Feeling: resentful, 7/10, hot face and tight jaw. Value: recognition and fairness.* Reading this back, the next step is obvious and calm: ask Rohit to credit each section by name in the next review.

A common mistake is mixing the trigger with a judgement ('Rohit is selfish'). Keep line one factual. After two weeks, read your log for patterns: the same people, times or situations will show up, and that is where your growth is.

examples.title: From 'stressed' to a useful word
examples.body:
Before: 'I am so stressed about the project.'

After: 'I feel overwhelmed (7/10) because three deliverables are due in the same week, and a little resentful because two teammates have not replied. My shoulders are tight.'

Action that follows: list the three deliverables, rank them, and send one clear message to the two teammates asking for a status by evening.
examples.takeaway: A precise word split one vague problem into two separate ones, each with its own next step.

examples.title: A trigger that pointed to a value
examples.body: Meera's mother says at dinner, 'Sharma ji's son got a package of twelve lakh. What are you doing?' Meera snaps and leaves the table. Later she writes her log: Trigger: comparison with a neighbour's son. Feeling: hurt and defensive, 8/10, tight throat. Value: being accepted for who I am, and respect for my effort.
examples.takeaway: The anger was really hurt. Once Meera knows the value, she can say 'I feel hurt when I am compared; I would like you to ask how my preparation is going' instead of snapping.

examples.title: Catching the body signal early
examples.body: During a team call, a senior says 'This code is not production ready.' Arjun notices his face getting hot and his typing getting faster. He labels it: 'embarrassed, 6/10'. Instead of replying instantly, he writes 'Thanks, noted. Can you point to the two main gaps so I fix them today?'
examples.takeaway: The body signal gave Arjun a few seconds of choice, and naming the feeling lowered its grip.

exercises.prompt: Your group project is due Friday. Two members have gone silent, you have three other submissions this week, and you keep thinking 'I am so stressed'. What is the most useful first step?

options.text: Keep telling yourself you are stressed and work through the night.
options.feedback: A broad word leads to a broad remedy (work harder) and ignores what is actually wrong.

options.text: Split the feeling: overwhelmed by the number of tasks, and resentful about the silent teammates. Then list tasks and message the teammates.
options.feedback: Two precise names point to two different actions: prioritise the list, and have a direct conversation.

options.text: Tell yourself it is nothing and carry on.
options.feedback: Ignoring the feeling does not remove it; it usually leaks out later as irritability.

options.text: Post a complaint about the teammates in the class group chat.
options.feedback: This acts on the resentment without checking facts and will damage trust.

exercises.why: Granularity turns a vague mood into specific problems. Overwhelm needs a shorter, ranked list; resentment needs a clear conversation.

exercises.prompt: The three lines of the emotion log are: trigger, feeling and body, and ____. Fill in the third line with one word that names what mattered to you (hint: it begins with 'v').
exercises.hint: Fairness, respect and belonging are examples.
exercises.why: The third line links the feeling to the value or need that felt threatened, which is what lets you choose a useful response.

exercises.prompt: Practise naming your feeling aloud to a friend.
exercises.setup: You are Kabir, a final-year student. Your faculty guide has just criticised your presentation in front of the class. Your close friend Sana finds you outside the seminar hall. Your goal is to describe your feeling precisely and decide on a next step.

turns.they: Hey, you left in a hurry. Are you okay?

options.text: I'm fine. It's nothing.
options.feedback: 'Fine' hides the feeling and ends the conversation.
options.reply: Okay... if you say so. You looked really upset though.

options.text: Honestly, I feel embarrassed, maybe 7 out of 10. My face is still hot.
options.feedback: A precise word, an intensity and a body signal give Sana something real to respond to.
options.reply: That sounds awful, being corrected in front of everyone. What did he actually say?

options.text: That teacher is the worst, he always targets me.
options.feedback: This is a judgement about him, not a description of your feeling.
options.reply: Hmm, maybe. But what happened exactly?

turns.they: What do you think hurt the most about it?

options.text: I guess it hit my need to look competent. I had prepared for two weeks.
options.feedback: You connected the feeling to a value (competence, effort), which is the point of self-awareness.
options.reply: That makes sense. You did work hard. Was any part of his feedback useful?

options.text: I don't know, I just want to forget it.
options.feedback: Avoiding the question skips the learning, though it is an understandable first reaction.
options.reply: Fair, we can talk later. But it might feel better if you work out what stung.

options.text: He should have said it privately.
options.feedback: A fair point about respect, but you have not yet named your own feeling or need.
options.reply: True, that would have been kinder. But how are you feeling about the feedback itself?

turns.they: So what do you want to do now?

options.text: Take ten minutes to cool down, then ask him which two slides to improve.
options.feedback: You regulate first and then turn the feeling into a constructive action.
options.reply: Good plan. I'll come with you if you want, and we can fix the slides tonight.

options.text: Skip the next class and avoid him all week.
options.feedback: Avoidance protects you for today but grows the problem.
options.reply: Hmm, that may make it harder to face him later.

options.text: Send him an angry email tonight.
options.feedback: Acting at the peak of the emotion usually creates a second problem.
options.reply: Please don't send anything tonight. Sleep on it first.
