exercises.why: Strong answers name the feeling with a precise word, mention a body signal, link it to a value, and then choose a calm next step instead of venting or hiding.

exercises.prompt: Recall one recent moment when you reacted strongly (for example, a comment from a family member, a delayed reply from a teammate, or feedback from a mentor). Write a three-line emotion log for it: trigger (factual), feeling with strength out of 10 and where you felt it in your body, and the value behind it. Then add one sentence on what you would do differently.

descriptors.0: No trigger given, or only a judgement about the person.
descriptors.1: Trigger mixed with judgement or blame.
descriptors.2: Mostly factual with one judgemental phrase.
descriptors.3: Camera-style facts: who said or did what, when.

rubric.label: Precise feeling, strength and body signal

descriptors.0: Only a broad word like 'bad' or 'stressed'.
descriptors.1: A feeling word but no strength or body signal.
descriptors.2: Precise word plus either strength or body signal.
descriptors.3: Precise word, a number out of 10 and a specific body location.

auto.label: Includes a strength such as 7/10 or 7 out of 10

descriptors.2: A value named but not clearly linked to the trigger.
descriptors.3: Value named and clearly linked to why the trigger hurt.

descriptors.0: No action is given at all.
descriptors.3: A specific, realistic action for next time.

exercises.modelAnswer: Trigger: In Tuesday's group call, Nikhil said, 'You did not finish the testing section,' while four others were listening. Feeling: embarrassed and a little defensive, 7/10, hot face and tight jaw. Value: being seen as reliable, and fairness, because I had told him on Sunday that the data was late. Next time I will take a breath, say 'The data reached me on Monday; I will finish by tomorrow noon,' and send the timeline in writing afterwards.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers keep line one factual, use a precise emotion word with a number and a body location, and link the feeling to a real value rather than to the other person's character. A common mistake is writing 'He is rude' as the trigger or 'I felt stressed' as the feeling. Score yourself honestly against each descriptor; if your log blames a person, rewrite line one as a camera would record it.

task.title: Three days of emotion logging
task.brief: Practise noticing, naming and linking feelings to values, using a three-line log.
steps: Choose a notes app or notebook and set a reminder for the same time each evening.
Each evening, pick the strongest emotional moment of the day and write three lines: trigger (factual), feeling with strength out of 10 and body signal, value or need.
Replace any broad word (fine, stressed, bad) with a more precise one.
After three entries, look for one pattern: a person, time of day or situation that repeats.
checklist: I wrote at least three entries
Each trigger is factual, with no judgement
Each entry has a precise emotion word and a number out of 10
I named one body signal that repeats
I wrote down one pattern I noticed
task.evidencePrompt: Write one of your log entries in three lines and the pattern you noticed.

quiz.prompt: Which statement shows the most emotional granularity?
options: I feel bad about the exam.
I feel anxious about tomorrow's viva and disappointed in my last mock score.
I am just not in a good mood.
quiz.why: It names two distinct feelings and their causes. 'Bad', 'stressed' and 'not in a good mood' are broad labels that cannot point to a specific action.

quiz.prompt: A teammate takes credit for your work and you feel furious. Which value was most likely threatened?
quiz.why: Anger at credit-taking usually signals that fairness and recognition were threatened. The other options do not connect to the trigger.

quiz.prompt: Tight jaw, hot face and shallow breathing are examples of body ____ that warn you a strong emotion is starting. (one word)
quiz.why: Body signals usually appear before you have words for the feeling, and give you a few seconds of choice.

quiz.prompt: Which is the best 'trigger' line for an emotion log?
options: Priya did not reply to my message about the deadline for two days.
Everyone ignores me in this team.
The whole project is a mess.
quiz.why: A trigger should be factual, like a camera recording. The others are judgements or generalisations that hide what actually happened.

bank.prompt: Rahul says, 'I'm stressed' before a client demo. After thinking, he realises he is afraid the demo will crash. Which action best matches the precise feeling?
options: Take a long break and ignore it
Rehearse the demo twice and prepare a backup recording
Blame the tester for earlier bugs
bank.why: Anxiety about a possible failure is best met with preparation. Breaks, blame or cancelling do not address the fear.

bank.prompt: Your cousin says, 'Still no job offer?' at a family function and you feel a flash of anger. What is the most useful next question to ask yourself?
options: Why is my cousin so rude?
How can I get back at them?
Why do I always get angry?
Which value or need felt threatened, such as respect or being accepted?
bank.why: Asking which value was touched turns a reaction into information. The other questions focus on blame or on a harsh generalisation about yourself.

bank.prompt: In the emotion log, line one should describe what happened as a ____ would record it. (one word, a piece of equipment)
bank.why: A camera records facts without opinions, which keeps the trigger line honest and free from blame.

cards.front: What is emotional granularity and why does it help?
cards.back: Using precise emotion words (overwhelmed, resentful, embarrassed) instead of broad ones (stressed, bad). A precise name points to a precise action.

cards.front: A reaction feels bigger than the event. What should you ask?
cards.back: Which value or need felt threatened: fairness, respect, competence, belonging, freedom? The trigger touched something you care about.
They appear before words do (tight jaw, hot face, sinking stomach). Noticing them gives you a few seconds of choice before you react.

cards.front: What are the three lines of the emotion log?
cards.back: 1. Trigger, stated factually. 2. Feeling with strength out of 10 and body signal. 3. The value or need behind it.

eq-1.reflection: Which broad word do you use most often to describe how you feel, and what three more precise words could replace it this week?

keyPoints: Self-awareness is the foundation: notice before you manage.
Replace broad words with precise ones, then rate them out of 10.
A strong reaction usually means a value was touched.
Body signals come first and give you a few seconds of choice.
Log three lines: trigger, feeling and body, value.
revision.redo: Right now, name your current feeling with a precise word, a number out of 10 and one body location, and write it in one line.

eq-2.title: Self-Regulation
eq-2.summary: Pause before you react, use the STOP technique, reframe the story you are telling yourself, and recover well after a misstep.
objectives: Use a deliberate pause to separate a feeling from the action that follows it.
Apply the four STOP steps and one reappraisal question in a heated moment.
Recover after a misstep with a short, specific repair instead of silence or over-apology.

explanation.heading: Between feeling and action there is a gap
explanation.body:
In the first lesson of this skill you practised naming emotions precisely. Naming is the first half; the second half is deciding what to do with the feeling. **Reacting** means the action follows the feeling in a split second: you snap, you send the angry message, you go silent for two days. **Responding** means you feel the same thing, but a short gap sits between the feeling and the action, and you choose.

The gap does not need to be long. Strong emotions peak and then fall; for most everyday irritations the sharpest part passes within a minute or two. A pause of even ten seconds, with one slow breath, is often enough to move you from reacting to responding. You are not hiding the feeling. You are choosing when and how it comes out.

explanation.heading: STOP: four steps for a heated moment
explanation.body:
STOP is a memorable routine for the moment you notice a rise in heat.

1. **S - Stop.** Freeze what you are about to say or type. Hands off the keyboard.
2. **T - Take a breath.** One slow breath in, a longer breath out. This calms the body signal you learned to spot earlier.
3. **O - Observe.** Name the feeling, rate it out of 10, and notice the body signal. 'Irritated, 7 out of 10, jaw tight.'
4. **P - Proceed.** Choose one action that fits your values: ask a question, ask for time, or reply briefly.

**Worked example.** In a group project chat, a teammate writes, 'Anyone who read the brief would know this slide is wrong.' You feel heat rise. Reacting would be: 'Maybe do it yourself then.' With STOP you stop typing, breathe, observe 'insulted, 7 out of 10', and proceed with: 'Fair, I may have missed something. Which part of the brief does it contradict?' The conflict never starts.

explanation.heading: Reappraisal: change the story, not the facts
explanation.body:
Much of the heat comes not from the event but from the story you attach to it. The facts are 'my team lead replied with one word: Noted.' The story might be 'She is angry with me.' Reappraisal means generating at least one other story that fits the same facts: 'She is replying from her phone between meetings.'

Use a simple question: **'What else could be true?'** List two alternatives, one neutral and one kind. You are not forcing yourself to believe the nicest story; you are loosening the grip of the first one so you can check it. Then, if it matters, check with a question: 'Does the draft need changes?'

A common mistake is suppression: telling yourself 'do not feel angry'. Suppressing usually makes the feeling louder. Reappraisal works because it changes the meaning, so the feeling reduces naturally.

explanation.heading: Recovering after a misstep
explanation.body:
Everyone snaps sometimes. Emotional intelligence is not never slipping; it is how fast and how well you repair. A good repair has three parts: **name what you did** specifically, **own it without excuses**, and **say what you will do differently**. For example: 'I raised my voice in the meeting when you changed the plan. That was not fair to you. Next time I will ask for a minute and speak to you after.'

Two common mistakes: waiting weeks because it feels awkward, and over-apologising so the other person has to comfort you. Keep it short, do it soon, and then change the behaviour. After the repair, note what the trigger was; this feeds your emotion log, and next time the pause will come a little earlier.

examples.title: The family expectation moment
examples.body:
At dinner, your uncle says, 'In IT you will never earn properly unless you leave this ABAP and do something government.' Heat rises: 8 out of 10, chest tight.

Reaction: 'You don't understand anything about my field!' and then a cold silence.

STOP response: breathe, observe 'defensive and dismissed', and reply calmly: 'I know you want me to be secure. I have thought about it; I can show you the plan after dinner.'
examples.takeaway: The feeling was identical in both versions. The pause changed the outcome, and the reply acknowledged the uncle's underlying value (security) without giving in.

examples.title: Reappraising a one-word reply
examples.body: You send your team lead a long update and receive 'Ok.' Story one: 'He thinks it was poor.' Alternatives: 'He is in a client call', 'Ok means he accepted it'. You ask: 'Please let me know if anything needs a change before the review.' He replies, 'All good, thanks.'
examples.takeaway: Alternatives came from the same facts, and a quick check replaced hours of worry.

examples.title: A short repair message
examples.body: After snapping at a project partner on a call, you message: 'I cut you off today and spoke sharply. That was not okay. I was anxious about the deadline, but that is my issue to manage. Can we go through your part again tomorrow? I will let you finish first.'
examples.takeaway: It names the act, owns it, gives a short reason without blaming, and states a change.

exercises.prompt: What is the main difference between reacting and responding?
options: Reacting means you feel the emotion; responding means you do not feel it.
Responding means a short gap exists between the feeling and the action, so you choose what to do.
Responding means you always stay silent until the feeling is gone.
Reacting is always loud, and responding is always polite agreement.
exercises.hint: Think about what happens between the feeling and the action.
exercises.why: Both involve feeling the emotion. The difference is the gap that lets you choose. Option 1 wrongly says you stop feeling; option 3 confuses a pause with permanent silence; option 4 treats responding as agreeing, which it is not.

exercises.prompt: In the STOP technique, what does the letter O stand for? (one word)
exercises.hint: You name the feeling and rate it out of 10.
exercises.why: O is Observe: name the feeling, rate it and notice the body signal before choosing what to do.

The best path pauses first, accepts the valid part of the criticism, commits to a concrete fix, and makes a calm request for next time. Counter-attacks, silence and self-attack all keep the heat in charge.
exercises.setup: You are a student in a group project. Rohan, a teammate, has just said in the group call that your section was 'copied and sloppy' in front of everyone. Your goal is to use STOP and keep the working relationship intact.

turns.they: Honestly, your section was copied and sloppy. We will lose marks because of it.

options.text: Say, 'Give me a second.' Take one slow breath, then say, 'That is harsh. Which parts concern you?'
options.feedback: You paused, named the sting in a calm way and asked for specifics.
options.reply: Mostly slides 4 and 5. Some lines look exactly like the source.

options.text: Say, 'At least I did my part. Where is yours?'
options.feedback: A counter-attack is a reaction. It turns a feedback issue into a fight.
options.reply: Oh, so now it is my fault? I am only saying what is true.

options.text: Say nothing and mute your mic for the rest of the call.
options.feedback: Not reacting is fine, but total silence leaves the issue unresolved and the heat inside you.
options.reply: Hello? Are you there? Fine, we will move on then.

turns.they: Slides 4 and 5. Some lines are word for word from the source.

options.text: Say, 'You are right to flag it. I will rewrite both in my own words by tomorrow evening. Could you review them?'
options.feedback: You accept the valid part, commit to a specific action and a time, and invite collaboration.
options.reply: Okay, that works. I will check them tomorrow night.

options.text: Say, 'I did not copy anything. You are exaggerating.'
options.feedback: You may be partly right, but flat denial without checking the slides escalates the argument.
options.reply: I am looking at it right now. It is the same sentence.

options.text: Say, 'Fine, I will rewrite everything. Sorry, sorry, it is all my fault, I am useless.'
options.feedback: Over-apologising and self-attack drains you and makes the issue about your feelings, not the slides.
options.reply: Uh, no, I did not say that. Let us just fix slides 4 and 5.

turns.they: Just fix them and we will see.

options.text: Say, 'Thanks. Also, next time please message me privately first; I find it easier to fix things that way.'
options.feedback: You set a calm, specific request for the future without blame.
options.reply: Fair enough. I should have done that. I will message you first.

options.text: Say, 'You should never criticise people in front of the group.'
options.feedback: The point is valid but the absolute language sounds like a lecture.
options.reply: I only said what the problem was. Anyway, send it by tomorrow.

options.text: Say nothing, and decide privately not to help Rohan again.
options.feedback: Silent resentment builds and nothing changes for the next project.

exercises.prompt: Yesterday you raised your voice at your team lead, Meena, when she changed the demo plan an hour before the client call. Today you must repair it. Write the exact message you would send (60 words or fewer is fine), including what you did, ownership, and what you will do differently.

descriptors.0: No mention of what actually happened.
descriptors.1: Vague wording such as 'sorry for yesterday' only.
descriptors.2: Mentions raising the voice but without context.
descriptors.3: Names the act and context: raised voice when the plan changed before the call.

rubric.label: Owns it without excuses or blame

descriptors.0: Blames Meena or the situation entirely.
descriptors.1: Apology followed by a 'but' that excuses the behaviour.
descriptors.2: Owns it, with a slight excuse.
descriptors.3: Clear ownership; any reason is given without shifting blame.

descriptors.1: Vague promise such as 'I will be better'.
descriptors.2: A change that is somewhat specific.
descriptors.3: A specific behaviour for next time, such as asking for a minute and raising concerns calmly.
Brief, calm and respectful.

exercises.modelAnswer: Hi Meena, yesterday I raised my voice when the demo plan changed before the client call. That was not okay and it was not fair to you. I was worried about the preparation, but I should have asked for five minutes instead. Next time I will tell you my concern calmly and we can decide together. Thank you for handling the call so well.
exercises.guidance: A strong repair is specific, short and forward-looking. Common mistakes are a vague 'sorry for yesterday', a long explanation that becomes an excuse, and apologising five times. Check that you named the exact behaviour and a future action you can really do. Score each criterion honestly against the model answer.

task.title: Run STOP in the wild
task.brief: Practise the pause on three small irritations today or tomorrow, and write down what you chose to do.
steps: Pick three mild triggers likely this week, such as a slow reply, a noisy room or a family comment.
When you notice heat, mentally say S, T, O, P and take one slow breath before acting.
Rate the feeling out of 10 before and after the pause.
Write one alternative story for each trigger using 'What else could be true?'
checklist: I used STOP at least twice
I rated the feeling before and after
I noted what I chose to do
task.evidencePrompt: Describe one moment you used STOP, the rating before and after, and what you did.

quiz.prompt: Which action best shows responding rather than reacting?
options: Replying instantly to a rude message to show you are not afraid.
Taking one breath, then replying briefly with a question.
Pretending the message did not bother you.
quiz.why: A short pause followed by a chosen reply is responding. Instant replies are reactions, deleting the chat is avoidance, and pretending is suppression.

quiz.prompt: Which is the correct order of STOP?
options: Observe, Stop, Proceed, Take a breath
Stop, Observe, Take a breath, Proceed
Take a breath, Stop, Proceed, Observe
Stop, Take a breath, Observe, Proceed
quiz.why: The order is Stop, Take a breath, Observe, Proceed. You freeze first, calm the body, name what you feel, and only then choose an action.

quiz.prompt: Your lead replied only 'Noted.' Which is a reappraisal?
options: I must not feel upset about this.
She is angry; I should stay away from her.
She may be busy and 'Noted' may simply mean she received it; I can check later.
quiz.why: Reappraisal finds another story that fits the same facts and then allows a check. Option 1 is suppression, option 2 keeps the same story, and option 4 is payback.

quiz.prompt: A good repair names what you did, owns it, and says what you will do ______. (one word)
quiz.why: The third part of a repair is the change in future behaviour: what you will do differently.

bank.prompt: You are about to type an angry reply to a classmate who missed a deadline, and your hands are shaking. What is the best first move?
options: Send the message, then apologise later.
Stop typing and take one slow breath before deciding anything.
Forward the chat to the professor immediately.
Ask others to take your side first.
bank.why: First, stop and breathe. Sending in anger or escalating to others before you have calmed down tends to make things worse.

bank.prompt: Which question best helps reappraise a situation?
options: Why does this always happen to me?
What else could be true here?
bank.why: 'What else could be true?' generates alternative stories that fit the facts. The others strengthen blame or hide the feeling.

bank.prompt: After snapping at a friend, should you repair soon or wait weeks until it feels less awkward? Answer with one word: soon or later.
bank.why: A repair works best soon and short. Waiting lets the hurt and the story grow.

cards.back: Reacting: action follows the feeling instantly. Responding: a short gap lets you choose the action. You still feel the emotion.

cards.front: What are the four STOP steps?
cards.back: Stop, Take a breath, Observe (name and rate the feeling), Proceed with one chosen action.

cards.front: What is reappraisal in emotional regulation?
cards.back: Changing the story you tell about the same facts. Ask 'What else could be true?' and check if it matters.

cards.front: Three parts of a good repair?
cards.back: Name what you did, own it without excuses, and say what you will do differently. Keep it short and do it soon.

eq-2.reflection: Think of a recent moment you reacted when you wish you had responded. What was the earliest body signal, and where could a ten-second pause have fitted in?

keyPoints: Feeling and action have a gap; use it.
STOP: Stop, Take a breath, Observe, Proceed.
Ask 'What else could be true?' before believing the first story.
Repair soon: name it, own it, change it.
Suppressing a feeling makes it louder; reframe instead.
revision.redo: Recall one irritation from today, rate it out of 10, write one alternative story, and say aloud what your STOP-proceed action would be.

eq-3.title: Empathy and Active Listening
eq-3.summary: Listen at a deeper level, reflect and paraphrase what you hear, validate feelings and ask open questions before offering any fix.
objectives: Recognise the three levels of listening and move up to focused listening.
Paraphrase and validate what someone says without judging or fixing.
Ask open questions that help the other person think and speak.

concepts.label: Open questions and not fixing too early

explanation.heading: Hearing is not listening
explanation.body:
In the last lesson you practised pausing before you react to your own emotions. Empathy is the mirror skill: noticing and understanding what another person feels. Most of us believe we listen well, yet we spend much of a conversation preparing our own reply. People feel respected when they are truly heard, and that feeling often matters more than the advice they receive.

There are three useful **levels of listening**. At level one, *internal listening*, your attention is on yourself: your opinion, your story, your next sentence. At level two, *focused listening*, your attention is on the speaker: the words, the tone, the pauses. At level three, *global listening*, you also notice the room, the energy and what is not being said. For most conversations the aim is a steady level two.

explanation.heading: Reflecting and paraphrasing
explanation.body:
**Paraphrasing** means saying back, in your own words, what you understood. **Reflecting** goes one step further and names the feeling underneath. Suppose your teammate Ankit says, "The client changed the requirement again, and I have already rewritten the report twice." A paraphrase: "So the scope moved after you had already redone the work." A reflection: "That sounds exhausting, and maybe a bit unfair."

These lines do three jobs. They prove you were listening, they let the speaker correct you ("not unfair, just worrying about the deadline"), and they slow the conversation so feelings can settle. Keep reflections tentative, using phrases like "it sounds like" or "I am guessing", because you are offering a guess, not a diagnosis.

explanation.heading: Validating before solving
explanation.body:
**Validation** means acknowledging that a feeling makes sense given the person's situation. It does not mean you agree with every opinion or that they are right. "Anyone would be nervous before a first technical interview" validates. "You should not be nervous, it is easy" dismisses.

The most common mistake is **fixing too early**. When a friend says she is stressed about an exam, you rush to give a study timetable. Often she wanted to be understood first. A good sequence is: listen, reflect, validate, and only then ask, "Would you like ideas, or do you mostly need me to listen?" That question alone prevents many arguments.

explanation.heading: Open questions and a practice routine
explanation.body:
A **closed question** invites yes or no: "Did you finish the work?" An **open question** invites a story: "How did the day go?" or "What was the hardest part?" Prefer *what* and *how* over *why*, since "Why did you do that?" can sound like blame. Useful follow-ups are "Tell me more" and "What happened next?"

To practise, choose one conversation a day and follow three rules: put the phone away, wait two seconds after they finish before you speak, and paraphrase once before sharing your view. Notice how often the speaker adds something new after you reflect. That extra detail is usually the real issue.

examples.title: Fixing versus listening
examples.body: Riya says, "My viva is on Monday and I keep blanking out." Version A, Sameer replies, "Just revise the slides three times, simple." Version B, he says, "Blanking out before a viva sounds really stressful. What happens when it occurs?" Riya then admits it only happens when she imagines the external examiner's face. Only after that does Sameer ask whether she wants practice questions.
examples.takeaway: The second reply reflects, validates and opens the topic, and it surfaces the real problem the advice would have missed.

examples.title: Levels of listening in a client call
examples.body: During a call with a client in Pune, a junior consultant notices the client's sentences getting shorter when the go-live date is mentioned. She stops taking notes, paraphrases the date concern and asks, "What worries you most about that timeline?" The client then reveals that his own manager has set an unrealistic target.
examples.takeaway: Noticing tone and pauses is focused listening, and it turned a routine call into useful information.

exercises.prompt: While a friend talks about her problem, you are mostly thinking about a similar story of your own to share. Which level is this?
exercises.why: Your attention is on your own story, which is internal listening (level one). Focused listening keeps attention on the speaker, and global listening also reads the wider situation.

exercises.prompt: Priya says, "The group is not replying and the submission is tomorrow." Which is the best reflection?
options: It is only a small assignment, relax.
You should message them again immediately.
Group work is always like this.
It sounds frustrating, with the deadline so close and no replies.
exercises.why: It names the feeling and the situation tentatively. The others dismiss, fix too early or generalise.

exercises.prompt: A junior says, "I made a mistake in the test data and I feel terrible." You are his senior. What is the best reply?

options.text: It is just test data, nobody will notice.
options.feedback: This minimises the feeling and tells him not to feel it.

options.text: Feeling bad makes sense when you care about your work. What happened?
options.feedback: It validates the feeling without excusing the mistake and invites the story.

options.text: You should have double-checked, so learn from this.
options.feedback: A lecture before listening makes people defensive.

options.text: Here is a five-step checklist to avoid errors.
options.feedback: A fix may help later, but offered first it skips the feeling.

exercises.why: Validation acknowledges that the feeling makes sense, then an open question invites detail before any solution.

exercises.prompt: Your cousin tells you, "I do not think engineering is for me, but my parents will be upset." Write the first four things you would say or ask: one paraphrase, one reflection of a feeling, one validation and two open questions. Do not give advice.

descriptors.3: Accurate paraphrase in your own words with no judgement.

descriptors.1: Names a wrong or harsh feeling.
descriptors.3: Names a likely feeling tentatively ("it sounds like").
Two genuine open what or how questions.
Entirely listening and exploring.

exercises.modelAnswer: So you are feeling unsure about the course, and you are worried about how your parents will react. It sounds like you are carrying two pressures at once. Anyone would find that heavy. What is it about engineering that does not feel right? How do you imagine your parents would take it if you told them?
exercises.guidance: A strong answer stays with the cousin: paraphrase, name a likely feeling, validate, and ask what and how questions. Common mistakes are adding advice such as "talk to them tonight", using why questions that sound like blame, and reflecting with certainty instead of guessing. Score yourself against the model.

task.title: One conversation, three listening moves
task.brief: Have one real conversation where you only use listening skills for the first five minutes, then log what you noticed.
steps: Pick a friend, sibling or classmate and ask how their week has been.
Put your phone away and wait two seconds before each reply.
Paraphrase at least twice and reflect one feeling tentatively.
Ask two open questions and hold back advice until they ask or you check.
Write down what new information appeared that you would not have heard otherwise.
task.evidencePrompt: Describe the conversation, one thing you reflected, and what new detail you learnt.

quiz.prompt: Which level of listening is the best default in a conversation?
quiz.why: Focused listening keeps your attention on the speaker and is the steady aim for most conversations.

quiz.prompt: Saying back in your own words what someone said is called ____. (one word)
quiz.why: Paraphrasing shows understanding and lets the speaker correct you.

quiz.prompt: Which statement validates?
options: Do not worry, it is nothing.
You should not feel that way.
It makes sense that you feel anxious before a first interview.
I felt worse than you at that age.
quiz.why: Validation says the feeling is understandable. The other options dismiss, correct or redirect to yourself.

quiz.prompt: Which is an open question?
options: What stood out for you in the training?
quiz.why: It cannot be answered with yes or no, so it invites a fuller answer.

bank.prompt: A colleague seems quiet after a review meeting. Which opening is most likely to help?
options: How are you finding the feedback so far?
You should not take reviews personally.
bank.why: A gentle what or how question invites sharing. A why question can feel like blame and a yes or no question is easy to dodge.

bank.prompt: In a team call, you notice one member has stopped speaking for ten minutes. This noticing is mostly:
bank.why: Noticing the group energy and what is not being said is global listening.

bank.prompt: Before offering a solution, a good question to ask is "Do you want ideas, or do you mostly need me to ____?" (one word)
bank.why: Checking what the person needs prevents fixing too early.

cards.front: What are the three levels of listening?
cards.back: Internal (attention on yourself), focused (attention on the speaker) and global (also the room, tone and silence). Aim for focused listening most of the time.
A paraphrase restates the content in your words. A reflection names the likely feeling, tentatively, such as "it sounds like you are frustrated".
Acknowledging that a feeling makes sense in the person's situation, without necessarily agreeing with every opinion or excusing a mistake.
Advice before understanding skips the feeling and often misses the real problem. Listen, reflect, validate, then ask whether they want ideas.

eq-3.reflection: Think of a recent conversation where you jumped to advice. What might the other person have said if you had reflected first?

keyPoints: Aim for focused listening, attention on the speaker.
Paraphrase content and reflect feelings tentatively.
Validate that feelings make sense without lecturing.
Ask open what and how questions and delay fixing.
revision.redo: In your next conversation paraphrase once before you share your view.

eq-4.title: Social Awareness and Relationships
eq-4.summary: Read group dynamics, give and receive feedback well, build trust, hold boundaries and repair relationships after conflict.
objectives: Read the roles and unspoken dynamics in a group before acting.
Give feedback using a clear structure and receive feedback without defending.
Set a respectful boundary and repair a strained relationship.

explanation.heading: Seeing the group, not just the person
explanation.body:
Last lesson you practised listening to one person. Social awareness widens the lens to a whole group. Every team, from a college project group to an SAP implementation team, has unwritten dynamics: who speaks first, who is ignored, who agrees quietly and complains later, and who decides in practice, whatever the organisation chart says.

Before a meeting, ask three questions. Who holds formal authority? Who holds informal influence? Who has gone quiet, and why might that be? Watch for signals such as someone repeatedly interrupted, a joke that lands badly or a topic everyone avoids. Observe first, then act: invite the quiet member with "Meera, you have worked on this module, what do you think?" rather than assuming agreement.

explanation.heading: Giving and receiving feedback
explanation.body:
Feedback is information about the effect of someone's behaviour. A reliable structure for giving it is **situation, behaviour, impact**, followed by a request. For example: "In yesterday's review (situation), you changed the test data without telling me (behaviour), so my results did not match and I lost an hour (impact). Could you message me before changing shared data?" It is specific, describes what anyone could have seen, and avoids labels like "careless".

Receiving feedback is harder. When it stings, use the pause from earlier lessons, then **listen, thank, clarify and decide**. Say "Thanks, can you give me one example?" Do not explain or defend in the moment. Afterwards, decide what to act on. Feedback is a gift of data even when delivered clumsily.

explanation.heading: Trust and boundaries
explanation.body:
**Trust** grows from small, repeated acts of reliability: doing what you said, on time, and telling people early when you cannot. It falls faster than it rises, so one hidden problem can cost months of goodwill.

A **boundary** is a limit that protects your time, energy or values, such as "I cannot take calls after 9 pm" or "I will not share your personal details without asking." Boundaries are not punishments. State them calmly and early, with a reason if useful, and offer an alternative: "I cannot review this tonight, but I can do it by 11 tomorrow." Boundaries that are never spoken are only resentments, and boundaries you never enforce teach people to ignore them.

explanation.heading: Repairing relationships
explanation.body:
Conflict happens in every close relationship. What matters is repair. A good repair has four parts: **acknowledge** what you did specifically, **own** the impact without excuses, **make amends** with a concrete action, and **change** the behaviour. Compare "Sorry if you felt bad" with "I mocked your idea in front of the group and that embarrassed you. I am sorry. I will talk to you privately first and I will credit your idea in the next meeting."

Timing matters. Repair soon, once emotions have cooled, and let the other person respond in their own way. Not everyone will forgive immediately, and a sincere attempt still builds your integrity.

examples.title: Feedback with structure
examples.body: Karthik tells a teammate, "In Thursday's demo you answered the client's pricing question, which was my area. I felt sidelined and the client got mixed messages. Next time, could you pass pricing questions to me?" The teammate replies, "I did not realise, thanks. I will pass them over."
examples.takeaway: Describing situation, behaviour and impact, then making one request, keeps the talk about actions rather than character.

examples.title: A repair after a missed deadline
examples.body: Aditi promised a module for a group project on Friday and delivered on Monday, so the team lost its testing time. She messages: "I missed Friday and you lost testing time. I am sorry. I have cleared my Tuesday evening to help test, and from now on I will tell you by Wednesday if I am at risk."
examples.takeaway: A repair names the specific harm, offers an action and changes the future behaviour, which rebuilds trust.

exercises.prompt: In a project meeting, one member has not spoken for 30 minutes while others dominate. The most socially aware move is to:
options: Invite them with a specific, low-pressure question about their work.
Ignore it, quiet people prefer silence.
Ask them publicly why they are silent.
exercises.why: A specific, easy invitation opens space without pressure. Silence is not agreement, and asking why in public can embarrass.

exercises.prompt: The feedback structure is situation, behaviour and ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Impact explains the effect of the behaviour on you, the team or the work.

exercises.prompt: A friend messages you at 11 pm every night asking for help with assignments, and you are losing sleep. What is the best step?

options.text: Keep replying and feel resentful.
options.feedback: Unspoken limits turn into resentment and hurt the friendship later.

options.text: Stop replying without any explanation.
options.feedback: It sets a limit but leaves your friend confused and hurt.

options.text: Tell her kindly that you cannot reply after 10 pm and offer to help between 6 and 8 pm.
options.feedback: A calm, early boundary with an alternative protects you and the relationship.

options.text: Tell her she is selfish for messaging so late.
options.feedback: Labelling her invites defence rather than change.

exercises.why: A boundary is stated calmly with a clear limit and a workable alternative.

exercises.prompt: You snapped at a teammate during a stressful review and criticised their work in front of others. Write the message you would send to repair this. Include a specific acknowledgement, ownership of the impact, an amends action and a change you will make.

descriptors.3: Names exactly what you said or did and where.

descriptors.2: Owns impact with a small excuse.
descriptors.3: Owns the impact clearly, no excuses.
Concrete action with timing.

descriptors.2: Promise to do better with one step.
descriptors.3: Specific behaviour change you can be held to.

exercises.modelAnswer: Hi Neha, in today's review I raised my voice and called your report sloppy in front of everyone. That was unfair and I am sorry; it must have been embarrassing. I would like to go through the report with you tomorrow at 11 and credit the parts that were strong when we present. From now on I will give feedback privately first and keep my voice calm even when I am under pressure.
exercises.guidance: A strong repair is specific, takes responsibility without excuses such as "I was stressed" as the main point, offers something concrete and names a behaviour change. Avoid "sorry if you felt hurt" and avoid asking for forgiveness in the same message. Score yourself honestly against the model.

task.title: Give one feedback and make one repair
task.brief: Practise the structured feedback format and, if relevant, one small repair or boundary in real life.
steps: Choose a recent small irritation with a friend or teammate.
Write feedback in the form situation, behaviour, impact, request and deliver it kindly in person or by message.
Listen, thank and ask one clarifying question if you receive feedback back.
If you owe someone an apology or need to set a boundary, write it using the four repair parts or the boundary format.
Note how the other person responded.
checklist: My feedback named a specific behaviour
I did not defend when I received feedback
I noted the other person's response
task.evidencePrompt: Write your feedback sentence and describe how it was received.

quiz.prompt: Informal influence in a group means:
options: The person with the highest designation
People whose views shape decisions regardless of title
quiz.why: Informal influence is real impact on decisions that does not depend on title.

quiz.prompt: When you receive feedback that stings, say thanks and ask for an ____ to understand it. (one word)
quiz.why: An example turns a vague remark into something specific that you can act on.

quiz.prompt: Which best builds trust at work?
options: Doing what you said and warning early when you cannot
quiz.why: Reliable follow-through and early honest warnings build trust steadily.

quiz.prompt: Which is the strongest apology?
options: I was stressed, you know how it is.
I dismissed your idea in the meeting, which embarrassed you. I am sorry and will raise concerns privately.
quiz.why: It names the act, owns the impact and commits to a change.

bank.prompt: Which feedback is most useful?
options: In today's code review three variables were unclear, which slowed my reading. Could you use full names?
People are saying you are lazy.
bank.why: It names the situation, behaviour and impact and makes a request, with no labels.

bank.prompt: A manager asks for opinions and everyone waits for the senior consultant to speak first. This shows:
bank.why: People deferring to one person shows how influence works in practice.

bank.prompt: A boundary should be stated calmly, early and with an ____ where possible. (one word)
bank.why: Offering an alternative keeps the relationship warm while protecting your limit.

cards.front: What three questions help read a group?
cards.back: Who holds formal authority? Who holds informal influence? Who is quiet and why? Observe before acting and invite quiet members specifically.
Situation, behaviour, impact, then a request. Describe what could be observed and avoid labels like careless or lazy.
State the limit calmly and early, give a reason if useful, offer an alternative and keep to it. Unspoken boundaries become resentments.

cards.front: Four parts of a good repair?
cards.back: Acknowledge the specific act, own the impact without excuses, make concrete amends and change the future behaviour.

eq-4.reflection: Which relationship in your life needs either a clear boundary or a repair, and what is the first sentence you would say?

keyPoints: Read formal and informal roles before you act in a group.
Give feedback as situation, behaviour, impact and request.
Trust comes from reliability, boundaries from calm clarity.
Repair by acknowledging, owning, amending and changing.
revision.redo: Write one situation, behaviour, impact sentence about something recent.

etiquette-1.title: First Impressions and Workplace Basics
etiquette-1.summary: Make a steady first impression through punctuality, greetings, handshakes, introductions and respectful everyday behaviour.
objectives: Apply a simple punctuality rule and handle a delay gracefully.
Greet, shake hands and introduce yourself and others correctly.
Remember names using a short repeat-and-use technique.

explanation.heading: Why the first minutes matter
explanation.body:
People form an initial view of you within moments, and then tend to read later behaviour through that view. Etiquette is not about being fancy. It is a set of small signals that say: I respect your time, I am paying attention, and I can be trusted around clients. For a fresher joining an IT services firm, those signals count even before anyone sees your code or your SAP knowledge.

The good news is that first-impression behaviours are learnable habits, not personality traits. Four are worth mastering: arriving on time, greeting well, introducing people correctly, and behaving considerately in shared spaces.

explanation.heading: Punctuality and handling delays
explanation.body:
Treat the start time as the time you are ready, not the time you leave home. A practical rule is **arrive 10 minutes early for interviews and client meetings, and 5 minutes early for internal meetings**. In Indian cities, add a buffer for traffic, metro delays or a late bus; plan for the bad day, not the average one.

If you will still be late, message **as soon as you know**, not when you are already late. A good message has three parts: the fact, your new arrival time, and an offer. Example: "Good morning Mr Verma, a metro delay means I will reach by 10:20, not 10:00. Please start without me or reschedule if you prefer." Do not over-apologise or give a long story. Once you arrive, give one short apology and move on.

explanation.heading: Greetings, handshakes and introductions
explanation.body:
Greet with a clear "Good morning" or "Namaste" while making brief eye contact and smiling. In many Indian offices a handshake is common, but some people prefer folded hands, especially across gender or age lines. Follow the other person's lead: if they offer a hand, shake it; if they fold their hands, return the gesture. A good handshake is firm but not crushing, lasts about two seconds, with eye contact.

For self-introductions, give name, role or context, and one hook: "Hello, I am Deepak Raj, an MCA student, currently learning SAP ABAP." When introducing two people, **introduce the junior to the senior first**: "Ma'am, this is Kiran, our new trainee. Kiran, this is Ms Rao, our delivery head." Use titles such as Sir, Ma'am or Mr/Ms until invited to use first names.

explanation.heading: Remembering names and everyday conduct
explanation.body:
Names are easy to lose in the first five seconds because you are thinking about your own reply. Use **hear, repeat, use**: listen fully, repeat the name back ("Nice to meet you, Priya"), then use it once more within the conversation. If you forget, ask again early rather than guess: "Sorry, I missed your name once more."

Everyday conduct completes the picture. Put your phone on silent and face down in meetings. Knock before entering a cabin. Keep your voice low in open offices, and avoid strong-smelling food at your desk. Say please and thank you to support staff, security guards and the cafeteria team as readily as to managers. People notice how you treat those who cannot help your career.

examples.title: A late-arrival message
examples.body: At 9:35 Rhea realises her cab is stuck and her 10:00 interview is at risk. She messages the HR coordinator: "Good morning Ms Singh, I am stuck in traffic near Sector 14 and will reach by 10:15. I am sorry for the inconvenience. Please let me know if you would prefer to reschedule."
examples.takeaway: The message is early, gives a specific time, and offers a choice, which shows respect without drama.

examples.title: Introducing a trainee
examples.body: In the corridor you meet your project lead with a new joiner. You say: "Sir, meet Aman, who joined the ABAP team today. Aman, this is Mr Khanna, our project lead." Mr Khanna shakes hands, Aman says "Pleased to meet you, sir" and repeats "Mr Khanna" once while asking about his own role.
examples.takeaway: Junior first to senior, a clear context line, and the name used again make the introduction smooth.

exercises.prompt: You expect to be 15 minutes late for a client meeting. What is the best first step?
options: Message as soon as you know, with a new arrival time and an offer
Hurry and apologise when you arrive
Wait to see whether traffic clears
Ask a colleague to explain later
exercises.why: Early notice with a specific time lets others adjust. Silence or a late apology wastes their time and looks careless.

exercises.prompt: When introducing two people, you first name the ____ person to the senior person. (one word)
exercises.why: The convention is to present the junior person to the senior one, as a sign of respect for seniority.

exercises.prompt: You meet a senior woman manager at a client site. She smiles and folds her hands in a namaste. What do you do?

options.text: Extend your hand anyway because handshakes are professional.
options.feedback: Ignoring her cue can feel awkward; follow the greeting style the other person chooses.

options.text: Return the namaste with a warm smile and a clear greeting.
options.feedback: Mirroring her greeting respects her preference and keeps the moment comfortable.

options.text: Nod briefly and walk on.
options.feedback: A nod without a greeting can feel dismissive to a senior person.

options.text: Say "Hey!" and wave.
options.feedback: Casual slang is too informal for a first meeting with a senior client contact.

exercises.why: Following the other person's lead on greeting style shows awareness and respect, while a clear verbal greeting keeps it warm.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact words you would say when introducing yourself to a new project lead on day one, followed by the exact words you would use to introduce a new colleague to your senior manager. Add one line on how you will remember the lead's name.

rubric.label: Self-introduction has name, context and hook

descriptors.2: Name and context, but no hook.
descriptors.3: Name, context and one specific hook.
Correct order with a context line for both people.
Consistently polite with correct titles.
Hear, repeat and use at least once, with timing.

exercises.modelAnswer: Hello, I am Deepak Raj, an MCA student who has just joined as a trainee in the ABAP team. I am keen to learn from you. Ma'am, this is Kiran, who joined our team this week from Pune. Kiran, this is Ms Rao, our delivery head. To remember the lead's name I will repeat it back when we meet and use it once more in my first question.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers are short, spoken-style and complete: your name, your context and a hook, then the junior introduced to the senior with a context line. A common mistake is introducing the senior to the junior or skipping titles. Score yourself on each part.

task.title: Practise a five-part first impression
task.brief: Rehearse greeting, introduction and name recall in a real setting this week.
steps: Write a 15-second self-introduction with name, context and a hook.
Say it aloud twice, with a smile and eye contact.
Use it with one new person at college, a meetup or online.
Apply hear, repeat, use to their name.
Note what felt natural and what to adjust.
checklist: I used it with a real person
task.evidencePrompt: Write your introduction line and one thing you would change next time.

quiz.prompt: For an internal team meeting, a sensible arrival time is:
quiz.why: Arriving slightly early means you start ready; arriving on the dot or late risks delaying others.

quiz.prompt: A good handshake is:
options: Soft and brief with no eye contact
Firm but not crushing, about two seconds, with eye contact
quiz.why: A firm, short handshake with eye contact projects confidence without discomfort.

quiz.prompt: The three steps for remembering a name are hear, repeat and ____. (one word)
quiz.why: Using the name again in conversation fixes it in memory and shows attention.

quiz.prompt: Which behaviour shows good office conduct?
options: Taking calls loudly at your desk
Knocking before entering a cabin and silencing your phone in meetings
Eating strong-smelling food at your desk daily
quiz.why: Small considerate acts such as knocking and silencing phones show respect for others' space and focus.

bank.prompt: Your train is delayed and you will miss a 10 am call start by 10 minutes. The best message says:
options: I will join at 10:10 due to a train delay; please start without me
bank.why: A specific time and a clear offer lets the team plan, unlike vague or dismissive messages.

bank.prompt: You forget the name of someone you met five minutes ago. Best action?
options: Admit it and ask again politely
Ask someone else behind their back
bank.why: Asking early is honest and respectful; guessing wrong or avoiding the name is worse.

bank.prompt: A security guard at the client site greets you each morning. Good etiquette is to:
options: Greet him back politely and thank him
Greet only if your manager is watching
bank.why: Courtesy to everyone, regardless of rank, reflects character and is noticed by colleagues.

cards.back: Arrive 10 minutes early for interviews and client meetings, 5 for internal ones; if delayed, message early with a new time and an offer.
Follow the other person's lead. A handshake is firm, about two seconds, with eye contact; return folded hands if offered.
Introduce the junior person to the senior person, with a short context line for each.
Hear, repeat, use: listen fully, repeat the name back, use it once more soon after.

etiquette-1.reflection: Think of a first meeting where someone left you with a strong impression. Which of their small behaviours created it, and which will you copy?

keyPoints: Arrive 10 minutes early for key meetings and message early if late.
Mirror the greeting style the other person chooses.
Introduce the junior to the senior with context.
Hear, repeat and use a name to remember it.
Courtesy to everyone, including support staff, is part of professionalism.
revision.redo: Say your 15-second introduction aloud once and check it has name, context and a hook.

etiquette-2.title: Email, Chat and Meeting Etiquette
etiquette-2.summary: Write clear emails, use CC, BCC and reply-all wisely, follow chat norms, set response times and behave well on video calls.
objectives: Structure a professional email with a clear subject and ask.
Choose To, CC, BCC and reply-all correctly.
Follow chat, response-time and video-call norms.

concepts.label: Chat norms on Teams and Slack

explanation.heading: Email that gets read and answered
explanation.body:
In the previous lesson you saw how greetings and punctuality shape first impressions. Written messages create the same impression at scale. A good email lets the reader act without writing back to ask what you meant.

Use a **specific subject line** with the topic and the action: "Action needed by Fri: approval for UAT test data" beats "Query". Open with a greeting, state the purpose in the first sentence, give only necessary background, and end with a clear ask and a date. Keep paragraphs short. Close with thanks and your name. Re-read once before sending, and check attachments are actually attached.

explanation.heading: To, CC, BCC and reply-all
explanation.body:
**To** is for people who must act. **CC** is for people who should know. **BCC** hides recipients from each other, so use it for large external groups where addresses should stay private, not to secretly watch a conversation. Secret BCCing a manager into a dispute damages trust.

**Reply-all** sends your answer to everyone. Before pressing it, ask whether every person needs your reply. "Thanks, noted" to a 60-person distribution list wastes sixty minutes of attention across the group. Reply only to the sender for acknowledgements, and reply-all only when your information changes what everyone does. When adding someone new to a thread, say so: "Adding Neha from the basis team."

explanation.heading: Chat norms and response times
explanation.body:
Teams and Slack are for quick, low-formality exchanges, but they are still workplace records. Write the whole request in one message instead of "Hi" followed by silence. Use threads to keep topics tidy, mention a person only when you need their action, and avoid late-night pings unless something is urgent. Choose the channel by urgency: chat for quick questions, email for formal decisions and external parties, a call for anything that has gone three messages without resolving.

Set expectations about response time. A common norm is to reply to emails within one working day and to chat within a few hours. If you cannot give a full answer, send a short holding reply: "Received, I will confirm by 4 pm tomorrow." Then actually do it.

explanation.heading: Video-call etiquette
explanation.body:
Join two minutes early, test audio and keep your camera on if the team norm is cameras on. Sit facing a light source, with a plain or blurred background and your camera at eye level. Stay muted when you are not speaking, because keyboard clicks and home noise distract everyone. Use the raise-hand feature or chat to take a turn.

Watch your attention. Looking at another screen is visible. If you must step away, say so in chat. Wear something suitable from the waist up and keep a charger and a backup network, such as your mobile hotspot, ready. If you are recording or taking notes, tell people. At the end, confirm owners and deadlines in a short written summary.

examples.title: Rewriting a weak email
examples.body: Before: Subject "Doubt". "Hi, I tried the report but it is not working. Please check." After: Subject "ZSALES_REPORT shows blank output in QA - input needed by Thu". "Hi Mr Iyer, the report returns blank for company code 1000 in QA since yesterday. I checked the selection variant and authorisations. Could you confirm whether the test data was refreshed by Thursday 5 pm? Thanks, Anita."
examples.takeaway: The improved email names the problem, the effort already made, the exact ask and a deadline.

examples.title: Reply-all avoided
examples.body: A trainer emails 80 trainees: "Please submit attendance sheets." Ravi replies only to the trainer: "Submitted, thanks." Another trainee replies to all with "Done!" and triggers 40 more replies.
examples.takeaway: Reply to the sender for acknowledgements and keep a large list quiet.

exercises.prompt: Which subject line is most professional?
options: Action by Fri 5 pm: approve UAT dates for sales module
exercises.why: A specific subject shows topic, action and deadline. The others are vague or alarmist.

exercises.prompt: To hide recipients' addresses from each other in a large external mailing, use the ____ field. (one word)
exercises.why: BCC conceals recipients from one another, so it suits privacy in big groups, not secret monitoring.

exercises.prompt: A manager asks for a status update by 3 pm. At 1 pm you realise you will only have the full answer tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: Say nothing and hope she forgets.
options.feedback: Silence breaks trust and leaves her unable to plan around the delay.

options.text: Send a holding reply with what you know and a firm time for the rest.
options.feedback: A short, honest update with a new time keeps her informed and shows ownership.

options.text: Send a long apology at 5 pm.
options.feedback: A late apology comes after the damage and gives no useful information.

options.text: Rush an incomplete answer and call it final.
options.feedback: Presenting a half-finished answer as complete risks errors that cost more later.

exercises.why: A timely holding reply with partial facts and a specific new time protects trust and gives the manager choices.

exercises.prompt: You need a senior colleague to review your SQL query before a client demo tomorrow at 11 am. Write the chat message you would send, then one line explaining why you chose chat or email.

rubric.label: Message is self-contained with the full ask

descriptors.3: Greeting, context, ask and deadline in one message.

rubric.label: States a deadline and time needed

descriptors.3: Deadline plus how long review should take.
Polite, brief, easy to answer.
Reason linked to urgency and formality.

exercises.modelAnswer: Hi Sameer, could you spare 15 minutes today to review my sales summary query? It joins VBAK and VBAP for last quarter and I want to be sure the totals are correct before the client demo tomorrow at 11 am. I have attached the query and the output. Thank you. I used chat because it is quick and informal, and I can move to a call if it gets complicated.
exercises.guidance: A strong message names the task, effort needed, deadline and attachments in one go. Common mistakes are sending just "hi", demanding, or burying the ask. Check your channel reason links to urgency.

task.title: Audit and rewrite one email
task.brief: Improve one real or imagined email using the structure from this lesson.
steps: Pick an email you sent recently, or invent one about a project doubt.
Rewrite the subject to include topic, action and deadline.
State the purpose in the first sentence and end with a clear ask.
Check To, CC and BCC choices.
Read it aloud once and cut anything unnecessary.
checklist: There is a clear ask and date
task.evidencePrompt: Paste your new subject line and the first two sentences of the email.

quiz.prompt: Reply-all is appropriate when:
options: You want to say thanks to a large list
Your reply changes what everyone needs to do
You want to impress the manager
You are unsure who sent it
quiz.why: Use reply-all only when everyone needs the information; acknowledgements go to the sender alone.

quiz.prompt: A conversation has gone back and forth for three chat messages without resolution. Best next step:
quiz.why: A quick call resolves misunderstandings faster than a long chat thread.

quiz.prompt: A common norm is to answer emails within one ____ day. (one word)
quiz.why: One working day is a widely accepted response window for non-urgent email.

quiz.prompt: On a video call you are not speaking. You should:
options: Walk around with the camera on
quiz.why: Staying muted removes background noise and keyboard sounds that distract others.

bank.prompt: You are emailing 200 applicants about interview timings. To protect privacy you should place their addresses in:
bank.why: BCC keeps addresses hidden from one another, which protects applicants' privacy.

bank.prompt: You received a complex request and need two days. Best reply today:
options: No reply until it is done
Received; I will send the full answer by Thursday noon
bank.why: A holding reply with a firm date sets expectations and shows responsibility.

bank.prompt: Your home internet is unreliable before an interview call. Best preparation:
options: Keep a mobile hotspot ready and join early to test
Switch camera off all the time
bank.why: A backup connection and an early test reduce the chance of disruption.

cards.back: Topic plus action plus deadline, for example "Action by Fri: approve UAT dates for sales module".
CC informs people openly. BCC hides recipients from each other and is for privacy in large groups, not secret monitoring.
A short message that confirms receipt and gives a specific time for the full answer, such as "I will confirm by 4 pm tomorrow".
Join early, test audio, mute when not speaking, face light, eye-level camera, and have a backup network.

etiquette-2.reflection: Which of your written messages recently left the reader with questions, and how would a clearer subject and ask have helped?

keyPoints: Subject lines carry topic, action and deadline.
To is for action, CC for information, BCC for privacy.
Reply-all only when everyone needs it.
Use the right channel and send holding replies.
Be muted, visible and prepared on video calls.
revision.redo: Rewrite one vague subject line from your inbox so it has topic, action and deadline.

etiquette-3.title: Meals, Events and Cross-Cultural Awareness
etiquette-3.summary: Handle business meals, corporate events, hierarchy, cultural differences and gifts with courtesy and good judgement.
objectives: Behave well at business meals and corporate events.
Read hierarchy and cultural differences without stereotyping.
Handle gifts and hospitality within ethical limits.

explanation.heading: Meals are working meetings with food
explanation.body:
After email and meeting etiquette, the next setting is the table. A business lunch or team dinner is not mainly about eating. It is a chance to build trust, and people notice how you handle it. Before you go, check any dietary needs, ask whether a vegetarian or Jain option exists, and learn who is hosting.

At the table, wait for the host to sit or begin. Place your phone away, order something easy to eat, since ribs or dishes that need heavy mess invite trouble, and avoid ordering the most expensive item unless the host suggests it. Chew with your mouth closed, pass dishes to the right if you are in a Western-style setting, and keep conversation light at first: travel, food, city, interests. Business topics follow the host's lead. If you do not drink alcohol, a simple "No, thank you, I will have a lime soda" is enough and needs no explanation.

explanation.heading: Corporate events and networking at them
explanation.body:
Training programmes, farewell parties and annual days are social but still professional. Arrive within the first hour, greet the senior people at your table, and speak with people from other teams rather than staying in your own group. Avoid alcohol or keep it very limited even if others do not, because tipsy behaviour is remembered for years. Do not gossip, argue about politics or religion, or post unflattering photos of colleagues.

Before leaving, thank your host and say goodbye to the people you spoke to. Follow up the next day with a short message to someone useful: "It was nice to hear about the SAP migration project."

explanation.heading: Hierarchy and cross-cultural awareness
explanation.body:
Indian workplaces often show hierarchy through titles, seating and who speaks first. Many clients in other countries expect a flatter style, where first names are used and juniors disagree openly. Neither is wrong. Your skill is to observe, ask when unsure and adjust. Useful differences include: some cultures prefer direct feedback while others hint; punctuality is strict in some and flexible in others; small talk is valued before business in some places and skipped in others.

Avoid stereotypes: treat a culture as a hint, not a rule about an individual. Practical steps: learn how to pronounce the person's name, use formal titles until invited otherwise, avoid jokes that depend on a culture or religion, and respect festivals and fasting. When you are unsure, say: "Please tell me if I do something that is not the norm here."

explanation.heading: Gifts and hospitality
explanation.body:
Small, modest gifts can be a courtesy, such as a box of sweets at Diwali to a team. They become a problem when they are expensive, secret, or given while a decision is pending, because they can look like a bribe. Many companies have a gift policy with a value limit. Check it, and when in doubt, decline politely or declare it to your manager.

How to decline: "That is very kind, but our policy does not let me accept it. I really appreciate the thought." If you give, choose something modest and suitable, and avoid items involving alcohol, leather or beef without knowing the recipient. Present with a short thank-you note. Hospitality such as a working lunch is normal; lavish trips are not.

examples.title: The lunch with a client
examples.body: Neha is invited to lunch with a client manager visiting from Germany. She arrives a few minutes early, waits for the host, orders a simple dish, and asks about the visitor's first trip to India. She talks business only after the host brings it up and thanks the host personally at the end.
examples.takeaway: Following the host, keeping choices simple and starting with light conversation make a meal comfortable for everyone.

examples.title: A gift offer
examples.body: A vendor sends Arjun an expensive smartwatch the week before a purchase decision. Arjun thanks the vendor, returns it, and informs his manager in writing that he did so, citing company policy.
examples.takeaway: Timing and value turn a gift into a conflict of interest, so decline and tell your manager.

exercises.prompt: At a business lunch hosted by your manager, when should you start eating?
options: After the host starts or invites everyone to begin
As soon as your food arrives
exercises.why: Following the host is the standard courtesy at business meals; starting early can seem careless.

exercises.prompt: A gift given while a business decision is pending can look like a ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Timing and value can turn a gift into an apparent bribe, which is why many firms limit or ban such gifts.

exercises.prompt: At the annual party your seniors are drinking and urge you to have a drink. You do not want one. What is the best response?

options.text: Accept to avoid awkwardness.
options.feedback: Giving in against your wish can lead to regret and reputation risk.

options.text: Say loudly that drinking is wrong.
options.feedback: Judging others creates tension and embarrasses the group.

options.text: Smile, say "No, thank you, I will have a mocktail," and continue chatting.
options.feedback: A short, friendly refusal with an alternative keeps the mood light and needs no justification.

options.text: Leave the party quietly.
options.feedback: Leaving without a word loses the chance to build relationships and may seem rude.

exercises.why: A polite, brief refusal with an alternative drink respects your choice without criticising others.

exercises.prompt: You are joining a first call with a client team from a country where first names are the norm, but your own manager is very formal. Write how you would open the call, how you would address people, and two cultural cautions you will keep in mind.

descriptors.3: Warm, brief opening with context and small talk.
Starts formal then follows their lead.
Two specific and respectful cautions.
Treats culture as a hint and checks individually.

exercises.modelAnswer: I would open with "Good morning, everyone, thank you for making time. I am Deepak, part of the ABAP support team." I would address people by title and surname until they invite first names, then follow their lead. Two cautions: avoid jokes about culture or religion, and note that time zones matter so I confirm the schedule in both time zones. I will treat these as hints and check what each person prefers.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer opens warmly, adapts address style gradually, and gives concrete cautions such as time zones or direct feedback. A common mistake is generalising about a whole country. Show that you will observe and ask.

task.title: Prepare a meal and event checklist
task.brief: Build a short personal checklist you will use before the next business meal or event.
steps: Write three things to check before a business meal, such as dietary options and the host.
Write three events behaviours: arrival, alcohol choice, thanks.
Write a two-line polite refusal for a gift.
Share the checklist with a friend and ask what they would add.
checklist: It is short enough to use
task.evidencePrompt: Paste your checklist and the gift refusal lines.

quiz.prompt: You are not sure what to order at a client dinner. Best approach:
options: A simple dish that is easy to eat
quiz.why: Simple, moderately priced dishes avoid mess and cost concerns, so attention stays on conversation.

quiz.prompt: After a corporate event, a good follow-up is:
options: A short next-day message to someone you met
quiz.why: A brief message turns a social moment into a relationship.

quiz.prompt: Treat a cultural pattern as a hint, not a ____ about an individual. (one word)
quiz.why: Culture offers hints; individuals vary, so observe and ask instead of assuming.

quiz.prompt: A supplier offers an expensive gift while you are choosing a vendor. You should:
options: Decline politely and tell your manager
quiz.why: Declining and disclosing protects you from a conflict of interest.

bank.prompt: You are vegetarian and invited to a team lunch. Best approach:
options: Tell the host in advance and ask about options
bank.why: Telling the host early lets them plan, avoiding awkward moments for everyone.

bank.prompt: A client from another country speaks very directly. You should:
options: Understand it as a style difference and clarify tone if needed
bank.why: Direct style is a cultural pattern; clarifying calmly keeps the relationship healthy.

bank.prompt: Which gift to a colleague at Diwali is most appropriate?
options: A modest box of sweets given openly
A secret gift to the manager only
bank.why: Modest, open gifts are a courtesy; costly or secret gifts raise ethical questions.

cards.front: First rule at a business meal?
cards.back: Follow the host: sit, order and eat when they do, choose simple dishes, and keep early talk light.
Mingle beyond your team, go easy on or skip alcohol, avoid gossip, thank the host and follow up.
Observe, ask politely, use titles until invited, avoid stereotypes and treat culture as a hint, not a rule.

cards.front: When is a gift a problem?
cards.back: When it is costly, secret, or given while a decision is pending; follow policy and tell your manager.

etiquette-3.reflection: Recall a time you felt unsure how to behave at a social or business gathering. What would you check or do differently next time?

keyPoints: Follow the host at meals and keep choices simple.
Events are professional: moderate behaviour, mingle, thank and follow up.
Treat culture as a hint and ask politely.
Decline costly or badly timed gifts and tell your manager.
revision.redo: Write one polite sentence you could use to decline a drink and one to decline a gift.

etiquette-4.title: Professional Ethics and Conduct
etiquette-4.summary: Practise confidentiality, honesty, owning mistakes, sensible social media conduct, respect, harassment awareness and managing up.
objectives: Protect confidential information in everyday situations.
Own mistakes quickly and honestly.
Recognise harassment and respond, and manage up respectfully.

concepts.label: Respect, harassment awareness and managing up

explanation.heading: Ethics is etiquette with consequences
explanation.body:
Earlier lessons covered greetings, messages and meals. Ethics goes deeper: it decides whether clients, managers and colleagues can trust you with real responsibility. In IT services you will see client data, source code, salary details and plans that are not public. Trust is the main thing you sell besides your skills.

Four habits carry most of the weight: keep confidences, tell the truth including about your own mistakes, behave carefully online, and treat people with respect while managing your relationship with your manager.

explanation.heading: Confidentiality in practice
explanation.body:
Confidential information includes client names and data, project details, unreleased products, internal pricing and colleagues' personal information. You will usually sign a non-disclosure agreement, but habit matters more than paperwork. Do not discuss client work in cabs, lifts, cafeterias or on public WhatsApp groups. Do not take screenshots of client systems for your personal portfolio. Do not copy production data to a personal laptop or pen drive. Lock your screen when you step away.

Worked example: a friend asks which bank you are working for and what the migration involves. A safe reply is: "I cannot discuss client details, but I can tell you I work in SAP finance support." You are helpful and still protect the client.

explanation.heading: Honesty and owning mistakes
explanation.body:
Everyone makes mistakes: a wrong transport request, a deleted table, a missed deadline. What matters is speed and honesty. Use a four-part script: **what happened, the impact, what you are doing about it, what you will do differently**. For example: "I released the wrong transport to QA. Testing is paused for the finance team. I have asked Basis to reverse it and will finish within an hour. From now on I will check the transport list with a colleague before release."

Do not hide, blame others or give vague excuses. Hidden mistakes grow. Reported early, most are small. Honesty also means not exaggerating skills on your CV or claiming credit for teammates' work.

explanation.heading: Social media, respect and managing up
explanation.body:
Treat every post as permanent and public. Do not share client or company information, complain about your employer, or post photos of colleagues without consent. Keep a separate professional profile and review privacy settings. Before posting, ask: would I be comfortable if my manager, a client and my parents saw this?

Respect means no teasing about appearance, caste, region, religion, gender or accent. **Harassment** is unwelcome conduct, such as comments, touching, repeated messages, or jokes, that makes someone uncomfortable or unsafe. In India, workplaces have an Internal Committee for sexual harassment complaints; know how to reach it. If you witness it, you can support the person, document what you saw and report it.

**Managing up** means helping your manager succeed: learn their priorities, send short regular updates, bring options with problems, and ask for feedback. Disagree privately and respectfully, with data.

examples.title: Owning a mistake
examples.body: Karan overwrote a test configuration. He messaged his lead within ten minutes: "I overwrote the QA config for the billing test. It affects tomorrow's demo. I have restored the backup and checked the values. I will take a backup before every change from now on."
examples.takeaway: Quick disclosure with impact and fix converts a mistake into evidence of reliability.

examples.title: A risky post
examples.body: Pooja posts a photo of her desk showing a client dashboard on her monitor with the caption "Another long day at Client X". A colleague points out customer names are visible, and she deletes the post and informs her manager.
examples.takeaway: Even background details can leak client information, so check screens before posting.

exercises.prompt: Which action is the safest for client data?
options: Using only approved systems and locking the screen when away
Copying production data to a personal pen drive for practice
Discussing the project loudly in a cab
Sharing screenshots in a friends' group
exercises.why: Approved systems and locked screens keep data inside the client's controls; the others create leaks.

exercises.prompt: A good mistake report covers what happened, the impact, the fix and what you will do ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Naming the change you will make is what turns an apology into prevention.

exercises.prompt: Your manager asks for a deadline you believe is unrealistic. What is the best approach?

options.text: Agree and quietly miss it.
options.feedback: Silent failure surprises your manager and damages trust.

options.text: Refuse openly in the meeting.
options.feedback: A flat refusal without data feels confrontational.

options.text: Privately show your estimate, explain the risks and propose options or a revised date.
options.feedback: Bringing data and options helps the manager decide and protects the project.

exercises.prompt: You accidentally emailed a client the wrong version of a test report that includes another client's name. Write the message you would send to your manager within the hour, using the four-part mistake script, and one step you would take to prevent a repeat.

Specific, checkable step.
