Impact: Client A may have seen another client's name. I have asked IT to recall the email and will call Client A within the hour to ask them to delete it. From now on I will have a colleague verify attachments before sending to external parties.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers are factual, quick and specific, and they escalate promptly. Avoid blame, vagueness and minimising the issue. Exposure of another client's name is a confidentiality matter, so your manager must know right away.

options: Copy production data to your laptop
Ask for masked or sample test data

finance-1.title: Income, Spending and Budgeting
finance-1.summary: Track where your money goes, split it into needs, wants and savings, build an emergency fund and pay yourself first.
objectives: Track one month of income and spending, including UPI and card payments, and read your cash flow.
Split a monthly income into needs, wants and savings and adapt the split to your situation.
Calculate an emergency fund target and set up a pay-yourself-first habit.

explanation.heading: Know where the money goes
explanation.body:
Most students and freshers can say roughly what they earn, a stipend or salary, but cannot say where it went by the 20th. **Cash flow** is simply money coming in minus money going out in a period, usually a month. If more goes out than comes in, you are running a deficit and covering it with savings, a parent or a loan. If less goes out, you have a surplus.

UPI makes spending feel weightless, because there is no cash leaving your hand. A ₹120 chai-and-snack, a ₹349 food order and a ₹199 subscription look small, but thirty of them make a large number. To track, export or scroll through one month of UPI, card and cash entries and put every item into a category: rent or hostel, food, travel, phone and internet, study costs, entertainment, shopping, other. The category totals, not the individual items, show you the pattern.

explanation.heading: Needs, wants and savings
explanation.body:
A popular starting guideline is the **50/30/20 split**: about 50 percent of income to needs, 30 percent to wants and 20 percent to savings and debt repayment. **Needs** are costs you cannot easily avoid: rent, groceries, commute, basic phone plan, insurance premiums, loan EMIs. **Wants** are things you can reduce without harm: eating out, extra subscriptions, new gadgets. **Savings** cover emergency fund, investments and extra loan repayment.

Treat it as a starting point, not a law. Worked example: a trainee earns ₹25,000 a month. The guideline gives ₹12,500 for needs, ₹7,500 for wants and ₹5,000 for savings. If rent and food alone cost ₹16,000, needs are 64 percent, so the trainee might trim wants to 16 percent and keep savings at 20 percent. A fresher who lives with family may have needs of only 30 percent and can save much more. The skill is to decide the split consciously.

explanation.heading: The emergency fund
explanation.body:
An **emergency fund** is money set aside only for shocks such as a sudden job loss, a medical bill or an urgent repair. It keeps you from borrowing on a credit card at high interest. A common target is **three to six months of essential expenses**, not of income. Essentials are your needs.

Example: essentials are ₹14,000 a month. Three months is 3 x 14,000 = ₹42,000 and six months is ₹84,000. If you can save ₹5,000 a month towards it, ₹42,000 takes 42,000 / 5,000 = 8.4 months, so about nine months. Keep this money somewhere safe and easy to reach, such as a savings account, separate from your daily account so you are not tempted. Someone with a stable family safety net may aim for the lower end; someone supporting parents or in an unstable job should aim higher.

explanation.heading: Pay yourself first
explanation.body:
If you save what is left at month-end, nothing is usually left. **Pay yourself first** means moving your savings amount out as soon as income arrives, ideally by an automatic standing instruction or SIP-style transfer on the day after payday. You then budget with the remaining money.

Start small. Even ₹1,000 a month builds the habit, and you can raise it with every raise or stipend increase. A common mistake is a budget so strict that it fails in week two. Build in a small "fun" line, and review once a month for ten minutes. Educational note: this lesson explains concepts, and your own numbers will differ.

examples.title: A month of UPI exposed
examples.body: Ananya, a 22-year-old intern earning ₹20,000, exported her month. Food delivery added up to ₹3,900 across 19 orders, which she had guessed at ₹1,500. Rent and mess were ₹9,000, travel ₹1,800, phone ₹400, shopping ₹2,500 and miscellaneous UPI transfers ₹1,600. She ended the month with only ₹800 left and no savings.
examples.takeaway: Category totals revealed a pattern that single payments hid; her guess was off by more than double.

examples.title: Paying yourself first
examples.body: After seeing this, Ananya sets a standing instruction of ₹2,000 to a separate savings account on the 2nd of each month. She caps food delivery at ₹2,000 with a weekly spending limit in her UPI app and drops one subscription of ₹199. After three months she has ₹6,000 saved without ever feeling a sharp cut.
examples.takeaway: Automating the saving first and trimming one want is easier than relying on month-end willpower.

exercises.prompt: A friend says, "I earn ₹30,000 and spend ₹33,000 in most months, but I am fine because I use my card." What does cash flow tell you?
options: She has a surplus because the card pays for it
Her income is too high to matter
She has a monthly deficit of ₹3,000 that debt or savings is covering
Cash flow only counts physical cash
exercises.why: Cash flow is money in minus money out, here minus ₹3,000. A card only delays payment. The other options ignore the deficit or misread what cash flow measures.

exercises.prompt: Essential expenses are ₹18,000 a month. A six-month emergency fund in rupees would be ₹____. (number only)
exercises.why: Six months of essentials is 6 x 18,000 = ₹1,08,000. The target is based on essentials, not on total income or wants.

exercises.prompt: You earn ₹30,000. Needs are ₹21,000, wants ₹7,000 and nothing is saved. Which adjustment is most sensible?

options.text: Ignore it, because the 50/30/20 split is a law and you cannot meet it.
options.feedback: The split is a guideline, so refusing to adapt it throws away a useful tool.

options.text: Cut wants to about ₹5,000 and move ₹2,000 to savings now, then raise savings as needs fall or income grows.
options.feedback: You start with a small realistic saving and adapt the guideline to your higher needs.

options.text: Stop all wants for six months and save ₹7,000 immediately.
options.feedback: A plan this strict usually collapses within weeks.

options.text: Save at month-end whatever remains.
options.feedback: Nothing is usually left at month-end, so savings stay at zero.

exercises.why: The split is a starting guideline. With high needs you adjust it, starting with a small automatic saving rather than a perfect plan.

exercises.prompt: Make a realistic monthly plan for a fresher earning ₹28,000. Write amounts for needs, wants and savings, state one thing you will cut or automate, and give an emergency fund target with the number of months it will take to reach it.

descriptors.2: All three groups with amounts that add up roughly to income.
descriptors.3: All three groups, amounts add up and are explained against needs.
One concrete action with an amount or schedule.

descriptors.2: Target based on months of expenses with rough time.
descriptors.3: Target from essentials, a monthly saving and months to reach it, correctly calculated.
Realistic with a small fun allowance.

exercises.modelAnswer: Income ₹28,000. Needs ₹15,500 (rent share, food, travel, phone), wants ₹6,500, savings ₹6,000. I will set a standing instruction of ₹6,000 on the 2nd and cap food delivery at ₹2,000. Essentials are ₹15,500, so a three-month fund is ₹46,500; at ₹4,000 a month towards it that is about 12 months, with the other ₹2,000 going to a long-term goal.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer has amounts that add up, one concrete change and a fund calculated from essentials, not income. Common mistakes are leaving no savings, budgeting wants at zero, and mixing up income with essentials. Check your arithmetic and rate yourself honestly against the model.

task.title: Track one week of spending

Put each into needs or wants and total each group.
Multiply the week by about four to estimate a month and compare it with your income.

quiz.prompt: Cash flow in a month is:
quiz.why: Cash flow compares what comes in with what goes out.

quiz.why: The guideline puts about 20 percent towards savings and debt repayment.

quiz.prompt: An emergency fund target is usually based on:
options: Three to six months of total salary
Three to six months of essential expenses
quiz.why: Essentials are what you must keep paying in an emergency, so the target is built on them.

options: Move savings out on payday before spending
Save only if there is money left
quiz.why: Saving first and automatically avoids the problem of nothing being left.

options: It is more expensive than cash
It feels weightless and many small payments add up unnoticed

bank.why: Paying yourself first means saving before you spend.

cards.front: What is cash flow and how do you track it?
cards.back: Money in minus money out for a month. Categorise a full month of UPI, card and cash payments and read the category totals.
About 50 percent needs, 30 percent wants and 20 percent savings and debt repayment. Adapt it to your real income and needs.

cards.front: How big should an emergency fund be?
cards.back: Three to six months of essential expenses, kept in a safe, easy-to-reach account separate from daily spending.

cards.front: How do you pay yourself first?
cards.back: Set an automatic transfer to savings for the day after payday and budget with what remains. Start small and raise it over time.

finance-1.reflection: Looking at your last month, which category surprised you most, and what one automatic saving will you set up this week?

The 50/30/20 split is a guideline you adapt.
Emergency fund is three to six months of essentials.
Automate saving on payday before you spend.

finance-2.title: Interest, Inflation and Compounding
finance-2.summary: Compare simple and compound interest with worked rupee calculations, use the rule of 72, and understand how inflation reduces real returns.
objectives: Calculate simple and compound interest for a given amount, rate and time.
Use the rule of 72 to estimate how long money takes to double.
Explain inflation and estimate a real return from a nominal return.

explanation.heading: Why interest matters
explanation.body: In the last lesson you tracked cash flow and learned to save first. Now the question is what saved money does while it waits. **Interest** is the price paid for using money. When you deposit, the bank pays you interest; when you borrow, you pay it. All figures in this lesson are illustrative round numbers, because real rates change often.

explanation.heading: Simple and compound interest
explanation.body:
**Simple interest** is calculated only on the original amount (the principal): SI = P x R x T / 100, where R is the yearly rate in percent and T is time in years. Example: ₹10,000 at 8 percent for 3 years gives 10,000 x 8 x 3 / 100 = ₹2,400, so the total is ₹12,400.

**Compound interest** is calculated on the principal plus the interest already earned. With yearly compounding the amount is P x (1 + R/100)^T. Same example: 10,000 x 1.08^3. Year 1: 10,800. Year 2: 11,664. Year 3: 12,597.12. Interest earned is ₹2,597.12, which is ₹197.12 more than simple interest. The gap looks small over 3 years but grows fast with longer time, because interest starts earning interest. This is why starting early beats saving more later.

explanation.heading: The rule of 72
explanation.body:
A quick way to estimate doubling time is the **rule of 72**: divide 72 by the yearly rate in percent. At 8 percent, 72 / 8 = 9 years to double. At 6 percent, 12 years. At 12 percent, 6 years. It is an approximation that works best for rates between about 6 and 12 percent, and it assumes compounding with no withdrawals.

Use it for sanity checks. If someone promises to double your money in two years, the rule implies a return of 72 / 2 = 36 percent every year, which should make you suspicious. It also shows the cost of high interest on debt: a loan at 24 percent doubles in about 3 years if unpaid.

explanation.heading: Inflation and real returns
explanation.body:
**Inflation** is the general rise in prices over time. If inflation is 6 percent, something costing ₹100 today costs about ₹106 next year, so each rupee buys less. Your **nominal return** is the percentage your money grew. Your **real return** is what remains after inflation, roughly nominal minus inflation. Example: money growing at 7 percent while inflation is 5 percent has a real return of about 2 percent. Precisely, 1.07 / 1.05 = 1.019, so 1.9 percent.

This is why cash under the mattress loses value, and why an account paying less than inflation slowly shrinks your buying power even though the balance rises.

explanation.heading: Time value of money
explanation.body: **Time value of money** says ₹1 today is worth more than ₹1 later, because today's rupee can earn interest and later rupees are eroded by inflation. Using our example, ₹12,597.12 received after 3 years at 8 percent is equal to ₹10,000 today. So when comparing offers, such as a ₹1,00,000 payment now versus ₹1,10,000 in two years, you need to ask what the money could earn. At 8 percent, ₹1,00,000 would become 1,00,000 x 1.1664 = ₹1,16,640 in two years, which beats ₹1,10,000.

examples.title: Two friends, one head start
examples.body: Kabir invests ₹5,000 at 8 percent for 9 years and Meera invests the same ₹5,000 for 18 years. By the rule of 72, money doubles every 9 years at 8 percent. Kabir has about ₹10,000. Meera has doubled twice: ₹20,000, not ₹15,000, though she held it only twice as long.
examples.takeaway: Doubling every period means extra time has an outsized effect.

examples.title: Real return check
examples.body: A fixed deposit offers 6.5 percent and the household inflation rate is 5.5 percent. Real return is about 1 percent. On ₹50,000, the balance after a year is ₹53,250, but things that cost ₹50,000 now cost about ₹52,750, so buying power rose only by about ₹500.
examples.takeaway: Always compare the rate with inflation before calling the result growth.

exercises.prompt: Simple interest on ₹20,000 at 5 percent per year for 2 years, in rupees, is ₹____. (number only)
Using the rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at 9 percent a year?
exercises.why: 72 / 9 = 8 years. Nine years confuses the rate with the time, and 12 years is the answer for 6 percent.

exercises.prompt: A relative says, "My savings account pays 3 percent and the balance only goes up, so I am safe." Inflation is about 5 percent. What is the best response?

options.text: Agree, because a rising balance means growth.
options.feedback: A rising balance can still buy less each year when inflation is higher.

options.text: Explain that the real return is about minus 2 percent, so buying power is slowly falling, and suggest comparing options for long-term money.
options.feedback: You correct the idea with real return and do not give a product pick.

options.text: Tell them to move everything into one risky product.
options.feedback: Abruptly chasing returns replaces one problem with another.

options.text: Say inflation does not affect savings.
options.feedback: Inflation affects every rupee you hold.

exercises.why: Real return is nominal return minus inflation. A balance that rises more slowly than prices is still losing buying power.

exercises.prompt: Explain to a friend why ₹1,00,000 today is not the same as ₹1,05,000 in two years. Use simple numbers: assume 6 percent yearly compounding and 5 percent yearly inflation. Calculate what ₹1,00,000 grows to in two years and say which option is better and why.

descriptors.3: Correct figure of ₹1,12,360 with working shown.
Picks with a reason tied to the figures.
Explains real return after inflation.
Friendly and clear to a non-expert.

exercises.modelAnswer: ₹1,00,000 at 6 percent for two years becomes 1,00,000 x 1.06 x 1.06 = ₹1,12,360. So ₹1,05,000 in two years is worth less than what I could have earned by waiting for nothing. Taking the money now and keeping it at 6 percent is better by about ₹7,360. With inflation at 5 percent, the real growth is only about 1 percent a year, so the gap in buying power is smaller, but the earlier money still wins.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer calculates 1.06 squared as 1.1236, gets ₹1,12,360, compares it with ₹1,05,000, and mentions inflation. Common mistakes are adding 12 percent instead of compounding, ignoring inflation, and stating a conclusion without numbers. Check arithmetic before scoring yourself.

task.title: Compound it yourself
task.brief: Use a spreadsheet or calculator to see compounding with your own illustrative numbers.
steps: Pick an amount you could imagine saving, such as ₹1,000, and a rate such as 8 percent.
Compute simple interest for 5 years and compound interest for 5 years and note the difference.
Apply the rule of 72 to the rate and check it against your compound figures.
Subtract an illustrative inflation of 5 percent and write the real return in one sentence.
checklist: I calculated simple and compound figures
I wrote one sentence about what I learned
task.evidencePrompt: Write your simple figure, your compound figure and the real return.

quiz.prompt: Compound interest differs from simple interest because it is calculated on:
quiz.why: Interest earns interest in compounding.

quiz.prompt: At 12 percent a year, money doubles in about ____ years. (number only)
If your money grows 6 percent and inflation is 4 percent, the real return is about:
quiz.why: Subtract inflation from the nominal return: 6 minus 4 is about 2 percent.

quiz.prompt: Time value of money means:
options: A rupee today is worth more than a rupee later
quiz.why: Today's rupee can earn returns, and future rupees are reduced by inflation.

bank.prompt: You deposit ₹10,000 at 10 percent compounded yearly. What is the balance after 2 years?
bank.why: Year one gives ₹11,000, and year two adds 10 percent of that, giving ₹12,100. Simple interest would give ₹12,000.

bank.prompt: An advertisement claims your money will double in 3 years. The yearly return it implies, by the rule of 72, is ____ percent. (number only)
bank.why: 72 / 3 = 24 percent every year, which is a very high claim and a reason for caution.

bank.prompt: A balance rises from ₹1,00,000 to ₹1,04,000 while prices rise 6 percent. Your buying power has:
bank.why: Growth of 4 percent is below 6 percent inflation, so the real return is negative.

cards.back: Simple: P x R x T / 100 on the principal only. Compound: P x (1 + R/100)^T, where interest also earns interest.
Divide 72 by the yearly percent return to estimate years to double. At 8 percent, about 9 years.

cards.front: How do you find a real return?
cards.back: Roughly nominal return minus inflation. Precisely, divide (1 + nominal) by (1 + inflation) and subtract 1.

cards.front: Why is money today worth more than later?
cards.back: Because it can earn interest now and later money loses buying power to inflation.

finance-2.reflection: Which of your current savings or goals is most affected by the length of time you hold it, and what does compounding suggest you should do about it?

keyPoints: Simple interest uses principal only; compound grows on itself.
Rule of 72 gives doubling time quickly.
Real return is nominal return minus inflation.
A rupee today is worth more than a rupee later.

finance-3.title: Investing Basics and Risk
finance-3.summary: Understand common Indian saving and investing options, SIPs, index funds, diversification, risk versus return and the warning signs of scams.
objectives: Describe what savings accounts, fixed deposits, PPF, EPF, mutual funds, index funds and gold are and how they differ.
Explain how SIPs, diversification and the risk-return trade-off work.
Spot common investment scam warning signs and verify an adviser safely.

concepts.label: Savings accounts, FDs, PPF and EPF
Mutual funds, index funds and SIPs

explanation.heading: A map, not a recommendation
explanation.body: After learning about compounding and inflation, the natural question is where money can grow. This lesson is educational, not personal advice. Rules, tax treatment and interest rates change, so check current details with the official source or a registered professional before acting. Think of this as a map of the main roads.

explanation.heading: Low-risk options
explanation.body: A **savings account** keeps money safe and instantly reachable, but pays low interest, so it suits your emergency fund and near-term spending. A **fixed deposit (FD)** locks money with a bank for a fixed period at a rate agreed in advance. Breaking it early usually carries a penalty. The **Public Provident Fund (PPF)** is a government-backed long-term savings scheme with a long lock-in. The **Employees' Provident Fund (EPF)** is a retirement saving to which you and your employer contribute from salary. Both have rules and rates that the government revises, so treat any number you hear as temporary. These options give predictability, but returns may barely beat inflation, which you saw last time.

explanation.heading: Mutual funds, index funds and SIPs
explanation.body:
A **mutual fund** pools money from many investors and a fund manager invests it in shares, bonds or both. You own **units**, priced at the **NAV** (net asset value per unit), and the price moves with the market. An **index fund** simply copies a market index such as a broad list of large companies, with low costs and no attempt to beat the market. A **SIP** (systematic investment plan) is not a product; it is a method of investing a fixed amount at regular intervals into a fund.

Example: ₹5,000 a month buys units at NAVs of ₹50, ₹40 and ₹62.50. That is 100 + 125 + 80 = 305 units for ₹15,000, an average cost of about ₹49.18 per unit, slightly below the simple average NAV of about ₹50.83. SIPs reduce the stress of timing the market, but they do not guarantee profit. Value can fall, especially over short periods.

explanation.heading: Risk, return and diversification
explanation.body:
**Risk** here means the chance that results differ from what you expect, including losing money. Higher potential **return** generally comes with higher risk, and no one can reliably give high returns with no risk. The longer your horizon, the more short-term swings you can ride out; money needed within a year or two should not sit in volatile assets.

**Diversification** means spreading money over different assets and sectors so that one failure does not wreck everything: "do not keep all your eggs in one basket". Gold is often used as a diversifier because its price does not always move with shares, though it can also fall and pays no interest. An index fund is diversified by design; putting your whole savings into one friend's start-up or a single stock is not.

explanation.heading: Spotting scams
explanation.body: Common warning signs are **guaranteed high returns**, pressure to decide today, promises of doubling money, requests to recruit friends, tips from social media or messaging groups, unregistered advisers, and requests to move money to personal accounts or wallets. Genuine investments clearly state that returns are not guaranteed. In India, advisers, brokers and funds should be registered with the market regulator, so ask for the registration number and check it on the regulator's official site yourself rather than from a link they send. Never share OTPs or PINs. If something is too good to be true, walk away and talk to someone you trust.

examples.title: Matching the goal to the tool
examples.body: Neha has three goals: ₹60,000 emergency fund, a laptop in 8 months, and a retirement saving she will not touch for 30 years. In general terms, the first two need safety and quick access, such as a savings account or short FD. The third can tolerate market swings, because there are decades to recover, and may use a diversified index fund.
examples.takeaway: Time horizon decides how much risk is sensible for each goal.

examples.title: A scam message
examples.body: A message in a Telegram group says: "Invest ₹10,000, get ₹30,000 in 15 days, guaranteed. Only 5 slots left. Bring two friends and earn extra." A return of 200 percent in 15 days would mean a 72 / ... rule-of-72 doubling in days, which no genuine investment can promise. Guaranteed, urgent, recruit-friends and no registration are four red flags at once.
examples.takeaway: Count the red flags; one is enough to pause and verify.

exercises.prompt: Which statement about a fixed deposit is correct?
options: It locks money for a set period at an agreed rate, and early withdrawal may carry a penalty
Its value changes daily with the share market
It is the same as a SIP
exercises.why: An FD is a fixed-term deposit with an agreed rate. It is not market-linked, not a SIP, and cannot promise to beat inflation.

exercises.prompt: Investing a fixed amount into a fund every month is called a ____. (three-letter abbreviation)
exercises.why: SIP stands for systematic investment plan; it is a method, not a product.

exercises.prompt: A "financial coach" you met online promises 25 percent monthly returns, says it is guaranteed, and asks you to transfer money to his personal UPI ID today. What should you do?

options.text: Send a small amount to test.
options.feedback: A small test still funds the fraud and invites bigger asks.

options.text: Decline, do not share OTPs or PINs, and check any claimed registration through the regulator's official site on your own.
options.feedback: Guaranteed returns, urgency and a personal account are red flags; verifying independently is the safe habit.

options.text: Send it quickly before slots end.
options.feedback: Pressure and urgency are classic scam tactics.

options.text: Ask him to send a screenshot of profits.
options.feedback: Screenshots are easily faked and prove nothing.

exercises.why: Guaranteed high returns, deadlines and personal accounts are classic scam signs. Verify independently and never rush.

exercises.prompt: You are 22 with ₹1,00,000 and three goals: a ₹30,000 emergency fund, a ₹40,000 purchase in 1 year, and ₹30,000 for a long-term goal 15 years away. In general terms (not advice), write how risk and time horizon affect what kind of option suits each goal, and why you would not put all of it in one asset.

descriptors.2: Links short goals to safer options.
descriptors.3: Links each goal to a sensible risk level with reasons.
Explains it with the goals as examples.

rubric.label: Notes no guarantees or checking rules

descriptors.3: Notes no guarantee and rules/rates change.
Clear, goal by goal.

exercises.modelAnswer: The emergency fund and the one-year purchase need safety and quick access, so a savings account or short deposit makes sense; a market fall could leave me short when I need the money. The 15-year goal can take swings, so a diversified fund may suit it, though returns are never guaranteed and rules change. Putting everything in one asset is risky because one failure would hit all three goals; spreading across assets limits the damage.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer treats each goal separately, uses time horizon, and states that returns are not guaranteed. Avoid naming a "best" product or promising returns. Common mistakes are using high-risk options for short-term money and thinking diversification removes all risk. Self-rate against the model.

quiz.prompt: EPF is mainly:
options: A retirement saving funded by employee and employer from salary
quiz.why: EPF accumulates from salary contributions for retirement.

quiz.prompt: A mutual fund unit is priced at its ____, short for net asset value. (abbreviation)
quiz.why: NAV is the per-unit value of the fund.

options: Putting everything in your best idea
Spreading money across different assets to reduce reliance on one
quiz.why: Spreading reduces the damage if one asset fails, but never removes risk.

quiz.prompt: Which is the biggest red flag?
options: A guaranteed high return with pressure to decide today
A fund stating returns are not guaranteed
quiz.why: Guaranteed high returns plus urgency are classic scam signals.

bank.prompt: In a SIP, the NAV is ₹50 in month one and ₹40 in month two. With ₹2,000 each month, how many units are bought in total?
bank.why: Month one buys 40 units and month two buys 50, a total of 90. Check: 2,000/50 = 40 and 2,000/40 = 50, so 90 units.

options: In a highly volatile asset for faster growth
In a safe, easily accessible option
bank.why: Short-term money should avoid volatility so that a market fall does not leave you short.

bank.prompt: A genuine investment cannot honestly offer ____ high returns. (one word)
bank.why: No honest investment can guarantee high returns because returns depend on risk and markets.

cards.front: What are FD, PPF and EPF in one line each?
cards.back: FD: fixed-term bank deposit at an agreed rate. PPF: government-backed long-term scheme. EPF: retirement saving funded by you and your employer. Rules and rates change.
A method of investing a fixed amount regularly into a fund. It is not a product, and it does not guarantee profit.
Higher potential return comes with higher risk. Short-term money needs safety; long horizons can tolerate swings. Spread across assets.
Guaranteed returns, urgency, doubling promises, recruiting friends, unregistered advisers and personal accounts. Verify registration yourself.

finance-3.reflection: Which of your financial goals has a short time horizon, and what does that suggest about how much risk you should accept for it?

Guaranteed high returns and urgency signal scams.

finance-4.title: Credit, Debt, Insurance and Taxes
finance-4.summary: Understand credit scores, credit card interest traps, EMIs, basic insurance, income tax concepts and how to stay safe from financial fraud.
objectives: Explain how a credit score works and how to protect it.
Calculate the true cost of an EMI loan and avoid credit card interest traps.
Describe term and health insurance, core income tax concepts and key fraud-safety habits.

concepts.label: Income tax concepts and fraud safety

explanation.heading: Borrowing and protection
explanation.body: Earlier lessons covered saving and investing. This one covers the other side: borrowing, protecting yourself and paying tax. It is educational; rates, tax rules and policy terms change, so read current documents before acting.

explanation.heading: Credit score and card interest
explanation.body:
A **credit score** is a number, usually three digits, that credit bureaus calculate from your borrowing history. Lenders use it to judge whether to give you a loan or card and at what rate. It is helped by paying every bill on time, keeping card use well below your limit, a long history, and few loan applications in a short time. It is hurt by late payments, defaults, and maxing out cards.

A credit card is an interest-free loan only if you pay the **full statement balance by the due date**. If you pay only the **minimum due**, interest is charged on the unpaid balance, often from the date of purchase, at a rate far higher than most loans. Illustrative example: ₹20,000 unpaid at 3 percent a month costs ₹600 in interest in one month, which is 36 percent a year. Add late fees and the balance can snowball. The rule: spend only what you can pay in full.

explanation.heading: EMIs and the real cost of a loan
explanation.body: An **EMI** (equated monthly instalment) is a fixed monthly payment covering principal and interest. The total cost is EMI x number of months. Example: borrowing ₹1,00,000 for 12 months with an EMI of ₹8,900 means you pay 8,900 x 12 = ₹1,06,800, so the extra cost is ₹6,800. Beware of **no-cost EMI** offers: the interest or processing fee is often built into the price or charged separately, so compare the total paid with the cash price. Before any loan, ask: what is the total cost, what are the fees, and can I afford the EMI with my essentials covered? A common guideline is to keep total EMIs well below a third of take-home pay.

explanation.heading: Term and health insurance
explanation.body: **Insurance** transfers a big financial risk to an insurer in exchange for a **premium**. **Term insurance** pays a lump sum to your family if you die during the term, and nothing if you outlive it. It is a pure protection product and generally cheaper when bought young, and it matters most if others depend on your income. A single student with no dependants may not need it yet. **Health insurance** pays for hospital costs up to a **sum insured**. Look at waiting periods, exclusions, co-payment clauses and whether hospitals nearby offer cashless treatment. Cover from an employer often ends when you leave, so a personal policy is worth considering. Never treat insurance as an investment, and always disclose your health history honestly, because hiding facts can lead to rejected claims.

explanation.heading: Tax concepts and fraud safety
explanation.body:
**Income tax** is charged on your **taxable income**, which is income minus eligible deductions and exemptions. Your employer deducts **TDS** (tax deducted at source) from salary and deposits it with the government. You receive a statement of this, such as Form 16. Filing a return reports your income and lets you claim a refund if too much tax was deducted. The tax system offers different regimes and slabs that the government revises, so check the current rules every year.

**Fraud safety:** never share OTPs, PINs or card CVV with anyone, including someone claiming to be a bank officer. You never need to enter a PIN to receive money; a "collect request" asks you to pay. Avoid remote-access apps at a stranger's request and check links before clicking. If you are defrauded, call your bank at once and report it on the national cybercrime helpline 1930 as fast as you can, because early reporting improves the chance of recovery.

examples.title: The minimum due trap
examples.body: Arjun buys a ₹30,000 phone on his card and pays only the minimum due of ₹1,500 for several months. Interest at an illustrative 3 percent a month on the remaining balance is about ₹855 in the first month. After paying ₹1,500 he still owes about ₹29,355, so most of his payment went to interest.
examples.takeaway: Paying only the minimum keeps you in debt while the interest quietly compounds.

examples.title: A fake bank call
examples.body: Priya gets a call: "Your account will be blocked; share the OTP just received to update KYC." She hangs up, calls the number printed on her bank card, and learns the bank never asks for OTPs on calls. She reports the number to the helpline.
examples.takeaway: Urgency plus an OTP request is a scam pattern; verify through an official number you looked up yourself.

exercises.prompt: Which habit helps a credit score the most?
options: Paying all dues on time and keeping utilisation low
Maxing out your card each month
Applying for many loans at once
exercises.why: On-time payments and low utilisation are the strongest positive signals. Maxing out and many applications hurt the score.

exercises.prompt: A loan of ₹50,000 has an EMI of ₹4,500 for 12 months. The total repaid is ₹____. (number only)
exercises.why: 4,500 x 12 = ₹54,000, so the loan costs ₹4,000 more than the amount borrowed.

exercises.prompt: You are 23, single, with no dependants, and your employer gives health cover for you. A friend urges you to buy a large term plan and a savings-linked policy today. What is the most sensible reaction?

options.text: Buy both immediately because insurance is an investment.
options.feedback: Mixing insurance with investment is a common mistake, and pressure is a bad reason to buy.

options.text: Check what your employer cover includes and ends, consider a personal health policy as you may lose cover when you leave, and revisit term cover when dependants appear.
options.feedback: You separate needs from sales pressure and plan for when cover ends.

options.text: Skip every policy forever.
options.feedback: You may be exposed if the employer cover ends or a family event changes your needs.

options.text: Buy whichever agent calls first.
options.feedback: Choosing by who calls first ignores your actual need and the policy terms.

exercises.why: Insurance should match real risks and dependants. Check existing cover and its limits before buying, and keep insurance separate from investing.

exercises.prompt: Write a short guide (for a friend starting their first job) with two points about how salary tax works (TDS, Form 16 and filing) and three habits to stay safe from UPI and phone fraud. Do not quote tax rates.

descriptors.3: Two accurate points covering TDS and filing or Form 16.
Three clear habits such as never sharing OTP or PIN and verifying calls independently.
Clear steps a beginner can follow.
Says rules change and to check current ones.

exercises.modelAnswer: Tax: your employer deducts TDS from salary and gives you Form 16 showing it. Filing a return reports your income and lets you claim a refund if too much was deducted; rules change, so check the current ones each year. Safety: never share OTPs or PINs, remember you never enter a PIN to receive money, and verify any bank call by dialling the number on your card. If cheated, call your bank and report at 1930 immediately.
exercises.guidance: A strong guide uses plain words, stays accurate, and gives concrete habits. Mistakes include quoting rates as permanent, saying a refund is automatic, or saying PIN is needed to receive money. Mark yourself honestly against the model.

task.title: Personal money safety check
task.brief: Audit your own setup for credit, insurance and fraud safety using general principles.
steps: List all cards and loans you have or expect, with the due date for each.
Write the total repayment of any EMI offer you have seen and compare with the cash price.
Check what health cover you have through family or employer and when it ends.
Write three fraud-safety rules and set app lock and UPI limits as appropriate.
checklist: I compared total cost with cash price
task.evidencePrompt: Write your three fraud rules and one thing you learned about your cover or dues.

quiz.prompt: A late credit card payment generally:
quiz.why: Late payments are recorded and lower your score.

quiz.prompt: Paying only the minimum due on a credit card means interest is charged on the unpaid ____. (one word)
quiz.why: Interest applies to the remaining balance, which is why the minimum due is a trap.

quiz.prompt: Term insurance pays:
options: A maturity bonus if you live
A lump sum to your family if you die within the term
quiz.why: Term cover is pure protection that pays on death during the term; health insurance covers hospital bills.

quiz.prompt: Which is true about UPI safety?
options: You must enter your PIN to receive money
You never need a PIN to receive money
Banks ask for OTPs on calls
Sharing CVV is safe with the bank
quiz.why: Entering a PIN approves a payment out, never an incoming credit.

bank.prompt: A phone costs ₹24,000 in cash. A "no-cost EMI" for 6 months totals ₹25,200. What is the better reading?
options: You pay ₹1,200 more than cash, so the cost is hidden in fees or price
The EMI is cheaper than cash
bank.why: Compare total paid with the cash price; here ₹1,200 extra is the hidden cost.

bank.prompt: Money deducted from your salary by the employer and deposited as tax is called ____. (three-letter abbreviation)
bank.why: TDS stands for tax deducted at source.

bank.prompt: Which feature is important to check in a health policy?
options: Waiting periods, exclusions and cashless hospitals
bank.why: Terms determine whether your claim is paid, so premium alone is a poor basis.

cards.front: How do you protect a credit score?
cards.back: Pay all dues on time, keep card use low against the limit, avoid many loan applications at once and check statements.

cards.front: What is the card minimum due trap?
cards.back: Interest is charged on the unpaid balance at high rates, so paying the minimum keeps you in debt. Pay the full statement balance by the due date.
Term pays your family a lump sum if you die in the term; health pays hospital bills up to the sum insured. Neither is an investment.
TDS is deducted from salary and shown on Form 16; filing can claim a refund. Never share OTP or PIN and report fraud quickly to the bank and 1930.

finance-4.reflection: Which borrowing or fraud risk in your own life are you least prepared for, and what is the first step you will take this week?

keyPoints: Pay credit card balances in full by the due date.
Total EMI cost is EMI times months; compare with cash.
Insurance protects against risk; it is not an investment.
Never share OTP or PIN; report fraud immediately.

gk-1.title: Indian Polity and Institutions
gk-1.summary: Understand the Constitution, fundamental rights, the three organs of government, federalism and how elections work, using only stable facts.
objectives: Name the six fundamental rights and tell them apart from directive principles and duties.
Explain how Parliament, the executive and the judiciary check one another.
Describe how power is shared between the Union and the states and how elections are run.

explanation.heading: The Constitution and your rights
explanation.body:
The Constitution of India was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950, which is why we celebrate Republic Day on that date. It is the supreme law: every other law, and every government action, must fit within it.

The most useful part for a citizen is **Part III, the fundamental rights**, found in Articles 12 to 35. There are six groups: right to equality (Articles 14 to 18), right to freedom (19 to 22), right against exploitation (23 and 24), right to freedom of religion (25 to 28), cultural and educational rights (29 and 30), and the right to constitutional remedies (Article 32). Article 21, the protection of life and personal liberty, has been read broadly by the courts, and the right to education for children aged 6 to 14 sits in Article 21A.

Two neighbours are often confused with these. **Directive Principles** (Part IV) are goals for the State, such as fair wages and public health. Courts cannot enforce them directly. **Fundamental Duties** (Article 51A) are duties of citizens, such as protecting public property. The right to property is no longer a fundamental right; since 1978 it is a legal right under Article 300A.

explanation.heading: Three organs, one system of checks
explanation.body:
Government works through three organs. The **legislature** makes laws. In India's Union Parliament this means the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. The Lok Sabha is the directly elected house, with a normal term of five years. The Rajya Sabha is a permanent house: members serve six-year terms and one-third retire every two years.

The **executive** carries laws out. The President is the formal head of state, but in practice acts on the advice of the Prime Minister and the council of ministers, who are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. If the Lok Sabha loses confidence in them, they must go. This is the parliamentary system.

The **judiciary** interprets laws and protects rights. The Supreme Court sits at the top, with high courts below it. Under Article 32 you can approach the Supreme Court directly for a fundamental right, and under Article 226 a high court. Courts can strike down a law that violates the Constitution; this is **judicial review**. In the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) the Supreme Court held that Parliament can amend the Constitution but not destroy its basic structure.

explanation.heading: Federalism: who decides what
explanation.body:
India is a union of states with a strong centre. The Seventh Schedule divides subjects into three lists. The **Union List** (defence, foreign affairs, currency) is for Parliament alone. The **State List** (police, public health, agriculture) is mainly for state legislatures. The **Concurrent List** (education, forests, marriage) allows both, and if they clash the Union law generally prevails.

A quick example: a state government runs its own police and public hospitals, but only the Union government can print currency or sign a treaty. A new law about a subject on the Concurrent List, say education, may be passed by Parliament and also by a state assembly. Knowing the lists lets you decide in seconds which government a news story is really about.

explanation.heading: How elections work
explanation.body:
The Election Commission of India, created under Article 324, conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. Every citizen aged 18 or above can vote, a limit lowered from 21 by the 61st Amendment in 1988. In Lok Sabha and assembly elections the system is **first past the post**: the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even without a majority of all votes cast.

Suppose three candidates in a constituency get 40,000, 35,000 and 25,000 votes. The first wins with 40 percent. Understanding this explains why a party can win many seats with a modest vote share. After results, the party or alliance that commands a majority in the Lok Sabha forms the government. To practise, take any news item about government and ask three questions: which organ is acting, under which list, and which article or rule applies.

examples.title: Which right is this?
examples.body: A college refuses admission to a student only because of her religion. This touches Article 15, part of the right to equality, which prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. If the matter is serious, the student can approach the high court under Article 226, or the Supreme Court under Article 32. A related news item about a state promising free nutrition schemes would instead be a Directive Principle, a goal rather than an enforceable right.
examples.takeaway: Match the facts to a group of rights first, then ask whether it is enforceable (a right) or aspirational (a directive principle).

examples.title: Whose job is it?
examples.body: A young entrepreneur in Faridabad asks who to complain to about a broken municipal road, a delayed passport and a change in customs duty. Roads and local bodies fall to the state and municipality (State List), passports are a Union subject (foreign affairs), and customs duty is a Union tax. Three problems, three levels of government.
examples.takeaway: The three lists let you route a problem to the right government instead of blaming everyone.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is NOT currently a fundamental right?
exercises.why: Property was removed from fundamental rights in 1978 and is now a legal right under Article 300A. The other three remain among the six groups.

exercises.prompt: The minimum age to vote in Indian elections is ____ years. (number)
exercises.why: The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18.

exercises.prompt: A state wants to start its own currency to help local traders. What is the correct position?

options.text: Allowed, since the state controls its economy.
options.feedback: Currency is on the Union List, so only the Union can control it.

options.text: Not allowed, because currency is a Union List subject reserved for Parliament and the central bank.
options.feedback: The Seventh Schedule places currency under the Union, so a state cannot issue one.

options.text: Allowed if the Rajya Sabha agrees.
options.feedback: The Rajya Sabha cannot hand a Union subject to a state this way.

options.text: Allowed because it is on the Concurrent List.
options.feedback: Currency is not on the Concurrent List.

exercises.why: Know the three lists: currency, defence and foreign affairs belong to the Union.

exercises.prompt: A law passed by Parliament is challenged because it seems to violate a fundamental right. In 4 to 6 sentences, explain which organ decides, how a citizen can approach it, and what it can do if the challenge succeeds.

descriptors.2: Names the Supreme Court or high court.
descriptors.3: Names the judiciary with its role as guardian of the Constitution.

auto.label: Mentions the judiciary or a court

descriptors.3: Mentions both Articles with the right court for each.

descriptors.2: Says the law can be struck down.
descriptors.3: Explains judicial review and striking down the unconstitutional part.
Clear and sequential.

exercises.modelAnswer: The judiciary decides. A citizen whose fundamental right is affected can go directly to the Supreme Court under Article 32 or to the relevant high court under Article 226. The court examines whether the law conflicts with the Constitution. If it does, the court can declare the law, or the offending part, unconstitutional and void. This power is called judicial review, and it makes the Constitution supreme over ordinary laws.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer names the judiciary, the two routes (Article 32 and 226) and judicial review. Common mistakes are saying the President or Parliament decides, or confusing the court striking down a law with the court making a new law. Mark yourself against each criterion honestly.

task.title: Map one news story to the system
task.brief: Pick any three government-related news items from this week and map each to the organ, list and level of government involved.
steps: Choose three items from a newspaper or news app.
For each, write which organ (legislature, executive, judiciary) is acting.
Write whether the subject is Union, State or Concurrent and the right or provision involved, if any.
Write one sentence in plain words summarising each.
checklist: Each has a list or level named
task.evidencePrompt: Paste your three mappings in one line each.

quiz.prompt: The Constitution of India came into force on:
quiz.why: It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. 15 August 1947 is independence.

quiz.prompt: To whom is the council of ministers collectively responsible?
quiz.why: In the parliamentary system the ministers answer to the directly elected Lok Sabha.

quiz.prompt: Police is mainly a subject of the:
quiz.why: Police and public order are on the State List.

quiz.prompt: In Lok Sabha elections, the candidate with the most votes wins under the ____ system. (three words, e.g. first ___ the post)
quiz.why: India uses first past the post, with no requirement of an absolute majority in the constituency.

bank.prompt: Which part of the Constitution lists goals the State should pursue, but which courts cannot directly enforce?
bank.why: Part IV, the Directive Principles, is non-justiciable. Part III holds the enforceable fundamental rights.

bank.prompt: Which body can declare a law unconstitutional?
bank.why: Judicial review is the courts' power to strike down laws that violate the Constitution.

bank.prompt: Which body conducts elections to Parliament and the state legislatures?
bank.why: Article 324 gives this task to the Election Commission of India.

cards.back: Equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies. They are in Part III, Articles 12 to 35.
The power of courts to test laws and executive acts against the Constitution and strike down those that violate it.

cards.front: Three lists in the Seventh Schedule?
cards.back: Union List (Parliament), State List (states), Concurrent List (both, Union law prevails in a clash).

cards.front: What is first past the post?
cards.back: The candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even without more than half of the votes.

gk-1.reflection: Which institution in this lesson affects your daily life most directly, and what would you want to understand better about how it works?

keyPoints: The Constitution is supreme law, in force since 26 January 1950.
Fundamental rights are enforceable; directive principles are not.
Parliament makes law, the executive carries it out, the judiciary interprets it.
Three lists decide who governs which subject.
Elections run by the Election Commission use first past the post.
revision.redo: Name the six rights groups and the three lists from memory in two minutes.

gk-2.title: Geography and Economy Basics
gk-2.summary: Pick up the essential geography of India and the world, and the core ideas of GDP, inflation, the Budget, the RBI and GST at concept level.
objectives: Place India's main physical features, climate pattern and time standard on a mental map.
Explain GDP, inflation, the Budget and the RBI's role in plain language.
Work out how GST is applied and shared with an illustrative example.

explanation.heading: Geography you should carry in your head
explanation.body:
Last time you saw how institutions share power. Geography and economy are the physical and money backdrop to all of it.

India sits in the northern and eastern hemispheres. The **Tropic of Cancer** (about 23.5 degrees north) passes through eight Indian states, roughly cutting the country into a tropical southern half and a subtropical northern half. India's **standard meridian** is 82.5 degrees east, which gives Indian Standard Time, five and a half hours ahead of UTC. The land has clear zones: the Himalayas in the north, the Indo-Gangetic plain of the Ganga and Yamuna, the Thar desert in the west, the Deccan plateau in the peninsula bounded by the Western and Eastern Ghats, and long coastlines on the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean.

The **south-west monsoon** brings most rainfall between June and September, which is why agriculture and food prices are so tied to it. Globally, Asia is the largest continent, the Pacific the largest ocean, and latitude and longitude form the grid that locates every place on Earth.

explanation.heading: GDP and inflation
explanation.body:
**Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** is the total market value of all final goods and services produced inside a country in a year. "Final" matters: the price of the steel is not added separately to the price of the car, or you would count the steel twice. **Nominal GDP** uses current prices; **real GDP** removes the effect of price changes so that you compare actual output.

**Inflation** is a sustained rise in the general price level, so each rupee buys less. In India it is commonly tracked with the Consumer Price Index (CPI). An illustrative example: if nominal GDP rises from 100 to 110 units while prices rise 5 percent, real growth is about 110 divided by 1.05, which is roughly 104.8, so about 4.8 percent, not 10. Mixing up nominal and real is the commonest mistake when reading economic news.

explanation.heading: The Budget and the RBI
explanation.body:
The **Union Budget**, called the Annual Financial Statement under Article 112, is the government's estimate of receipts and expenditure for the financial year, which runs from 1 April to 31 March. Receipts come from taxes (income tax, GST, customs) and borrowing; expenditure covers salaries, subsidies, defence, interest and infrastructure. The **fiscal deficit** is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowing. If a government spends 120 and earns 100 without borrowing, the deficit is 20, which must be borrowed.

The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, established in 1935, is the central bank. It issues currency notes (except one-rupee notes, which the government issues), regulates banks, manages foreign exchange and runs **monetary policy**. Its main tool is the **repo rate**, the rate at which it lends to banks. Raising the rate makes loans costlier and cools inflation; cutting it encourages borrowing and growth. Budgets are fiscal policy by the government; interest-rate decisions are monetary policy by the RBI.

explanation.heading: GST in a nutshell
explanation.body:
The **Goods and Services Tax**, introduced on 1 July 2017, is an indirect tax charged on the supply of goods and services, replacing many separate central and state taxes. It is **destination-based**: the tax goes to the state where the goods or services are consumed. A **GST Council** with the Union and states decides rates.

When a sale is within one state, tax is split into **CGST** (Centre) and **SGST** (state). When it crosses states, **IGST** is charged and shared. An illustrative example: a laptop bag costs ₹1,000 before tax, and the rate is 18 percent, so GST is ₹180 and the buyer pays ₹1,180. Within one state, ₹90 goes to the Centre and ₹90 to the state. Rates change over time, so learn the mechanism and check the current rate when you need it.

examples.title: Reading a headline correctly
examples.body: A headline says "Economy grows 9 percent in rupee terms" in a year when prices rose 6 percent. A careful reader asks whether it is nominal or real. Real growth is about 1.09 divided by 1.06 minus 1, roughly 2.8 percent. The same headline, read properly, tells a very different story.
examples.takeaway: Always ask whether a figure is nominal or adjusted for inflation.

examples.title: Splitting a GST bill
examples.body: You buy a printer from a shop in Faridabad for ₹5,000 plus an illustrative 18 percent GST. GST is ₹900, total ₹5,900. As the sale is inside Haryana, ₹450 is CGST and ₹450 is SGST. If the shop were in Delhi shipping to you, IGST of ₹900 would be charged instead.
examples.takeaway: Calculate GST on the pre-tax price; split equally into CGST and SGST for a same-state sale.

exercises.prompt: Which line passes through India and roughly divides it into tropical and subtropical halves?
exercises.why: The Tropic of Cancer at about 23.5 degrees north crosses eight Indian states. The equator and Tropic of Capricorn lie south of India.

exercises.prompt: A product costs ₹2,000 before tax and attracts an illustrative 18 percent GST. The total price in rupees is ____. (number only)
exercises.why: 18 percent of 2,000 is 360, so the total is 2,360.

exercises.prompt: Which body sets the repo rate?
exercises.why: The RBI runs monetary policy and sets the repo rate. The Finance Ministry presents the Budget; the GST Council sets GST rates.

exercises.prompt: Nominal GDP of an imaginary country grows from 200 to 230 units while prices rise 10 percent. In 4 to 6 sentences, calculate the approximate real growth and explain why the headline 15 percent figure misleads.

descriptors.3: Real growth about 4.5 percent shown correctly.
Defines both and links the gap to inflation.
Says part of the 15 percent is only higher prices, not more output.
Clear steps.

exercises.modelAnswer: The nominal rise is 30 on 200, which is 15 percent. But prices rose 10 percent, so real GDP is 230 divided by 1.10, about 209.1, a growth of roughly 4.5 percent. The headline misleads because most of the increase reflects higher prices rather than more goods and services produced. Real GDP is the better measure of actual output.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer divides by one plus inflation instead of simply subtracting, though subtraction gives a rough 5 percent. Common mistakes are treating nominal growth as real growth or forgetting the base. Check your numbers before judging yourself.

task.title: Decode a bill and a headline
task.brief: Use one real shopping bill and one economic headline to apply GST and nominal-vs-real ideas.
steps: Find any bill showing GST, or imagine one with a pre-tax price you pick.
Verify the CGST plus SGST equals the total tax and recompute it.
Find one headline with a growth or price figure.
Write whether the figure is nominal or real, or unclear, and what extra detail you would need.
checklist: I wrote what extra detail I would need
task.evidencePrompt: Write the bill amounts and your verdict on the headline.

quiz.prompt: India's standard meridian used for Indian Standard Time is:
quiz.why: IST is based on 82.5 degrees east, five and a half hours ahead of UTC.

quiz.prompt: The measure of the total value of final goods and services produced in a year is called ____. (abbreviation)
quiz.why: GDP counts final goods and services produced within a country in a year.

quiz.prompt: The fiscal deficit equals total expenditure minus:
quiz.why: It measures how much the government must borrow after counting all non-borrowed receipts.

quiz.prompt: On a sale between two states, the tax charged is:
quiz.why: Inter-state supplies attract IGST, which is later shared between the Centre and the destination state.

bank.prompt: Which season brings most of India's annual rainfall?
bank.why: The south-west monsoon delivers most rain, driving agriculture and food prices.

bank.prompt: A bank raises loan rates after the central bank raises the repo rate. The central bank's name abbreviation is ____. (three letters)
bank.why: The Reserve Bank of India runs monetary policy and sets the repo rate.

bank.prompt: A shop sells a book for ₹500 before tax with an illustrative 12 percent GST within the same state. How much is CGST?
bank.why: Total GST is ₹60; half, ₹30, is CGST and half is SGST.

cards.back: Nominal uses current prices; real removes price changes. Use real figures to judge actual growth in output.
Fiscal policy is the government's taxes and spending in the Budget. Monetary policy is the RBI's control of interest rates and money supply.
CGST and SGST split GST for same-state sales; IGST applies to sales between states and is shared afterwards.
Tropic of Cancer crosses eight states; standard meridian is 82.5 degrees east; monsoon rain is June to September.

gk-2.reflection: Which price or tax you pay regularly could you now explain better, and what would you check on your next bill?

keyPoints: The Tropic of Cancer crosses India and IST uses 82.5 degrees east.
GDP counts final output; use real GDP to judge growth.
Inflation is a rise in the general price level.
The Budget is fiscal policy; the RBI handles monetary policy.
GST splits into CGST and SGST for same-state sales; IGST for inter-state.
revision.redo: Compute 18 percent GST on ₹2,500 and split it into CGST and SGST.

gk-3.title: History, Science and Environment
gk-3.summary: Link key turning points in world and Indian history, the scientific method and everyday science, and the basics of climate and environment.
objectives: Place major world and Indian historical turning points in order and explain why they mattered.
Apply the scientific method and spot correlation versus causation in daily claims.
Explain the greenhouse effect, ozone layer and weather versus climate in simple words.

explanation.heading: History as a chain of turning points
explanation.body:
Earlier lessons covered institutions and the economy. Both are shaped by history, and history is easiest to remember as a short chain of turning points rather than a list of dates.

For India: the Indus Valley Civilisation reached maturity around 2500 BCE with planned cities. The Maurya Empire, with Ashoka in the third century BCE, united much of the subcontinent. The Mughal Empire began after the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. The revolt of 1857 was the first large-scale challenge to the East India Company's rule, after which the Crown took direct control. Under Gandhi, the Salt March of 1930 and the Quit India movement of 1942 mobilised the masses, and India became independent on 15 August 1947.

For the world: Gutenberg's printing press (about 1450) spread knowledge cheaply, the French Revolution (1789) spread ideas of liberty and equality, the Industrial Revolution (from the late eighteenth century) changed how goods were made, and the Second World War (1939 to 1945) led to the United Nations. For each turning point ask: what changed, and what did it cause next?

explanation.heading: The scientific method
explanation.body:
Science is not a list of facts; it is a method for finding out when we are wrong. The steps are: observe something, ask a question, form a **hypothesis** (a testable explanation), run an experiment or collect data, analyse it, and share the result so others can repeat it.

A good experiment changes one factor while keeping others constant. Example: a student claims that studying with music improves coding marks. A fair test uses similar tasks, the same time of day and the same person, once with music and once without. If many people show a gain, the evidence strengthens.

The classic trap is **correlation is not causation**. Ice-cream sales and drowning cases both rise in summer, but ice cream does not cause drowning; heat causes both. Whenever a claim says "X causes Y", ask whether a third factor could explain both, and whether the sample was big enough.

explanation.heading: Science in daily life
explanation.body:
Basic physics and biology show up everywhere. Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level, but at lower temperatures at high altitude because air pressure is lower, which is why food cooks slowly in hill stations and why a **pressure cooker** raises the pressure so food cooks faster. Newton's first law explains why you lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly: your body keeps moving. Light bends when it passes between materials, which is why a straw looks bent in water.

In biology, green plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make food and release oxygen, a process called **photosynthesis**. Vaccines train the immune system to recognise a germ without causing the full disease. DNA carries the instructions that make living things. Ordinary habits connect to this: washing hands removes germs, and boiled water kills many disease-causing organisms.

explanation.heading: Climate and environment basics
explanation.body:
**Weather** is what is happening in the atmosphere today; **climate** is the pattern over many years, commonly around 30. A cold day does not disprove climate change, any more than one good exam proves a student is excellent.

The **greenhouse effect** is natural: gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour trap heat and keep Earth warm enough for life. The concern is that burning coal, oil and gas adds extra carbon dioxide, trapping more heat and raising average temperatures. The **ozone layer** high in the atmosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation; it was damaged by certain chemicals, and the Montreal Protocol (1987) successfully phased those out. The Paris Agreement (2015) is a global agreement to limit warming well below 2 degrees Celsius. Biodiversity, the variety of living species, supports food, water and medicine, so protecting forests and wetlands is also practical self-interest.

examples.title: Testing a study claim
examples.body: Aman says, "Everyone who tops our class wakes up at 5 a.m., so early waking gives high marks." A sharper reading notes that toppers might also sleep earlier, study more consistently or have fewer distractions. To test the claim, you would compare similar students who changed only their wake-up time for a month.
examples.takeaway: Look for a third factor and a fair comparison before accepting a cause.

examples.title: Reading a hot-day argument
examples.body: A friend says a cool morning in Dehradun in June shows global warming is a myth. The answer is the weather-climate distinction: one day is weather. Climate is judged from many years of averages across many places.
examples.takeaway: Single events are weather; patterns over decades are climate.

exercises.prompt: Which event came first?
exercises.why: The sequence is 1857, Salt March (1930), Quit India (1942), independence (1947).

exercises.prompt: A testable explanation that you check with an experiment is called a ____. (one word)
exercises.why: A hypothesis is a testable explanation, the second step after observation and a question.

exercises.prompt: Why does food cook faster in a pressure cooker?
options: It lowers the boiling point of water
It adds more heat from the stove
It raises the pressure so water boils at a higher temperature
It removes oxygen from the food
exercises.why: Higher pressure raises water's boiling point, so food reaches a higher temperature. Lowering the boiling point would cook slower.

exercises.prompt: A classmate says, "It snowed heavily last week, so global warming is false." In 4 to 6 sentences, explain the difference between weather and climate and how the greenhouse effect is meant to be understood.

descriptors.3: Weather is short-term; climate is a long-term pattern, about 30 years.
Natural heat-trapping; extra gases raise temperatures.
Shows why one snowfall does not disprove a trend.
Polite and persuasive.

exercises.modelAnswer: Weather is the condition on a particular day, while climate is the average pattern over many years, usually around thirty. One heavy snowfall is weather and cannot show the long-term trend. The greenhouse effect is natural, since gases like carbon dioxide trap heat and keep Earth habitable. Extra gases from burning fuels trap more heat, so the long-term average temperature rises even though individual days can still be cold.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer separates short-term from long-term, explains the greenhouse effect as natural plus enhanced, and stays polite. Common mistakes are saying the greenhouse effect itself is harmful or that cold days prove nothing without saying why.

task.title: Fact-check a daily claim
task.brief: Take one health, science or environment claim from social media and test it using the scientific method.
steps: Write the claim exactly as you saw it.
Write what hypothesis it implies and what evidence would support or contradict it.
Check for correlation versus causation, sample size and a third factor.
Write a verdict: supported, unsupported or unclear, with one reason.
checklist: I checked for a third factor
I wrote a verdict with a reason
task.evidencePrompt: Paste the claim and your verdict with one reason.

quiz.prompt: India became independent on:
quiz.why: Independence was on 15 August 1947; 26 January 1950 marks the Constitution.

quiz.prompt: "Ice-cream sales and drownings rise together" best illustrates:
quiz.why: Both are driven by summer heat, so one does not cause the other.

quiz.prompt: Plants make food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide in a process called ____. (one word)
quiz.why: Photosynthesis is how green plants produce food and release oxygen.

quiz.prompt: The Montreal Protocol of 1987 concerned:
quiz.why: It phased out chemicals that damaged the ozone layer.

bank.prompt: Which invention around 1450 helped spread knowledge cheaply across Europe?
bank.why: Gutenberg's printing press made books far cheaper.

bank.prompt: A fair experiment on whether a new study app improves scores should:
options: Change one factor and keep the others the same
bank.why: Controlling variables isolates the effect of the one factor.

bank.prompt: The pattern of weather over many years, commonly about 30, is called ____. (one word)
bank.why: Climate is the long-term pattern; weather is the day-to-day state.

cards.back: Revolt of 1857, Salt March 1930, Quit India 1942, independence 15 August 1947, Constitution in force 26 January 1950.
Two things rising together do not mean one causes the other; a third factor or chance may explain both.
Higher pressure raises the boiling point of water, so food cooks at a higher temperature and faster.
Weather is short-term conditions; climate is the long-term average pattern, around 30 years.

gk-3.reflection: Which claim did you accept recently without testing it, and how would you check it now?

keyPoints: History is a chain of turning points with causes and effects.
Scientific method: observe, hypothesise, test, share.
Correlation is not causation.
Weather is a day; climate is decades.
The greenhouse effect is natural; extra gases enhance it.
revision.redo: Pick one claim you heard today and name the missing evidence.

gk-4.title: Following the World and Remembering It
gk-4.summary: Know the main international organisations, build a sustainable news routine, remember what you read with notes and mnemonics, and verify claims before sharing.
objectives: Describe what the UN, WTO and IMF do and how they differ.
Set up a daily news routine and a knowledge notebook that actually gets reviewed.
Use mnemonics and verification habits to remember accurately and avoid misinformation.

explanation.heading: Who does what internationally
explanation.body:
The **United Nations** was founded in 1945 after the Second World War to maintain peace and promote cooperation. It is headquartered in New York. Its main organs include the **General Assembly**, where every member state has one vote; the **Security Council**, with 15 members, five of them permanent (China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States) holding a veto; the **International Court of Justice** at The Hague; and the Secretariat led by the Secretary-General.

The **World Trade Organization (WTO)**, set up in 1995 as successor to the GATT, is based in Geneva. It provides rules for trade between countries and a forum to settle trade disputes. The **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and the **World Bank** came from the Bretton Woods conference of 1944 and sit in Washington DC. The IMF promotes monetary stability and lends to countries with balance-of-payments problems, while the World Bank finances development projects such as roads and schools. A one-line way to remember: UN for peace, WTO for trade, IMF for monetary stability, World Bank for development.

explanation.heading: A news routine that lasts
explanation.body:
The earlier lessons gave you facts; this one gives you the habit of keeping them fresh. Most people fail at news by overdoing it: three hours of scrolling leaves nothing behind. A sustainable routine is **20 to 30 minutes daily**.

A workable pattern: spend 10 minutes scanning headlines from one or two reliable newspapers, 10 minutes reading one story in depth, and 5 minutes writing a note. Choose a mix: one national, one international, one economy or science item. Avoid reading only breaking news; follow stories over weeks to see how they develop.

Then build a **knowledge notebook**, on paper or a notes app. For each item write the fact, why it matters, and a question you could be asked about it. On Sundays, spend 15 minutes reviewing the week's notes and turning the best five into flashcards. Without review, notes become a graveyard.

explanation.heading: Mnemonics and the memory palace
explanation.body:
Memory is helped by structure, vivid images and repetition at spaced intervals. A **mnemonic** is a memory aid. An acronym example: for the six fundamental-rights groups you could build a short sentence from their first letters. A rhyme or story works for lists of dates.

The **memory palace** (method of loci) uses a place you know well, say your home in Faridabad. Place one vivid image per item along a fixed route: to remember the five permanent members of the Security Council, imagine a giant dragon at the gate (China), a baguette on the sofa (France), a bear in the kitchen (Russia), a tea cup on the table (UK) and a burger on the bed (US). Walk the route in your mind to recall them. Make images exaggerated, funny and sensory. Then review at increasing gaps: next day, after three days, after a week.

explanation.heading: Verifying before you believe or share
explanation.body:
Forwarded messages claiming "a new law from tomorrow" or "scientists warn" spread because they provoke emotion. Build a short verification habit.

1. **Pause** when a claim makes you angry or excited.
2. **Find the source**: who said it, and can you see the original statement or document?
3. **Check the date**: old stories are often recirculated as new.
4. **Read laterally**: open other reliable outlets and see whether they report the same fact.
5. **Look for numbers and context**: a percentage with no base, or a screenshot with no link to the original, is weak.

Example: a forward says "WTO bans all online payments in India from next month." The WTO sets trade rules between countries; it does not ban domestic payment systems. That mismatch with what the institution actually does is itself a warning sign. If you cannot verify it, do not share it.

examples.title: A one-page Sunday review
examples.body: Priya keeps a notebook with three columns: fact, why it matters, possible question. Her Sunday entry: "IMF lends to countries with balance-of-payments problems. Matters because it shapes news about loans. Question: which institution funds development projects? (World Bank)." She converts five such entries into flashcards and reviews them again on Wednesday.
examples.takeaway: A fact, a reason and a question turn reading into usable knowledge.

examples.title: Checking a forwarded message
examples.body: A WhatsApp forward says "UN announces new world currency from next week." Rohan checks: the UN does not issue currency; there is no source link; the screenshot has no date. He searches reliable news outlets and finds nothing. He does not forward it and replies in the group with the reasons.
examples.takeaway: Match the claim with what the institution can actually do, and look for the original source.

exercises.prompt: Which organisation provides rules for trade between countries and a forum for settling trade disputes?
exercises.why: The WTO (1995, Geneva) handles trade rules. The IMF deals with monetary stability and the World Bank with development finance.

exercises.prompt: The number of permanent members of the UN Security Council is ____. (number)
exercises.why: Five permanent members hold a veto: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States.

exercises.prompt: A forward says "RBI will cancel all ₹500 notes tomorrow, tell everyone". You feel anxious. What is the best step?

options.text: Forward it to family groups to be safe.
options.feedback: Forwarding unverified alarming claims spreads panic.

options.text: Pause, look for the original statement, and check reliable news outlets or the official source before acting.
options.feedback: Pausing and checking the source and other outlets is the core verification habit.

options.text: Ignore it only because it was forwarded by many people.
options.feedback: Popularity does not verify a claim, and ignoring without checking means you cannot reassure others.

options.text: Rush to the bank and withdraw cash.
options.feedback: Acting on an unverified claim can cost you and spread panic.

exercises.why: Verification beats reaction: pause, find the source, read laterally.

exercises.prompt: Design a 25-minute daily news routine for yourself. In 4 to 6 sentences, state what you read, for how long, how you record it and when you review it weekly.

descriptors.3: Clear minutes for each step totalling about 25.
Notebook with fact, why it matters and a question.
Specific day, minutes and flashcards.
Sustainable for months.

exercises.modelAnswer: Every morning for 10 minutes I scan headlines from one national and one international newspaper, then read one story in depth for 10 minutes. In the last 5 minutes I write a note in my notebook with the fact, why it matters and a question. Every Sunday I spend 15 minutes reviewing the notes and turning the best five into flashcards for the coming week.
