Use coaching when the person has the ability but needs clarity; give direct advice when they lack knowledge or the situation is urgent.

explanation.heading: Running one-to-ones
explanation.body:
A **one-to-one** is a regular, private conversation between a leader and one team member, even 15 minutes every two weeks. It is not a status report. Use a simple agenda: 1. their topics first (concerns, blockers, growth), 2. progress on agreed actions, 3. feedback both ways, 4. next steps. Let them set the agenda and take short notes.

Student version: a group leader meets each member briefly before a big submission, asking "What is going well, what is blocking you, and what do you need from me?" People raise problems early in private, long before a public failure.

explanation.heading: Making feedback a habit
explanation.body:
Feedback works when it is frequent, timely and small, not saved for the end of the semester. Give it within a day or two while the situation is fresh, in private if it is corrective and in public if it is praise (if the person is comfortable). Aim for more positive than corrective feedback; specific praise tells people what to repeat.

Also ask for feedback yourself: "What is one thing I could do differently to make the group run better?" Leaders who accept feedback make it safe for others. Receive it by listening, thanking and asking for examples, not by defending.

examples.title: SBI correction
examples.body: Before: "You are always late to group calls." After: "On Tuesday and Thursday you joined the call 15 minutes late (behaviour). We started without your module's update, and I had to repeat the decisions later (impact). Is something making the time difficult? Could we move the call or could you send your update in advance?"
examples.takeaway: Observable facts plus impact invite problem-solving instead of defence.

examples.title: GROW conversation
examples.body: Sana: "I cannot learn this reporting tool." Leader: "What would success look like in two weeks?" (Goal) "Build one report on my own." "What have you tried?" (Reality) "Watched videos but never practised." "What options do you have?" (Options) "Practise with a sample, ask Rahul for 20 minutes." "What will you do first?" (Will) "Tonight, build a small report, and ask Rahul tomorrow."
examples.takeaway: Four questions led Sana to her own plan, which she is more likely to follow.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is the Behaviour part of an SBI statement?
options: You submitted the sheet without checking the totals.
exercises.why: Behaviour describes what was observable. "Careless" is a judgement, "upset" is impact and the last is the situation.

exercises.prompt: In the GROW model, the R stands for ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Reality explores where the person is now and what is in the way.

exercises.prompt: In a one-to-one, your teammate spends the time giving a status update on tasks. What is the best response?

options.text: Continue; status is important.
options.feedback: Status can be shared elsewhere, and the personal conversation is lost.

options.text: Ask what is going well, what is blocking them and what they need from you.
options.feedback: The meeting is meant for blockers, growth and support.

options.text: End the meeting early.
options.feedback: You lose the chance to learn about issues.

options.text: Give a list of faults.
options.feedback: It turns a support space into an attack and kills openness.

exercises.why: One-to-ones are for the person: blockers, needs and growth, not just status.

exercises.prompt: A teammate often uploads code with no comments and later no one can understand it. Write SBI feedback in 4 to 6 sentences, including a question or request at the end.

descriptors.3: Specific time or place.
Purely observable with no labels.
Clear effect on team or result.
Open question and a specific request.

exercises.modelAnswer: In Tuesday sprint review, the payment module code you uploaded had no comments. When Meera needed to fix the refund bug, she spent two hours working out what it did, and we missed the evening test. How did the day go for you on this? Could you add short comments on each function before you push from now on?
exercises.guidance: Strong feedback is specific, factual and about impact, then invites the person to respond. Weak feedback uses words such as always or lazy. Compare with the model honestly.

task.title: Give one piece of SBI feedback
task.brief: Give one SBI feedback message, positive or corrective, to a friend or teammate within the next two days.
steps: Pick a real recent situation.
Write the three parts in one or two sentences each.
Deliver it in private and end with a question.
Listen without defending.
Note their response.
task.evidencePrompt: Write your S, B and I statements and the reply you got.

quiz.prompt: What does SBI stand for?
quiz.why: SBI gives structure: when, what you saw and its effect.

quiz.prompt: Which question belongs to Options in GROW?
options: What do you want to achieve?
What could you do about it?
quiz.why: Options explores possible actions; goal, reality and will have other questions.

quiz.prompt: A one-to-one agenda should start with the ____ topics. (one word)
quiz.why: Letting the team member set the agenda builds openness.

quiz.prompt: Which is the better habit?
options: Save all feedback for the semester end
Give small, timely feedback within a day or two
quiz.why: Timely, small feedback is fresh and easier to act on.

bank.prompt: Which is better positive feedback?
options: In today call you summarised the three decisions in a minute, and the client confirmed straight away
bank.why: It names the situation, behaviour and impact so the person knows what to repeat.

bank.prompt: A new member asks how to fix a production bug that needs urgent help. The leader should:
options: Give direct guidance, then coach later
bank.why: Coaching suits non-urgent growth; urgent knowledge gaps need direct help.

bank.prompt: To make it safe for others, leaders should also ask for ____ themselves. (one word)
bank.why: Receiving feedback well models the behaviour you want.

cards.back: Situation, Behaviour, Impact: say when it happened, what you observed without judging, and what effect it had, then invite their view.

cards.front: What are the four GROW stages?
cards.back: Goal, Reality, Options and Will (way forward). Ask questions at each stage so the person finds their own plan.
Short, regular and private: their topics first, actions progress, feedback both ways, next steps, with brief notes.
Make it frequent, timely and small, specific in praise, private for correction and ask for feedback yourself.

leadership-3.reflection: Which feedback do you currently avoid giving, and how could SBI make it easier to say?

keyPoints: SBI keeps feedback factual and specific.
GROW uses questions to build ownership.
One-to-ones are for the person, not just status.
Small timely feedback beats a big late review.
revision.redo: Write one SBI positive statement for someone you worked with this week.

leadership-4.title: Leading Teams Through Change
leadership-4.summary: Understand how teams develop, run focused meetings, choose a decision method and keep a student or early-career team steady in uncertainty.
objectives: Recognise the four stages of team development and respond to each.
Run a meeting with purpose, agenda, decisions and action owners.
Choose a decision method and lead calmly when things are uncertain.

explanation.heading: How teams develop
explanation.body:
Earlier lessons covered leading individuals; now consider the team. Bruce Tuckman's model describes four stages that most new teams pass through:

- **Forming**: polite, unsure, looking for direction. Leader job: clarify purpose and roles.
- **Storming**: disagreements about method, roles and influence. Leader job: keep it task-focused, set working norms and listen.
- **Norming**: agreed ways of working appear. Leader job: reinforce habits and share ownership.
- **Performing**: the team works smoothly and solves its own problems. Leader job: step back and remove obstacles.

A final-year project group typically storms in week three, when two members realise they pictured different projects. This is normal, not failure. Teams that skip the storming conversation often meet it later at a worse time.

explanation.heading: Meetings that work
explanation.body:
Most meetings waste time because nobody knows their purpose. Before calling one ask: **could this be a message?** If not, prepare:

1. **Purpose and desired outcome**: "Decide the database design" is better than "discuss database."
2. **Agenda with times** sent in advance, with only the people who are needed.
3. **Roles**: one person facilitates, one takes notes.
4. **Close with decisions and actions**: who does what by when, read aloud before ending.
5. **Send notes** within a day.

Keep it to 30 minutes where possible. Start on time, and park off-topic points on a list instead of debating them. A weekly 20-minute stand-up asking "done, next, blocked" works well for student teams.

explanation.heading: Deciding as a team
explanation.body:
Choose the method to fit the decision:

- **Leader decides** after consulting: quick, good for urgent or minor decisions, but lowers buy-in.
- **Vote**: fair and fast for choices between clear options, but can leave a hurt minority.
- **Consensus**: everyone can live with the choice; slow, best for important decisions affecting everyone.

Say which method you are using before the discussion starts, so people do not feel cheated. A useful check is "Can everyone live with this and support it?" After deciding, record it, so it is not reopened every meeting. Disagree and commit means voicing doubts, then backing the final decision fully.

explanation.heading: Leading in uncertainty
explanation.body:
Requirements change, the client shifts the scope, or a key member falls sick. In uncertainty people look to the leader for steadiness. Four habits help:

1. **Say what you know and what you do not**, plainly. Do not pretend.
2. **Set a short horizon**: "For the next week we will do these three things."
3. **Communicate more often**, even a two-line update.
4. **Involve the team** in options and stay calm in tone.

Example: when the faculty guide changes the project topic a month before the deadline, a leader names the facts, resets the plan in one meeting and assigns the first week's tasks, rather than venting or freezing.

examples.title: A storming-stage fix
examples.body: In week three, Kabir and Anita argue over whether to build a mobile app or a website. The leader, Divya, calls a 30-minute meeting: purpose is to decide the platform. She uses consensus, asks each to state interests (speed, demo ease), lists criteria, and the group picks the website for the demo with a mobile-friendly layout. She records the decision in the group chat.
examples.takeaway: Naming the method and criteria turned a personal clash into a task decision.

examples.title: Agenda for a short meeting
examples.body: Subject: 25-min check-in, Wednesday 6 pm. Purpose: decide what to demo on Saturday. 1. Status of each module (5 min). 2. Risks (5 min). 3. Decide demo scope (10 min). 4. Actions (5 min). Facilitator: Divya; notes: Anita.
examples.takeaway: A timed agenda with a decision and roles keeps a meeting short and productive.

exercises.prompt: A team quarrels about roles in week three. Which stage is this and what should the leader do?
options: Storming; keep it task-focused and agree norms
exercises.why: Conflict over roles and methods is storming. Stepping back or waiting lets it worsen.

exercises.prompt: A meeting should end by reading out decisions and action owners with ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Actions need names and dates so they happen.

exercises.prompt: Your team must decide the fest venue today, and it is a small choice between two halls. Which method is best?

options.text: Long consensus process
options.feedback: Consensus for a small, urgent choice wastes time.

options.text: A quick vote after listing pros and cons
options.feedback: A vote is fast and fair for a clear choice between options.

options.text: Wait for the principal to decide
options.feedback: It delays a decision the team can take.

options.text: Do not decide
options.feedback: Postponing leaves the team stuck.

exercises.why: Use quick methods for small clear choices and save consensus for important ones.

exercises.prompt: Your guide changes your project topic three weeks before the final submission. Write a short message (4 to 6 sentences) to your team that states what you know, what you do not, the next week plan and what you need from them.

descriptors.3: Both stated plainly.
A concrete one-week plan with owners.
Calm and reassuring.
A specific ask and time for the next update.

exercises.modelAnswer: Team, the guide has changed our topic to a hospital queue tracker, effective now. What we know: the deadline is unchanged and we can reuse our login and database design. What we do not know yet: whether he accepts the same report format. This week: Arun redesigns the tables by Wednesday, Neha adapts the screens by Friday and I will meet the guide tomorrow. Please send me your concerns by tonight; I will update the group tomorrow at 6 pm.
exercises.guidance: Strong messages are calm, factual and action-oriented. Weak ones vent or ask everyone to wait. Compare honestly against the model.

task.title: Run one proper meeting
task.brief: Lead one short team meeting with agenda, roles and written actions.
steps: Decide the purpose and the outcome you want.
Send an agenda with times beforehand.
Assign a facilitator and a note taker.
End by reading decisions and actions with owners and dates.
Send notes the same day.
checklist: I stated a purpose and outcome
I ended with actions, owners and dates
task.evidencePrompt: Paste your agenda and your list of actions.

quiz.prompt: Which is the final stage of Tuckman model as listed here?
quiz.why: The stages go forming, storming, norming, performing.

quiz.prompt: Before calling a meeting ask whether it could be a ____. (one word)
quiz.why: Many meetings are only information sharing that a message can do.

quiz.prompt: Which method gives the strongest buy-in for an important decision?
quiz.why: Consensus aims for everyone to be able to support the choice, at the cost of time.

quiz.prompt: In uncertainty, a leader should:
options: State what is known and unknown and set a short plan
quiz.why: Honesty and a short-horizon plan keep the team steady.

bank.prompt: A new club committee meets for the first time and members are polite but unsure. The leader should mainly:
bank.why: Forming teams need direction and clarity.

bank.prompt: Which is the best meeting objective?
options: Decide who writes each chapter of the report by Friday
bank.why: A decision-focused outcome keeps the meeting short and useful.

bank.prompt: Voicing doubts and then fully supporting the final decision is called disagree and ____. (one word)
bank.why: It keeps debate open before and unity after the decision.

cards.back: Forming, storming, norming, performing. Leaders clarify at forming, steady conflict at storming, reinforce habits at norming and remove obstacles at performing.
Clear purpose and outcome, timed agenda, facilitator and note taker, actions with owners and dates, and notes sent after.
Leader decides for urgent or minor matters, vote for clear options and consensus for important decisions. Name the method first and record the result.
State what is known and unknown, set a short horizon plan, communicate often and involve the team calmly.

leadership-4.reflection: Think of a group you were in that got stuck. Which stage was it in, and what would have helped?

keyPoints: Storming is normal; handle it with norms.
Meetings need a purpose, agenda and actions.
Match decision method to the decision.
Be honest, short-horizon and calm in uncertainty.
revision.redo: Write a one-line purpose and three agenda items for your next meeting.

negotiation-1.title: Interests, Positions and Preparation
negotiation-1.summary: Separate what people say they want from why they want it, know your walk-away alternative, and fill in a one-page preparation sheet before any negotiation.
objectives: Explain the difference between a position and an interest with an everyday example.
Define BATNA, reservation point and ZOPA and use them to judge whether a deal is worth taking.
Complete a preparation sheet for a real upcoming negotiation.

explanation.heading: Positions hide interests
explanation.body:
Most people think negotiation is a tug of war over one number. A **position** is what someone demands: "I want a flat at ₹12,000 a month." An **interest** is the reason behind it: "I can only spend ₹14,000 in total on housing, and I need a quiet place to study." Positions collide; interests can often be combined.

Two roommates in Faridabad argue over the single bedroom with the balcony. Position: "I want that room." Asking *why* reveals that one wants morning sunlight for yoga and the other wants a door that closes for night calls. A rota, a curtain or a swap of study desk can satisfy both. The skill is to ask "What would having that give you?" before you argue about the thing itself.

The common mistake is to negotiate only on positions, which forces a winner and a loser and often damages the relationship.

explanation.heading: BATNA and reservation point
explanation.body:
Your **BATNA** is your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you will actually do if no deal is reached. It is your real source of power. A student with a second offer in hand negotiates calmly; a student with no alternative feels forced to accept anything.

Your **reservation point** is the worst deal you would still accept. It comes from your BATNA. If your alternative is a freelance project paying ₹20,000 a month, a job offering ₹18,000 is below your reservation point unless it brings something else you value, such as training or stability. Decide this number before the conversation, in a calm moment, because pressure makes people say yes to bad deals.

Work on improving your BATNA before negotiating. Applying to two more companies often does more than any clever phrase.

explanation.heading: ZOPA: the zone of possible agreement
explanation.body:
The **ZOPA** is the range where both sides can say yes. Suppose you are selling a used laptop. You will not accept less than ₹22,000 (your reservation point). The buyer will not pay more than ₹27,000. The ZOPA runs from ₹22,000 to ₹27,000, so a deal is possible. If the buyer's ceiling were ₹20,000 there would be no ZOPA, and walking away would be the right result, not a failure.

You rarely know the other side's limit, so you estimate it by research and by asking questions. Knowing the ZOPA may not exist protects you from forcing a bad agreement.

explanation.heading: The preparation sheet
explanation.body:
Fill in one page before you negotiate:

1. **My interests**, ranked: what matters most, what matters a little.
2. **Their likely interests**: what pressures and goals do they have?
3. **My BATNA** and **reservation point**.
4. **Their likely BATNA**.
5. **Target**: an ambitious but defensible outcome.
6. **Tradeable items**: things cheap for me but valuable to them, such as a faster payment or a longer commitment.
7. **Facts and standards** that support my ask.

Practise by preparing small negotiations first: a rent increase, a freelance fee or a group project deadline. Ten minutes of preparation usually decides the result more than forty minutes of talking.

examples.title: Two interns, one laptop
examples.body: Aman and Sana share one office laptop. Aman says, "I need it every afternoon." Sana says, "No, I need it every afternoon." Asked why, Aman needs it for a 3 pm client demo; Sana needs it to finish a report due by 6 pm. They agree Aman takes it from 2:30 to 4, Sana from 4 to 6.
examples.takeaway: Different interests (a demo slot, a deadline) allowed a split that both positions ruled out.

examples.title: Freelance fee with a BATNA
examples.body: Rohit is offered ₹6,000 for a website. His BATNA is a college-notice-board project paying ₹5,000 with little effort. He sets his reservation at ₹5,500, target ₹8,000, and lists tradeables: delivery in 10 days instead of 7, free first-month fixes. The client's budget is ₹7,000, so the ZOPA is ₹5,500 to ₹7,000. They settle at ₹6,800 with the longer timeline.
examples.takeaway: Knowing the walk-away number and a tradeable made it easy to reach a deal inside the ZOPA.

exercises.prompt: Which statement is an interest rather than a position?
options: I need to keep housing costs low so I can save for my certification fee.
I will not pay more than ₹9,000 rent.
exercises.why: An interest explains why: saving for a certification. The others state demands, which are positions. Asking why uncovers interests.

exercises.prompt: The worst deal you would still accept, derived from your alternatives, is called your ____ point. (one word)
exercises.why: The reservation point is the walk-away limit that comes from your BATNA.

exercises.prompt: Choose a real upcoming negotiation (rent, a freelance fee, a project deadline, a salary talk). Write a short preparation sheet: your top interest, their likely interest, your BATNA, your reservation point and one tradeable item.

descriptors.3: Both sides interests ranked and reasoned.

descriptors.2: BATNA and a number or limit.
descriptors.3: Concrete BATNA with a limit that follows from it.
An item cheap for you and valuable to them.
Specific to a real situation.

exercises.modelAnswer: Situation: asking my landlord to hold rent at ₹9,000 next year. My interest: predictable costs for exams. Likely their interest: no vacancy gap. BATNA: a similar room 2 km away at ₹9,500 with a deposit. Reservation: ₹9,500 total. Tradeable: a two-year commitment and on-time rent via UPI on the 1st.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer names interests on both sides, gives a real alternative and a limit that follows from it, and finds something cheap for you but valuable to them. Common mistakes are listing only demands and setting a reservation point with no alternative behind it. Compare your sheet with the model honestly.

exercises.prompt: You will sell your old phone only for ₹8,000 or more. The only buyer says his absolute ceiling is ₹6,500. What is the best response?

options.text: Accept ₹6,500 to avoid the hassle.
options.feedback: Dropping below your reservation point means you accept a deal worse than keeping the phone.

options.text: Recognise there is no ZOPA, thank him and look for other buyers.
options.feedback: With no overlap, walking away is the correct result. Your BATNA of selling elsewhere or keeping it is better.

options.text: Insist he must pay ₹8,000.
options.feedback: Pushing a buyer past his stated limit wastes time and harms goodwill.

options.text: Lie that another buyer offered ₹9,000.
options.feedback: Fabricating an offer is dishonest and easy to expose.

exercises.why: When the ranges do not overlap there is no ZOPA, and a good negotiator is willing to walk away.

task.title: Prepare one real negotiation
task.brief: Pick a real negotiation coming up in the next month and complete the seven-line preparation sheet.
steps: Choose the negotiation and the other person.
Write your ranked interests and your guess at theirs.
Write your BATNA, reservation point and target.
List at least two tradeable items and one supporting fact.
Ask yourself whether a ZOPA probably exists.
checklist: I named interests, not only positions
My reservation point comes from a real alternative
I estimated the other side limit
task.evidencePrompt: Write your BATNA, reservation point and top tradeable item.

quiz.prompt: What is the best question for uncovering an interest?
quiz.why: Asking what something gives the person moves from the demand to the need behind it.

quiz.prompt: The acronym BATNA stands for Best Alternative To a Negotiated ____. (one word)
quiz.why: BATNA is your best alternative if no agreement is reached.

quiz.prompt: You will accept at least ₹50,000 and the client will pay at most ₹60,000. The ZOPA is:
quiz.why: The ZOPA is the overlap where both can say yes. The midpoint is only one possible outcome inside it.

quiz.prompt: Which belongs on a preparation sheet?
options: Interests, BATNA, reservation point, target and tradeables
A script to repeat word for word
A list of weaknesses of the other person
quiz.why: Preparation maps both sides and your limits; a fixed script or personal attacks do not help.

bank.prompt: Two team members both insist on presenting the final slide. Which step is most likely to resolve it?
options: Let the manager choose by seniority
Ask each what presenting last means to them
Take turns every week without discussing why
bank.why: Learning the interests, such as visibility or a closing summary, may allow a solution that suits both.

bank.prompt: A candidate with two offers negotiates more calmly than one with none because:
bank.why: A strong alternative lowers the fear of walking away, which is the source of negotiating strength.

bank.prompt: If the seller needs at least ₹30,000 and the buyer can pay at most ₹25,000, how many rupees of overlap exist? (number)
bank.why: The buyer ceiling is below the seller floor, so there is no ZOPA and no overlap.

cards.back: A position is what you demand; an interest is why you want it. Ask what the demand would give you, because interests can often be combined where positions cannot.
Your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement: what you will really do if there is no deal. It sets your reservation point and your confidence.
The zone of possible agreement: the overlap between your reservation point and theirs. If there is no overlap, no deal should be forced.

cards.front: Name four items on a preparation sheet.
cards.back: Your ranked interests, their likely interests, your BATNA and reservation point, a target and tradeable items, supported by facts.

negotiation-1.reflection: Think of the last time you agreed to something under pressure. What alternative did you have that you forgot to consider?

keyPoints: Ask why to find interests behind positions.
Know your BATNA and reservation point before talking.
A deal only exists if the ZOPA exists.
Prepare on one page: interests, limits, target, tradeables.
revision.redo: Pick one upcoming small negotiation and write your BATNA, reservation point and one tradeable in two minutes.

negotiation-2.title: Tactics and Conversation
negotiation-2.summary: Use anchoring, careful concessions, good questions, silence and framing to steer a negotiation, and answer objections without getting defensive.
objectives: Make a first offer that is ambitious yet defensible and explain why anchoring matters.
Trade concessions in shrinking steps and ask for something in return.
Respond to an objection with a question and a reframe instead of an argument.

explanation.heading: Anchoring: the first number
explanation.body:
In the last lesson you prepared interests, a BATNA and a target. Now you use them in conversation. The first number spoken tends to pull the final result towards it; this is **anchoring**. If you quote ₹15,000 for a freelance logo and the client counters ₹9,000, the deal will likely land near ₹12,000. Had you opened at ₹11,000, it would land near ₹10,000.

A good anchor is ambitious but defensible: you can explain it with a reason. "₹15,000 includes three concepts, two revisions and source files" holds up; "₹15,000 because I want it" does not. If the other side anchors first with a very low figure, do not counter inside their range. Pause, restate your reasons and give your own number with its justification.

explanation.heading: Concessions: small, slower, never free
explanation.body:
A **concession** is something you give up. Three rules make them powerful. First, never concede without asking for something: "I can deliver in five days if we agree on ₹13,000." Second, make concessions **smaller each time**, from ₹1,500 to ₹700 to ₹300, which signals you are nearing your limit. Third, concede slowly and label it as a cost to you, so it is valued.

The common mistake is the large first concession, which teaches the other side that your price was padded and invites a second request.

explanation.heading: Questions and silence
explanation.body:
Questions give you information and control. Prefer **open questions**: "What budget did you plan for this?" "What would make this a good outcome for your team?" Closed questions get yes or no and tell you little. Ask one question, then stop.

**Silence** is a tool. After you state a number, stay quiet. Many people rush to fill the gap with a discount. Count to five in your head. The same applies after their answer: a short pause often brings the real reason out.

Use **summaries** to check understanding: "So the main concern is timeline, not price, is that right?" It shows listening and prevents solving the wrong problem.

explanation.heading: Framing and objections
explanation.body:
**Framing** is how a request is presented. "This saves your team four hours a week" frames the price as a gain; "This costs ₹13,000" frames it as a loss. Link your ask to their interests.

When someone says "Your price is too high," do not defend. Use three steps: 1. *Acknowledge*: "I understand budget is tight." 2. *Ask*: "Compared with what, and what number works?" 3. *Reframe or trade*: "If we remove the source files, I can do ₹11,000." Often "too high" means "I need a reason," "I have a lower budget," or "I need to justify it to my boss". Asking finds out which one.

examples.title: Concession ladder
examples.body: Meera freelances social-media posts and opens at ₹8,000 a month. The client asks for ₹6,000. Meera replies, "I can go to ₹7,400 if you commit for three months." Client pushes. She moves to ₹7,100 for a 30-day payment term, then says ₹7,000 is her best and holds with silence. The client agrees at ₹7,000.
examples.takeaway: Steps shrank (600, 300, 100) and every concession bought something: commitment and fast payment.

examples.title: Objection handled
examples.body: Interviewer HR: "Your expectation looks above our band." Candidate: "I understand there is a band. Could you share what range you have for this role, and which parts of my profile are driving the gap?" HR names communication skills. Candidate offers examples of client calls from an internship and suggests reviewing after six months.
examples.takeaway: A question replaced a defence, revealing the real objection and opening a trade.

exercises.prompt: A client opens by offering far less than your range. The best response is:
options: Restate your value with reasons and give your own number
Counter just above their number to be fair
exercises.why: Countering within their range lets their anchor control the outcome. Give your own reasoned anchor instead.

exercises.prompt: Concessions should get ____ each time, to signal you are near your limit. (one word)
exercises.why: Shrinking steps show you are running out of room.

exercises.prompt: A client says: "Your quote of ₹12,000 for the website is too high." Write your reply in three parts: acknowledge, ask a question, then reframe or trade.

descriptors.3: Warm and specific acknowledgement.
Open question that finds the real objection.
Links price to their interest and trades a feature or term.

exercises.modelAnswer: I understand the budget needs to feel right. What number or what part of the quote are you comparing it with? If your limit is ₹10,000, I can do that by removing the admin dashboard, which you can add later. If speed matters more, I can keep the full scope with payment in two parts.
exercises.guidance: Strong replies stay calm, ask what the price is compared with, and offer something in return for any reduction. Common mistakes are arguing about worth or discounting immediately. Compare with the model answer honestly.

exercises.setup: You are a final-year student selling a handmade project kit as a side income. A junior wants it cheaper. Your list price is ₹1,500, your reservation point is ₹1,100. You are the seller.

turns.they: Can you make it ₹900? Other kits are cheaper.

options.text: Sure, ₹900 then.
options.feedback: You are below your limit and made a huge free concession.

options.text: I cannot do ₹900. Which kit are you comparing with, and what does it include?
options.feedback: A question tests the comparison and keeps you in control.
options.reply: It has fewer components and no manual.

options.text: No, the price is fixed.
options.feedback: Rigid refusal gives no path forward.

turns.they: Mine is simpler, but it is ₹1,000.

options.text: Mine includes the manual and a spare part. I can do ₹1,350 if you take it today.
options.feedback: You justify value and trade with a smaller concession for a condition.
options.reply: Hmm, ₹1,350 still feels a bit high.

options.feedback: Dropping straight to their number gives away more than needed.

options.text: That is rude to compare.
options.feedback: Defensiveness damages the relationship.

turns.they: Can you do ₹1,200? That is my budget.

options.text: ₹1,250, and I will help you set it up.
options.feedback: A last small concession, with service, stays above your reservation point.

options.text: ₹1,200 and I lose all profit.
options.feedback: Complaining of loss without a trade weakens your stance.

options.text: ₹1,100, my absolute lowest.
options.feedback: Revealing your limit ends negotiation and leaves no room.

exercises.why: Ask before conceding, shrink each concession and attach a trade; do not reveal your limit.

task.title: Run a small anchored negotiation
task.brief: Use anchoring, a question and a traded concession in one real conversation this month, such as a freelance quote, a rent matter or an online purchase from a small seller.
steps: Prepare a reasoned first number.
Open with the number and one reason, then stay quiet.
Ask one open question about their situation.
Concede only against something in return, in shrinking steps.
Afterwards note what worked.
checklist: I opened with a reasoned number
I used at least one pause
I did not concede for free
task.evidencePrompt: Write your opening number, one question you asked and what you traded.

quiz.prompt: Why does an opening number matter?
options: It pulls the final outcome towards it
quiz.why: Anchors shape later expectations, so open with a defensible but ambitious figure.

quiz.prompt: Never concede without asking for something in ____. (one word)
quiz.why: Trade, do not give; each concession should buy something.

quiz.prompt: After you state your price, the strongest move is to:
quiz.why: Silence lets the other party respond; rushing usually produces a needless discount.

quiz.prompt: When told "too expensive," first:
options: Acknowledge and ask what they compare it with
quiz.why: A question finds the real concern before you trade.

bank.prompt: A seller of a second-hand bike writes ₹45,000 "for reasons: low mileage, new tyres, full service history". This anchor is strong because it is:
bank.why: Defensible anchors carry reasons, so they resist being dismissed.

bank.prompt: A question that cannot be answered with just yes or no is an ____ question. (one word)
bank.why: Open questions bring information and keep the other person talking.

bank.prompt: Your concessions to a vendor were ₹500, ₹500, ₹500. What does this pattern suggest?
options: There is more room, so keep asking
bank.why: Equal steps suggest unlimited room. Shrinking steps signal a limit.

cards.back: The first number tends to pull the outcome towards it. Make it ambitious but defensible with a reason, and do not counter inside a lowball anchor.
Never give without getting, make each one smaller than the last, and concede slowly. Large early concessions invite more requests.

cards.front: Why use open questions and silence?
cards.back: Open questions reveal interests and constraints; silence after a number often draws out concessions or the real reason.
Acknowledge the concern, ask a question to find the real issue, then reframe in terms of their interests or trade something.

negotiation-2.reflection: When did you last fill a silence with a discount or a concession? What might you say or not say next time?

keyPoints: Anchor first with a reasoned, ambitious number.
Shrink concessions and trade, never give free.
Ask open questions and use silence.
Answer objections with acknowledge, ask, reframe.
revision.redo: Write a reasoned opening number and one open question for any negotiation you expect this week.

negotiation-3.title: Offers and Salary Negotiation
negotiation-3.summary: Read an Indian job offer correctly, from CTC to in-hand pay, and learn how a fresher can research, time and phrase a respectful negotiation.
objectives: Break a CTC figure into fixed, variable, joining bonus and in-hand components.
List the non-salary terms worth checking in an offer, such as notice period and bond.
Write a respectful counter for an entry-level offer using research and timing.

concepts.label: Offer anatomy and CTC vs in-hand

explanation.heading: Reading an offer: CTC is not salary
explanation.body:
After preparing a BATNA and learning tactics, the biggest negotiation most early-career people face is a job offer. In India, offers quote **CTC** (cost to company): the total a company spends on you in a year. It is not what reaches your bank account.

Typical parts: **fixed pay** (basic, HRA, allowances), **variable pay** (a bonus linked to performance, not guaranteed), employer **PF contribution**, **gratuity** and sometimes insurance. A **joining bonus** is a one-time amount, often repayable if you leave within a set period. Your **in-hand** pay is lower again, because employee PF, professional tax and income tax are deducted.

Illustration with simple numbers: a ₹4,80,000 CTC might comprise ₹4,20,000 fixed and ₹60,000 variable. Divided by twelve, fixed is ₹35,000 a month, but in-hand may be around ₹30,000 after deductions, and the variable may pay out only partly. The exact split varies by company, so always ask for a **written breakup**.

explanation.heading: Terms beyond the number
explanation.body:
Other terms can matter as much as ₹20,000 a year:

- **Notice period**: 30, 60 or 90 days. A long notice reduces your freedom to move.
- **Service agreement or bond**: a promise to stay for a period or pay a penalty. Read the amount and the conditions.
- **Probation**: length, and whether pay or benefits differ.
- **Training and role**: which team, which technology, and whether ABAP or other work is promised. An entry-level role that builds skills can beat a slightly higher offer with no learning.
- **Location, shifts, relocation and work mode.**
- **Variable pay rules** and the date of the first review.

Never accept orally or on a call alone; get the offer letter and read every page.

explanation.heading: Research and timing
explanation.body:
Research gives your ask a standard. Learn the typical range for the role, city and company type from peers, seniors, college placement cells and your network. Use ranges, not single numbers, and do not claim figures you cannot support.

Timing matters. Negotiate after you have a written offer and before you accept; interest is highest then. Avoid giving your current or expected salary early, if you can say "I would like to understand the range for this role first." Large service firms hiring in campus batches often have fixed bands, so room may be small; smaller firms and off-campus hires are more flexible.

explanation.heading: A respectful counter for freshers
explanation.body:
Start with gratitude and enthusiasm, then make one clear request backed by a reason. Ask for the whole package, not only the base.

Example: "Thank you for the offer, I am excited to join the SAP team. Based on my certification work and the range I have seen for similar roles, could the fixed pay be ₹4,20,000 instead of ₹3,90,000? If that is difficult, I would value a six-month review or a training allowance."

Offer an alternative if the answer is no: a review date, a joining bonus or a shorter notice period. Accept the outcome gracefully. A fresher who asks politely rarely loses an offer, and a clear no is still useful information. Never bluff another offer you do not hold.

examples.title: Understanding two offers
examples.body: Offer A: CTC ₹4,00,000, all fixed, 90-day notice. Offer B: CTC ₹4,30,000 with ₹50,000 variable paid on company performance, 30-day notice and a one-year bond of ₹1,00,000. Monthly fixed: A is about ₹33,300; B is ₹3,80,000 divided by twelve, about ₹31,700. Kavya prefers A for steadier pay, but notes the notice and asks if it can be cut to 60 days.
examples.takeaway: Comparing fixed pay and terms, not headline CTC, changes which offer looks better.

examples.title: Fresher counter in an email
examples.body:
Subject: Offer for Associate Consultant - a question

Dear Ms Iyer, thank you for the offer; I am keen to join. I noticed the fixed component is ₹3,60,000. Given my SAP training and the ranges I have seen for similar roles, could we revisit it to ₹3,90,000? If the band is fixed, I would appreciate clarity on training and the review cycle. Thank you for considering this.
examples.takeaway: Gratitude, one specific ask, a reason and a fallback keep it respectful and effective.

exercises.prompt: An offer states CTC ₹6,00,000. What is the most accurate statement?
options: It is the total yearly cost to the company, not the in-hand amount
It is your fixed pay only
exercises.why: CTC includes variable pay and employer contributions and excludes deductions, so in-hand is lower.

exercises.prompt: A promise to stay for a set period or pay a penalty is called a service ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Service agreements or bonds can cost you freedom to leave, so read them.

exercises.prompt: You receive a verbal offer on a call, and the recruiter immediately asks for your current salary. What is your best move?

options.text: Quote your current salary at once.
options.feedback: Early disclosure can anchor the offer to your old pay.

options.text: Thank them, ask for the range for the role and the written offer, and discuss after reviewing it.
options.feedback: You gather information and keep negotiating leverage until the offer is written.

options.text: Reject the offer on the call.
options.feedback: You have no complete information, so rejecting is premature.

options.text: Accept immediately to show enthusiasm.
options.feedback: Accepting before reading the written terms removes the chance to negotiate.

exercises.why: Seek the range and a written offer before discussing numbers.

exercises.prompt: You have an offer as a Trainee Developer with fixed pay of ₹3,60,000 and want ₹3,90,000. Draft a short respectful counter (4 to 6 sentences) with gratitude, a reason and a fallback request.

descriptors.3: Genuine gratitude with interest in the role.

descriptors.2: A reason from skills or range.
descriptors.3: A specific reason tied to value and research.
A clear number plus the component it refers to.
A flexible fallback such as review, training or notice period.

exercises.modelAnswer: Dear Mr Rao, thank you for the offer; I am excited about joining the team. Based on my project and certification work and the range I have seen for similar trainee roles, could the fixed pay be ₹3,90,000? If the band is fixed, I would appreciate a six-month review or a training allowance. Thank you for considering this.
exercises.guidance: A strong counter is warm, specific and brief, with one reason and a fallback. Common mistakes are demanding an unsupported number, comparing with friends or bluffing other offers. Check yours against the model honestly.

task.title: Decode a real or sample offer
task.brief: Take a real offer or a sample you find from a peer and break it into parts, then draft a counter.
steps: Write CTC, fixed, variable, joining bonus and estimated in-hand.
List notice period, bond, probation and training terms.
Note the range you found from at least two people.
Draft a four-sentence counter email.
checklist: My counter includes thanks, reason and fallback
task.evidencePrompt: Paste your counter draft and the number you are asking for.

quiz.prompt: Which part of CTC is least guaranteed?
quiz.why: Variable pay depends on performance or company results.

quiz.prompt: Which term most limits your ability to change jobs?
options: A long notice period and a bond
quiz.why: Notice periods and bonds create time and money costs for leaving.

quiz.prompt: The best time to negotiate is after a written offer and ____ you accept. (one word)
quiz.why: After acceptance your leverage is gone.

quiz.prompt: Which counter is strongest?
options: My friend got more, so match it.
Thank you; based on my skills and the market range, could we revisit fixed pay to ₹3.9 lakh?
I need more because rent is high.
quiz.why: It is grateful, specific and evidence-based; others are demanding or need-based.

bank.prompt: A fixed pay of ₹3,60,000 per year equals how many rupees per month before deductions? (number)
bank.why: 3,60,000 divided by 12 is 30,000 per month before deductions.

bank.prompt: Which is a good source for pay research?
options: Seniors, placement cells and peers in similar roles
bank.why: Several grounded sources give a range you can defend.

bank.prompt: The recruiter says the band is fixed. What is a sensible reply?
options: Thanks; could we agree a six-month review or a training allowance?
I will tell others about it
bank.why: Moving to non-salary items keeps the relationship and may still add value.

cards.back: CTC is the total yearly cost to the company, including variable pay and employer contributions. In-hand is lower after PF, tax and other deductions; ask for the breakup in writing.
Notice period, bond or service agreement, probation, training and role, location and work mode, variable pay rules and review dates.
Collect ranges from seniors and peers, and negotiate after the written offer but before acceptance; avoid quoting current pay early.
Thank them, make one specific ask with a reason, offer a fallback such as a review or training, and accept the answer gracefully.

negotiation-3.reflection: What would matter more to you in a first job than ₹20,000 extra a year, and how would you ask for it?

keyPoints: CTC is not in-hand pay; get the breakup.
Check notice, bond, probation and training.
Research ranges and negotiate before accepting.
Counter with thanks, one reason and a fallback.
revision.redo: Take any offer or job advert and list its fixed, variable and three non-salary terms.

negotiation-4.title: Everyday and Difficult Negotiations
negotiation-4.summary: Handle pressure tactics calmly, stay ethical, close agreements clearly and follow up, using realistic practice scenarios.
objectives: Recognise common pressure tactics and respond without panic.
Apply an ethics test to avoid manipulation and keep the relationship.
Close with a written summary and follow-up for everyday agreements.

explanation.heading: Common pressure tactics
explanation.body:
You have learned preparation, tactics and offers. Real negotiations sometimes include pressure. Recognising the tactic is half of resisting it.

- **Deadline pressure**: "This offer expires in an hour." Reply: "I want to decide properly. Could I have until tomorrow evening?" Genuine deadlines can usually flex a little.
- **Good cop, bad cop**: one person is harsh, another sympathetic. Respond to the proposal, not the performance.
- **The nibble**: after agreement, a small extra request, such as "include free maintenance too." Reply: "That was not in our scope; I can add it for a fee."
- **Lowball and bluff**: an absurdly low number to move your anchor. Do not counter inside it.
- **Take it or leave it**: check your BATNA; if it is better, leave politely.

A good rule: **slow down**. Say "Let me think and get back to you" and use the time.

explanation.heading: Ethics: firm without manipulating
explanation.body:
Negotiators are tempted to bluff: "I have another offer," when they do not. Besides being wrong, it is risky. Claims get checked, and trust in your industry circle is small and lasting.

A useful test with three questions: **Would I be comfortable if the other side saw exactly what I am doing? Would I be comfortable if my college seniors heard about it? Am I telling the truth about facts?** You may keep your reservation point private and choose what to emphasise, but you may not invent facts. Hard on the problem, soft on the person: disagree about terms without insulting the other party.

Everyday example: when a tenant asks a landlord for a lower deposit, naming a real alternative flat is honest leverage; claiming a false offer is not.

explanation.heading: Closing and follow-up
explanation.body:
Agreements fade without a clear close. Close in four steps:

1. **Summarise** the terms aloud: price, date, scope, payment method.
2. **Check** for confusion: "Have I missed anything?"
3. **Write** it down the same day, in a short message or email. For example: "To confirm: ₹7,000 per month for three months, payment by the 5th via UPI, starting 1 November."
4. **Follow up** on the date promised and thank them.

If you cannot reach agreement, close the conversation anyway: "Let us pause here and revisit on Friday after checking numbers." This keeps the door open.

explanation.heading: Practising and reviewing
explanation.body:
Negotiation is a skill built by reps, not by reading. Practise with low-stakes cases: canteen group orders, deadline swaps with project partners, a gym membership, a rickshaw fare, a second-hand purchase. Use the three-minute review after each one: What was my goal? What did I trade? What did I say that helped or hurt? What will I do differently?

When the stakes are high, role-play with a friend: ask them to play a tough counterpart, then switch roles to learn how it feels from their side. Keep notes in one place so lessons accumulate.

examples.title: The nibble after agreement
examples.body: Arjun agrees to design a poster for a fest for ₹2,000. As he sends the final file, the organiser says, "Please also make Instagram and WhatsApp versions, it is only a small change." Arjun answers, "Happy to. The two extra sizes are ₹600 together, and I can send them by tonight." The organiser agrees.
examples.takeaway: Naming the extra as a separate, priced item turned a free grab into a fair trade.

examples.title: Closing message
examples.body: After a call about a shared flat, Neha writes: "Confirming what we agreed: rent ₹9,500 including maintenance, deposit of two months, move-in 1 December, water and electricity split equally. Please reply yes if this matches your understanding." The owner replies yes and later cannot dispute the deposit.
examples.takeaway: A short written summary turns a spoken agreement into a shared record.

exercises.prompt: A vendor says "This price is only valid for the next 30 minutes." What is the best response?
options: Ask politely for a bit more time and check your alternatives
exercises.why: Many deadlines can flex; slowing down protects your decision. Panic payment or insult serves no one.

exercises.prompt: After agreeing terms you should send a written ____ the same day. (one word)
exercises.why: A written summary prevents misunderstandings later.

exercises.prompt: A manager asks you, "Do you have competing internship offers?" and you have none. Write your honest reply in 3 to 4 sentences that stays positive and still states a researched stipend range.

descriptors.3: Clearly honest without weakening your position.
Specific reason for wanting this team.
A researched range with a reason.

exercises.modelAnswer: I do not have another offer at the moment, but this team is my first choice because of its SAP work. From seniors and the placement cell, I understand stipends for similar roles run between ₹12,000 and ₹15,000. Could we look at the upper part of that range given my project experience?
exercises.guidance: Strong answers admit the lack of an offer without apology, show real interest and give a researched range. Common mistakes are bluffing, which is dishonest and risky, or saying nothing, which loses your ask. Score honestly against the model.

exercises.setup: You are a fresher who accepted a verbal job offer. HR now says on call that the joining date and the bond terms are changed. You want to protect your position calmly. You are the candidate.

turns.they: The bond is now two years instead of one, and you must confirm today.

options.text: Fine, I will confirm.
options.feedback: Agreeing under pressure to a major new term is risky.
options.reply: Thank you, we will send the letter.

options.text: This changes our earlier discussion. Please send the revised terms in writing, and I will respond by tomorrow evening.
options.feedback: You slow down, ask for writing and set a reasonable reply time.
options.reply: Okay, I can send it in an hour. Tomorrow evening is fine.

options.text: This is unfair. I will complain to everyone.
options.feedback: Threats escalate and harm your reputation.
options.reply: There is no need to be rude.

turns.they: The bond was always two years; our offers all carry it.

options.text: The earlier message I received states one year. Could we check it together? I would like to continue if we can align.
options.feedback: You use facts calmly and keep the door open.
options.reply: Let me check the email trail and revert today.

options.text: You are lying.
options.feedback: Accusations end the cooperation.
options.reply: I do not appreciate that tone.

options.text: Then I accept.
options.feedback: Giving in ignores contradicting evidence.

turns.they: I checked; a one-year bond was a mistake. What else can we do to settle it?

options.text: One year as originally stated, with the same joining date. Please confirm in the revised letter.
options.feedback: You restate the agreed term and ask for it in writing.
options.reply: Yes, I will send it today.

options.text: Remove the bond completely.
options.feedback: A new demand after they corrected the error may feel like overreach.

options.text: Whatever, I do not care.
options.feedback: Disengaging leaves terms unclear.
options.reply: Then we will proceed as in the letter.

exercises.why: Slow down, use written facts and restate the agreement.

task.title: Practise with an everyday negotiation
task.brief: Run one low-stakes negotiation this week and finish with a written close.
steps: Pick a small case: a group order, a deadline swap, a purchase.
Write your goal, limit and one tradeable.
Hold the conversation using one tactic from this skill.
Send a same-day message summarising what was agreed.
Do the three-minute review.
checklist: I had a goal and a limit
task.evidencePrompt: Write the agreed terms and one thing you will do differently.

quiz.prompt: What is the nibble?
options: A small extra request made after agreement
quiz.why: The nibble asks for a small add-on at the end; respond by pricing it.

quiz.prompt: Which is acceptable in ethical negotiation?
quiz.why: You may protect private information but must not lie about facts.

quiz.prompt: The first step in closing is to ____ the agreed terms aloud. (one word)
quiz.why: Summarising checks that both sides understood the same terms.

quiz.prompt: What is the best way to improve negotiation skill?
options: Practise in low-stakes cases and review each
quiz.why: Deliberate practice and review build skill faster than reading.

bank.prompt: Two interviewers, one harsh and one friendly, ask you to lower your expectations. What should you do?
options: Respond to the proposal itself and ask for time
bank.why: Good cop, bad cop is a performance; judge the offer and slow down.

bank.prompt: Which test checks if a tactic is ethical?
options: Would I be comfortable if the other side saw exactly what I am doing?
Is it legal in my city?
bank.why: Transparency, truthfulness and long-term trust are the standard, not just effectiveness.

bank.prompt: Two days after a verbal agreement you realise terms are unclear. What kind of message would have prevented it? (one word)
bank.why: A written confirmation sent the same day prevents disputes.

cards.back: Deadline pressure, good cop and bad cop, the nibble, lowball or bluff, and take it or leave it. Slow down, ask for time and check your BATNA.
Would I be comfortable if they saw my tactic? Am I truthful about facts? You may keep limits private but not invent facts; be hard on the problem, soft on the person.
Summarise aloud, check for gaps, send a written confirmation the same day and follow up on the promised date.
Use low-stakes cases and friend role-plays, then run a three-minute review: goal, trade, what helped, what to change.

negotiation-4.reflection: Which pressure tactic would make you give in fastest, and what one sentence will you use to slow it down?

keyPoints: Slow down against pressure and ask for writing.
Be truthful: private limits are fine, invented facts are not.
Close with a same-day written summary.
Practise small and review each time.
revision.redo: Write a three-line confirmation message for any agreement you made this week.

networking-1.title: Networking Foundations
networking-1.summary: Understand networking as giving first and building genuine relationships, use weak ties, set a clear goal and find people through college, alumni and online communities.
objectives: Explain networking as building relationships rather than collecting favours.
Describe why weak ties often open doors and how to use them.
Set a networking goal and list five places to find the right people.

explanation.heading: What networking really is
explanation.body:
Many students hear "networking" and picture awkward events where people hand out cards and ask for jobs. That picture is wrong, and it makes people avoid something useful. **Networking** is simply building and maintaining genuine professional relationships: people who know what you do, whom you trust, and who might share information, advice or an introduction. In India a large share of jobs and opportunities travel through conversations, and for an entry-level candidate with no experience, a few good relationships can matter as much as a perfect CV.

The core principle is **giving first**. Instead of asking "What can I get?", ask "How can I be useful?" Useful can be small: sharing an article, congratulating someone on a project, answering a question in a community, or offering your notes. Giving builds goodwill and makes later requests natural.

explanation.heading: Weak ties and your starting network
explanation.body:
Sociologist Mark Granovetter found in his research that people often learn about jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends. These acquaintances are **weak ties**. Your close friends know the same people and information you do. A weak tie, such as a senior from college now working at a services firm, moves in a different circle and sees opportunities you cannot.

So you do not need dozens of close friends in the industry. You need a wide set of light, friendly connections and the habit of keeping them warm. Everyone starts with more than they think: classmates, teachers, seniors, internship supervisors, relatives' colleagues and people you meet on courses.

explanation.heading: Start with a goal
explanation.body:
Networking without direction becomes random. Write a one-line **goal**: "In the next three months I want to understand what an entry-level ABAP consultant does day to day, and meet four people who work in SAP." This tells you who to look for and what to ask. Goals can also be to learn about a company, get feedback on your CV, or find a study partner.

A useful split is learn, connect, contribute. Learn means gaining information; connect means meeting people; contribute means giving something back. A healthy week has a bit of each.

explanation.heading: Where to find people
explanation.body:
Look first where trust already exists. **College**: teachers, placement cell, seniors and alumni, many of whom enjoy helping juniors from their own institution. **Communities**: SAP learning groups, local developer meetups, college clubs and student chapters of professional bodies. **Online**: LinkedIn, professional forums and open-source or learning communities where you can answer questions and share small projects. **Events**: webinars, workshops and college seminars.

Example: Aman wants to learn about SAP careers. He lists five places: his placement cell, two alumni from his BCA batch, an SAP forum, a local meetup and a teacher who once worked in a consulting firm. In a week he has identified three specific people to contact. Quality beats quantity: five real conversations beat 500 unanswered connection requests.

examples.title: Giving first in practice
examples.body: Meena sees a senior post on LinkedIn that his team is looking for interns. She does not message him asking for a referral. She comments with a useful link to a free SQL practice set, thanks him for sharing, and weeks later asks him two questions about his day-to-day work. He replies warmly and mentions a vacancy.
examples.takeaway: Small, genuine contributions create goodwill, and the opportunity followed from the relationship rather than a demand.

examples.title: A weak tie in action
examples.body: Imran's close friends all apply to the same three companies. A former classmate, whom he talks to only occasionally, mentions that a mid-sized consulting firm is hiring freshers for an ABAP training batch. Imran applies and gets interviewed.
examples.takeaway: Distant acquaintances reach different circles, so they surface opportunities your close circle never sees.

exercises.prompt: Which approach best reflects giving first?
options: Sharing a helpful resource and thanking someone for their post
Messaging a stranger for a job on day one
Collecting as many contacts as possible
Waiting for others to approach you
exercises.why: Giving builds goodwill without demanding anything. Asking for a job immediately or collecting contacts does not create a relationship.

exercises.prompt: People you know slightly, such as an old classmate in another company, are called weak ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Weak ties connect you to different circles and often bring new information.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best networking goal?
options: Speak to four people working in SAP in three months to learn about the role
exercises.why: It is specific, measurable and tied to learning. The others are vague or purely outcome-based.

exercises.prompt: List five specific places or groups, relevant to you, where you could meet people in your target field. For each, write one low-pressure thing you could do or give there this month.

descriptors.3: Five specific, relevant places.
A concrete action for each.
Mostly giving or learning first.
College, community and online mixed.

exercises.modelAnswer: One: placement cell, ask for a list of alumni in IT services. Two: my BCA alumni group, congratulate a senior on a new role. Three: a local developer meetup, attend one session and ask one question. Four: an SAP forum, answer one beginner question. Five: my teacher with consulting experience, ask for advice on the first year of work and offer to share my project.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer lists real places you can reach, mixes college, community and online, and gives each a small action that is more about learning or giving than asking for a job. Avoid vague entries like "LinkedIn" with no action. Score yourself honestly.

task.title: Map your starting network
task.brief: List the people you already know and choose three to contact with a giving-first message.
steps: Write a list of 15 people: teachers, seniors, classmates, relatives' colleagues, internship contacts.
Mark five as weak ties working in or near your target field.
Write a one-line networking goal for three months.
Choose three people and write one useful thing you could share or ask for each.
checklist: My goal is specific and dated
I planned a giving-first step for three people
task.evidencePrompt: Write your goal and the three people with the step for each.

quiz.prompt: The giving-first principle means:
options: Looking for ways to be useful before asking for help
quiz.why: You contribute and build goodwill first, so later requests feel natural.

quiz.prompt: Why do weak ties often help find opportunities?
options: They move in different circles with different information
quiz.why: Weak ties reach circles you do not, so they hear about things you would miss.

quiz.prompt: A good networking goal is specific and has a time limit; for example, "meet four people in SAP in three ____". (one word)
quiz.why: A time frame makes the goal measurable and prompts action.

quiz.prompt: Which is a good first place to look for contacts?
options: College alumni and teachers, where trust already exists
quiz.why: Shared institutions create trust, so alumni and teachers often respond.

bank.prompt: You want to learn about careers in data analytics but know nobody. What is a sensible starting step?
options: Ask your placement cell for alumni in analytics and join one community
Wait until you have a job
Post that you need a job
bank.why: Starting with institutional links and a community gives warm, relevant entry points.

bank.prompt: Sharing a helpful article with a thank-you note is an example of ____ first. (one word)
bank.why: Giving first means offering value before asking for anything.

bank.prompt: Which networking message shows a clear goal?
options: I am exploring SAP ABAP roles and would value ten minutes about your first year
bank.why: It states why you are writing and what small thing you ask.

cards.back: Offering something useful, such as a resource, thanks or help, before asking for anything. It builds goodwill that makes later requests natural.

cards.front: What are weak ties and why do they matter?
cards.back: Acquaintances outside your close circle. They connect you to different groups and information, so they often bring job leads.

cards.front: What does a good networking goal look like?
cards.back: One specific, time-bound line, such as meeting four SAP professionals in three months to learn what the job involves.

cards.front: Where can a student find people?
cards.back: College teachers, seniors and alumni, student clubs and communities, online forums and professional networks, workshops and webinars.

networking-1.reflection: Who among your acquaintances may know something useful about your target career, and what could you offer them first?

keyPoints: Networking means genuine relationships, not collecting favours.
Give first with small, real contributions.
Weak ties open different circles.
Set a specific goal and start where trust already exists.
revision.redo: Name one weak tie and one useful thing you could share with them this week.

networking-2.title: Conversations and Introductions
networking-2.summary: Prepare a short self-introduction, make small talk with open questions, remember names and handle events with a simple plan.
objectives: Deliver a clear ten-second and thirty-second self-introduction.
Start and sustain small talk with open questions and genuine curiosity.
Use simple techniques to remember names and prepare for an event.

explanation.heading: A short, clear introduction
explanation.body:
In the first lesson you set a goal and found places to meet people. Now you need to say who you are in a way that is easy to remember. A strong **self-introduction** has three parts: *who you are*, *what you do or are learning*, and *a hook*, a hint of what you are curious about or can help with.

Ten-second version: "Hi, I am Deepak, an MCA student in Faridabad learning SAP ABAP." Thirty-second version adds the hook: "Before this I built web apps with Node.js, and now I am curious how SAP teams handle reporting for clients." The hook gives the other person something to respond to. Avoid reading out your whole CV, using vague phrases like "I am just a student", or apologising. Practise aloud until it sounds natural, and adjust for context: a teacher, a recruiter and a fellow student need different emphasis.

explanation.heading: Small talk with open questions
explanation.body:
Small talk feels pointless until you see its job: it builds enough comfort for deeper conversation. Start with something shared: the event, the speaker, the venue or the place. "What brought you to this session?" works better than "Do you come here often?" because it is **open**, inviting a story rather than yes or no.

A simple loop is **ask, listen, follow up, share**. Ask an open question. Listen for a detail they mention, such as "I moved from testing to development". Follow up on that detail: "What made you switch?" Then share something short of your own. Most people like to talk about their work and experiences, so curiosity makes you memorable. Avoid interrogation by balancing questions and sharing, and avoid sensitive topics such as salary, religion and politics with new acquaintances.

explanation.heading: Remembering names
explanation.body: Remembering a name is a small signal of respect. Three steps help. First, **pay attention** when you hear it, which means not thinking about your own reply. Second, **repeat it** at once: "Nice to meet you, Kavya." Third, **use it** once or twice in the conversation and link it to something, such as an image or fact: "Kavya, who works on SAP reporting in Gurugram." If you forget, say honestly, "I am sorry, I have forgotten your name. Could you remind me?" It is far better than guessing. After the event, jot down names and one fact for each.

explanation.heading: Handling events
explanation.body: Events become manageable with a plan. Before: know the purpose, check who is attending, set a small goal such as speaking to three new people, and prepare your introduction and two questions. During: arrive early, when groups are small, and approach people standing alone or groups with open space. To join a group, stand near, listen, and add a comment when there is a pause. To leave gracefully, say "It was great talking to you. I am going to meet a few other people. Can I connect with you on LinkedIn?" After: within 48 hours, send a short note to each person, which the next lesson covers in detail.

examples.title: Two self-introductions
examples.body: Weak: "Hi, I am just a final-year student, nothing special, looking for any job." Strong: "Hi, I am Sana, a final-year BCA student. I have built two small inventory apps in SQL and C#, and I am exploring ABAP for reporting roles. What is your team's work like?" The strong version states identity, evidence and a question.
examples.takeaway: A hook and a question turn an introduction into the start of a conversation.

examples.title: Following up on a detail
examples.body: At a college seminar, Rohit asks the speaker, "What made you choose consulting?" The speaker mentions travelling to client sites. Rohit follows up: "What is a typical first week at a client site like?" The speaker lights up and shares a story, and later remembers Rohit.
examples.takeaway: Following up on a detail they mention shows real interest and keeps the conversation going.

exercises.prompt: Which is the best element to end a 30-second introduction with?
options: A hook that shows your interest or invites a question
exercises.why: A hook gives the listener something to respond to. Apologies and marks lists weaken the introduction and a job request is premature.

exercises.prompt: A question that invites a story, such as "What brought you here?", is called an ____ question. (one word)
exercises.why: Open questions cannot be answered with yes or no.

exercises.prompt: You meet someone, shake hands, and forget their name five minutes later. What should you do?

options.text: Avoid using any name for the whole conversation.
options.feedback: Avoiding it hides the problem and misses the chance to connect.

options.text: Guess a name and hope it is right.
options.feedback: A wrong guess embarrasses both people.

options.text: Say "Sorry, I have forgotten your name, could you remind me?" and repeat it.
options.feedback: Being honest is respectful and quickly solves it.

options.text: Check their name tag only after leaving.
options.feedback: It is too late to use the name in conversation.

exercises.why: An honest quick request and repeating the name builds trust better than hiding the lapse.

exercises.prompt: You will attend a one-day SAP community meetup next Saturday, knowing nobody. Write your plan: a goal, your 30-second introduction, two open questions you will ask, and how you will end a conversation politely.

descriptors.3: Small, specific and realistic.
Identity, evidence and a hook.
Two open what or how questions.
Polite with a follow-up such as connecting.

exercises.modelAnswer: Goal: speak to three new people and collect two names with one fact each. Introduction: Hi, I am Aarav, an MCA student; I built web apps with Node.js and I am now learning ABAP, curious about how consultants handle reports. Questions: What brought you to this session? How did you start in SAP? Exit: It was great meeting you; I am going to say hello to a few others. May I connect with you on LinkedIn?
exercises.guidance: A strong plan has a small goal, an introduction with identity, evidence and a hook, two open questions starting with what or how, and a warm exit with a next step. Avoid plans that say only "be confident". Score yourself against the model.

task.title: Practise introductions and open questions
task.brief: Say your introduction to three people and hold three short conversations using the ask, listen, follow up, share loop.
steps: Write your ten-second and thirty-second introductions and say them aloud twice.
Speak to three people, which can be classmates, a teacher or an online meetup attendee.
In each conversation ask two open questions and follow up on one detail.
Repeat each name and write down names with one fact afterwards.
checklist: I wrote two versions of my introduction
I followed up on a detail each time
I recorded three names and facts
task.evidencePrompt: Write your 30-second introduction and one follow-up question that worked.

quiz.prompt: What are the three parts of a strong introduction?
options: Who you are, what you do or learn, and a hook
quiz.why: Identity, current focus and a hook make an introduction memorable.

quiz.prompt: The loop for small talk is:
quiz.why: It balances curiosity with sharing and keeps conversation flowing.

quiz.prompt: After hearing a name, repeat it immediately and ____ it in conversation. (one word)
quiz.why: Using a name once or twice helps memory and shows respect.

quiz.prompt: The best time to arrive at a networking event is:
quiz.why: Early arrival makes joining small groups easier.

bank.prompt: At a seminar, the person next to you says they work in supply chain. Which follow-up question is best?
options: What kind of problems do you solve in supply chain?
bank.why: It is open, curious and on topic. The others are closed, judgemental or too personal.

bank.prompt: A short self-introduction can include a ____ that invites the other person to respond. (one word)
bank.why: The hook or question gives the other person a way into the conversation.

bank.prompt: You want to leave a conversation politely. What works best?
options: Say you enjoyed it, mention you will meet others, and offer to connect
bank.why: A warm closing and a next step keeps the relationship positive.

cards.back: Who you are, what you do or are learning, and a hook showing a curiosity or interest. Keep a ten-second and a thirty-second version.

cards.front: What is the small talk loop?
cards.back: Ask an open question, listen for a detail, follow up on it, then share something short of your own. Avoid salary and politics.
Pay attention, repeat the name at once, use it once or twice, link it to a fact and note it afterwards. If you forget, ask honestly.

cards.front: What is a simple event plan?
cards.back: Set a small goal, prepare an introduction and two questions, arrive early, join open groups, exit politely and follow up within 48 hours.

networking-2.reflection: When did a conversation with a stranger go well, and which of its moves could you repeat deliberately?

keyPoints: Introduce yourself with identity, focus and a hook.
Use open questions and follow up on details.
Repeat and use names; ask if you forget.
Plan events with a small goal and a polite exit.
revision.redo: Say your 30-second introduction aloud once and refine one sentence.

networking-3.title: Outreach and Follow-Up
networking-3.summary: Write short cold messages, request informational chats, ask for referrals respectfully, follow up at the right time and keep a simple contact tracker.
objectives: Write a short, specific cold message that makes saying yes easy.
Run an informational chat and ask about referrals respectfully.
Follow up on time and keep a simple contact tracker.

explanation.heading: Writing a cold message
explanation.body:
Last lesson you practised conversations face to face. Often you need to contact someone you have never met. A **cold message** works when it is short, specific and easy to answer. Use four parts: **who you are** in one line, **why this person** (a genuine reason), **a small ask**, and **thanks with an easy exit**.

Example: "Hello Ms Gupta, I am Deepak, an MCA student learning SAP ABAP. I read that you moved from development to functional consulting at your firm, which is the path I am considering. Could I ask you two questions over a ten-minute call, or by message if that is easier? Thank you for considering it, and I understand if you are busy."

Avoid "Please help me get a job", walls of text, copy-paste messages with the wrong name, and asking for more than a person can give. Specific beats generic every time.

explanation.heading: Informational chats
explanation.body:
An **informational chat** is a short conversation, usually 10 to 20 minutes, where you learn about someone's work and path. It is not a job interview and you do not ask for a job. Prepare three to five questions: "How did you get started?", "What does a typical week look like?", "What skills mattered most in your first year?", "What would you do differently?", and "Who else would you suggest I speak to?"

Respect their time by starting on schedule, keeping to the length, and listening more than you talk. At the end, thank them and mention one thing you will do with the advice. People remember students who act on suggestions.

explanation.heading: Asking for referrals
explanation.body: A **referral** means an employee recommends you for an opening, which often gets an application noticed. Ask only after some relationship exists, and make it easy and low-pressure. Do your homework: find a specific vacancy, check that you meet the basics, and send a short summary plus your CV. "Would you be comfortable referring me, or is there anyone better to ask? I understand if you would rather not." Never expect a referral from someone who has not seen your work or spoken to you. Whatever the answer, thank them, because a gracious reply keeps the relationship intact.

explanation.heading: Follow-up and a contact tracker
explanation.body:
Most outreach fails because of silence, not rejection. People are busy.
