examples.takeaway: One star, one link and one question tell you more when you return than a page of yellow.

examples.title: Choosing the right speed
examples.body: Tuesday: you need the due date and marks split in a 12-page assignment brief - you scan. Wednesday: you want to know if an article on project management is relevant - you skim. Thursday: you study the chapter on joins for your exam - you read with SQ3R.
examples.takeaway: The task decides the speed. Use the fastest speed that still achieves your purpose.

exercises.prompt: In SQ3R, which step involves closing the book and explaining a section in your own words?
exercises.hint: It is the step with the Rs in the middle: Read, then ...
exercises.why: Recite is the recall step. Survey is a preview, Question turns headings into questions, and Review comes at the end to go over everything again.

exercises.prompt: You need to find the deadline date in a long email thread and ignore everything else. Which speed is this: reading, skimming or scanning? Write one word.
exercises.hint: You are looking for one specific item.
exercises.why: Scanning is a targeted search for a specific item. Skimming is for the gist, and careful reading is for understanding and remembering.

exercises.prompt: You are reading a chapter for an exam and you notice you have highlighted nearly every sentence. What is the best next step?

options.text: Keep going; highlighting shows you are working hard.
options.feedback: When everything is highlighted, nothing stands out, and the highlighting replaces thinking.

options.text: Stop, remove most marks, and for each section write one margin note in your own words plus one question.
options.feedback: Correct: choosing one main idea per section forces understanding and creates review material.

options.text: Switch to a different colour for the rest of the chapter.
options.feedback: A new colour changes the look but not the problem that you are marking without deciding what matters.

options.text: Read the chapter twice without marking anything.
options.feedback: Rereading passively gives a false feeling of knowing; you need to produce something, such as notes or questions.

exercises.why: Active reading selects and rephrases. Fewer, better marks plus margin notes in your own words turn the page into something you can review.

exercises.prompt: Imagine you must read a 15-page article titled 'How Companies Migrate to the Cloud' before a client call tomorrow. Describe your plan: state your purpose, say what you would look at in your preview, write two heading-style questions you would ask, and say which parts you would read carefully and which you would skim.

descriptors.1: A vague purpose such as 'to learn about the cloud'.
descriptors.2: A purpose tied to the situation but not specific about what to extract.
descriptors.3: A purpose tied to the client call that states what you need to be able to say or ask.

descriptors.1: Mentions looking at the article but not what to look at.
descriptors.2: Names two preview elements such as title and headings.
descriptors.3: Names three or more elements, such as title, headings, first sentences, summary or conclusion.

auto.label: Mentions at least two preview elements

descriptors.1: One question, or questions that are too broad.
descriptors.2: Two questions that are relevant but generic.
descriptors.3: Two specific questions that match likely headings and the purpose.

descriptors.0: No difference between sections is given.
descriptors.1: Says to read everything carefully or to skim everything.
descriptors.2: Names one careful section and one skimmed section without a reason.
descriptors.3: Matches each part to reading, skimming or scanning with a reason linked to the purpose.

exercises.modelAnswer: My purpose is to be able to explain the main migration approaches and ask two sensible questions on tomorrow's client call. In a three-minute preview I would read the title, the introduction, every heading, the first sentence of each section and the conclusion. My questions: 'What are the main ways to migrate to the cloud?' and 'What risks do companies face during migration?' I would read the sections that answer those questions carefully, skim the case studies for the headline result, and scan for any cost figures I might need.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers connect the plan to the client call, so the purpose is something you can test: 'I can explain three migration approaches'. Questions should be built from likely headings, not generic prompts. A common mistake is saying you will read all 15 pages carefully; with limited time, selecting what to read closely is the skill. Compare your plan with the model answer and score honestly.

task.title: Run SQ3R on one real chapter
task.brief: Apply purpose, preview, questions, annotation and recitation to a chapter or article you choose.
steps: Choose a chapter or an article of five to ten pages from a book, course material or an article you already have, and write one sentence stating why you are reading it.
Spend three minutes surveying it: title, headings, first lines, diagrams, summary. Turn each heading into a question on a sheet of paper.
Read one section at a time. Mark at most one main idea and one question per page, and write short margin notes in your own words.
After each section, close the book and write or say the answer to your question; then review all your answers at the end.
checklist: I wrote my purpose before starting
I made a question from each heading
I limited my marks to the main ideas and questions
I recited each section's answer without looking
task.evidencePrompt: Name what you read, state your purpose, and write two of your questions with your answers.

quiz.prompt: Why do you set a purpose before reading?
options: It tells you how closely to read and what to look for.
It replaces the need to understand the text.
It guarantees you will remember everything.
quiz.why: A purpose guides your attention and your speed. It does not shorten the text, replace understanding or guarantee memory.

quiz.prompt: What does the Q in SQ3R ask you to do?
options: Quote the author in your notes.
Quit if the chapter is difficult.
quiz.why: Q is for Question: convert headings into questions so you read to find answers. The other options are not part of the method.

quiz.prompt: Complete the rule: for each section, mark the main idea, not every ______. (one word)
quiz.why: Highlighting every sentence hides what matters. Choose the main idea and add your own words in the margin.

quiz.prompt: You want to decide quickly whether a long report is relevant to your project. Which speed fits?
quiz.why: Skimming gives the gist so you can decide. Careful reading is too slow for a first decision, scanning looks for one item only, and reciting is a recall step.

bank.prompt: After reading a section on 'How garbage collection works', you close the book and cannot explain it without looking. What does this tell you?
options: The book is badly written and you should stop.
You understood it, but your memory is poor.
You do not understand it yet and should reread the section, then try again.
You should move on; recall is not needed.
bank.why: Failing to recite shows a gap in understanding at the exact moment you can fix it. Blaming the book or skipping recall leaves the gap.

bank.prompt: You need the name of a single parameter in a 60-page technical manual. Which speed do you use: reading, skimming or scanning? Write one word.
bank.why: Scanning looks for one specific item and ignores the rest, which is the quickest way to find a parameter name.

bank.prompt: A colleague hands you a report and says 'read this'. What is the best first move?
options: Start at page one and read to the end.
Ask what you need from it, then preview the headings and summary with that purpose in mind.
Highlight the first paragraph of each page.
Put it aside until you have a free afternoon.
bank.why: Knowing the purpose and previewing first lets you choose the right speed. Reading from page one ignores the purpose, and highlighting or delaying does not help you read it well.

cards.front: What do you do before you read in an active way?
cards.back: Set a purpose (why and what for), then preview the title, headings, first lines, visuals and conclusion for two or three minutes.

cards.front: What do the letters in SQ3R stand for?
cards.back: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review. Recite, saying the answer without looking, is the step that exposes gaps.
Sparingly: one main-idea mark, question marks where confused, short margin notes in your own words and arrows for links.
Reading: careful, to understand. Skimming: fast, for the gist. Scanning: targeted, to find one item.

reading-2.reflection: Think of the last long text you read. Did you read it with a purpose, and which of the three speeds should you have used?

keyPoints: Set a purpose and preview before you read.
SQ3R: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review.
Turn headings into questions.
Mark the main idea and write notes in your own words.
Match the speed (reading, skimming, scanning) to the purpose.
revision.redo: Pick any page you read today, state its main idea aloud without looking, then check yourself.

reading-3.title: Reading Non-Fiction and Technical Text
reading-3.summary: Read papers, documentation and long articles by structure, summarise in your own words and slow down deliberately for dense passages.
objectives: Use the structure of a text, conclusion first, to decide how deeply to read.
Summarise a section in your own words without looking back.
Apply a slow-reading routine to dense technical documentation.

explanation.heading: Read the map before the territory
explanation.body:
In the previous lesson you learned to set a purpose and preview before reading. Non-fiction and technical text reward that habit even more, because they are built with structure: titles, headings, abstracts, summaries, diagrams and conclusions. A story is meant to be read in order; a technical article is not.

For a research paper or long report, read in this order: title, abstract (or executive summary), headings, the **conclusion**, then any figures and tables. Only then decide what to read in full. Reading the conclusion first sounds like cheating, but it tells you what the author wants you to believe, so you can judge the evidence with a question in mind: "Do these results really support that claim?"

Example: you are preparing an MCA seminar on cloud migration. A 20-page case study opens with an abstract of 150 words. Five minutes on the abstract, headings and conclusion shows that only sections 3 and 5 relate to your topic. You save an hour.

explanation.heading: Summarise in your own words
explanation.body:
The fastest test of understanding is to close the page and explain a section aloud or on paper without looking. If you cannot, you did not understand it; you only recognised the words. This is why highlighting alone fails: it feels productive but moves nothing into memory.

Use the **stop-and-say rule**. After each section, close the book and write one to three sentences: "This section says that... because... which matters since...". Then check against the text and fix errors. Keep summaries about one tenth of the original length. A common mistake is copying phrases: if you reuse the author's sentences, you are transcribing, not thinking. Change the vocabulary, use an example from your own life, such as comparing a database index to the index at the back of a textbook.

explanation.heading: Slowing down for dense material
explanation.body:
Skimming is a skill for deciding, but dense material needs deliberate slowness. Signs you are in dense territory: new vocabulary every sentence, formulas, long chains of conditions, or the same paragraph re-read three times without sense.

A slow-reading routine:

1. Read the paragraph once at normal speed to get the gist.
2. Mark every term you cannot define and look each one up or infer it from context.
3. Read again slowly, turning each sentence into plain words.
4. Make a tiny example. If the text describes an ABAP internal table with a header line, write three sample rows.
5. Summarise in one sentence.

If you are stuck after two passes, read an easier source first and come back. That is not weakness; it is sequencing.

explanation.heading: Documentation and long articles
explanation.body:
Technical documentation is a reference, not a novel. Start with the overview or "concepts" page to learn the vocabulary, then follow one tutorial from start to end, and only then use the reference pages when you need a specific detail. Read code samples by running or tracing them, and change one thing to see what happens.

For long articles and reports, break the reading into sessions of 20 to 30 minutes with a clear stopping point at a heading. Before each session write the question you want answered. Afterwards, add one line to a running summary so the whole piece builds into a page you can reuse. Do not read a 40-page manual from the first line; read the table of contents first and pick the path you need.

examples.title: Triage of a research paper
examples.body: Priya has to cite one paper in her project report. She reads the abstract (what was tested), the conclusion (what was found), and glances at two charts. The paper compares query performance across indexing methods, and the conclusion says B-tree indexes were fastest for range queries. That is exactly what she needs, so she reads the method section in full and skips the literature review.
examples.takeaway: Structure tells you where to spend your attention before you invest an hour.

examples.title: Stop-and-say on a dense paragraph
examples.body: Paragraph: "Normalisation reduces redundancy by decomposing relations so that each non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key." Amit closes the book and writes: "Each column in a table should describe only that table's ID, so the same fact is not stored twice. Example: store the customer's city once in a customer table, not in every order row."
examples.takeaway: A plain-language rewrite with an example proves you understood, not just recognised, the sentence.

exercises.prompt: You must decide quickly whether a 30-page industry report is useful for your project. What is the best first move?
options: Read the abstract or summary, the headings and the conclusion
exercises.why: Summary, headings and conclusion reveal the claim and whether it matters. Starting at page 1 wastes time, and the references alone cannot tell you the findings.

exercises.prompt: After reading a section, you close the book and write the main points without looking. This is the ____-and-say rule. (one word)
exercises.why: The stop-and-say rule asks you to pause after each section and restate it from memory.

exercises.prompt: You re-read the same paragraph about foreign keys three times and it still does not make sense. What is the best next step?

options.text: Keep re-reading faster until it clicks.
options.feedback: Repeating the same pass rarely produces new understanding.

options.text: Mark the unknown terms, define them, then rewrite each sentence in plain words with a small example.
options.feedback: Defining terms and building an example turns dense text into something you can check.

options.text: Skip it and pretend you understood.
options.feedback: Gaps in basics tend to break later sections.

options.text: Highlight the whole paragraph in yellow.
options.feedback: Highlighting feels like progress but tests nothing.

exercises.why: Dense text yields to slow, structured work: define, paraphrase, exemplify.

exercises.prompt: Choose a paragraph of at least 100 words from any textbook or documentation. Write a summary in your own words (30 to 60 words), then give one example of your own, and list one thing you were unsure of. Include the original topic in your first line.

descriptors.2: Own words but missing a point.
descriptors.3: Accurate, concise, in own words.
Original, concrete example from your own experience.
Names the exact term or step and how you will check it.
Within the target range.

exercises.modelAnswer: Topic: database indexes. Summary: An index is a separate sorted structure that lets the database jump to rows without scanning the whole table, at the cost of extra storage and slower writes. Example: like the subject index at the back of a book that points to page numbers. Unsure: how the database chooses between two indexes; I will check by reading about query plans.
exercises.guidance: Strong summaries are about a quarter to a half of the original length, avoid the author's phrases and include an example you invented. Honest gaps are a good sign, not a weakness. Mark yourself by comparing with the model.

task.title: Structure-first reading
task.brief: Read one real non-fiction or technical document using structure, stop-and-say and a slow pass on one hard paragraph.
steps: Pick a document of at least five pages from your course, an ABAP reference or a long article.
Preview the title, abstract or intro, headings and conclusion; write what you expect to learn.
Read one section, close it and write a three-sentence summary in your own words.
Choose one dense paragraph and use the five-step slow routine.
Note one idea you will use.
checklist: I wrote a summary without looking
I defined unknown terms in a dense paragraph
I noted one idea to use
task.evidencePrompt: Paste your expected learning, one summary and one term you defined.

quiz.prompt: A sensible order for scanning a research paper is:
options: Page 1 to the end without stopping
Only the last paragraph of the appendix
quiz.why: Abstract, headings and conclusion give you the shape and the claim.

quiz.prompt: Which proves you understood a section?
options: You explained it in your own words without looking
quiz.why: Recall in your own words tests understanding directly.

quiz.prompt: A first step with a dense paragraph is:
options: Read it once for the gist and mark unknown terms
quiz.why: Gist first, then define the unknown terms.

quiz.prompt: How should you approach a new tool's documentation?
options: Start with the overview and one tutorial, then use the reference as needed
Read the reference from A to Z
quiz.why: Overview and a tutorial build vocabulary; reference is for lookups.

bank.prompt: Why read a paper's conclusion early?
options: It gives the claim so you can test the evidence against it
It saves you from reading anything
bank.why: Knowing the claim lets you read the evidence critically.

bank.prompt: A good summary is typically about what fraction of the original length? Answer as a number like 1/10.
bank.why: Around one tenth forces you to keep only the key ideas.

bank.prompt: You need the exact parameters of one function in an unfamiliar library. Which part of the documentation fits best?
options: The reference page for that function
A story-like blog about the library history
bank.why: Reference pages are for specific details once you know the concepts.

cards.back: Title, abstract or summary, headings, conclusion, figures, then read in full only the parts you need.
After each section close the text and write one to three sentences in your own words, then check and fix.
Gist pass, mark unknown terms, plain-words pass, tiny example, one-sentence summary.
Overview first, one tutorial end to end, then reference pages for details; run code and change one thing.

reading-3.reflection: Which type of text do you currently read front to back that you could triage by structure instead?

keyPoints: Read structure and conclusion before deciding how deep to go.
Prove understanding by summarising from memory.
Dense text needs deliberate slow passes, definitions and examples.
Documentation: overview, tutorial, then reference.
revision.redo: Take one article you saved and summarise it using only abstract, headings and conclusion, then decide whether to read more.

reading-4.title: Retention and Turning Reading into Action
reading-4.summary: Take Cornell notes, practise recall, review on a spaced schedule, link ideas and convert each book into a one-page action plan.
objectives: Take Cornell-style notes that include cues and a summary.
Review notes on a spaced schedule using recall rather than rereading.
Write a book-to-action page and prune your reading list.

explanation.heading: Why we forget what we read
explanation.body:
Last time you learned to read by structure and summarise in your own words. The next problem is that even good reading fades: within a few days most details are gone unless you do something with them. Retention comes from effort at retrieval, not from the number of times your eyes pass over the page. Reading a book and doing nothing with it is like attending a gym and watching others lift.

Three tools fix this: structured notes, spaced recall, and an action page that turns ideas into behaviour.

explanation.heading: Cornell notes and recall
explanation.body:
**Cornell notes** split a page into three zones: a wide right column for notes, a narrow left column for **cues** (questions or keywords), and a bottom strip for a **summary** in two or three sentences. While reading, write short notes in your own words on the right. Afterwards, write a question in the left column for each block of notes, such as "Why does normalisation reduce update anomalies?". Finally, summarise the page at the bottom.

The left column is the secret. Cover the right column and answer the cues aloud; this is **recall practice**. Check, mark what you missed and repeat later. Compare two students: one rereads the chapter three times, the other reads once and tests herself with cues three times. The second remembers more, even though she spent less time looking at the text.

explanation.heading: Spaced review and linking ideas
explanation.body:
**Spaced review** means revisiting notes at growing gaps: roughly one day, one week, one month. At each review you do recall first (cover and answer), then check. Put three small dates in your calendar when you finish a book chapter. If you answer easily, extend the gap; if you fail, shorten it. Even ten minutes per review beats a four-hour cram.

**Linking ideas** makes knowledge useful. Whenever you learn something, ask: where else does this apply? How does it connect to something I already know? Example: reading about "single responsibility" in a software book, you link it to the idea of focusing a Pomodoro on one task, and to ABAP function modules that should do one job. Write the link in the margin or in a notes app so that ideas form a network, not isolated facts.

explanation.heading: Book-to-action page and your list
explanation.body:
At the end of each book or long article, write a **book-to-action page**: one page with (1) the three ideas that mattered most, (2) one action you will try within seven days, (3) one thing you will stop or change, and (4) the date you will review the page. Example for a time-management book: "Idea: plan backward. Action: plan this week's project milestones on Sunday. Review: 14 days."

Finally manage your reading list. A list is a queue, not a guilt pile. Keep it short, about five items, order by relevance to your current goals, and prune anything you no longer want. Abandoning a book at page 50 because it does not serve you is a sensible decision. Reading ten books and acting on one beats the reverse.

examples.title: A Cornell page on indexes
examples.body: Right column: "Index = sorted lookup structure; speeds reads, slows writes; best on columns used in WHERE and JOIN." Left cues: "What is an index?" "Trade-off?" "Where to add one?" Bottom summary: "Indexes speed searching but cost storage and write time, so add them only on frequently queried columns."
examples.takeaway: Cues turn passive notes into a self-test you can use at every review.

examples.title: Spaced review calendar
examples.body: Neha finishes Chapter 4 on Monday. She sets three reminders: Tuesday (5 minutes, cover and answer the cues), the following Monday (5 minutes), and the Monday a month later (5 minutes). At the one-week review she misses two cues and marks them, then reviews those two again after three days.
examples.takeaway: Short, recalled, spaced reviews take minutes and beat rereading the chapter the night before an exam.

exercises.prompt: In Cornell notes, what goes in the narrow left column?
options: Cues such as questions or keywords
The full text of the chapter
exercises.why: Cues let you cover the notes and test yourself. The full text belongs nowhere in your notes, and drawings are optional.

exercises.prompt: Reviewing at growing gaps such as one day, one week and one month is called ____ review. (one word)
exercises.why: Spaced review revisits notes at increasing intervals.

exercises.prompt: You just finished a book on communication. What is the best way to close it out?

options.text: Put it on the shelf and start the next one.
options.feedback: Without action the ideas fade in a week.

options.text: Write a one-page summary with three ideas, one action to try within a week, and a review date.
options.feedback: Converting ideas to a dated action makes the reading change your behaviour.

options.text: Re-read it from the start immediately.
options.feedback: Rereading is passive and slower than recall plus action.

options.text: Tell friends you finished it.
options.feedback: Telling is not using.

exercises.why: Reading pays off only when at least one idea becomes a small, dated action.

exercises.prompt: Take one idea from anything you read recently. Write the idea in one sentence, link it to two different areas of your life or studies (for example ABAP, college, family, finances), and write one cue question and one seven-day action.

descriptors.3: Clear and in your own words.
Two specific links with explanation.
Open question that tests understanding.
Specific action with a date or day within seven days.

exercises.modelAnswer: Idea: do one thing per work block. Links: in ABAP a function module should do one job; in college, working on one subject per evening stops half-finished notes. Cue: why does single-tasking improve quality? Action: this Thursday I will run two 25-minute single-task blocks on the project report.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer states the idea in your own words, makes links that explain something (not just name topics), and produces a cue and an action you can check in a week. Typical mistakes are vague actions such as "be better". Score honestly.

task.title: Build your retention system
task.brief: Make one Cornell page, schedule spaced reviews and write a book-to-action page for something you have read.
steps: Pick a chapter or article and make a Cornell page with notes, at least four cues and a summary.
Schedule three reviews: tomorrow, in a week and in a month.
Do the first recall review with the notes covered.
Write a book-to-action page: three ideas, one action, one stop or change, a review date.
Prune your reading list to five items.
checklist: My Cornell page has cues and a summary
My action is specific and within seven days
My reading list has five items or fewer
task.evidencePrompt: List your cues count, review dates and your seven-day action.

quiz.prompt: Cornell notes have these zones:
quiz.why: The cue column, notes column and summary strip work together.

quiz.prompt: Which study method produces stronger memory?
options: Reading once then testing yourself on cues
quiz.why: Retrieval effort strengthens memory more than passive exposure.

quiz.prompt: Linking an idea to something you already know:
options: Builds a network that makes it easier to remember and use
quiz.why: Connections give an idea more retrieval paths and more uses.

quiz.prompt: Which belongs on a book-to-action page?
options: One action to try within seven days
A list of books you did not read
quiz.why: The page exists to turn ideas into a small dated action.

bank.prompt: You easily answered every cue at your one-week review. What is a sensible next gap?
options: One more week later is too short; try about a month
bank.why: Easy recall means you can stretch the interval.

bank.prompt: After taking notes, write a ____ at the bottom in two or three sentences. (one word)
bank.why: The bottom strip of a Cornell page is the summary.

bank.prompt: You have a reading list of 40 books and feel guilty. What is the best step?
options: Keep about five relevant ones and prune the rest
bank.why: A short, relevant queue is easier to act on; pruning is healthy.

cards.back: A page with a notes column, a cue column for questions and a summary strip, so you can cover and self-test.
Recall first, then check, at spaced gaps of about one day, one week and one month.
Connections to what you already know make ideas easier to remember and apply in more places.
Three key ideas, one action within seven days, one thing to change and a review date, plus a pruned reading list.

reading-4.reflection: Think of the last book or course you finished: what is one idea from it you could turn into a seven-day action today?

keyPoints: Retention needs retrieval, not rereading.
Cornell notes give you cues for self-testing.
Review at one day, one week and one month.
Write an action page and keep your reading list short.
revision.redo: Make four cue questions for a chapter you read last week and answer them without looking.

research-1.title: Framing Questions and Search Strategy
research-1.summary: Turn a vague topic into answerable questions, build a keyword list, choose the right kind of source and keep a search log.
objectives: Convert a vague topic into two or three narrow, answerable research questions.
Build a keyword list with synonyms and use search operators as ideas (exact phrase, exclude, site type, date range).
Tell primary sources from secondary sources and keep a short search log.

explanation.heading: A topic is not a question
explanation.body:
Most weak research starts with a topic: 'SAP careers', 'cloud computing', 'AI in banking'. A topic has no edges, so you can read for days and never know whether you have finished. A **question** has edges. It tells you what a good answer looks like and when to stop.

To narrow a topic, add four things: **who** (which group or place), **what exactly** (which measurable aspect), **when** (which period) and **why you need it** (the decision it supports). Take the topic 'SAP careers'. A narrowed question is: *What skills do entry-level SAP ABAP job descriptions at Indian IT services firms ask for most often?* Now you know the sources (job postings, firm career pages), the output (a ranked list of skills) and the finish line (about 15 to 20 postings reviewed).

A good test: can you imagine the answer fitting in one or two sentences, with evidence? If not, split the question. Two or three small questions beat one huge one.

explanation.heading: Keywords, synonyms and operators
explanation.body:
Search tools match words, not meaning, so the words you choose decide what you find. Write a keyword list before you search. For each core idea list **synonyms**, **related terms** and **how an expert would say it**. For 'entry-level SAP ABAP skills' you might list: fresher, graduate trainee, junior, associate consultant; ABAP, ABAP on HANA, SAP development; skills, requirements, qualifications, responsibilities.

Most search tools support a few ideas, whatever the exact symbols are. Learn them as concepts:

- **Exact phrase**: wrap words in quotation marks to match them together, as in 'associate consultant' rather than the two words anywhere.
- **Exclude**: put a minus sign before a word to drop an unwanted meaning, such as removing 'salary' when you want skills.
- **Site or domain type**: restrict results to one organisation, or to a type such as government or education pages.
- **Date range**: limit results to recent years when the field changes fast.
- **File type**: ask for reports or presentations rather than blog posts.

Worked example: a search for the single word *python* returns snakes and tutorials. Searching for *'python' 'data cleaning' tutorial -snake* narrows it. If the first search returns noise, change one thing at a time so you learn which change helped.

explanation.heading: Primary and secondary sources
explanation.body:
A **primary source** is the original: the dataset, the court order, the company's annual report, the interview recording, the research paper that ran the experiment. A **secondary source** describes or interprets primary material: a news article about the report, a textbook, a blog summary. A **tertiary** source, such as an encyclopaedia, collects secondary sources.

Why it matters: every retelling can drop a detail, round a number or add spin. When a news story says 'a survey found 70% of graduates are unemployable', the primary source is the survey itself, with its sample size, date and question wording. Use secondary sources to get oriented and find the primary one; use the primary source to confirm the claim.

The same document can be primary or secondary depending on your question. A newspaper column is secondary for 'what does the study show?' but primary for 'how did the media describe the study?'.

explanation.heading: Keep a search log
explanation.body:
A search log is a short running table: **date, query, tool, what you found, usefulness (1 to 3), next move**. It costs one line per search and saves you from repeating dead ends, losing a good page, or forgetting where a number came from. It also makes your work checkable by a teammate, which matters in a client project.

Example line: *12 Oct | 'ABAP fresher' requirements -salary | job portal | 6 useful postings, 3 duplicates | 2 | try 'associate consultant SAP' next.* After ten lines, patterns appear: which keywords worked, which sources repeat each other. Common mistake: collecting links without recording the question they answer. Practise by logging every search for your next assignment, even the quick ones.

examples.title: From vague topic to three questions
examples.body:
Topic: 'Digital payments in India'.

Narrowed questions:
1. How did the number of UPI transactions per month change between two chosen years, according to the payment network's own published statistics? (primary source, numbers)
2. What reasons do small shopkeepers give for accepting or refusing UPI? (interviews or surveys, secondary or primary)
3. What are the most common UPI fraud methods described by banks or regulators? (official advisories)

Each question names a group, a measurable thing and a source type.
examples.takeaway: Each narrowed question can be answered with evidence and has a clear finish line, unlike the original topic.

examples.title: Improving a failing search
examples.body:
Goal: find how many hours a week students spend on phones.

Attempt 1: phone use students. Result: shopping pages and phone reviews.
Attempt 2: 'screen time' 'university students' survey. Result: better, but many are 10 years old.
Attempt 3: 'screen time' 'university students' survey, with the date range set to the last five years, excluding 'children'. Result: three surveys with sample sizes.
examples.takeaway: Use synonyms and the expert phrase ('screen time'), then exact phrase, then date and exclusion; change one thing per attempt.

examples.title: Two search-log lines
examples.body:
09 Oct | 'ABAP fresher' skills | job portal | 5 postings, all ask for SQL and OOP basics | 3 | open each firm's careers page.
10 Oct | 'SAP ABAP syllabus' | training institute pages | marketing text, no depth | 1 | skip institute sites, try official learning content.
examples.takeaway: A useful log records the result and the next move, so the next session starts instantly.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is the best-framed research question for a college project?
options: What are the three most reported types of online fraud against individuals in India in the last two years, according to official advisories?
exercises.hint: Look for a group, a measurable aspect, a time period and a source type.
exercises.why: The second option names who (individuals in India), what (three most reported fraud types), when (last two years) and where evidence comes from (official advisories). The others are topics or opinion questions with no finish line.

exercises.prompt: You want to find pages containing the exact words 'data warehouse' together, not separately. Which punctuation should you wrap around the phrase? Write the name of the mark (two words).
exercises.hint: The mark is used in writing to show spoken words.
exercises.why: Wrapping a phrase in quotation marks asks the search tool to match those words together in that order, which removes many irrelevant results.

exercises.prompt: Your manager says: 'Find out about remote work.' Write two narrowed research questions that would let you give a useful answer for an IT services team, and for each name the type of source you would use and whether it is primary or secondary.

descriptors.1: Questions are still broad (no group, time or measure).
descriptors.2: Questions have most of: group, measure, period; one is still loose.
descriptors.3: Both questions name who, what, when and could be answered in one or two evidenced sentences.

descriptors.1: Sources named but do not suit the questions.
descriptors.2: Suitable sources named; primary or secondary label missing or wrong once.
descriptors.3: Suitable source for each question, correctly labelled primary or secondary.

auto.label: Labels at least one source as primary or secondary

descriptors.1: Only a vague link to a decision.
descriptors.3: Both questions clearly support a decision the team would make.

exercises.modelAnswer: Q1: What share of employees at Indian IT services firms reported higher or lower productivity after moving to hybrid work, according to published surveys from the last three years? Source: the original survey reports from research firms or company disclosures (primary), cross-checked with news summaries (secondary). Q2: Which collaboration practices (daily stand-ups, written updates, overlap hours) do team leads say worked best for hybrid teams? Source: interviews or published case notes from team leads (primary) and HR journals (secondary). Both help decide our team's office-day policy.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers split 'remote work' into questions with a group, a measure and a time frame, and link each to a decision. A common mistake is to write a narrower topic, such as 'Remote work and productivity', which is still not a question. Label sources honestly: a news article about a survey is secondary even if it quotes numbers.

exercises.prompt: A news article says 'A new report shows 8 in 10 freshers lack job-ready coding skills.' You need to quote this in a presentation tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: Quote the article, since a reputable newspaper published it.
options.feedback: The newspaper is a secondary source; it may have rounded, simplified or dropped caveats. You cannot judge the claim without the report.

options.text: Find the report named in the article, check sample size, date and the question wording, then cite the report.
options.feedback: Correct: you move from the secondary to the primary source and verify what the number actually measures.

options.text: Search for other articles repeating the same number and quote the most popular one.
options.feedback: Repeating articles often copy each other; popularity is not verification, and you still have not seen the original.

options.text: Leave out the statistic entirely.
options.feedback: Safe, but you lose useful evidence that could be verified in a few minutes.

exercises.why: The efficient move is to trace to the primary source. Secondary coverage is useful for finding the report, but the report itself shows how the figure was produced.

task.title: Frame, search, log
task.brief: Pick a real topic you need to know about and run a small, logged search.
steps: Choose a topic from your studies or job search (for example, how SAP ABAP freshers are hired).
Write two narrowed questions using who, what, when and why.
List at least eight keywords and synonyms, then run three searches, changing one thing each time (exact phrase, exclusion or date range).
Log each search as one line: date, query, what you found, usefulness 1 to 3, next move.
Mark whether each useful result is primary or secondary.
checklist: I listed eight or more keywords and synonyms
I ran three searches and logged each
I labelled sources primary or secondary
task.evidencePrompt: Paste your best narrowed question and one search-log line.

quiz.prompt: What makes a research question better than a topic?
options: It is longer and more formal.
It tells you what a good answer looks like and when to stop.
It always has a yes or no answer.
It can be searched with a single keyword.
quiz.why: A question sets edges: group, measure and period. Length and formality do not help, many good questions are not yes/no, and a single keyword search is the opposite of focused.

quiz.prompt: A search for 'java' keeps returning coffee pages. Which change best fixes this?
options: Use a minus sign to exclude 'coffee' or add 'programming language'.
Search the same word again, more slowly.
quiz.why: Excluding the unwanted meaning or adding context narrows results. Repeating, padding with unrelated words and capital letters do not change what the tool matches.

quiz.prompt: Which is a primary source for the question 'What did the company report as its yearly revenue?'
options: A blog post summarising the results
A news article quoting an analyst
The company's own published annual report
quiz.why: The annual report is the original document. The others describe or interpret it and may contain errors.

quiz.prompt: Name one thing a search log line should record besides the query. (one word, such as the date)
quiz.why: A log line records date, query, tool, what was found, usefulness and the next move, so you never repeat a dead end or lose where a fact came from.

bank.prompt: A student wants to research 'student stress'. Which narrowed version is best?
options: What are the top three self-reported stressors among first-year engineering students in India in survey studies from the last five years?
bank.why: It names the group, measure, period and evidence type. The others are topics, a loaded question or a claim.

bank.prompt: You read a blog that says 'Government data show road accidents fell last year.' What should you do first?
options: Share it, since it cites government data.
Find the government publication the blog refers to and read the figure there.
Search for other blogs saying the same thing.
Ask the blog author in the comments.
bank.why: The blog is a secondary source; the government publication is primary. Other blogs may just copy the first, and the author's reply is not documentary evidence.

bank.prompt: Your search for 'cloud certification' gives few results. Name the kind of word you should add to your list to widen it, such as 'credential' for 'certification'. (one word)
bank.why: Adding synonyms and related terms captures pages that use different words for the same idea.

cards.front: What four things narrow a topic into a question?
cards.back: Who (group or place), what exactly (measurable aspect), when (period) and why (the decision it supports).

cards.front: Name four search operators as ideas.
cards.back: Exact phrase (quotation marks), exclude (minus), site or domain type, and date range. Change one thing per search.
Primary is the original (data, report, paper, recording). Secondary interprets or reports on it. Trace claims back to the primary.

cards.front: What goes in a search log line?
cards.back: Date, query, tool, what you found, usefulness 1 to 3, and the next move.

research-1.reflection: Think of a time you searched for something and gave up or accepted a poor answer. Which of today's steps (narrower question, better keywords, primary source, log) would have changed the result?

keyPoints: A topic has no edges; a question names who, what, when, why.
Build a keyword and synonym list before you search.
Operators as ideas: exact phrase, exclude, site type, date range.
Trace secondary claims to the primary source.
Log every search with a next move.
revision.redo: Take any vague topic you heard today and write one narrowed question with who, what and when in two minutes.

research-2.title: Evaluating Sources
research-2.summary: Judge whether a source deserves trust by checking authority, evidence, incentives and recency, and by reading laterally.
objectives: Judge a source on authority, evidence, incentives and recency instead of how professional it looks.
Use lateral reading to learn who is behind a page before trusting what it says.
Spot sponsored, thin or low-quality content and decide how much weight it deserves.

explanation.heading: Trust is earned by checks, not by looks
explanation.body:
In the previous lesson you framed a question and searched for sources. Now comes the harder part: deciding which of the pages you found deserve belief. A clean layout, a confident tone and a .org address prove almost nothing, because anyone can buy a template in an afternoon. Judge the source on four checks instead: **authority**, **evidence**, **incentives** and **recency**.

Think of it as a quick audit, not a verdict. Most sources are neither perfect nor worthless; your job is to decide how much weight each deserves for *this* question.

explanation.heading: Authority and evidence
explanation.body:
**Authority** asks: does this author or organisation have a reason to know? Look for relevant expertise and a track record on this specific topic. A cardiologist writing about heart disease has authority; the same cardiologist writing about cryptocurrency does not. Authority is always *topic-specific*.

**Evidence** asks: what does the claim rest on? Strong sources show their working: data with a stated method, named studies, original documents, or direct quotes with context. Weak sources use phrases like *experts say*, *studies show* or *everyone knows* with nothing you can trace. A claim with no way to check it is an opinion wearing a lab coat.

**Recency** matters differently by topic. A 2012 article about a programming framework may describe a version nobody uses; a 2012 article about how photosynthesis works is still fine. Ask whether the facts in this area change quickly, then check the date the page was published or last updated.

explanation.heading: Incentives: who gains if you believe this?
explanation.body:
Every source has a reason to exist. A newspaper wants readers, a company wants customers, a charity wants donations, a coaching institute wants admissions. An incentive does not make a source false, but it tells you which direction errors are likely to lean.

Watch for sponsored content: articles paid for by a brand, written to look like independent journalism. Signs include labels such as *partner content* or *advertorial*, a product named in nearly every paragraph, comparisons where one option always wins, and a button to buy or enrol at the end. A review site that earns a commission on each link clicked is also not neutral, even if it writes well.

A useful question: *would this page exist if the product were bad?*

explanation.heading: Lateral reading: leave the page to judge the page
explanation.body:
Professional fact-checkers do not study a site by reading its About page, because the site wrote that page about itself. They open new tabs and ask what *other* sources say about the site. This is **lateral reading**: moving sideways to check who is behind a source, rather than reading deeper into it.

Worked example. You find a page called *National Institute for Digital Careers* claiming that 9 out of 10 ABAP freshers get placed within a month. Instead of reading the page closely, you search for the institute name alone. You find that its address matches a coaching centre selling a paid course, that no university lists it, and that the figure appears only on its own pages. Verdict: low authority, no traceable evidence, strong incentive. You would not use the number, though you might note the institute exists.

Make it a habit: before you read a page for what it says, spend two minutes finding out what others say about it. Common mistake: judging by design, or trusting a page because it appeared first in a search.

examples.title: Two articles on the same salary claim
examples.body:
Source A is a placement brochure: *Our ABAP graduates earn very high salaries.* No figures, no method, photo of smiling students, enrol button on every screen.

Source B is a survey report from an industry body: 1,200 respondents, the question wording, the date of collection and the margin of error all stated, with a note that freshers in smaller cities reported lower figures.

Scoring on the four checks: A fails evidence and incentives; B shows its method and admits limits.
examples.takeaway: The more a source shows its working and admits limits, the more weight it earns; vague warmth plus a sales button lowers it.

examples.title: Lateral reading in four moves
examples.body: You meet a blog, *TechPulse Daily*, praising a laptop. Open a new tab. 1) Search *TechPulse Daily who owns*. 2) Find it is run by a laptop reseller. 3) Check two independent testers on the same model. 4) Return to the blog and read it as marketing, with the independent results as your main evidence.
examples.takeaway: Two minutes outside the page told you more than twenty minutes inside it.

examples.title: Recency and topic speed
examples.body: You need a how-to for configuring a feature in a software tool. The best-looking guide is from six years ago. You check the tool's own release notes and find the menu was redesigned. Meanwhile, a six-year-old explanation of how a binary search works is still correct.
examples.takeaway: Match your date check to how fast the topic changes.

exercises.prompt: A well-known physician publishes a long article claiming a particular smartphone is the best for students. How should you rate her authority on that claim?
options: High, because doctors are trusted experts in general.
High, because the article is long and detailed.
Low for this claim: her expertise is in medicine, not phones, and authority is topic-specific.
Cannot be judged at all without reading the article twice.
exercises.hint: Ask what she is actually trained to know.
exercises.why: Authority is specific to the topic. Her medical expertise does not transfer to phone comparisons. Length and detail (option 2) are not authority, and you can judge her relevance without re-reading (option 4).

exercises.prompt: What name is given to the habit of opening new tabs to see what other sources say about a site, instead of reading deeper into the site itself? (two words)
exercises.hint: Starts with the word lateral.
exercises.why: This is lateral reading: moving sideways to check who is behind a source before trusting its own description of itself.

exercises.prompt: Read this extract from a web page and evaluate it in 60-100 words: "TOP 5 Best Online Courses for ABAP in 2026 - Our expert team tested every course! SkillRocket Academy is number one and rated 5/5 by 98% of students. Click Enrol Now to get 40% off today only. Other courses lack mentoring and placement help." Name at least two incentive or evidence red flags and say how you would check the page laterally.

descriptors.1: One vague flag, such as "looks like an advert".
descriptors.2: Two flags named but one is not explained.
descriptors.3: At least two flags clearly explained, such as the number-one ranking the page benefits from, the unexplained 98% figure, urgency pressure and the dismissal of rivals.

auto.label: Mentions at least two relevant terms such as incentive, advert, evidence or urgency

descriptors.3: Proposes concrete outside checks, such as who owns SkillRocket, independent student reviews, and whether any neutral body lists these courses.
Clear verdict, for example treat as marketing and not as evidence, with reasoning linked to the flags.

exercises.modelAnswer: This page looks like marketing rather than independent evaluation. The top-ranked course is also the one with the enrol button, which is an incentive to rank it first, and the 98 per cent rating has no stated sample, method or source. The urgency phrase today only is a pressure tactic. I would search who owns the academy, read independent student discussions about it, and see whether any neutral body or employer mentions the course. Until then I would treat the page as an advert, not as evidence.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer names specific red flags from the extract (ranked first by a seller, unexplained 98 per cent, pressure to buy now, belittling competitors) and proposes checks outside the page. Common mistakes: saying the page is fake (it may simply be biased), or only saying it looks unprofessional. Score yourself on whether each flag is tied to a quote and each check could really be done in two minutes.

exercises.prompt: You are preparing a college talk and find a striking statistic on a polished website called Indian Youth Skills Council: "72% of graduates cannot write a correct email." It has no named author. The talk is tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: Use the statistic; the site looks official and the claim sounds plausible.
options.feedback: Looks and plausibility are not evidence. You would be repeating an untraceable number to an audience.

options.text: Search for the council itself, then look for the original survey; if neither can be found, drop the number or call it unverified.
options.feedback: Right: lateral reading on the organisation, then trace the figure to its source. If you cannot, you protect your credibility by not stating it as fact.

options.text: Use it but add "some studies say" to soften it.
options.feedback: Softening words do not fix a claim with no source; you are still passing it on.

options.text: Skip statistics entirely and use only your own opinions.
options.feedback: Over-correcting. Verified numbers strengthen a talk; the fix is checking, not avoiding evidence.

exercises.why: The statistic has no author, method or origin, and the organisation is unknown. Check who they are laterally, trace the number, and only use it if both hold up.

task.title: Audit one real source
task.brief: Pick a page you recently relied on and audit it with the four checks and a lateral search.
steps: Choose a real article, blog post or video description you used in the last two weeks.
Write one line each for authority, evidence, incentives and recency.
Open a new tab and spend two minutes finding what others say about the author or site.
Give the source a trust rating from 1 to 5 and write what it is still good for.
checklist: I chose a real source I actually used
I did at least one lateral search
I gave a rating and a limited use
task.evidencePrompt: Write the source type, your rating, and the biggest red flag or reason for trust you found.

quiz.prompt: Which author has the most relevant authority for a claim about how SAP pricing models changed over time?
options: A famous cricketer who uses SAP software in his business.
A licensing analyst who has published on enterprise software contracts for years.
A student blogger with many followers.
A news anchor who covered a software company once.
quiz.why: Relevant, topic-specific experience gives authority. Fame and followers do not.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence offers evidence you can actually check?
options: Experts agree this method is the best.
Everyone in the industry already knows this.
The 2023 survey of 800 freshers, described in the appendix, found 61% used the method.
quiz.why: Only the last names a survey, a year, a sample and a figure you can look up. The others are vague appeals with nothing to trace.

quiz.prompt: A phone review ends with "Buy now" links and the site earns a fee from each sale. What is the best conclusion?
options: Treat it with caution and cross-check with an independent tester, since the fee creates a lean toward positive reviews.
The review is automatically trustworthy because it is detailed.
Ignore every review that has any links.
quiz.why: An incentive shows the likely direction of bias; it does not prove falsehood (option 1) and it is not a reason to dismiss every link (option 4). Detail alone (option 3) does not remove the incentive.

quiz.prompt: Fact-checkers judge an unfamiliar site by leaving it and searching for what others say. In one word, what do they avoid relying on first, since the site wrote it about itself: the "About" ____?
quiz.why: The About page is the site's own description of itself, so it cannot independently confirm its own trustworthiness. Lateral reading looks outside it.

bank.prompt: You read a 2014 blog post explaining the steps to install a development tool. What should you do first?
options: Follow it step by step since it was written by someone confident.
Check whether the tool has changed since 2014, because installation steps change quickly.
Assume it is wrong because it is old.
Trust it if it has many comments.
bank.why: Fast-changing topics need a date check against current documentation. Old is not automatically wrong (option 3), but confident tone and comments (options 1, 4) do not prove it still works.

bank.prompt: A news-style article is labelled "Partner Content" and mentions a brand in every paragraph. In one word, what kind of content is it likely to be (starts with s)?
bank.why: Partner content paid for by a brand is sponsored content: written to promote, even when it looks like independent reporting.

bank.prompt: A charity publishes a report saying its own programme was a huge success. Which factor most limits how much weight you should give it?
options: It is a charity, and charities are never honest.
It is evaluating its own work and benefits from the positive result, so independent evaluations should be sought.
It was published as a PDF.
bank.why: The incentive is self-assessment; independent evaluations reduce that conflict. Option 2 is an unfair generalisation, and format or length is irrelevant.

cards.front: What does "authority" mean when judging a source?
cards.back: Having relevant, topic-specific expertise or a track record on this exact subject. A doctor is an authority on medicine, not on phones.

cards.front: Name three signs of a source showing its evidence.
cards.back: Named data with method, traceable studies or documents, and quotes with context. Vague phrases such as "experts say" signal missing evidence.

cards.front: Why does an incentive matter, and what question exposes it?
cards.back: It shows which way errors are likely to lean. Ask who gains if you believe this, and whether the page would exist if the product were bad.

cards.front: What is lateral reading, in one line?
cards.back: Opening new tabs to see what others say about a source before reading deeper into it, instead of trusting its self-description.

research-2.reflection: Think of a source you trusted quickly in the past, perhaps a video, a forwarded message or a coaching site. Which of the four checks would have changed your opinion, and what would you do differently now?

keyPoints: Judge on authority, evidence, incentives and recency, not looks.
Authority is topic-specific.
Ask who gains if you believe this.
Read laterally: leave the page to judge the page.
Match the date check to how fast the topic changes.
revision.redo: Pick any article from your feed today and spend two minutes on a lateral search about its publisher; note one thing you learned.

research-3.title: Fact-Checking Claims
research-3.summary: Trace claims to their source, test numbers, quotes and images, and spot common misinformation tactics.
objectives: Trace a claim back to its original source.
Check a number, quote or image for context.
Recognise common misinformation tactics and confirm with two independent sources.

explanation.heading: Start at the source
explanation.body:
Most viral claims are repeated, not reported. A post says "A new study proves coffee cures diabetes" and gives no link. The first job is to **trace the claim to its origin**: who said it first, in what document, on what date. Look for the primary source: the study itself, the official notification, the full speech. If a news article cites a report, find the report. If you cannot find an origin after a reasonable search, treat the claim as unverified.

Ask three quick questions: Who is making the claim? What is their evidence? What would they gain if you believe it? A coaching centre advertising its own results, a company praising its own product and an anonymous account selling a remedy all have reasons to exaggerate. That does not make them wrong, but it means their claims need independent confirmation before you rely on them or forward them.

explanation.heading: Numbers, quotes and images
explanation.body: Check **numbers** for units, time period and comparison. "Sales rose 200%" may mean from 1 to 3. Ask "compared with what?" and "how many in total?". For **quotes**, search for the exact words with the speaker's name; a quote with no date or place is suspect. For **images**, ask when and where the photo was taken. Old photos are often reposted as new events. A reverse image search shows earlier appearances, and details such as signs, language, weather and shadows can contradict the caption.

explanation.heading: Two independent sources
explanation.body: One source is not enough, and two copies of the same story do not count as two. **Independent** means they obtained the information separately, for example a government dataset and a newspaper's own investigation. Prefer sources with accountability: named authors, correction policies and a record of accuracy. If reliable sources disagree, report the disagreement instead of picking one.

explanation.heading: Common misinformation tactics
explanation.body: Misinformation often uses recognisable tricks. **Emotional triggers** such as outrage or fear push you to share before thinking. **Fake authority** uses phrases like "doctors say" without names. **Cherry-picking** shows only the data that supports a point. **Missing context** crops a video or quote. **False urgency** says "share before it is deleted". When you feel a strong urge to forward something, pause and check first. Sharing is an action with consequences. A false health tip, fake job notice or fabricated rumour can mislead real people, cost them money or damage someone's reputation. Making a two-minute check your habit is a small act of responsibility.

examples.title: Tracing a statistic
examples.body: A message claims "80% of engineers lose jobs to automation". Tracing shows the figure came from a speaker's slide estimating tasks, not jobs, and with no study cited. Verdict: unsupported.
examples.takeaway: Follow the number back to what was actually measured.

examples.title: An old photo
examples.body: A photo of flooded streets is captioned as this week's rain. A reverse search finds it in a news article from four years ago in another city.
examples.takeaway: Dates and places in the original source can expose recycled images.

exercises.prompt: The first step when checking a viral claim is to:
options: Trace it to its original source
exercises.why: The original source tells you what was actually said or found.

exercises.prompt: Two sources count only if they are ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Copies of one story are not independent confirmation.

exercises.prompt: Choose a claim you have seen recently (describe it in a sentence). List the steps you would take to check it and any tactic it uses.

descriptors.3: Clear and specific.
Concrete steps including source tracing and two independent sources.
Tactic named with evidence from the claim.

exercises.modelAnswer: Claim: a forwarded message says a new law will ban cash from next month. Steps: search for the official notification, check the ministry's statement, look for two independent newspapers reporting the same details, and confirm the date. Tactic: false urgency and fake authority because it says "doctors and officials confirm" without names.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers name the claim, trace it to a primary source, seek two independent confirmations and identify a recognisable tactic such as false urgency.

exercises.prompt: A dramatic photo is shared with a caption about an event today. What do you do?

options.text: Share it because it looks real.
options.feedback: Looking real is not verification.

options.text: Run a reverse image search and look for the earliest appearance and original caption.
options.feedback: Finding the original context reveals recycled images.

options.text: Count the likes.
options.feedback: Popularity is not accuracy.

options.text: Ask commenters to confirm.
options.feedback: Comments are weak evidence.

exercises.why: Verify the image origin and date.

task.title: Fact-check one claim
task.brief: Check one real claim from your messages or social feeds.
steps: Copy the claim exactly.
Find its original source or write that you could not.
Find two independent sources or note that they disagree.
Write a verdict: supported, unsupported or unclear, with reasons.
checklist: I looked for two independent sources
I wrote a verdict with reasons
task.evidencePrompt: Write the claim, your verdict and the strongest evidence you found.

quiz.prompt: A primary source is:
quiz.why: Primary sources are closest to the facts.

quiz.prompt: To check a number you should ask:
options: Compared with what, in what period?
quiz.why: Context and comparison give numbers meaning.

quiz.prompt: Which is a misinformation tactic?
options: False urgency like "share before it is deleted"
quiz.why: Urgency pushes sharing before thinking.

quiz.prompt: A reliable source usually has named authors and a ____ policy. (one word)
quiz.why: Correction policies show accountability.

bank.prompt: If you cannot find a claim's origin, treat it as:
bank.why: No origin means no verification.

bank.prompt: A reverse image search helps to find:
bank.why: Earlier appearances reveal context.

bank.prompt: Cherry-picking means:
bank.why: It hides data that does not fit.

cards.back: Trace the claim to its original source, not the latest repost.
Units, time period, comparison and total counts.
They obtained the information separately, not by copying each other.
Emotional triggers, fake authority, cherry-picking, missing context, false urgency.

research-3.reflection: What is one type of forwarded message you tend to believe too quickly, and what will you check before sharing next time?

keyPoints: Trace to the origin.
Check numbers, quotes and images for context.
Independent sources matter.
Pause when emotions spike.
revision.redo: Check one more forwarded message with the four-step method.

research-4.title: Synthesis and Research Briefs
research-4.summary: Compare sources, state confidence honestly, attribute properly and write a one-page research brief.
objectives: Compare sources and note where they agree and differ.
State a confidence level with reasons.
Write a one-page brief with attribution.

explanation.heading: From facts to understanding
explanation.body:
Finding facts is only half of research. **Synthesis** means combining what several sources say into a clear answer to your question. A list of summaries is not synthesis; synthesis says, "Three sources agree on X, one disagrees on Y because of Z, so the best current view is W."

Start with your question in one sentence, because without it every source seems equally relevant and your notes grow without direction. Good questions are narrow and decision-oriented, such as "Which database should our project use for 500 users?" rather than "Tell me about databases". Then read each source only for what it adds to that question, and record claim, evidence and date for each.

explanation.heading: Comparing sources
explanation.body: Make a small table: rows are sources, columns are claims. Mark where sources **agree**, where they **differ** and where one is **silent**. Ask why differences exist: different dates, definitions, sample sizes or interests. Give more weight to sources that are recent, close to the data, transparent about method and free from obvious bias. Do not average conflicting claims; explain them. If one report says 40 per cent and another 60 per cent, the middle value 50 is probably wrong for both, but the reason for the gap may be the most valuable finding. Note it in your brief so the reader can judge for themselves.

explanation.heading: Confidence and attribution
explanation.body:
Be honest about how sure you are. Use three levels. **High**: several independent, reliable sources agree and evidence is direct. **Medium**: good sources but limited, dated or partly conflicting evidence. **Low**: single source, indirect evidence or strong disagreement. State the level and the reason in one line.

**Attribution** means saying where each claim comes from: "According to the 2024 annual report of X..." Attribution lets readers check you, protects you from error and avoids passing others' work off as your own. Quote exactly when wording matters and paraphrase otherwise, always with the source.

explanation.heading: The one-page brief
explanation.body: A research brief is for a busy reader. Use this structure: **Question** (one sentence), **Bottom line** (two or three sentences with confidence), **Key evidence** (three to five bullets with sources), **Disagreements and gaps**, **Recommendation or next step**. Keep to one page. Put the answer first, because most readers stop early. Remove anything that does not help the decision. Use plain words, short sentences and numbers with units. Before sharing, read the brief once as the reader and ask whether they could act on it in two minutes.

examples.title: A brief on laptops
examples.body: Question: Which RAM size should a student buy for web development? Bottom line: 16 GB, medium confidence. Evidence: two reviews and two vendor guides agree on 16 GB for multiple tools. Gap: no direct benchmark for the student's stack. Next step: check the college lab setup.
examples.takeaway: Answer first, confidence stated, gaps honest.

examples.title: Differences explained
examples.body: Two reports give different internet user counts. One counts monthly users and the other daily users; one is from 2021 and the other from 2024.
examples.takeaway: Differences often come from definitions and dates.

exercises.prompt: Where sources conflict, you should:
exercises.why: Understand differences in date, definition and method.

exercises.prompt: A single indirect source supports only ____ confidence. (one word)
exercises.why: Single or indirect evidence means low confidence.

exercises.prompt: Write a mini research brief (question, bottom line with confidence, three evidence bullets with sources, one gap and next step) on a topic of your choice. Use clearly invented source names if needed, such as "Source A".

descriptors.3: Clear with a level and reason.
Three attributed bullets.
Both a real gap and a next step.

exercises.modelAnswer: Question: Should our hostel group buy a shared router? Bottom line: Yes, medium confidence, because three of four sources show lower per-person cost and one flags signal limits. Evidence: Source A (price list) shows Rs 1,800 per router; Source B (user review) reports stable speeds for four users; Source C (manual) lists a 30 m range. Gap: no measurement in our building. Next step: test one borrowed router for two days.
exercises.guidance: Strong briefs lead with the answer and its confidence, attribute each claim and name a real gap. Avoid long background.

exercises.prompt: You want to use a statistic from an article in your brief. What is the best way?

options.text: Use it without a source because it is common knowledge.
options.feedback: Statistics need a source.

options.text: State the figure and name the article, author and date.
options.feedback: Clear attribution lets readers verify it.

options.text: Rewrite it as if you calculated it.
options.feedback: That misrepresents your work.

options.text: Quote the whole article.
options.feedback: Long quotes bury your own synthesis.

exercises.why: Name the source so claims can be checked.

steps: Write the question in one sentence.
Gather three sources and note claim, evidence and date for each.
Write the bottom line with a confidence level.

task.evidencePrompt: Paste your question and bottom line with confidence.

quiz.why: Synthesis answers a question using several sources.

quiz.prompt: High confidence needs:
quiz.why: Agreement across independent sources supports high confidence.

quiz.prompt: Attribution helps readers to:
quiz.why: They can verify where each claim comes from.

quiz.why: Busy readers want the answer at the top.

options: I am sure because it is online.
Medium confidence: good sources but limited data.

bank.why: One page forces clarity.

cards.back: Make a table of sources against claims; mark agree, differ and silent; explain differences.
High: independent sources agree. Medium: good but limited. Low: single or indirect evidence.
Saying who said what, where and when, so readers can check it.
Question, bottom line with confidence, key evidence, gaps, next step.

research-4.reflection: Think of a recent decision you made from one source. What would a second and third source have added?

keyPoints: Synthesis combines sources into an answer.
Explain differences instead of averaging.
State confidence with reasons.
Lead a brief with the answer.
