stress-1.title: Understanding Stress
stress-1.summary: Learn what stress is, how it shows up in body and behaviour, and how to run a quick baseline check.
objectives: Explain the stress response and the difference between a stressor and stress.
Recognise your own early warning signs across body, mind and behaviour.
Run a two-minute baseline check and rate your current load.

explanation.heading: What stress actually is
explanation.body:
Stress is the body and mind preparing to meet a demand. When you sense a challenge, such as an exam, a deadline or a hard conversation, your nervous system releases hormones including adrenaline and cortisol. Your heart rate rises, breathing quickens, muscles tense and attention narrows. This is the **stress response**, and it evolved to help you act fast.

The response is useful in short bursts. A student who feels a spike of alertness before an exam often performs better than one who feels nothing. The problem begins when the alarm keeps ringing with no recovery. Constant activation without rest wears down sleep, mood, concentration and health.

explanation.heading: Stressor versus stress
explanation.body:
Keep two words apart. A **stressor** is the demand or event: a deadline, noisy hostel, an unclear project brief, a family expectation. **Stress** is your reaction to it: the tight chest, racing thoughts, irritability. The same stressor produces different stress in different people, and in the same person on different days.

This distinction matters because it shows two levers. You can change or remove some stressors, for example by clarifying a brief or moving a deadline. You can also change how your body and mind respond, using skills you will learn in the next lessons. Treating every problem as only a stressor, or only a reaction, leaves one lever unused.

explanation.heading: Early warning signs
explanation.body:
Stress rarely announces itself as "I am stressed". It shows up as signals in three channels. **Body:** tension in neck and jaw, headaches, stomach discomfort, tiredness, disturbed sleep. **Mind:** racing thoughts, difficulty concentrating, constant worry, feeling overwhelmed. **Behaviour:** irritability, procrastination, skipping meals, scrolling late at night, withdrawing from friends.

Everyone has a personal signature. One person notices it first in sleep, another in a short temper. Learning your first two or three signals gives you an early warning system, because acting at "mildly tense" is far easier than acting at "overwhelmed".

explanation.heading: Helpful and harmful stress, and a baseline check
explanation.body:
Stress is most helpful when the demand is challenging but achievable and you recover afterwards. It becomes harmful when it is intense, long-lasting, or leaves no recovery time. A useful test: **Do I feel energised and focused, or drained and stuck?**

The **two-minute baseline check** has three steps. First, rate your stress from 0 to 10 right now. Second, scan body, mind and behaviour for your top signals. Third, name the main stressor in one sentence. Do this at the same time each day for a week and you will see patterns, such as Sunday evening spikes or a rise after late nights. This is a wellbeing skill, not a diagnosis. If stress feels unmanageable or lasts for weeks, talking to a doctor or counsellor is a sensible step.

examples.title: Same stressor, different stress
examples.body: Two students receive the same project deadline. Asha feels a surge of focus, makes a plan and sleeps normally. Rohan feels tightness in his chest, avoids opening the file and stays up scrolling. The stressor is identical; the stress responses differ.
examples.takeaway: Stress lives in the reaction, which means the reaction can be trained.

examples.title: A baseline check entry
examples.body: Tuesday, 9 pm. Stress 6/10. Body: tight shoulders, slept 5 hours. Mind: replaying a client call. Behaviour: skipped lunch, short with roommate. Main stressor: unclear feedback from the client.
examples.takeaway: Naming the stressor in one sentence makes it solvable: the next step is to ask the client for specifics.

exercises.prompt: A pending project deadline is best described as:
exercises.why: A stressor is the external demand; the stress is your reaction to it. The deadline is the demand, so it is the stressor.

exercises.prompt: Name the three channels in which early stress signals show up: body, mind and ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Signals appear in body, mind and behaviour, such as procrastination or withdrawing from friends.

exercises.prompt: Write your own baseline check: a 0-10 stress rating, your top two signals in body/mind/behaviour, and the main stressor in one sentence. Then name one small action that targets the stressor.

descriptors.3: Clear rating with context for the number.
Two or more specific signals across channels.

rubric.label: States the stressor in one sentence

descriptors.3: One crisp sentence naming the demand.

rubric.label: Names a small action on the stressor

descriptors.2: Action is reasonable but not small.
descriptors.3: Small, specific, doable action.

exercises.modelAnswer: Wednesday evening: stress 7/10. Body: tight neck, only 5 hours of sleep. Behaviour: I keep checking my phone instead of starting the report. Stressor: I do not know what the client wants in section 3. Action: I will send the client two specific questions tomorrow at 10 am.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer gives a number, two concrete signals and a one-sentence stressor, then a small action such as sending one message. Avoid vague words like "bad" and avoid large actions like "fix everything". Score honestly against the model.

exercises.prompt: You have felt wired and irritable for three weeks, sleeping badly, and you keep postponing a task you usually enjoy. A friend says, "Everyone is stressed, just push through." What is the best response?

options.text: Push through and say nothing.
options.feedback: Ignoring a three-week pattern lets it grow. Pushing through with no recovery is the harmful pattern.

options.text: Treat it as a signal: do a baseline check, add recovery time, and consider talking to someone you trust or a professional.
options.feedback: Persistent signals deserve action early, including support if they do not ease.

options.text: Take on more work to feel in control.
options.feedback: More load without recovery usually deepens the problem.

options.text: Wait for it to disappear after exams.
options.feedback: Waiting can work for short bursts but not for weeks of disrupted sleep and mood.

exercises.why: Weeks of disrupted sleep, mood and motivation are a signal to act: reduce load, restore recovery and seek support if it persists.

task.title: Seven-day baseline log
task.brief: Start a daily two-minute stress baseline and keep it for a week.
steps: Pick a fixed time each day, ideally evening.
Write the 0-10 rating, top two signals and the main stressor in one sentence.
Do the first entry now.
After day 7 look for patterns in time of day and stressor type.
task.evidencePrompt: Paste today's entry: rating, signals and stressor.

quiz.prompt: During the stress response, which change is expected?
options: Faster heart rate and tense muscles
quiz.why: The stress response speeds the heart, tenses muscles and narrows attention to prepare for action.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence uses "stress" correctly as a reaction?
options: My chest feels tight when I think of the exam.
The exam stress is on Friday.
I scheduled my stress for Monday.
quiz.why: Stress is the reaction (tight chest). The exam is the stressor.

quiz.prompt: Which is a behavioural early warning sign?
quiz.why: Skipping meals and withdrawing are behaviours; racing thoughts are mind, tight shoulders and headache are body.

quiz.prompt: Stress is most helpful when you have enough ____ afterwards. (one word)
quiz.why: Short, manageable stress followed by recovery is helpful; stress without recovery becomes harmful.

bank.prompt: Which pattern most suggests stress has become harmful?
options: A short burst of nerves before a presentation
Weeks of poor sleep, irritability and avoidance
bank.why: Long-lasting disruption without recovery is the harmful pattern.

bank.prompt: Clarifying an unclear brief with your manager mainly works on:
bank.why: Clarifying removes ambiguity at the source, the stressor.

bank.prompt: Why did the stress response evolve?
options: To help us act quickly in a challenge
bank.why: It prepares the body to act quickly, which is useful in short bursts.

cards.front: What happens in the stress response?
cards.back: Adrenaline and cortisol rise: faster heart rate, quicker breathing, tense muscles, narrowed attention, ready to act.
Stressor = the demand or event. Stress = your body and mind reaction to it.

cards.front: Three channels of early warning signs?
cards.back: Body (tension, sleep), mind (racing thoughts), behaviour (procrastination, withdrawing).
When it is intense or long-lasting and recovery time is missing.

stress-1.reflection: Which of your early warning signs appears first, and what usually triggers it?

keyPoints: Stress is a reaction; a stressor is the demand.
Signals show up in body, mind and behaviour.
Short stress with recovery is helpful; no recovery is harmful.
A two-minute daily check reveals your patterns.
revision.redo: Do a two-minute baseline check now and write the rating and stressor in one sentence.

stress-2.title: Calming the Body
stress-2.summary: Use slow breathing, muscle release, movement and sleep habits to lower physical tension quickly.
objectives: Use extended-exhale and box breathing for one to three minutes.
Release tension with progressive muscle relaxation and short movement breaks.
Build three sleep habits that protect recovery.

explanation.heading: Why start with the body
explanation.body:
When you are tense, thinking your way to calm is hard because the body is feeding alarm signals to the brain. Calming the body first sends the opposite signal: it is safe to slow down. The tools in this lesson are fast, free and invisible, so you can use them before an interview or in a meeting.

Think of the body as a dashboard with a few dials: breathing rate, muscle tension, movement and sleep. You cannot directly order your heart to slow down, but you can turn the dials that feed it. Each tool below turns one dial. Practise them when you are calm, for a minute or two, so they become automatic. Skills you have never practised rarely appear at the moment of highest pressure, which is exactly when you most need them.

explanation.heading: Breathing that actually calms
explanation.body:
Slow breathing works largely because a longer exhale engages the part of the nervous system that slows the heart. Try **extended exhale breathing**: inhale through the nose for 4 counts, exhale slowly through the mouth for 6 to 8 counts. Repeat for one to three minutes. Another is **box breathing**: inhale 4, hold 4, exhale 4, hold 4. If holding makes you uncomfortable or dizzy, skip the holds and just breathe slowly.

Keep breaths gentle, not deep and forced. Over-breathing can cause lightheadedness. If you feel dizzy, return to normal breathing. Practise once when you are calm so it is easy when you are not.

explanation.heading: Muscle release and movement
explanation.body:
**Progressive muscle relaxation** means tensing one muscle group for about five seconds, then releasing for ten, moving through hands, arms, shoulders, face, stomach, legs and feet. The contrast teaches you what tension feels like so you can release it. Skip any area that is painful or injured.

Movement is the other lever. A five-minute walk, stretching your neck and shoulders, or climbing stairs uses the energy the stress response created. Aim for a short movement break every 60 to 90 minutes of seated work.

explanation.heading: Sleep as recovery
explanation.body: Sleep is where the body recovers from stress, and stress in turn damages sleep. Three habits help most. **Consistent timing:** wake at roughly the same time daily. **Screen wind-down:** stop scrolling 30 to 60 minutes before bed because bright screens and endless content keep the mind alert. **Worry dump:** write tomorrow's tasks and worries on paper before bed so your mind does not rehearse them. Most adults need around 7 to 9 hours. If sleep problems last for weeks despite good habits, speak to a doctor.

examples.title: Breathing before a viva
examples.body: Outside the exam room, Meera does six rounds of inhale for 4 and exhale for 7. Her shoulders drop and her voice steadies as she walks in.
examples.takeaway: A longer exhale is the core of the technique; it works in under two minutes.

examples.title: A worry dump
examples.body: At 10:15 pm Arjun writes: "Tomorrow: send invoice, finish slide 5. Worry: client may reject the plan. Next step: ask for feedback at 11 am." He sleeps without replaying the plan.
examples.takeaway: Writing converts looping thoughts into a next step.

exercises.prompt: Which breathing pattern best calms the body?
options: Inhale for 4 and exhale slowly for 6 to 8
Fast deep breaths through the mouth
Hold breath as long as possible
exercises.why: A longer exhale engages the calming branch of the nervous system. Fast or forced breathing can cause dizziness.

exercises.prompt: In progressive muscle relaxation you tense a muscle group for about five seconds and then ____ it. (one word)
exercises.why: The contrast between tension and release teaches the body what relaxed feels like.

exercises.prompt: Write your own three-point sleep wind-down plan for tonight, including a specific time for stopping screens, one worry-dump step and your wake time.

descriptors.3: Screen stop and wake time both specific.

auto.label: Includes at least one clock time

descriptors.3: Specific step with where and how.

rubric.label: Plan is realistic and doable tonight

descriptors.3: Clearly doable with your actual schedule.

exercises.modelAnswer: Tonight: screens off at 10:30 pm and phone charging outside my bed. At 10:35 I write tomorrow's three tasks and one worry on paper with a next step. Lights out by 11:00 and wake at 6:45 am, the same as weekdays.
exercises.guidance: A good plan has clock times, a written worry-dump and fits your real evening. Avoid plans like "sleep better". Compare with the model and rate yourself.

exercises.prompt: Five minutes before a live demo your hands shake and your heart races. Which action is best?

options.text: Tell yourself to stop being nervous.
options.feedback: Commands to yourself rarely calm the body.

options.text: Breathe in for 4 and out for 7 for two minutes, and relax your shoulders.
options.feedback: Slow breathing with a long exhale quickly lowers arousal and is invisible.

options.text: Drink three strong coffees.
options.feedback: Caffeine can increase shakiness and heart rate.

options.text: Skim the whole project again quickly.
options.feedback: Last-minute rushing adds tension instead of reducing it.

exercises.why: Fast, discreet calming skills beat self-commands or stimulants before a short performance.

task.title: Two-minute breathing practice
task.brief: Practise extended exhale breathing today at a calm moment.
steps: Sit comfortably and set a two-minute timer.
Inhale through the nose for 4 and exhale slowly for 6 or more.
Rate your tension 0-10 before and after.
Plan one trigger moment tomorrow where you will use it.
task.evidencePrompt: Write your before and after ratings and tomorrow's trigger.

quiz.prompt: Why does a longer exhale help?
options: It engages the calming part of the nervous system
quiz.why: A long exhale slows the heart and signals safety to the body.

quiz.prompt: When using muscle relaxation you should:
options: Skip any painful or injured area
Hold tension for a full minute
quiz.why: Skip painful or injured areas; tension is brief and then released.

quiz.prompt: Which habit best protects sleep?
options: Sleeping in two hours on weekends only
quiz.why: A consistent wake time stabilises your body clock.

quiz.prompt: Writing tomorrow's tasks and worries on paper before bed is called a worry ____. (one word)
quiz.why: A worry dump moves looping thoughts onto paper with a next step.

bank.prompt: In box breathing, the counts are:
bank.why: Box breathing is inhale 4, hold 4, exhale 4, hold 4. Skip holds if uncomfortable.

bank.prompt: A good movement break during long study sessions happens about every:
bank.why: A short break every 60 to 90 minutes uses stress energy and resets focus.

bank.prompt: You cannot stop thinking about tomorrow at night. Best step?
options: Write tasks and worries with a next step
bank.why: Writing converts looping thoughts into next steps and lets the mind rest.

cards.back: Inhale through the nose for 4, exhale slowly for 6-8. Repeat for one to three minutes. Stay gentle.

cards.front: How does progressive muscle relaxation work?
cards.back: Tense a muscle group about 5 seconds, release for about 10, move through the body. Skip painful areas.
Consistent wake time, screen wind-down 30-60 minutes before bed, and a worry dump on paper.

cards.front: When should you speak to a doctor about sleep?
cards.back: If sleep problems last for weeks despite good habits.

stress-2.reflection: Which body-calming tool will you actually use this week, and at what exact moment?

keyPoints: Calm the body first; thinking comes easier after.
Long exhale is the core of calming breath.
Release muscles and move every 60-90 minutes.
Protect sleep with a fixed wake time and a worry dump.
revision.redo: Do one minute of extended-exhale breathing now and note how your shoulders feel.

stress-3.title: Calming the Mind
stress-3.summary: Use reframing, the circle of control, worry time and journaling to quiet anxious thinking.
objectives: Separate what you control, influence and cannot control.
Reframe an alarming thought into a balanced one.
Contain worry with scheduled worry time and short journaling.

explanation.heading: Thoughts shape stress
explanation.body: Last lesson you calmed the body. Now the mind. The same event can feel threatening or manageable depending on what you tell yourself about it. "I will fail this interview and my career is over" produces far more stress than "This interview is hard, and I can prepare for it". You cannot stop thoughts from arriving, but you can examine them rather than obey them.

explanation.heading: The circle of control
explanation.body:
Draw three circles. In the **control** circle put things fully in your hands: your preparation, effort, reply time, how you speak to people. In the **influence** circle put things you can affect but not decide: the interviewer's impression, a teammate's mood. Outside is **no control**: the economy, other candidates, the weather, past events.

Stress grows when energy flows to the outer circle. Move attention to the inner circles and choose one action there. Example: you worry whether the client will like the demo (influence). Control actions: rehearse twice, prepare two backup slides, send the agenda in advance.

explanation.heading: Reframing a thought
explanation.body:
Reframing means testing a thought and replacing it with a more accurate one. Use three questions. **Evidence:** what facts support or contradict this thought? **Alternatives:** what else could be true? **Usefulness:** does believing this help me act well?

Take "I froze in the demo, so I am bad at presenting." Evidence against: two earlier demos went fine and the freeze lasted ten seconds. Alternative: I was under-rehearsed on that section. Balanced thought: "One section went badly. I will rehearse that part and try again." A good reframe is realistic, not fake positivity.

explanation.heading: Worry time and journaling
explanation.body:
Trying not to worry usually backfires. Instead give worry a **scheduled slot**: 10 minutes, same time daily, away from bed. When a worry appears at other times, jot a two-word note and tell yourself it has an appointment. In the slot, write each worry and ask: can I act on this? If yes, write the next step. If no, write "no control" and let it go.

A short **journal entry** of three lines also helps: what happened, what I felt, what I will do next. Keep it under five minutes and write by hand if you can, because slowing down helps you notice patterns. Over a few weeks, reread old entries: you will often see that most feared outcomes never happened, and that you coped better than you expected. That evidence makes the next reframe easier. If anxious thoughts are constant, interfere with daily life or last for weeks, speak to a counsellor or doctor.

examples.title: Sorting a worry
examples.body: Worry: "What if my seniors judge my code review comments?" Control: write comments politely with reasons. Influence: ask a peer to preview one. No control: whether a senior is in a bad mood. Chosen action: draft comments in the "what, why, suggestion" format.
examples.takeaway: Moving to the inner circles turns a worry into a plan.

examples.title: A balanced reframe
examples.body: Thought: "Everyone will see I do not know SQL." Evidence: I have passed two SQL quizzes and one query bug was my only miss. Balanced: "I am still learning joins; I will practise three queries a day for a week."
examples.takeaway: Check evidence, allow alternatives, then choose a useful thought.

exercises.prompt: Which item belongs in the circle of CONTROL for an interview tomorrow?
options: How well you prepare your answers tonight
Whether the panel is in a good mood
exercises.why: Your own preparation is fully in your control; the others are outside it.

exercises.prompt: The three reframing questions are evidence, alternatives and ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Ask whether believing the thought helps you act well: usefulness.

exercises.prompt: Choose a worry you have now. Write the thought, one piece of evidence for and against it, and a balanced replacement thought plus one control action.

descriptors.3: Specific evidence on both sides.
Realistic, specific and useful.
Specific action within your control.

exercises.modelAnswer: Thought: "I will fail the technical round." For: I have not practised arrays recently. Against: I solved four similar problems last month and the round tests basics. Balanced: "I may be rusty, but I can practise basics." Action: solve three array problems tonight and review the mistakes tomorrow morning.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers use real evidence for both sides, avoid forced positivity and end in an action within your control. Avoid actions like "make them like me".

exercises.prompt: At 11 pm you are lying awake worrying about a deadline that you cannot finish tonight. What helps most?

options.text: Keep thinking until you solve everything.
options.feedback: Rumination in bed rarely solves problems and delays sleep.

options.text: Write the worry and the first next step on paper, then tell yourself it will be handled at tomorrow's worry slot.
options.feedback: Parking the worry with a next step reduces mental looping.

options.text: Scroll your phone to forget about it.
options.feedback: Scrolling keeps the mind alert and can worsen sleep.

options.text: Tell yourself you must not think about it.
options.feedback: Suppression often increases intrusive thoughts later.

exercises.why: Containing worry with a note and a next step beats suppression or scrolling.

task.title: Run a worry through all three tools
task.brief: Take one real worry through the circle of control, reframing and worry time.
steps: Write the worry in one sentence.
Place its parts into control, influence and no-control.
Write evidence for and against, then a balanced thought.
Schedule a 10-minute worry slot for tomorrow.
task.evidencePrompt: Write the worry, the balanced thought and your control action.

quiz.prompt: Stress grows when attention goes mainly to:
quiz.why: Energy spent on things outside your control leaves nothing for action.

quiz.prompt: A good reframe is:
quiz.why: Reframes must fit the evidence and help you act.

quiz.prompt: Scheduled worry time works because:
options: It forces you to worry more
It gives worry a container so it stops leaking into the day
quiz.why: A defined slot contains worry and lets you postpone it.

quiz.prompt: Things you can affect but not decide belong in the circle of ____. (one word)
quiz.why: Influence covers what you can affect but not decide, like a teammate's mood.

bank.prompt: Which is the best balanced thought after a poor quiz score?
options: I missed these topics; I can revise them
bank.why: It is realistic and points to action.

bank.prompt: Outside your worry slot a worry appears. What do you do?
options: Argue with it for an hour
Jot a short note and return to the task
bank.why: A brief note postpones the worry to its slot.

bank.prompt: Which action is within your control before a client call?
options: Preparing an agenda and two questions
bank.why: Preparation is in your control; client emotions are only influenced.

cards.back: Control (your actions), influence (can affect, cannot decide), no control (leave it).
Evidence? Alternatives? Is this thought useful?
A fixed 10-minute daily slot. Note worries briefly outside it; in the slot write next steps or "no control".
If anxious thoughts are constant, interfere with daily life, or last for weeks.

stress-3.reflection: Which worry keeps returning, and which circle does it truly belong in?

keyPoints: Examine thoughts instead of obeying them.
Spend energy in the control and influence circles.
Reframe with evidence, alternatives and usefulness.
Give worry a scheduled slot.

stress-4.title: Sustainable Load
stress-4.summary: Set boundaries, build recovery rituals, spot burnout warning signs and write a personal stress plan.
objectives: Set one realistic boundary that protects recovery.
Recognise burnout warning signs and know when to ask for professional help.
Write a personal stress plan with triggers, tools and supports.

explanation.heading: Load, not just coping
explanation.body: Breathing and reframing help in the moment, but if your workload never leaves room for recovery, no technique will keep up. Sustainable performance comes from managing **load** across weeks: how much you take on, how you protect rest, and how early you notice trouble. Think of it like a phone battery: apps drain it, charging restores it, and a phone that is never charged fails.

explanation.heading: Setting boundaries
explanation.body:
A **boundary** is a clear limit about your time, energy or availability. Examples: "I do not reply to work chat after 9 pm", "I can take this on if the deadline moves to Friday", "I need one evening a week free". Good boundaries are specific, stated calmly and early, and offered with an alternative where possible: "I cannot join tonight; I can review the draft tomorrow morning."

Boundaries feel awkward at first, especially with seniors or family. Start small and observe that most people accept clear, polite limits. Saying yes to everything usually results in lower quality for all tasks. A useful test before agreeing: ask yourself what you will have to drop or delay if you say yes, and whether you are willing to drop it. If the honest answer is no, say so kindly. Protecting your capacity is part of being reliable, because people trust someone who delivers what was promised.

explanation.heading: Recovery rituals and burnout signs
explanation.body:
Recovery is not laziness. Build small rituals: a 10-minute walk after lunch, a phone-free meal, a weekly activity that has nothing to do with work or study, regular sleep, time with people who energise you.

**Burnout** is long-term exhaustion from sustained, unmanaged stress. Warning signs include persistent exhaustion that rest does not fix, cynicism or detachment from things you used to care about, declining performance despite effort, and feeling helpless. If you notice several of these for weeks, or feel hopeless or unsafe, **reach out to a doctor, counsellor or helpline and tell someone you trust**. Asking for help early is a strength, and professionals are better placed than any article to guide you.

explanation.heading: Your personal stress plan
explanation.body: A **stress plan** is a one-page note you write when calm. Include: **my signals** (top three early signs), **my triggers** (situations that reliably raise stress), **my tools** (two body tools and two mind tools you have practised), **my boundaries** (one or two), **my people** (two people you can talk to) and **my red line** (the signs after which I will seek professional help). Review it monthly. Having decided in advance removes the burden of deciding when you are already tired.

examples.title: A polite boundary
examples.body: Manager: "Can you take this ticket tonight?" Reply: "I am at capacity tonight. I can start first thing tomorrow and have a draft by noon. Would that work?"
examples.takeaway: State the limit, offer an alternative, ask for agreement.

examples.title: A stress plan excerpt
examples.body: Signals: poor sleep, short temper, skipping meals. Triggers: back-to-back deadlines, unclear feedback. Tools: extended-exhale breathing, 10-minute walk, worry slot, journaling. People: my sister, my mentor. Red line: two weeks of exhaustion despite rest, then I book a doctor visit.
examples.takeaway: Decisions made in advance are easier to follow under pressure.

exercises.prompt: Which boundary statement is best?
options: I cannot do tonight, but I can deliver a draft by noon tomorrow.
exercises.why: A good boundary is specific, calm and offers an alternative.

exercises.prompt: Persistent exhaustion that rest does not fix, along with cynicism and declining performance, are warning signs of ____. (one word)
exercises.why: These are classic burnout signs, and several lasting weeks call for support.

exercises.prompt: Write a six-line personal stress plan: signals, triggers, tools, boundaries, people and your red line (the point at which you will seek professional help).

descriptors.3: All six parts.
Concrete and personal.

rubric.label: Clear red line including seeking help

descriptors.3: Clear red line that includes contacting a professional or trusted person.

exercises.modelAnswer: Signals: poor sleep, headaches, short temper. Triggers: exam week, unclear feedback. Tools: extended-exhale breathing, 10-minute walk, worry slot, journal. Boundaries: no study after 11 pm; one free evening weekly. People: my brother and my mentor. Red line: two weeks of constant exhaustion or hopeless feelings, then I will book a doctor or counsellor appointment and tell my brother.
exercises.guidance: Strong plans are specific, short and include a red line involving professional help. Avoid vague lines like "relax more". If you ever feel unsafe or hopeless, contact a local emergency number or a helpline immediately.

exercises.prompt: For six weeks you have felt exhausted despite sleep, stopped caring about projects you loved, and your marks are slipping. What is the best move?

options.text: Push harder; it is only a phase.
options.feedback: Six weeks of these signs is not a short phase, and pushing harder can deepen it.

options.text: Tell someone you trust and book an appointment with a doctor or counsellor, while reducing load where possible.
options.feedback: Early professional support plus reduced load is the right response.

options.text: Avoid everyone until it passes.
options.feedback: Withdrawal tends to worsen your isolation.

options.text: Switch courses immediately without talking to anyone.
options.feedback: A big decision under exhaustion is risky; get support first.

exercises.why: Sustained signs call for help and a lighter load, not more pressure or isolation.

task.title: Draft your one-page stress plan
task.brief: Write the six-part stress plan and share it with one trusted person.
steps: Write signals, triggers and tools from the last three lessons.
Add one or two boundaries with wording you can use.
Name two people and your red line.
Share the plan with one person and ask them to check in monthly.
task.evidencePrompt: Write your red line and one boundary sentence.

quiz.prompt: A boundary should usually be:
quiz.why: Specific, calm and early boundaries work best.

quiz.prompt: Which is a recovery ritual?
options: A phone-free meal and a daily walk
quiz.why: Rituals that restore energy include walks and phone-free meals.

quiz.prompt: Which is a burnout warning sign?
quiz.why: Sustained exhaustion with detachment and falling performance is a burnout signal.

quiz.prompt: A stress plan includes a red line: the signs after which you will seek ____ help. (one word)
quiz.why: The red line names when you will contact a doctor or counsellor.

bank.prompt: Which reply sets a boundary politely?
options: I can only do this by Friday; shall I proceed on that basis?
bank.why: It states a limit and invites agreement.

bank.prompt: Why protect weekly free time?
bank.why: Recovery restores energy and keeps quality high.

bank.prompt: If you feel hopeless or unsafe, the right step is to:
options: Contact a helpline, doctor or trusted person right away
bank.why: Reach out immediately; professionals and trusted people can help.

cards.back: State the limit, offer an alternative, ask for agreement. Be specific and early.
Walks, phone-free meals, regular sleep, a non-work activity each week, time with energising people.
Persistent exhaustion, cynicism or detachment, falling performance, helplessness. Seek help if weeks-long.
Signals, triggers, tools, boundaries, people, red line.

stress-4.reflection: Which boundary would protect your recovery most, and what exact words will you use to state it?

keyPoints: Manage load across weeks, not just in the moment.
Boundaries are specific, calm, early and offer an alternative.
Recovery rituals are part of performance.
Burnout signs lasting weeks call for professional help.
revision.redo: Reread your stress plan and update one trigger or tool.

tech-1.title: A Method for Debugging
tech-1.summary: Replace guesswork with a repeatable loop: reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, test, fix and verify.
objectives: Apply the reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, test, fix, verify loop to a bug.
Read an error message and stack trace to find the first line worth checking.
Narrow a bug down quickly using binary search and rubber-duck explanation.

explanation.heading: Debugging is a method, not a mood
Read the error message before anything else
explanation.body:
An error message is the program telling you exactly what it knows. Read it in three parts: the **type** (TypeError, ReferenceError, SyntaxError), the **message**, and the **stack trace**, which lists the calls that led there, most recent first.

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'city')
    at formatAddress (order.js:14:28)
    at printLabel (label.js:6:10)
    at main (app.js:22:3)
```

This says: at line 14 of order.js, the code tried to read `.city` of something that was `undefined`. Start at the top frame inside your own code. But the top line is where it *crashed*, not always where the *mistake* is. Often `printLabel` passed in an undefined address, so follow the trace one frame down if line 14 looks fine.

The same habit applies in SAP work. A short dump or a system message such as a failed database read has a program name, a line and a reason. Copy the exact text into your notes. Paraphrasing loses the clues.

explanation.heading: Binary search: halve the problem
explanation.body:
When you do not know where the bug lives, do not read all 400 lines. Put a check at the midpoint, for example `console.log(total)` after line 200. If the value is already wrong there, the bug is in the first half; if it is still right, it is in the second half. Repeat. Each check halves the suspect area, so even 1,000 lines need at most about ten checks.

The same idea works elsewhere. With version control you can bisect commits: mark a good old commit and a bad new one, and test the commit in the middle. With a long input file, delete half the rows and see if the failure remains. With a configuration, disable half the settings.

The common mistake is changing three things at once. If the bug disappears you will not know which change fixed it, and if a new bug appears you will not know which change caused it.

explanation.heading: Rubber ducks and honest verification
explanation.body:
Rubber-duck debugging means explaining your code, line by line, out loud to an object or a patient friend. Explaining forces you to state what the code actually does rather than what you assumed it does, and the gap is often exactly where the bug is. Say things like 'this line sets total to zero; this loop runs while i is at most the length...' and you may hear the mistake yourself.

Before you ask a senior for help, prepare three things: what you expected, what happened instead (with the exact error text), and what you already tried. This takes five minutes, often solves the problem on its own, and makes you look like someone who is easy to help.

Finally, keep a short bug note: symptom, cause, fix. After a few weeks you will see patterns, such as off-by-one errors, undefined values and wrong data types, and you will find them faster.

examples.title: Shrinking a failing report
examples.body:
A sales report script crashes on a file of 5,000 rows. You cut the file to 2,500 rows: still crashes. Cut to 1,250: no crash. The bad row is in the 1,250 you removed. After three more halvings you find row 1,873 has an empty amount field, and the code calls `.toFixed(2)` on `undefined`.

Hypothesis: empty amounts are not handled. Test: run the script on that single row. Fix: treat a blank amount as 0 or skip it with a warning. Verify: the full 5,000-row file runs, and the single row runs.
examples.takeaway: Isolation by halving found one bad row in about six experiments, with no reading of 5,000 lines.

examples.title: Reading a trace from the top
examples.body: 'ReferenceError: totl is not defined at calc.js:9'. Line 9 reads `return totl * rate;`. The type says a name was used that does not exist, and the name is `totl`. A typo for `total`. Fix the spelling, run again, and confirm the output.
examples.takeaway: Error type plus message plus line number usually names the problem outright. Read all three before touching the code.

examples.title: A good help request
examples.body: 'I expected the discount to be 10% for orders above 5,000 rupees. For an order of 5,000 exactly I get 0%. The code on line 31 uses `>`. I tried 5,001 and it works. I suspect the boundary should be `>=`, but I am not sure whether 5,000 itself qualifies.'
examples.takeaway: Expectation, actual result, evidence and a hypothesis let a colleague answer in one minute.

exercises.prompt: A script sometimes prints a wrong total, but you cannot tell when. What should you do first?
options: Find the exact input or steps that make the bug appear every time.
Add try/catch around everything to hide the error.
Ask for a code review before testing anything.
exercises.hint: You cannot confirm a fix for something you cannot trigger.
exercises.why: Reproducing the bug reliably comes first, because every later step and the final verification depend on it. Rewriting guesses at the cause; try/catch hides the symptom; and review without a failing case has nothing concrete to examine.

exercises.hint: marks[3] does not exist.
exercises.why: On the last pass i is 3, and marks[3] is undefined. 60 + 70 + 80 + undefined gives NaN, because arithmetic with undefined is not a number.

exercises.prompt: Your colleague says: 'The login page works for me but fails for the client on their office laptop. Fix it.' Write a short debugging plan of 4 to 6 steps. Use the words reproduce, isolate and verify, and say what exact information you would ask for before changing any code.

descriptors.0: No recognisable method; jumps straight to changing code.
descriptors.1: Mentions one or two steps but out of order or without detail.
descriptors.2: Most steps present in a sensible order.
descriptors.3: Reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, test, fix and verify all appear in a logical order.

descriptors.1: Asks something vague such as 'what is wrong?'.
descriptors.2: Asks for either the exact error text or the browser and version.
descriptors.3: Asks for exact error text or screenshot, browser, steps taken and differences from your setup.

rubric.label: One change at a time and a check

descriptors.0: Plans to change several things at once.
descriptors.1: Changes are mentioned but not controlled.
descriptors.2: Plans small changes and a re-test.
descriptors.3: Changes one thing at a time and re-tests the original failing case afterwards.

exercises.modelAnswer: 1. Ask the client for the exact error message or a screenshot, the browser and version, and the steps they follow. 2. Reproduce it: try the same browser, version and account on my side. 3. Isolate: compare their setup with mine, for example extensions, cookies, time zone and network proxy, changing one factor at a time. 4. Form a hypothesis, such as a blocked cookie, and test it. 5. Fix the cause in code or give the client a settings change. 6. Verify with the original failing steps on their laptop and re-check my own setup still works.
exercises.guidance: A strong plan starts with evidence, not code. Look for specific requests such as the exact error text, browser version and steps. A common mistake is saying 'I will debug the code' without ever reproducing the failure, or listing several changes made together. Score each criterion honestly against the model answer.

exercises.prompt: A 400-line data-cleaning script finishes without error, but the final CSV has wrong totals. You know the input was correct and the script is split into about ten steps. You have 20 minutes before a review. What do you do?

options.text: Read all 400 lines carefully from the top, hoping to spot it.
options.feedback: Reading can work but is slow, and you may not notice a subtle fault you have already read three times.

options.text: Print the running total after the fifth step. If it is already wrong, look at steps 1 to 5; if not, look at 6 to 10. Repeat on the half that holds the fault.
options.feedback: Binary search: each check halves the suspect lines, so four or five checks find the faulty step.

options.text: Change several likely lines at once and see whether the totals come right.
options.feedback: Multiple simultaneous changes hide which one mattered and can introduce new bugs.

options.text: Wrap the whole script in try/catch so that it stops complaining.
options.feedback: The script already runs without error; the fault is wrong output, not an exception.

exercises.why: When you know the output is wrong but not where, a midpoint check halves the search space every time. It is faster and more dependable than reading everything or changing lines blindly.

task.title: Debug with a written log
task.brief: Fix one real bug in your own code using the full loop and a short written log.
steps: Pick a small bug from a college project or practice code. If you have none, plant one: change a < to <= in a loop.
Write the symptom, the exact error text if any, and the steps that reproduce it.
Write one hypothesis, test it with a print or breakpoint, and note the result.
Fix it, re-run the original case plus one nearby case, and write one line on the cause.
checklist: I reproduced the bug before changing code
I wrote a hypothesis before testing
I changed one thing at a time
I verified with the original case and a nearby case
task.evidencePrompt: Write the symptom, your hypothesis, the cause and the fix in a few lines.

quiz.prompt: Which order is the correct debugging loop?
options: Reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, test, fix, verify
quiz.why: You need a reliable failure first, then a small case, then a stated guess, a test of it, a fix of the cause and a final check. The other orders fix or verify before understanding the problem.

quiz.prompt:
Which line of this trace should you open first?

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'city')
    at formatAddress (order.js:14:28)
    at printLabel (label.js:6:10)
```
options: label.js line 6, because it is lower in the list
Any line; the trace order is random
order.js line 14, the top frame in your own code
quiz.why: Traces list the most recent call first, so the top frame shows where the crash happened. If that line looks correct, follow the next frame to find who passed in the undefined value.

quiz.prompt: You are searching 1,000 lines for a bug and halve the suspect range with each check. About how many checks are needed at most? Write a number.
quiz.why: 1,000 halved repeatedly reaches one line after about ten steps, since 2 to the power 10 is 1,024.

quiz.prompt: Why does explaining code aloud to a rubber duck help find bugs?
options: It forces you to state what the code actually does instead of what you assumed.
The duck's reactions point to the faulty line.
Speaking aloud makes the compiler run faster.
It replaces the need to test the fix.
quiz.why: The benefit is in your own explanation: slowing down exposes assumptions that differ from reality. Nothing external happens, and testing is still required.

bank.prompt: You fixed a bug where a discount failed for an order of exactly 5,000 rupees. What is the best verification?
options: Run the original 5,000 case and a nearby case such as 4,999 and 5,001.
Assume it is fixed because the code compiles.
Ask a teammate to read the code once.
bank.why: A nearby-case check confirms you fixed the boundary without breaking the neighbours. Compiling proves nothing about logic, and a single case may hide a new fault.
Array indexes run from 0 to length minus 1, so items[3] is outside the array. Reading it gives undefined rather than an error.

bank.prompt: A form stopped working after one of 40 recent commits. You know commit 1 was fine and commit 40 is broken. Which approach finds the culprit fastest?
options: Test commit 1, then 2, then 3, in order.
Test commit 20, then keep halving whichever side holds the first failing commit.
Read every diff before testing anything.
bank.why: Halving finds the first bad commit in about six tests (2 to the power 6 is 64, which is more than 40). Linear testing could take up to 39, and reverting everything throws away the good work.

cards.front: List the six steps of the debugging loop.
cards.back: Reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, test, fix, verify. Change one thing at a time and re-run the original failing case at the end.

cards.front: How do you read a stack trace?
cards.back: Note the error type and message, then open the top frame in your own code. If that line is fine, follow the next frame down to the caller.
Check the midpoint of the code, data or commit history. Decide which half contains the fault, then repeat. Each check halves the suspect area.

cards.front: What do you bring when asking a senior for help?
cards.back: What you expected, what actually happened with the exact error text, and what you already tried.

tech-1.reflection: Think of the last bug that cost you more than an hour. Which step of the loop did you skip, and how would doing it have changed the time spent?

keyPoints: Reproduce first; you cannot verify what you cannot trigger.
Read error type, message and top stack frame before editing.
Halve the suspect area instead of reading everything.
Change one thing at a time, then re-run the original case plus a neighbour.
Explain the code aloud to expose wrong assumptions.
revision.redo: Take any short function you wrote recently, plant one off-by-one bug, then find it again using a single midpoint print and one sentence of hypothesis.

tech-2.title: Relational Data and SQL Thinking
tech-2.summary: Understand tables, keys and joins through SAP customer and sales order tables, and write SELECT queries that are precise and efficient.
objectives: Explain tables, primary keys and foreign keys using SAP header and item tables.
Write SELECT queries with WHERE, JOIN and GROUP BY and predict the result set.
Avoid SELECT star and database selects inside loops.

explanation.heading: Tables, rows and keys
explanation.body:
In the debugging lesson you learned to isolate a problem methodically. Data problems need the same care, and that starts with understanding how relational data is organised. A **table** stores one kind of thing, with one **row** per record and one **column** per attribute. A **primary key** is the column (or combination of columns) that identifies a row uniquely. A **foreign key** is a column that refers to the primary key of another table.

SAP gives a classic example. Table **KNA1** holds general customer master data, with the customer number KUNNR as its key. Table **VBAK** is the sales order header: one row per order, key VBELN, and a KUNNR column pointing to the customer. Table **VBAP** holds the order items: one row per item, key VBELN plus POSNR (item number), with columns such as MATNR (material) and KWMENG (order quantity). One customer has many orders, and one order has many items. This one-to-many shape is why data is split into header and item tables instead of one giant table.

explanation.heading: SELECT, WHERE and JOIN
explanation.body:
A query reads like a sentence: **SELECT** which columns, **FROM** which table, **WHERE** which rows. For example:

```
SELECT vbeln, erdat, netwr
  FROM vbak
  WHERE kunnr = '0000001000'
    AND erdat >= '20250401'.
```

This returns the number, creation date and net value of orders for one customer from a given date. A **JOIN** combines tables through matching keys. An **inner join** keeps only rows that match on both sides; a **left outer join** keeps every row from the left table and fills missing right-side columns with empty values. To list orders with customer names you would join VBAK to KNA1 on KUNNR. To list items you join VBAK to VBAP on VBELN.

When reading a result, ask: how many rows should come back? Joining a header to its items returns one row per item, so an order with four items appears four times. Forgetting this is a common cause of inflated totals.

explanation.heading: GROUP BY and aggregates
explanation.body:
**GROUP BY** collapses rows into groups and **aggregates** summarise each group: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX. To find total order value per customer:

```
SELECT kunnr, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(netwr) AS total
  FROM vbak
  GROUP BY kunnr.
```

Every selected column that is not an aggregate must appear in GROUP BY. Use WHERE to filter rows before grouping, and HAVING to filter groups afterwards, such as customers with more than ten orders. A useful habit is to work out one group by hand from three sample rows before trusting the query.

explanation.heading: Fast, careful queries
explanation.body:
Two habits matter in ABAP and in any database work. First, **never use SELECT star** unless you truly need every column. Fetching 200 columns when you need three wastes memory and network time. Name the columns you need. Second, **never run a database select inside a loop**. If you loop over 5,000 orders and select the customer name each time, you make 5,000 database round trips. Instead select the customers once, using a join or a single query with all the keys, and look results up in an internal table in memory.

Also filter in the database with WHERE rather than fetching everything and filtering in the program, and use key fields in WHERE conditions where possible, because indexes on keys make them fast. Check the first result with a small sample before running on production-sized data.

examples.title: Orders with customer name
examples.body: Task: list order number, order date and customer name for April 2025. Query: SELECT vbak~vbeln, vbak~erdat, kna1~name1 FROM vbak INNER JOIN kna1 ON kna1~kunnr = vbak~kunnr WHERE vbak~erdat BETWEEN '20250401' AND '20250430'. If an order referred to a customer missing in KNA1, an inner join would drop it, whereas a left outer join would keep it with an empty name.
examples.takeaway: State what rows you expect, then choose the join type that matches the question.

examples.title: Loop select versus one select
examples.body: Slow version: LOOP AT orders and inside it SELECT SINGLE name1 FROM kna1 for each order, causing one database call per order. Better: select all needed customers once, with the keys from the orders, into an internal table sorted by KUNNR, then READ TABLE inside the loop. For 5,000 orders that is one database call instead of 5,000.
examples.takeaway: Database round trips are expensive; move lookups into memory after one read.

exercises.prompt: In SAP, which column links a sales order header in VBAK to its customer in KNA1?
exercises.why: KUNNR is the customer number, a foreign key in VBAK that points to the key of KNA1. POSNR is the item number and MATNR is the material.

exercises.prompt: To summarise total order value for each customer you use SUM together with the clause GROUP ____. (one word)
exercises.why: GROUP BY groups the rows and SUM aggregates each group.

exercises.prompt: You inner join VBAK to VBAP on VBELN. An order with 3 items appears in the result:
options: Three times, one row per item
Three times only if the net value is above zero
exercises.why: A join returns one row for every matching pair, so a header appears once per item. This is why header totals are inflated when summed after the join.

exercises.prompt: A colleague wrote code that loops over 3,000 sales orders and, inside the loop, selects the customer name from KNA1 for each one. Explain what is wrong, how many database calls it makes, and describe the better approach in steps. Mention the SELECT star habit too.

descriptors.1: Says it is slow without reason.
descriptors.3: Names select in a loop and round-trip cost.
States about 3,000 calls versus one.

descriptors.2: Mentions a join or single select.
descriptors.3: Select once into an internal table, then read in memory or use a join.
Explains why selecting only needed columns saves memory and time.

exercises.modelAnswer: The code makes one database call per order, about 3,000 round trips, which is slow. A better approach is to collect the customer numbers, select the customer names once into an internal table, or join VBAK to KNA1 in one query, then read the name from memory inside the loop. Also select only the columns needed instead of SELECT star, which wastes memory and transfer time.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer names the loop select, counts the calls, and offers one read plus an in-memory lookup or a join. Common mistakes are saying only that the program is slow, suggesting more hardware, or forgetting to limit columns. Score yourself against the model.

task.title: Sketch a header and item query
task.brief: Design and write queries for orders and customers on paper or in a text file, then predict the results.
steps: Draw three small tables with 3 rows each: customers, order headers and order items, using the key names KUNNR, VBELN and POSNR.
Write a query listing orders for one customer, then a join adding customer name.
Write a GROUP BY query for total value per customer.
Work out by hand the number of rows each query should return and write it next to the query.
checklist: My tables have keys that link
I wrote a join and a GROUP BY
I predicted the row counts before running anything
I selected named columns, not star
task.evidencePrompt: Paste one of your queries and the row count you predicted.

quiz.prompt: A primary key is:
options: A column or set of columns identifying a row uniquely
quiz.why: It identifies each row uniquely, like VBELN for an order header.

quiz.prompt: Which join keeps all rows from the left table even if there is no match on the right?
quiz.why: A left outer join keeps every left row and fills empty values where there is no match.

quiz.prompt: To filter groups after grouping, for example customers with more than ten orders, use the clause ____. (one word)
quiz.why: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups afterwards.

quiz.prompt: Which is the better practice?
options: Select needed columns once, then look up in memory
Fetch everything and filter in the program
quiz.why: One targeted read followed by in-memory lookups avoids repeated database trips.

bank.prompt: A report joins an order header to its items and sums the header net value. The totals look too high. Most likely reason?
options: The header value repeats once per item row
bank.why: Each item row repeats the header columns, so summing the header value multiplies it by the item count.

bank.prompt: In a table of student marks, the roll number that identifies each student uniquely is the ____ key. (one word)
bank.why: A column that uniquely identifies each row is the primary key.

bank.prompt: Why select only the columns you need instead of SELECT star?
options: It saves memory and data transfer
bank.why: Fewer columns means less data moved and stored, which makes programs faster.

cards.front: What are KNA1, VBAK and VBAP?
cards.back: KNA1 is customer master general data (key KUNNR), VBAK is the sales order header (key VBELN) and VBAP holds the order items (VBELN plus POSNR).
Inner join keeps only matching rows on both sides. Left outer join keeps all left rows and fills empty values where the right side has no match.
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters the groups after aggregation, for example SUM or COUNT conditions.
Do not use SELECT star when you need a few columns, and do not run a database select inside a loop. Read once, then look up in memory.

tech-2.reflection: Think of a report or app you have built. Where did it fetch data one row at a time, and how would you restructure it?

keyPoints: Header and item tables link through keys like VBELN.
Joins return one row per matching pair, so predict row counts.
GROUP BY with aggregates summarises; HAVING filters groups.
Name columns and avoid selects inside loops.
revision.redo: Write a join query from memory and predict its row count from three sample rows.

tech-3.title: Version Control and Collaboration
tech-3.summary: Use the Git mental model of commits, branches, merges and pull requests, write useful commit messages, resolve simple conflicts and undo safely.
objectives: Explain commits, branches, merges and pull requests with a clear mental model.
Write commit messages that others can understand months later.
Resolve a simple merge conflict and undo mistakes safely.

explanation.heading: The Git mental model
explanation.body:
Last lesson you worked on safe, efficient data access. Today is about keeping code safe and shared. **Git** is a version control system: it records the history of your project so you can see what changed, go back and work with others without overwriting each other.

The key idea is that Git stores **snapshots**. A **commit** is a snapshot of the whole project at a moment, with a message, an author and a pointer to the previous commit. Changes move through three places: your **working directory** (files you edit), the **staging area** (changes chosen for the next commit, using git add) and the **repository** (saved commits, using git commit). Because commits are cheap and local, you can commit often and nothing is lost until you choose.

explanation.heading: Commit messages that help
explanation.body:
A commit message is a note to a future teammate, often yourself in three months. Good messages explain **what changed and why**, in a short first line of roughly 50 characters, in the imperative: "Fix tax rounding in invoice total". A longer body can follow after a blank line if the reason is not obvious.

Compare "changes", "fix" and "final version 2" with "Add input check for empty order number" or "Handle missing customer in report query". The second group lets people search history and understand intent. Keep one logical change per commit: do not mix a bug fix, a rename and a new feature, because small commits are easy to review and easy to undo.

explanation.heading: Branches and pull requests
explanation.body:
A **branch** is an independent line of work. The main branch holds stable code. For each task you create a branch, for example feature/order-report, commit there, and the main branch stays safe. When the work is ready you open a **pull request** (PR): a request to merge your branch into main, with a description and a review by teammates. A **merge** combines the histories.

A healthy flow is: pull the latest main, create a branch, make small commits, push the branch, open a PR, respond to review comments, then merge. Keep branches short-lived, because the longer a branch lives, the more it drifts from main and the harder the merge. Write PR descriptions that explain the goal, how you tested, and anything the reviewer should look at closely.

explanation.heading: Conflicts and safe undo
explanation.body:
A **merge conflict** happens when two branches changed the same lines. Git cannot decide, so it marks the file:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
tax = amount * 0.18
=======
tax = amount * rate
>>>>>>> feature/rate-param
```

The part above the equals line is your current branch; below is the incoming branch. Read both, decide the correct final code (here probably the parameter version), delete the marker lines, test, then stage and commit.

For undoing, prefer safe tools. **git restore** discards uncommitted edits to a file. **git revert** creates a new commit that reverses an earlier one, safe on shared branches because history is not rewritten. **git reset --hard** destroys uncommitted work and rewriting pushed history upsets teammates, so avoid both unless you fully understand them. Before risky steps, run git status and make a backup branch.

examples.title: Before and after commit messages
examples.body: Weak history: "update", "changes", "fix again". Strong history: "Add validation for negative quantity in order form", "Fix off-by-one error in pagination", "Move database config to environment variables". A teammate searching for the pagination bug finds the right commit in seconds.
examples.takeaway: Imperative, specific messages make history searchable and reviewable.

examples.title: Resolving a conflict calmly
examples.body: Two students changed the same line in config.js: one set the port to 3000, the other made it read from an environment variable. Git marks the conflict. They read both versions, agree the environment variable with a default of 3000 is best, delete the markers, run the app, then commit with "Resolve conflict: read port from environment".
examples.takeaway: Conflicts are a conversation between two intentions; decide, remove markers, test and commit.

exercises.prompt: Which sequence moves a change into saved history?
exercises.why: You edit in the working directory, stage with git add, then record with git commit. Commit cannot come before staging.

exercises.prompt: Which commit message is best?
options: Fix rounding error in invoice tax total
exercises.why: It says what changed and where, in the imperative. The others tell a future reader nothing.

exercises.prompt: You have finished a small feature on your own branch and the main branch is protected. What is the best next step?

options.text: Push straight to main to save time.
options.feedback: Bypassing review risks breaking stable code and ignores team rules.

options.text: Open a pull request with a clear description and how you tested, and ask for review.
options.feedback: A PR with context lets teammates review and merge safely.

options.text: Keep the branch for a month and merge everything at once.
options.feedback: Long-lived branches drift from main and create painful conflicts.

options.text: Email the files to a teammate.
options.feedback: This bypasses version control and loses history.

exercises.why: Short-lived branches merged through reviewed pull requests keep main stable.

exercises.prompt: You merged main into your branch and Git reports a conflict in a file. Explain, step by step, how you would resolve it and verify the result. Then say which command you would use to undo a pushed commit on a shared branch and why.

descriptors.3: Explains markers and chooses the correct final code from both sides.
Removes markers, runs tests, stages and commits.
Chooses revert and explains history is not rewritten.
Mentions git status or a backup branch before risky steps.

exercises.modelAnswer: I open the conflicted file, read the version between the markers, and talk to the other author if needed. I choose the correct final code, delete the marker lines, run the app and tests, then stage the file and commit. To undo a pushed commit on a shared branch I use git revert, because it adds a new commit that reverses the change without rewriting history others have pulled. Before risky steps I run git status and make a backup branch.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer follows read, decide, clean markers, test, stage and commit, then names git revert for shared history. Common mistakes are deleting one side blindly, forgetting to test, and recommending reset hard on pushed commits. Score yourself honestly.

task.title: Practise Git in a sandbox repository
task.brief: Create a throwaway repository and practise the full cycle including a conflict.
steps: Create a folder, run git init and make a first commit with a clear message.
Create a branch, change one line and commit it, then change the same line on main and commit.
Merge the branch and resolve the conflict by editing the markers.
Use git revert on one commit and check the history with git log.
checklist: I made at least three commits with good messages
I created and merged a branch
task.evidencePrompt: Paste your git log lines and describe how you resolved the conflict.

quiz.prompt: What is a commit?
options: A snapshot of the project with a message and a link to the previous commit
quiz.why: Commits are snapshots linked in a chain, which forms the project history.

quiz.prompt: Good commit messages are written in the ____ mood, such as "Add check" rather than "Added check". (one word)
quiz.why: The imperative style reads like an instruction and is the usual convention.

quiz.prompt: A pull request is:
options: A request to merge a branch, usually with review
quiz.why: It proposes merging your branch into another and gives teammates a place to review.

quiz.prompt: Which undo is safest on a shared branch?
quiz.why: Revert adds a new commit that reverses the old one and leaves shared history intact.

bank.prompt: You see <<<<<<< and >>>>>>> markers in a file. What do they mean?
options: A merge conflict needs manual resolution
bank.why: Markers show where two branches changed the same lines and a person must decide the result.

bank.prompt: You fixed a bug and renamed a variable across files in one go. Best practice?
options: Two commits, one per logical change
bank.why: One logical change per commit makes review and undo simple.

bank.prompt: A long-lived branch is risky because it drifts from main and causes painful ____. (one word)
bank.why: The longer a branch lives, the more its changes overlap with others and the harder merging becomes.

cards.front: What are the three places a change moves through in Git?
cards.back: Working directory (edit), staging area (git add) and repository (git commit). Commits are local snapshots until you push them.

cards.front: What makes a commit message good?
cards.back: A short imperative first line saying what changed and why, one logical change per commit, and no vague words like fix or update alone.

cards.front: Why use branches and pull requests?
cards.back: Branches isolate work so main stays stable. Pull requests let teammates review before merging. Keep branches short-lived.

cards.front: How do you handle a conflict and undo?
cards.back: Read both sides, choose the correct code, delete markers, test and commit. Undo shared commits with git revert, not reset.

tech-3.reflection: Look at the last ten commit messages in any of your projects. Which would a teammate not understand, and how would you rewrite one?

keyPoints: A commit is a snapshot; stage then commit.
Messages explain what and why in the imperative.
Short-lived branches merge through reviewed pull requests.
Resolve conflicts deliberately and use revert for shared undo.
revision.redo: Rewrite one vague commit message from your own project in imperative form.

tech-4.title: Clean Code, Testing and Review
tech-4.summary: Write readable code with good names and small functions, test edge cases, review code kindly and understand how ABAP changes travel through transport requests.
objectives: Apply naming, small functions and why-comments to make code readable.
Write unit tests that cover normal cases and edge cases.
Give and receive code review, and describe how ABAP changes move through transports.

explanation.heading: Code is read more than written
explanation.body:
Earlier lessons covered debugging, data access and version control. Now we ask how to write code that others, and your future self, can understand. Most of a developer's time goes to reading existing code, so readability is a productivity tool, not decoration.

Start with **names**. A name should reveal intent: compare `lv_x` with `lv_overdue_days`, or `proc1` with `calculate_late_fee`. Use consistent conventions, since SAP teams usually follow prefixes such as lv_ for local variables and lt_ for local tables. Keep **functions small**: each should do one thing at one level of detail, ideally fitting on one screen. If you struggle to name a function without using "and", it probably does two jobs.

**Comments** should explain *why*, not repeat *what*. "Add 1 to counter" is noise; "Use 30 days because the contract allows a grace period" is valuable. If a comment explains confusing code, try renaming or splitting the code first.

explanation.heading: Unit tests and edge cases
explanation.body:
A **unit test** runs a small piece of code with known input and checks the output. ABAP has a built-in framework, ABAP Unit, where test classes are marked FOR TESTING and use assertions to compare expected and actual values. Other languages have similar tools, such as Jest for JavaScript.

Good tests cover the normal case and the **edge cases**, the boundaries where bugs live. For a late-fee function charging 2 percent after 30 days, test 29 days (no fee), 30 days (boundary), 31 days (fee), 0 days, a negative number and an empty input. Write the test name as a sentence, such as "no_fee_within_grace_period". Tests protect you when you change code later: if they still pass, you probably did not break anything. Tests that need a long setup often signal functions that are too large.

explanation.heading: Code review
explanation.body:
In a **code review**, a teammate reads your change before it is merged. It catches bugs, spreads knowledge and keeps style consistent. As an author, keep changes small, explain the purpose, and run tests before asking. As a reviewer, comment on the code, not the person, ask questions rather than issuing orders ("What happens if the table is empty?") and separate must-fix issues from preferences by marking the latter "nit".

As the author, treat feedback as information, say thanks, and ask when unclear. A reviewer's confusion usually means the code is confusing. Do not defend; improve it. Praise good work too, because a review that only lists faults teaches people to avoid reviews.

explanation.heading: How ABAP changes travel
explanation.body:
ABAP development usually happens in a **landscape** of separate SAP systems. Developers work in the **development system** (DEV), where code is changed. Changes are recorded in a **transport request**, a container listing the objects changed, such as programs, tables or classes. After the request is released, it is imported into the **quality or test system** (QAS), where testers check it against realistic data. Only after approval is it imported into **production** (PRD), where real business runs. Developing directly in production is avoided because a mistake affects live users.

Conceptually this mirrors git branches and releases: develop in isolation, test, then promote. Good habits include giving the request a descriptive text, keeping related changes in one request and never mixing unrelated work, so a transport can move cleanly and be traced if something goes wrong.

examples.title: Renaming for clarity
examples.body: Before: FORM calc USING p1 p2. IF p1 > 30. p2 = p2 * 1.02. ENDIF. ENDFORM. After: FORM apply_late_fee USING iv_days_overdue CHANGING cv_amount. IF iv_days_overdue > gc_grace_days. cv_amount = cv_amount * gc_late_fee_factor. ENDIF. ENDFORM. The logic is unchanged, but a new team member now sees the rule without asking.
examples.takeaway: Good names and named constants turn magic numbers into readable business rules.

examples.title: Edge-case tests for a late fee
examples.body: Rule: 2 percent fee after 30 days. Tests: 29 days, fee 0; 30 days, fee 0; 31 days, fee 2 percent; 0 days, fee 0; negative days, a clear error. The writer realises the original code used greater-or-equal and charged on day 30, so the boundary test exposes a bug before it reaches users.
examples.takeaway: Boundaries are where off-by-one errors hide, so test just below, at and just above them.

exercises.prompt: Which comment adds the most value?
options: Use a 30-day cut-off because the contract allows a grace period
exercises.why: It explains why, which the code cannot show. The others repeat what the code already says.

exercises.prompt: A discount function gives 10 percent for orders of 1,000 rupees or more. Which test input is the most important boundary check?
exercises.why: Boundaries, here exactly 1,000, are where comparison mistakes such as greater-than versus greater-or-equal appear.

exercises.prompt: In a review you spot a function with no check for an empty input table. What is the best comment?

options.text: This is sloppy, you obviously did not think.
options.feedback: Personal criticism blocks learning and invites defence.

options.text: What happens if the input table is empty? It looks like it would raise an error here.
options.feedback: A specific question about behaviour is respectful and actionable.

options.text: Just write "fix it" and leave.
options.feedback: It gives no reason or detail, so the author learns nothing.

options.text: Approve silently and fix it yourself later.
options.feedback: Silent fixes hide the lesson and may surprise the author.

exercises.why: Good review comments are specific, about the code, and phrased to invite a response.

exercises.prompt: Explain to a new joiner, in your own words, how an ABAP change moves from a developer to live users. Name the three kinds of system, what a transport request is, and why you do not change code directly in production.

descriptors.3: All three with their purposes.
Container of changed objects that is released and imported along the landscape.
Mentions live users, untested changes and traceability.
Clear step-by-step flow.

exercises.modelAnswer: Developers change code in the development system. Their changes are recorded in a transport request, which is a container listing the changed objects such as programs and tables. Once released, the request is imported into the quality or test system, where testers check it with realistic data. After approval it is imported into production, where real users work. We avoid editing production directly because untested changes could break live business and be hard to trace.
exercises.guidance: A strong answer gives the order DEV, test, production, explains the transport request as a container of changes, and gives a risk-based reason. Weak answers confuse transports with emails or skip the test system. Score yourself against the model.

task.title: Clean one piece of your code and write tests
task.brief: Take a function from a past project, improve it and add unit tests with edge cases.
steps: Pick a function between 10 and 40 lines from your own project.
Rename two unclear variables or the function itself, and replace one magic number with a named constant.
Write at least four tests: normal, boundary, empty or zero, and invalid input.
Ask a friend, or imagine a reviewer, to give two comments in the "What happens if...?" style and respond to them.
checklist: I replaced a magic number with a name
I wrote at least four tests including a boundary
task.evidencePrompt: Paste your before and after names and list your four test cases.

quiz.prompt: A function name containing "and", such as validate_and_save, suggests:
options: It probably does two jobs and should be split
It must be a database call
quiz.why: One function should do one thing, so "and" signals two responsibilities.

quiz.prompt: Test just below, at and just above a limit; these limit values are called ____ cases. (one word)
quiz.why: Edge or boundary cases are where off-by-one errors often occur.

quiz.prompt: A good reviewer comment is:
options: Specific, about the code and phrased as a question or suggestion
quiz.why: Specific, respectful comments help the author improve the code.

quiz.prompt: In an ABAP landscape, changes are made in development and then imported in order to:
quiz.why: Changes are tested in the quality system before moving to production.

bank.prompt: What does a transport request contain?
options: A list of changed objects such as programs, tables and classes
bank.why: It is a container that carries changed development objects through the landscape.

bank.prompt: A hard-coded number like 30 with no explanation in code is called a magic ____. (one word)
bank.why: Replacing a magic number with a named constant explains its meaning.

bank.prompt: You get a review comment that stings. The best first response is to:
options: Thank the reviewer and ask for an example if unclear
bank.why: Reviews are information, and a calm clarifying question moves things forward.

cards.back: Names that reveal intent, small single-purpose functions, named constants instead of magic numbers, and comments that explain why rather than what.

cards.front: Which cases should unit tests cover?
cards.back: The normal case, boundaries just below, at and above limits, zero or empty inputs and invalid inputs. Name tests as sentences.

cards.front: How do you review kindly and effectively?
cards.back: Comment on the code, not the person, ask questions, separate must-fix from nits and praise good work. Authors say thanks and improve confusing code.

cards.front: How does an ABAP change reach production?
cards.back: It is recorded in a transport request in development, released, imported to the quality or test system, approved, then imported to production.

tech-4.reflection: Which piece of your own code would confuse you if you opened it in six months, and what two changes would make it clear?

keyPoints: Names reveal intent and functions do one thing.
Comments explain why, not what.
Test normal, boundary, empty and invalid cases.
Review the code kindly; changes travel DEV, test, production by transport.
revision.redo: Pick one function and rename one variable and one constant for intent.

time-1.title: Time Audit and Priorities
time-1.summary: See where your hours really go, sort tasks with the Eisenhower matrix, and put your hardest work in your best hours.
objectives: Run a simple time audit and read the totals honestly.
Sort tasks into the four Eisenhower quadrants and explain why important is not the same as urgent.
Match demanding work to your high-energy hours.

explanation.heading: You cannot manage hours you have not seen
explanation.body:
