The reverse outline shows that paragraph 4 does not support the main message about performance. Move it to a different document or delete it, and add a paragraph on the fix for the slow server.
examples.takeaway: Summarising each paragraph in one line exposes repetition (1 and 2) and off-topic material (4).

exercises.prompt: In a PEEL paragraph, which part tells the reader why the evidence proves the point?
exercises.hint: It is the step many beginners skip.
exercises.why: The Explain step connects evidence to the point. Point states the claim, Evidence provides the proof, and Link connects the paragraph to the next idea or the main message.

exercises.prompt: In a one-page brief for a decision-maker, which section should appear near the top because the reader most needs it? Answer with one word.
exercises.hint: It is the answer, not the background.
exercises.why: Decision-makers need the recommendation early; background and options exist to justify it.

exercises.prompt: Situation: your project group of five students keeps missing deadlines because tasks are assigned verbally in a WhatsApp group and get buried. Using these facts: in the last sprint, 4 of 9 tasks were late; two members said they never saw their task; a shared task board would take under an hour to set up. Write ONE PEEL paragraph (60 to 110 words) arguing that the group should adopt a shared task board.

rubric.label: Clear point in the first sentence

descriptors.1: Claim appears but late or is vague.
descriptors.2: Claim is in the first sentence but mildly vague.
descriptors.3: First sentence clearly recommends the shared task board.

rubric.label: Specific evidence from the facts given

descriptors.1: Vague facts such as 'many tasks were late'.
descriptors.2: Uses one number or fact accurately.
descriptors.3: Uses at least two given facts accurately (4 of 9 late; two members never saw their task).

auto.label: Uses a fact from the sprint data

rubric.label: Explains why the evidence supports the point

descriptors.1: Reasoning is implied but not stated.
descriptors.2: States a reason, but it is generic.
descriptors.3: States that verbal assignment in a busy chat leads to missed tasks and that a visible board gives each person a fixed place to check.

descriptors.2: Ends with a recommendation but no step.
descriptors.3: Ends by linking to the action: set up the board (under an hour) and use it from the next sprint.

exercises.modelAnswer: The group should move task assignment from WhatsApp to a shared task board. In the last sprint, 4 of our 9 tasks were late, and two members said they never saw the message assigning their task. This shows that the chat buries decisions under daily conversation, so people cannot find what they own. A board gives each task one visible place, with a name and a date. Setting it up takes under an hour, so we can start with the next sprint.
exercises.guidance: A strong paragraph opens with the claim, uses the numbers exactly as given, then does the explaining: why a buried chat causes late work and why a board fixes it. Weak answers repeat the facts without reasoning, exaggerate ('everyone always misses everything') or add facts that were not provided. Score each part separately, and rewrite the weakest part once.

exercises.prompt: You are drafting a one-page brief recommending that your team adopt automated tests. Your reverse outline reads: 1. Manual testing takes 6 hours per release. 2. Two bugs reached production last month. 3. Our new intern is very enthusiastic. 4. Automated tests could cut testing to 1 hour. 5. Recommendation and first step. What should you do with paragraph 3?

options.text: Keep it; it adds a human touch and the reader will like the personality.
options.feedback: Warmth is fine elsewhere, but here it does not support the recommendation and weakens the logical flow.

options.text: Cut it or move it elsewhere, because it does not support the main message of the brief.
options.feedback: Correct. The reverse outline shows a paragraph with no link to the recommendation. Every paragraph in a brief should earn its place.

options.text: Move it to the start so the brief opens with something friendly.
options.feedback: This puts an irrelevant point in the most prominent position and delays the main message.

options.text: Expand it to three paragraphs so the brief looks more thorough.
options.feedback: Padding makes a brief longer without making it more persuasive.

exercises.why: A reverse outline is a test: each paragraph must support the main message. Paragraphs 1, 2 and 4 build the case; 5 closes it; 3 does not belong.

task.title: Outline and PEEL a real recommendation
task.brief: Plan and draft a short recommendation about something real in your studies or work.
steps: Choose a real decision (a tool for your project, a study plan, a hostel or lab issue) and write your main message in one sentence.
List three to four supporting points as an outline, with one fact or example for each.
Draft one PEEL paragraph for the strongest point, making sure the Explain step is present.
Do a reverse outline of your list: one line per point, and delete anything that does not support the message.
checklist: Main message is one clear sentence
Each outline point has specific evidence
Paragraph includes all four PEEL parts
task.evidencePrompt: Write your main message and the first sentence of your PEEL paragraph.

quiz.prompt: What should you write first when planning a report?
options: The conclusion, so you can end quickly
The main message as one sentence, followed by supporting points
A list of every fact you know
The headings only, with no message
quiz.why: A one-sentence main message gives the whole document a spine, and supporting points follow from it. A list of every fact lacks direction, and headings alone do not say what you are arguing.

quiz.prompt: What does the L in PEEL stand for?
quiz.why: L is Link: connect the paragraph back to the main message or forward to the next idea.

quiz.prompt: Which sentence uses the strongest evidence?
options: Our website is terrible and everybody hates it.
The checkout page takes about 12 seconds to load, and 18 of 50 test users abandoned it.
Many people say the page is slow.
It is obvious that the page needs work.
quiz.why: It gives specific, checkable figures. The others rely on adjectives, vague 'many people' or an appeal to the obvious.

quiz.prompt: A reverse outline has one line per what? Answer with one word.
quiz.why: In a reverse outline you summarise each paragraph in one line, so repetition and off-topic material become visible.

bank.prompt: A paragraph begins 'Our canteen is the problem' and then lists five complaints with no explanation. Which PEEL part is mainly missing?
options: Explain, because the facts are not tied to a point or reason
Point, because the first sentence is too short
Link, because there is no heading
Evidence, because five complaints are too many
bank.why: The paragraph has a vague claim and facts but no reasoning connecting them. Having five items of evidence is not a flaw, and headings are unrelated to Link.

bank.prompt: Name the one-page-brief section that states the owner and date for each action. Use two words.
bank.why: The Next steps section turns the recommendation into owners and dates, so something actually happens.

bank.prompt: You write: 'Traffic to our app page doubled, so users are clearly happier.' What is wrong with the evidence?
options: Traffic growth does not show satisfaction, so the evidence does not match the claim.
It should cite an authority instead of data.
bank.why: More visits can arise from marketing, curiosity or problems that make people return. Satisfaction needs matching evidence such as ratings, complaints or retention.

cards.front: What are the sections of a one-page brief?
cards.back: Purpose, Background, Options or findings, Recommendation, Next steps (with owner and date). Put the recommendation near the top for decision-makers.
Point, Evidence, Explain, Link. Claim first, proof second, reason why the proof matters third, then connect to the main message.
It is specific, checkable and matches the claim. Use data, a real example or an authority, and state honest limits like sample size.

cards.front: How do you test the logical flow of a draft?
cards.back: Reverse outline: one line per paragraph. Merge repeats, cut or move lines that do not support the main message, and check transitions.

writing-3.reflection: Think of a time you tried to convince someone in writing or in a meeting. Which of the four parts of PEEL was weakest in what you said, and what evidence could you have added?

keyPoints: Write the main message as one sentence before drafting.
PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.
Specific, checkable evidence beats adjectives.
Match evidence to the claim.
Reverse outline: one line per paragraph; cut what does not support the message.
revision.redo: Pick any paragraph you wrote recently and label its P, E, E and L; add the missing part in one sentence.

writing-4.title: Editing and Revision
writing-4.summary: Improve any draft in separate passes for structure, sentences, words and proofreading, and use feedback well.
objectives: Edit a draft in four ordered passes instead of one messy read.
Use reading aloud and a personal checklist to catch errors.
Receive feedback without defensiveness and apply it selectively.

explanation.heading: Draft and edit are different jobs
explanation.body:
In earlier lessons you learned to write clearly, to structure emails and to build arguments. The final skill is editing, and most weak writing is simply unedited writing. The reason people skip it is that they try to edit while drafting, which slows both. Draft first, quickly. Then edit as a separate task, ideally after a break of at least an hour; a draft read the next morning shows its flaws.

The key technique is **multiple passes, each with one focus, from big to small**. If you fix commas in a paragraph you will later delete, the time is wasted. Large problems first, small ones last.

explanation.heading: The four passes
explanation.body:
**Pass 1: Structure.** Does the piece answer the reader's question? Is the main message first or clearly signposted? Is the order logical? Use a reverse outline, then move, merge or delete whole paragraphs.

**Pass 2: Sentences.** Look at each paragraph. Shorten long sentences, change passive to active, make sure each sentence adds something new. Aim to cut 10 to 20 percent of the words.

**Pass 3: Words.** Replace vague or padded words with precise ones: *utilise* becomes *use*, *in order to* becomes *to*, *due to the fact that* becomes *because*, *very important* becomes *critical* or is simply removed. Delete filler such as *basically*, *actually*, *kindly* and *needful*. Check that names, numbers and terms are used consistently.

**Pass 4: Proofread.** Spelling, grammar, punctuation, dates, amounts, names, attachments. Do this last, slowly, and change the way you see the text: increase the zoom, print it, or read from the last line to the first.

Worked example. Draft: *We are in the process of making an attempt to utilise a new tool in order to improve the speed.* After words and sentences passes: *We are testing a new tool to improve speed.* Fourteen words became eight, and nothing was lost.

explanation.heading: Read aloud, then check against your own list
explanation.body:
Your eyes forgive errors that your ears catch. **Reading aloud**, or using a text-to-speech voice, exposes missing words, clumsy rhythm, repeated phrases and sentences that run out of breath. If you stumble, the reader will too. Mark each stumble and fix it.

Build a **personal checklist** from your own recurring mistakes, as you did in the first English lesson. A useful list has five to eight items, for example: *Is the main point in the first two lines? Is every ask dated? Any 'revert back' or 'discuss about'? Names and numbers checked against the source? Attachment included? Subject line specific?* Keep it where you write, and update it each month. A checklist beats memory because errors you do not see are, by definition, ones you will not remember to look for.

For high-stakes documents, ask for a **fresh pair of eyes**. Another person finds what you cannot, because you read what you meant to write.

explanation.heading: Taking feedback well
explanation.body:
Feedback is information about how your text lands, not a judgement of you. When someone gives you comments: **listen first** and avoid explaining; **ask a clarifying question** such as 'Which part lost you?'; **separate the symptom from the suggested fix**. A reader may say 'This paragraph is boring' (symptom) and propose a rewrite (fix); the symptom is reliable even if the fix is not.

Then decide. Apply feedback that matches your purpose and reader; note and thank for feedback you decline, and if two reviewers disagree, return to the reader and purpose. When you ask for feedback, **be specific**: 'Is the recommendation clear in the first paragraph?' gets a better answer than 'Thoughts?' After applying changes, thank the reviewer and tell them what you changed; people give better feedback to those who use it.

examples.title: Four passes on one paragraph
examples.body:
Draft: 'Basically, due to the fact that the server is very slow, we are of the opinion that it is important to the project that the migration of the database should be done by the team in the coming week.'

Pass 2 (sentences, active voice): 'The server is very slow, so the team should migrate the database next week.'
Pass 3 (words): 'The server is slow, so we should migrate the database next week.'
Pass 4 (proofread, add a date): 'The server is slow, so we should migrate the database in the week of 20 October.'
examples.takeaway: Thirty-seven words became sixteen. Each pass had one job, and the final proofread caught the missing date.

examples.title: Reading aloud catches what eyes miss
examples.body:
Written: 'Please find attached the the report for your review and feedback on the same.'

Read aloud, the learner trips on the repeated 'the' and the clumsy 'on the same'. Fixed: 'Please find the report attached. I would value your feedback by Friday.'
examples.takeaway: Stumbles when reading aloud flag repeated words, awkward phrases and missing details such as a deadline.

examples.title: Responding to vague feedback
examples.body:
Reviewer: 'Your proposal feels long.'

Learner: 'Thanks. Which section lost you?' Reviewer: 'The background, I did not know what you wanted until page two.'

Change made: moved the request to the opening line and cut background from 250 to 80 words.
examples.takeaway: A clarifying question turned a vague comment into a specific, fixable problem.

exercises.prompt: What is the best order for edit passes?
exercises.hint: Go from big problems to small ones.
exercises.why: Large issues come first so you do not polish text you later delete. Proofreading comes last, after the content has settled.

exercises.prompt: Edit the phrase 'in order to' to its shortest correct form. Write the one word that replaces it.
exercises.hint: Two words are redundant here.
exercises.why: 'In order to' almost always shortens to 'to' without any loss of meaning.

exercises.prompt: Edit this status update for a manager. Rewrite it in no more than 45 words, keeping every fact: 'Basically, due to the fact that the testing of the login module has been completed by us, we are now in a position to start the testing of the payment module, which is expected to be started on Monday 20 October and to be completed within a period of three days, if there are no delays.'

descriptors.1: One fact missing (login done, payment testing starts, Monday 20 October, three days, conditional on no delays).
descriptors.2: All facts present but one is distorted.
descriptors.3: All five facts present and accurate.

auto.label: Keeps at least five key words from the original

descriptors.0: Still over 60 words or passive and padded.
descriptors.1: Shorter but over 45 words, or filler remains.
descriptors.2: At or under 45 words with a small amount of padding.
descriptors.3: Under 45 words, active voice, no filler.

rubric.label: Reads smoothly and in logical order

descriptors.1: Order is acceptable but rhythm is clumsy.
descriptors.2: Clear order with one awkward phrase.
descriptors.3: Past, next step, dates, condition: clear order and natural rhythm when read aloud.
No spelling, punctuation or date errors.

exercises.modelAnswer: We have finished testing the login module. Payment module testing starts on Monday 20 October and should take three days, if there are no delays.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers lead with what is done, then what is next, then the date, duration and condition. Cut 'basically', 'due to the fact that' and 'in a position to'. A common mistake is trimming facts, such as dropping 'if there are no delays', to hit the word count. Read your version aloud and count the words honestly before scoring.

exercises.prompt: You share a project report with two reviewers. Reviewer A says the opening is too long. Reviewer B says the opening is perfect but the recommendation is hidden. Your reader is a busy department head who will decide in one meeting. What is the best response?
options: Ignore both reviewers; you wrote the report and you know it best.
Follow Reviewer A because shorter is always better.
Ask each what specifically lost them, then decide using your reader and purpose: tighten the opening and move the recommendation to the top, since a decision-maker needs it first.
Rewrite the whole report so everyone is satisfied.
exercises.why: The best response uses feedback as information, probes the symptom, and decides by purpose and reader. Both comments point at the same problem: the main point arrives late for a decision-maker. Ignoring reviewers wastes insight, following one blindly or rewriting everything is inefficient.

task.title: Four-pass edit with a checklist
task.brief: Edit a real piece of your writing through four passes and build your checklist.
steps: Choose a real draft of 150 to 300 words (an email, assignment paragraph or report section) and leave it for at least an hour.
Do pass 1 (structure) and pass 2 (sentences), then pass 3 (words) cutting at least 10 percent of the length.
Read the result aloud and mark every stumble; fix them, then proofread slowly for names, numbers and dates.
Write a checklist of five to eight items based on the errors you found.
checklist: I did the passes in order, one focus each
The final version is at least 10 percent shorter
I read it aloud and fixed stumbles
I wrote a checklist from my own errors
task.evidencePrompt: State the word count before and after, and list two items on your checklist.

quiz.prompt: Why should proofreading be the last pass?
options: It is the least important step.
You might polish text that you later delete or rewrite.
Spell checkers work better at the end.
quiz.why: Content changes during the earlier passes, so correcting commas first wastes effort. Proofreading is important, but only worthwhile once the text is settled.

quiz.prompt: What does reading your draft aloud mainly help you find?
options: Awkward rhythm, repeated words, missing words and sentences that are too long
quiz.why: Your ears detect rhythm and clumsy phrases that your eyes skip. It does not tell you facts such as a deadline, and structural choices are made in pass 1.

quiz.prompt: A personal editing checklist should mainly be built from:
options: A grammar textbook's full list of rules
Your own recurring errors and the needs of your readers
quiz.why: It is short and works because it targets mistakes you actually make. A textbook list is too long to use and borrowed phrases may not fit your errors.

quiz.prompt: When feedback is vague ('this feels long'), what should you ask for? Answer with one word that completes: 'Which ____ lost you?'
quiz.why: Asking which part lost the reader turns a vague symptom into a specific, fixable problem.

bank.prompt: Which change belongs in the 'words' pass?
options: Moving the conclusion to the top
Checking that the date is correct
Deleting a paragraph that repeats another
bank.why: The words pass replaces vague or padded words. Moving or deleting paragraphs is a structure change, and checking dates is proofreading.

bank.prompt: Besides reading aloud, name one trick for seeing proofreading errors by changing how the text looks, such as printing it or reading it from the last line to the first. Write the word 'backwards', 'print' or 'zoom'.
bank.why: Changing the format, order or size makes your brain read what is actually written rather than what you expect.

bank.prompt: A senior colleague tells you your report summary 'doesn't land'. What is the best first reply?
options: Explain why the summary is actually fine.
Say nothing and rewrite it overnight.
Thank them and ask which sentence lost them and what they expected to see.
Ask someone else to rewrite it.
bank.why: A thanks plus a clarifying question reveals the real problem and keeps the person willing to help. Defending the summary or guessing the fix wastes the information.

cards.front: What are the four edit passes in order?
cards.back: Structure, sentences, words, proofread. Move from big problems to small ones, and give each pass one focus.
Ears catch what eyes skip: missing or repeated words, clumsy rhythm and overlong sentences. Fix every place you stumble.

cards.front: What should be on your personal editing checklist?
cards.back: Five to eight items from your own recurring errors: main point first, dated ask, known grammar slips, numbers and names checked, attachment included.

cards.front: How do you handle feedback well?
cards.back: Listen first, ask which part and why, separate symptom from suggested fix, decide by reader and purpose, then thank the reviewer.

writing-4.reflection: Which edit pass do you most often skip, and what is one small habit (a break, reading aloud, a checklist) that would make you do it?

keyPoints: Draft first, edit later, and edit in separate passes.
Order: structure, sentences, words, proofread.
Read aloud and fix every stumble.
A short personal checklist beats memory.
Ask which part lost the reader; decide by purpose.
revision.redo: Take one paragraph you wrote today, cut it by 15 percent without losing facts, and read it aloud once.

final.title: Final Assessment: Your 60-Day Review
final.intro: This is the final assessment of the 60-day programme. It samples all 26 skills. Part A is auto-graded from lessons you completed. Part B has a decision scenario, a role-play, a 90-day plan and a claim evaluation. It measures demonstrated ability rather than completion, so answer honestly and in detail. You can retake it later.

items.prompt: Three weeks before a campus placement drive you realise you have not done any serious preparation and you are anxious. What is the best plan?

options.text: Panic and study all night every night.
options.feedback: Sleep loss and panic reduce learning.

options.text: List the key topics, plan daily focus blocks with review, protect sleep and ask a senior for a mock interview.
options.feedback: A structured plan with recovery works.

options.text: Give up on the drive.
options.feedback: Giving up ignores the three weeks you still have.

options.text: Copy answers without understanding.
options.feedback: Copying does not build real skill.

items.why: A realistic plan, focus blocks and rest beat panic.

items.setup: Your manager asks you to take on an extra urgent task while you already have a deadline on Friday. You want to stay cooperative while protecting quality.

turns.they: Can you also take this urgent report? It is due Friday too.

options.text: Sure, no problem, I will do everything.
options.feedback: Agreeing silently risks quality and burnout.

options.text: I want to help. I have the module due on Friday. If I take this report, one of them will need to move. Which is the priority?
options.feedback: It states the limit, offers help and asks for a decision.

options.text: No, that is not my job.
options.feedback: A blunt refusal damages cooperation.

turns.they: The report is a priority. The module can move to Monday.

options.text: Okay, I will work on both anyway.
options.feedback: Ignoring the offered change creates overload.

options.text: Thank you. I will deliver the report by Friday noon and the module by Monday noon, and confirm this by email.
options.feedback: Clear dates and written confirmation.

options.text: Fine, whatever.
options.feedback: A sulking reply weakens trust.

turns.they: I might need help with testing the report too.

options.text: I cannot, I am busy.
options.feedback: A flat no without alternative is unhelpful.

options.text: I can test it for two hours on Thursday afternoon. Could someone else cover the rest?
options.feedback: A clear limit with an alternative.

options.text: Why does everything come to me?
options.feedback: Complaining does not solve the issue.

items.why: State limits, offer help, ask for priorities and confirm in writing.

items.prompt: Write a 90-day plan for your own next step (for example, getting your first SAP ABAP role). Include a specific goal with a date, three monthly milestones, weekly habits with time blocks, a money or resources plan, a plan B and how you will review progress.

descriptors.3: Specific, measurable and dated.
Three milestones and weekly time-blocked habits.
Both specific.
Review dates with adjustment rules.

items.modelAnswer: Goal: receive at least two ABAP trainee interview calls and complete one end-to-end ABAP report project by 15 January. Month 1: finish core ABAP topics and 30 practice programs. Month 2: build the report project and apply to twenty companies. Month 3: complete ten mock interviews and follow up with contacts. Weekly: Monday to Friday 7 to 9 pm focus blocks, one weekend review session, 30 minutes of networking messages. Resources: Rs 3,000 for a course and a free practice system access. Plan B: apply also for junior web-development roles. Review: every Sunday check progress against milestones, adjust the next week and cut tasks if I am behind.
items.guidance: Strong plans are specific, dated, realistic and include milestones, weekly time blocks, resources, plan B and scheduled reviews. Avoid vague statements such as "work hard".

items.prompt: You read this claim in a forwarded message: "A new study proves that AI tools will replace all programmers within two years, so learning to code is pointless." Write 100 to 140 words evaluating the claim: what you would check, what tactics it uses, what a fair conclusion would be and how confident you are.

descriptors.3: Source tracing, study details and independent sources.
Absolute words, vague authority and urgency identified.
Balanced conclusion with stated confidence and reasons.

items.modelAnswer: I would first find the study itself and check who ran it, the sample, the date and what it actually measured; "proves", "all" and "pointless" are absolute words, and "a new study" is vague authority. I would look for two independent sources and reports from developers. The claim also uses fear to push a conclusion. A fair view is that tools will change many coding tasks, but evidence for replacing all programmers in two years is weak. My confidence that the claim is exaggerated is medium to high until I see the study.
items.guidance: Strong answers trace the claim to its source, notice absolute wording and fear tactics, look for independent evidence and finish with a balanced conclusion and honest confidence level.

week-1.title: Week 1 Assessment: Foundations
week-1.intro: This assessment checks whether you can apply the week's ideas on goals, time, English, reading, discipline and stress in realistic situations. Part A is auto-graded from your completed lessons. Part B asks you to decide, role-play and write. Take your time and answer as you would in real life.

items.prompt: It is 9 pm. You planned two hours of SQL practice today, but you spent the evening on messages and have a mock test tomorrow at 10 am. What is the best move?

options.text: Skip practice and hope the test goes well.
options.feedback: Hope is not a preparation plan.

options.text: Do a focused 50-minute block now on the weakest topic, phone away, and plan the rest for early morning.
options.feedback: A short focus block on the weak area is realistic and effective.

options.text: Study until 4 am without breaks.
options.feedback: Sleep loss will hurt tomorrow's performance.

options.text: Move the test to next week without asking.
options.feedback: You cannot unilaterally change commitments.

items.why: A realistic recovery plan protects sleep and uses focus on the weakest topic.

items.setup: You are in a short mock interview and the interviewer asks you to introduce yourself. You feel nervous and your voice is shaky.

turns.they: Please tell me a little about yourself.

options.text: Um, I am, like, a student, I guess.
options.feedback: Fillers and hedges lower the impression of confidence.
options.reply: Could you tell me more about your studies?

options.text: Take one slow breath, then: "I am Deepak, an MCA student in Faridabad with a web-development background, aiming for an ABAP role."
options.feedback: A breath and a clear structured introduction show calm.
options.reply: Good. What drew you towards ABAP?

options.text: I will say everything about my whole life now.
options.feedback: Too long and unfocused for an introduction.
options.reply: That is a lot. Let us move on.

turns.they: What drew you towards ABAP?

options.text: I do not know, it just seemed good.
options.feedback: A vague answer shows little preparation.

options.text: I like solving business problems with code, and ABAP is central to SAP systems used by many large companies.
options.feedback: It is specific, honest and links interest to the role.
options.reply: That is clear. How are you preparing?

options.text: Everyone says it pays well.
options.feedback: Money alone is a weak motive to state.

turns.they: How are you preparing for the role?

options.text: I study when I can.
options.feedback: Vague; please give specifics.

options.text: I practise daily: one focus block on ABAP basics, weekly mini programs and a written review of my errors.
options.feedback: Specific habits show discipline and a system.

options.text: I am not preparing yet.
options.feedback: This statement undermines your candidacy badly.

items.why: Calm breathing and specific, structured answers make a strong first impression.

items.prompt: Write a short plan (about 100 words) for the next two weeks that includes one specific goal, how you will break it into weekly steps, when each day you will do a focus block and a reading habit to support it.

descriptors.3: Specific and measurable with a date.
Weekly steps with daily time blocks.
A specific daily reading habit linked to the goal.

items.modelAnswer: Goal: finish 40 ABAP practice problems by 28 October. Week 1: 20 problems on internal tables and loops; week 2: 20 on database reads and review of mistakes. Daily: a 50-minute focus block at 7 pm with my phone in another room. Reading: 20 minutes every morning of ABAP documentation and notes, writing two lines of summary. I will review progress each Sunday and adjust.
items.guidance: Strong plans have a measurable goal with a date, weekly steps, specific daily times and a reading habit that supports the goal. Avoid general statements like "study more".

week-2.title: Week 2 Assessment: Thinking and Communicating
week-2.intro: This assessment tests how you think and communicate under realistic conditions: evaluating claims, writing clearly, reading emotions, staying calm and acting with confidence. Part A uses auto-graded questions from lessons you completed. Part B has a decision scenario, a role-play and a short writing task.

items.prompt: A teammate says: "Everyone knows that this framework is the best. Only beginners disagree." You have doubts about it for your project. What is the best response?

options.text: Agree to avoid conflict.
options.feedback: Agreeing silently leaves your doubts unexamined.

options.text: Ask what evidence supports it for this project and share one specific concern calmly.
options.feedback: It tests the claim and respects the person.

options.text: Say they are being arrogant.
options.feedback: This attacks the person, not the claim.

options.text: Ignore the meeting.
options.feedback: Disengaging solves nothing at all.

items.why: Critical thinking asks for evidence while emotional intelligence keeps the tone respectful.

items.setup: You disagree with a classmate's plan during a group project meeting. They sound frustrated when you raise a concern.

turns.they: I think my plan is fine. Why are you objecting now?

options.text: You always do this and it is annoying.
options.feedback: Blame escalates the conflict.
options.reply: Forget it, do whatever you want.

options.text: I can hear you are frustrated. I like the structure; my concern is the deadline in week three. Can we check it together?
options.feedback: It acknowledges emotion, names a specific issue and invites collaboration.
options.reply: Okay, show me where the issue is.

options.text: Fine, you are right.
options.feedback: Giving in quickly avoids the issue and may cost later.

turns.they: How could the deadline be a problem?

options.text: It just feels wrong.
options.feedback: A feeling without facts is weak.

options.text: The testing task is after the submission date in the schedule. Moving testing one week earlier would fix it.
options.feedback: Concrete fact plus a proposed solution.

options.text: Never mind.
options.feedback: Withdrawing leaves the issue unresolved.

turns.they: Can you update the plan and send it?

options.text: Maybe later, if I remember.
options.feedback: Vague commitments reduce trust.

options.text: Yes, I will send the updated plan by tonight at 8 pm.
options.feedback: Clear commitment with a time.

options.text: Why do I always have to do the work?
options.feedback: Complaining weakens team cooperation badly.

items.why: Acknowledge feelings, name concrete issues and make specific commitments.

items.prompt: Write a short, clear email (about 100 words) to a senior asking for one day's extension on a task because a dependency has not been delivered. Include facts, impact, a proposed new date and a polite close.

descriptors.3: Clear subject and request at the start.
Specific facts and impact.
Specific new date and professional tone.

items.modelAnswer: Subject: Request for one-day extension on report task. Hello Mr Verma, I am writing to request one extra day on the sales report. The data file from the finance team arrived at 4 pm today instead of yesterday, so I could start the analysis only now. I propose to submit by 12 noon on Thursday instead of Wednesday evening. I will share a draft of sections one and two by tomorrow 3 pm so you can review them early. Thank you for understanding. Regards, Deepak.
items.guidance: Strong emails state the request first, give the specific reason with facts, propose a concrete new date and keep a polite professional tone. Avoid excuses or blame.

week-3.title: Week 3 Assessment: Problem-Solving, Research and Digital Skills
week-3.intro: This assessment checks how you solve problems, check information and use digital tools responsibly. Part A is auto-graded from lessons you completed. Part B has a decision scenario, a role-play and a short written analysis. Treat the questions as real work situations.

items.prompt: A report you wrote in SQL suddenly shows twice the usual sales total after a join was added. What do you do first?

options.text: Send it because the number is bigger.
options.feedback: Bigger numbers can come from errors.

options.text: Check the row counts before and after the join and look for duplicates caused by the join keys.
options.feedback: Testing the cause with row counts is systematic debugging.

options.text: Delete the join and say nothing.
options.feedback: You might fix it but learn nothing.

options.text: Blame the database.
options.feedback: Blame is not diagnosis.

items.why: Debugging starts by testing the most likely cause with evidence.

items.setup: A friend forwards you a message claiming that a new government rule bans a common payment method from next month and asks you to share it widely.

turns.they: Quick, share this before it gets deleted!

options.text: Okay, sharing now.
options.feedback: False urgency is a misinformation tactic.

options.text: Let me check the original source first; I will look for the official notification and two independent reports.
options.feedback: It applies source tracing and independence checks.

options.text: I do not care about this.
options.feedback: Ignoring does not help your friend.

turns.they: Why do you need to check? It looks official.

options.text: Because I said so.
options.feedback: It does not explain the reason.

options.text: Official-looking messages can be edited or old. I want to see the date and the original notice.
options.feedback: It explains the checks in plain words.

options.text: I do not trust anything.
options.feedback: Blanket distrust is not a method.

turns.they: I found nothing yet. What do we do now?

options.text: Share it anyway.
options.feedback: Unverified claims should not be shared.

options.text: Treat it as unverified, tell the group it is unconfirmed and check the ministry website tomorrow.
options.feedback: It communicates uncertainty honestly and plans a next check.

options.text: Say it is fake.
options.feedback: You have no proof it is fake either.

items.why: Trace the origin, look for independent confirmation and state uncertainty honestly.

items.prompt: You used a generative tool to draft a summary of a technical article for your study group. Write 90 to 120 words explaining how you will verify and responsibly use the output before sharing it.

descriptors.3: Specific checks against the source.
Hallucinations, outdated facts and bias explained.
Takes responsibility and discloses use.

items.modelAnswer: I will not share the summary as it is. First I will read the original article and compare each key claim, number and name with the source. I know tools can invent facts, miss recent changes or reflect bias, so I will mark anything I cannot verify and remove it. I will rewrite the summary in my own words, add the article link and note that a tool helped with a first draft. I remain responsible for the accuracy of what I share, and I will not put private information into any tool.
items.guidance: Strong answers describe concrete checks against the original source, name specific limits such as invented facts, and accept responsibility for accuracy with disclosure.

week-4.title: Week 4 Assessment: Working With People
week-4.intro: This assessment checks how you behave and decide when working with people: etiquette, presentation, emotions, conflict, networking and stress. Part A is auto-graded from the lessons you completed. Part B has a decision scenario, a role-play and a written task.

items.prompt: You are invited to an on-campus company event the day after an all-night project push. You are tired and your formal clothes are unwashed. What is the best approach?

options.text: Skip the event without telling anyone.
options.feedback: Silent absence can look unprofessional.

options.text: Prepare clean, neat, simple clothes, arrive on time and keep introductions short and polite.
options.feedback: Basic grooming and punctuality create a good impression.

options.text: Wear the same crumpled clothes and avoid eye contact.
options.feedback: Poor presentation signals low care.

options.text: Arrive late and leave early.
options.feedback: This signals low interest in the host.

items.why: Neat basics, punctuality and polite manners matter more than expensive clothing.

items.setup: At a networking event you promised a senior engineer you would send a resume, but you forgot for a week. You now message them to follow up.

turns.they: Hi, I remember we met. Did you send your resume?

options.text: Sorry, I forgot, whatever.
options.feedback: A careless tone weakens trust.

options.text: I am sorry for the delay. I missed sending my resume after we met. I have attached it now with two lines on my ABAP training.
options.feedback: A brief apology with immediate repair.
options.reply: Thank you, I will have a look.

options.text: I was busy, and you also did not follow up.
options.feedback: Blaming the other person damages the relationship.

turns.they: Thanks. What kind of role are you looking for?

options.text: Anything works.
options.feedback: A vague answer gives them nothing to act on.

options.text: An entry-level SAP ABAP developer role at a services firm. I am building small reports and practising daily.
options.feedback: A specific target with evidence of effort.

options.text: Whatever pays most.
options.feedback: Focusing on money alone gives a poor impression.

turns.they: I might know someone. Can you send a short note I can forward?

options.text: I do not have time to write.
options.feedback: Refusing the help they offer loses the chance.

options.text: Certainly. I will send a three-line summary by tomorrow noon.
options.feedback: Clear commitment that makes the favour easy.

options.text: Maybe sometime next month.
options.feedback: Delays reduce the momentum quickly.

items.why: A brief apology, a specific ask and quick follow-through build networking trust.

items.prompt: You have three deadlines this week, you are sleeping badly and a teammate has not replied. Write 100 to 130 words describing how you would prioritise, protect your recovery and handle the unresponsive teammate.

descriptors.3: Clear ordering by deadline and importance.
Specific sleep and stress tools.
Clear follow-up with a deadline and escalation path.

items.modelAnswer: I would list the three tasks, rank them by deadline and impact, and start with the earliest important one in a 50-minute focus block each morning. I would stop work at 11 pm, use slow breathing and a shutdown ritual to protect sleep, and schedule a short walk daily. For the teammate, I would send a clear message today asking for their part by tomorrow noon, offering a quick call if they are stuck, and tell my lead by Thursday if there is still no reply, with facts.
items.guidance: Strong answers rank tasks, protect rest with concrete habits and follow up with the teammate politely, with a deadline and an escalation step. Avoid blaming or vague promises.

week-5.title: Week 5 Assessment: Careers, Money, Negotiation and Presenting
week-5.intro: This assessment checks how you plan a career, handle money decisions, negotiate and present. Part A is auto-graded from completed lessons. Part B has a decision scenario, a negotiation role-play and a written task. Answer as you would on the job.

items.prompt: You receive your first stipend of Rs 20,000. You have no savings and a Rs 4,000 monthly phone instalment. What is the most sensible first move?

options.text: Spend most of it on gadgets.
options.feedback: This leaves no safety margin.

options.text: Make a simple budget, set aside a small emergency fund first and track spending for the month.
options.feedback: A budget and emergency fund are basic foundations.

options.text: Lend all of it to a friend.
options.feedback: Large loans without planning are risky.

options.text: Put it all into one risky investment.
options.feedback: Putting everything in a risk is unwise.

items.why: Build a budget and a small buffer before taking risks.

items.setup: You receive a job offer from an IT services firm. The salary is slightly below the range you researched for entry-level roles, and you want to negotiate respectfully.

turns.they: We are happy to offer you the role at this salary. Please confirm.

options.text: I will take it, no questions.
options.feedback: Accepting without discussion forfeits your chance.

options.text: Thank you, I am excited about the role. Based on my research for similar entry-level roles, could we discuss a figure closer to the middle of that range?
options.feedback: Appreciation, evidence and a clear request.
options.reply: Let me see what is possible.

options.text: This is too low. Give me more.
options.feedback: Demanding without reasons rarely works.

turns.they: The budget is limited. What would make this work for you?

options.text: Whatever you can do.
options.feedback: This gives away your position.

options.text: I would value a slightly higher base, or a joining bonus and a review after six months. Which is easier for you?
options.feedback: Offers flexible options with a trade-off.
options.reply: We can look at a six-month review.

options.text: Nothing else matters.
options.feedback: Inflexibility closes off useful options.

turns.they: We can do a six-month review with a revised figure. Does that work?

options.text: Yes, please put it in writing.
options.feedback: Confirming and requesting it in writing protects you.
options.reply: Of course, we will email it.

options.text: I guess so.
options.feedback: A weak reply risks later misunderstanding.

options.text: No, never mind then.
options.feedback: Walking away without trying options wastes the progress.

items.why: Prepare evidence, ask for a specific outcome, explore options and confirm in writing.

items.prompt: You have five minutes to present your learning project to a panel. Write 100 to 130 words describing your core message, a three-part structure with time split and how you will handle one tough question.

descriptors.3: One-sentence claim with a reason.
Three parts with minutes.
Acknowledge, answer briefly, check.

items.modelAnswer: Message: A daily practice routine can make a beginner ready for ABAP tasks in eight weeks. Structure: one minute opening with a hook about interview rejections, three minutes with three points (habit, practice problems, review of errors) and one minute close with a call to join the group. If asked why not another language, I will acknowledge the question, explain that the target role uses ABAP, answer briefly and ask if that addresses their concern.
items.guidance: Strong answers give one claim with a reason, a clear three-part time split and a calm structured response to a question. Avoid listing many messages.

week-6.title: Week 6 Assessment: Leadership, Creativity and Knowledge
week-6.intro: This assessment checks how you lead, generate ideas, adapt and communicate what you know. Part A is auto-graded from lessons you completed. Part B has a decision scenario, a leadership role-play and a written task. Think about what you would genuinely do.

items.prompt: You lead a three-person project. One member is repeatedly late with tasks, and the deadline is in five days. What is the best step?

options.text: Redo their work silently every time.
options.feedback: This hides the problem and burns you out.

options.text: Talk privately, ask what is blocking them, agree a specific plan with check-in times and adjust the load if needed.
options.feedback: It combines empathy, clarity and accountability.

options.text: Announce their failures to the whole group.
options.feedback: Public blame damages trust.

options.text: Ignore it until the deadline passes.
options.feedback: Waiting makes the situation worse.

items.why: Good leaders address the issue early, privately and with a plan.

items.setup: Your team's client has just changed an important requirement, and a teammate is upset because their work may be wasted.

turns.they: This is so unfair. All my work is wasted!

options.text: That is just how it goes, deal with it.
options.feedback: Dismissing feelings damages trust.
options.reply: You do not care at all.

options.text: I understand why that is frustrating. Let us look at what can be reused and plan the changes together.
options.feedback: It validates feelings and moves to action.

options.text: Maybe we should blame the client.
options.feedback: Blame does not help the project.

turns.they: Some of it can be reused, but the deadline has not moved.

options.text: We will work through the night.
options.feedback: Overwork is not a plan.

options.text: Let us list the changes, estimate each, agree what is essential and discuss moving one item with the client.
options.feedback: Impact assessment and options are the right response.

options.text: We should refuse the change.
options.feedback: Refusing flatly harms the relationship.
options.reply: The client will not like that.

turns.they: Who will talk to the client about the timeline?

options.text: Not me, ask someone else.
options.feedback: Avoiding responsibility weakens leadership.

options.text: I will, and I will send a written summary of the impact and options today.
options.feedback: Taking ownership and confirming in writing.

options.text: Wait and see what they say.
options.feedback: Waiting loses valuable time here.
options.reply: We do not have much time.

items.why: Acknowledge feelings, assess impact, give options and take ownership of communication.

items.prompt: Your campus library has long queues at peak hours. Write 100 to 130 words: reframe the problem as two How Might We questions, list at least four varied ideas and state how you would test the best one cheaply.

descriptors.3: Two different open HMWs.
Four or more varied ideas.
Cheap test with a clear measure.

items.modelAnswer: HMW 1: How might we make the first hour of the library peak less crowded? HMW 2: How might we let students borrow without queueing? Ideas: self-checkout kiosks, a mobile pre-booking list, a pickup shelf, staggered class-wise slots, a returns drop box. Cheap test: for one week, set up a pickup shelf for pre-booked books and measure average waiting time compared with the previous week using a simple tally sheet.
items.guidance: Strong answers reframe with open questions, offer varied ideas and propose a cheap test with a measurable result. Avoid proposing an expensive solution first.

week-7.title: Week 7 Assessment: Negotiation, Teams and Finance
week-7.intro: This assessment deepens what you have practised: negotiating, resolving team conflict, leading change and thinking about money and evidence. Part A is auto-graded from lessons you completed. Part B has a decision scenario, a conflict role-play and a written task.

items.prompt: A social media post promises "guaranteed 30% monthly returns" from a new investment scheme and says it is limited to the first 50 people. What is the best response?

options.text: Invest quickly before slots end.
options.feedback: False urgency and guaranteed returns are warning signs.

options.text: Treat it as a likely scam, check regulator registration and avoid sending any money.
options.feedback: Guaranteed high returns and pressure are classic red flags.

options.text: Invest a small amount to test it.
options.feedback: Even a small amount can be lost and may lead to more demands.

options.text: Share it with friends to help them.
options.feedback: Sharing spreads possible fraud.

items.why: No legitimate investment can guarantee extreme returns, and urgency is a warning sign.

items.setup: Two team members both want to present the final demo to the client. You are the project lead and need to resolve it fairly.

turns.they: I should present. I did most of the work!

options.text: Fine, you can present.
options.feedback: Giving in without discussion ignores the other person.

options.text: Let us each say why this matters to us. What do you want from presenting?
options.feedback: It looks for interests behind positions.
options.reply: I want to show my module to the client.

options.text: Nobody will present then.
options.feedback: This punishes both people.

turns.they: I want to present because my part is the most visible to the client.

options.text: Then you are both wrong.
options.feedback: Judging does not solve the problem.

options.text: So each of you wants your module shown. Could each present your part for five minutes, with one of you opening and the other closing?
options.feedback: It creates an option that meets both interests.

options.text: Flip a coin.
options.feedback: A coin toss ignores interests but is quick.

turns.they: That works, but who will decide the order?

options.text: I do not care, decide yourselves.
options.feedback: Avoiding the decision invites a new dispute.

options.text: I will propose the order based on the demo flow and send it in writing, and we review it after the client call.
options.feedback: A clear agreement that is written and reviewed.

options.text: The loudest person decides.
options.feedback: This is unfair and unprofessional.

items.why: Find interests, create options and agree in writing with a review.

items.prompt: Write 100 to 130 words: a simple monthly budget plan for a first-job salary of Rs 30,000 (you decide the categories and amounts), including one saving goal and one item you would negotiate or reduce.

descriptors.3: Categories with amounts that add up.
Specific amount, purpose and date.
Specific item with a method.

items.modelAnswer: Rent and food Rs 12,000; transport Rs 3,000; phone and internet Rs 1,000; learning Rs 2,000; family Rs 4,000; emergency fund Rs 4,000; personal Rs 3,000; buffer Rs 1,000. Goal: build an emergency fund of Rs 30,000 by next March by saving Rs 4,000 a month. I will reduce rent by sharing a flat and negotiate a monthly transport pass to cut travel costs.
items.guidance: Strong answers give categories with amounts that add up to the salary, a specific saving goal with a date and a concrete way to reduce a cost.

week-8.title: Week 8 Assessment: Integration
week-8.intro: This assessment integrates careers, conflict, presenting and networking with everything before it. Part A is auto-graded from lessons you completed. Part B has a decision scenario, an interview role-play and a written task. Combine skills as you would in a real workplace.

concepts.label: Career Planning and Personal Branding: applied

items.prompt: You reach an interview 20 minutes early. The receptionist asks you to wait, and the interviewer is delayed by 30 minutes. What is the best behaviour?

options.text: Complain loudly about the delay.
options.feedback: Complaining creates a poor first impression.

options.text: Wait calmly, review your notes, keep your phone silent and greet people politely.
options.feedback: Patience and courtesy are part of professionalism.

options.text: Leave and send an angry message.
options.feedback: Leaving without discussion damages your chances.

options.text: Scroll videos with sound on.
options.feedback: Noise and distraction look careless.

items.why: Everyone you meet may influence the decision, so stay patient and polite.

items.setup: You are in an interview for an entry-level SAP ABAP role. The panel will ask about your preparation, a failure and a conflict at work.

turns.they: Tell us about a time you failed and what you learned.

options.text: I have never failed.
options.feedback: Claiming no failures sounds unreal.

options.text: I failed a mock technical test because I had not practised under time limits. I did a post-mortem, took three timed practice sets and improved from 40 to 70 per cent.
options.feedback: A specific story with analysis and results.

options.text: It was my teacher's fault.
options.feedback: Blaming others suggests low responsibility.

turns.they: How do you handle disagreement in a team?

options.text: I avoid people I disagree with.
options.feedback: Avoidance cannot work in teams.

options.text: I clarify what matters to each of us, offer options and agree on a specific next step, in writing if needed.
options.feedback: It shows interest-based problem solving.

options.text: I just do what the loudest person says.
options.feedback: Passive compliance is not a strategy.

turns.they: Do you have any questions for us?

options.text: No questions.
options.feedback: A good candidate usually asks something.

options.text: What would the first 90 days look like for a trainee, and how is learning supported?
options.feedback: A thoughtful question that shows planning.

options.text: How soon can I get a raise?
options.feedback: This focuses on pay before contribution.

items.why: Use specific stories, constructive conflict habits and thoughtful questions in interviews.

items.prompt: Write 100 to 130 words: a follow-up message to a senior professional you met last week that thanks them, reminds them of your conversation, makes one specific small request and offers something useful in return.

descriptors.3: Specific thanks recalling the conversation.
Specific and easy to grant.
Real offer with a warm, professional tone.

items.modelAnswer: Dear Ms Rao, thank you for the time you gave me at the campus event last Thursday. Your point about writing clean ABAP and testing small programs stayed with me. I have started a weekly mini-program habit based on it. If you are open to it, could I send you a short summary of my practice projects and ask for two lines of feedback? I would be happy to share the notes I made from the session with other students in return. Thank you again. Regards, Deepak.
items.guidance: Strong messages are short, specific about the earlier conversation, make a small clear ask and offer something in return. Avoid asking for a job directly in the first message.
